stories.title: Several belugas from Marineland have health issues, Chicago aquarium says
stories.summary: Shedd Aquarium says in a Friday statement it is conducting round-the-clock supervision and teams are monitoring the whales' health.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .

A Chicago aquarium says several of the belugas that were transferred to its site from Ontario’s Marineland have health issues.

Shedd Aquarium says in a Friday statement it is conducting round-the-clock supervision and teams are monitoring the whales’ hydration, breathing rates, swim patterns, social interaction and other behaviours.

The aquarium’s update comes after it reported last week that two of the three whales that died at its site in a week’s span were belugas from Marineland, a theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont., that closed after it ran out of money.

Shedd has said that Peekachu, one of the Marineland belugas, died on Aug. 25 at its site two weeks after being relocated.

A 20-year-old beluga named Rain, that was moved from Marineland to the Chicago park in mid-August, also died, as well as a 34-year-old beluga that had lived for decades in Chicago.

Amid the spate of deaths, the Shedd Aquarium says there is still uncertainty surrounding the health of the remaining animals and it is awaiting lab results as the park investigates the deaths.

“Some of the rescued belugas are showing more encouraging signs than others, but several have presented clinical concerns,” Shedd wrote in the statement Friday. “Their condition can change from day to day and, at times, hour to hour.”

The aquarium said belugas get most of their hydration through the fish they eat and while some of the rescued whales are eating regularly, others are not.

As a whole, Shedd said none of the belugas are “where we want them to be from a health standpoint.”

The Marineland belugas were given a clean bill of health in the days before their relocations, with Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson responsible for giving the final approval.

Marineland, which is now up for sale, completed the largest collective move of captive whales the world has ever seen last week, shipping 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums in the United States and Spain over several weeks.

The final move last week brought an end to whale captivity in Canada.

Before their transfers, Marineland threatened to euthanize them if it did not get an emergency cash infusion after the federal government blocked an earlier plan to move the whales to China.

Multiple whales have died after being relocated.

In 2021, Marineland moved five whales to Mystic Aquarium in Connecticut.

Two of those whales died within a year of the move and the third died two years after the transfer. Mystic said the whales had pre-existing conditions while Marineland said they were healthy when they left.

Nineteen belugas, one killer whale and one dolphin died at Marineland between 2019 and 2025.

— with files from Liam Casey

The hallways of the Longueuil school, just south of Montreal, came back to life last week with the arrival of 55 students between the ages of four and 21.

Funded by Quebec’s Education Department, Jacques-Ouellette is the only French-language school in the province specializing in students with visual impairments.

While the school is part of the Marie-Victorin school service centre in the Longueuil area, it also welcomes children from about 10 other school service centres to meet their specialized needs.

“It’s case by case all the time,” Blondin said. “One will read braille, another will read print but can see 18-point type, another needs 36-point type to read. Another can only see using a video magnifier.”

Choquette said continuing to teach braille also helps preserve the physical skills needed to read it.

“It’s about providing an accessible paper book for free, just as we do for sighted people,” he said. “That helps keep the language alive.”

stories.title: Several belugas transferred from Marineland have health issues, Chicago aquarium says
stories.summary: Shedd Aquarium says it is conducting round-the-clock supervision and teams are monitoring the whales’ health
stories.content:
A Chicago aquarium says several of the belugas that were transferred to its site from Ontario’s Marineland have health issues.

Shedd Aquarium says in a Friday statement it is conducting round-the-clock supervision and teams are monitoring the whales’ hydration, breathing rates, swim patterns, social interaction and other behaviours.

The aquarium’s update comes after it reported last week that two of the three whales that died at its site in a week’s span were belugas from Marineland, a theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont., that closed after it ran out of money.

Shedd has said that Peekachu, one of the Marineland belugas, died on Aug. 25 at its site two weeks after being relocated.

A 20-year-old beluga named Rain, that was moved from Marineland to the Chicago park in mid-August, also died, as well as a 34-year-old beluga that had lived for decades in Chicago.

Amid the spate of deaths, the Shedd Aquarium says there is still uncertainty surrounding the health of the remaining animals and it is awaiting lab results as the park investigates the deaths.

“Some of the rescued belugas are showing more encouraging signs than others, but several have presented clinical concerns,” Shedd wrote in the statement Friday. “Their condition can change from day to day and, at times, hour to hour.”

The aquarium said belugas get most of their hydration through the fish they eat and while some of the rescued whales are eating regularly, others are not.

As a whole, Shedd said none of the belugas are “where we want them to be from a health standpoint.”

The Marineland belugas were given a clean bill of health in the days before their relocations, with Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson responsible for giving the final approval.

Marineland, which is now up for sale, completed the largest collective move of captive whales the world has ever seen last week, shipping 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums in the United States and Spain over several weeks.

The final move last week brought an end to whale captivity in Canada.

Before their transfers, Marineland threatened to euthanize them if it did not get an emergency cash infusion after the federal government blocked an earlier plan to move the whales to China.

Multiple whales have died after being relocated.

In 2021, Marineland moved five whales to Mystic Aquarium in Connecticut.

Two of those whales died within a year of the move and the third died two years after the transfer. Mystic said the whales had pre-existing conditions while Marineland said they were healthy when they left.

Nineteen belugas, one killer whale and one dolphin died at Marineland between 2019 and 2025.

content_blocks.text: Trainer Taylor-Lee Dell says goodbye to beluga whale "Tofino," the last whale in captivity in Canada, before being transported by a group of experts from Marineland and several U.S. aquariums onto a truck via a sling before being moved to an aquarium in the U.S., in the final transfer of whales out of the closed park, in Niagara Falls, Ont., ON Monday, Aug. 31, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Carlos Osorio
By The Canadian Press
Posted September 6, 2026 1:55 pm.
Last Updated September 6, 2026 2:00 pm.
Chicago — A Chicago aquarium says several of the belugas that were transferred to its site from Ontario’s Marineland have health issues.

Shedd Aquarium says in a Friday statement it is conducting round-the-clock supervision and teams are monitoring the whales’ hydration, breathing rates, swim patterns, social interaction and other behaviours.

The aquarium’s update comes after it reported last week that two of the three whales that died at its site in a week’s span were belugas from Marineland, a theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont., that closed after it ran out of money.
Shedd has said that Peekachu, one of the Marineland belugas, died on Aug. 25 at its site two weeks after being relocated.
A 20-year-old beluga named Rain, that was moved from Marineland to the Chicago park in mid-August, also died, as well as a 34-year-old beluga that had lived for decades in Chicago.
Amid the spate of deaths, the Shedd Aquarium says there is still uncertainty surrounding the health of the remaining animals and it is awaiting lab results as the park investigates the deaths.

“Some of the rescued belugas are showing more encouraging signs than others, but several have presented clinical concerns,” Shedd wrote in the statement Friday. “Their condition can change from day to day and, at times, hour to hour.”
The aquarium said belugas get most of their hydration through the fish they eat and while some of the rescued whales are eating regularly, others are not.
As a whole, Shedd said none of the belugas are “where we want them to be from a health standpoint.”
The Marineland belugas were given a clean bill of health in the days before their relocations, with Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson responsible for giving the final approval.

Marineland, which is now up for sale, completed the largest collective move of captive whales the world has ever seen last week, shipping 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums in the United States and Spain over several weeks.
The final move last week brought an end to whale captivity in Canada.
Before their transfers, Marineland threatened to euthanize them if it did not get an emergency cash infusion after the federal government blocked an earlier plan to move the whales to China.
Multiple whales have died after being relocated.
In 2021, Marineland moved five whales to Mystic Aquarium in Connecticut.

Two of those whales died within a year of the move and the third died two years after the transfer. Mystic said the whales had pre-existing conditions while Marineland said they were healthy when they left.
Nineteen belugas, one killer whale and one dolphin died at Marineland between 2019 and 2025.

stories.title: ‘New step in life’: Thousands of post-secondary students arrive in London
stories.summary: As first-year students arrive at residence on Western University campus, they are greeted with a fun and cheeky song by upper-year students.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
As first-year students arrive at residence on Western University campus, they are greeted with a fun and cheeky song by upper-year students.

“First years out the car, first years out the car!” they chanted.

Once they step out of the vehicle, they ask the student’s name and program.

It’s a way to break the ice for those venturing into new territory and moving out for the first time.

“I’m most excited about being able to leave my house because now I have so much more freedom,” said Gavin Chen, a medical science student from Scarborough, Ont.

“I can stay out longer and stuff like that.”

Thousands of students are moving to London this weekend at Western, Kings University, and Fanshawe College.

“It’s an exciting day for Western and the local community, welcoming 6,800 students to campus and moving into residence through new homes, away from home,” said Chris Alleyne, Associate VP, Housing and Ancillary Services at Western.

“It takes a village, certainly, to welcome the entirety of the student population back over the next couple of days.”

With the largest first-year residence program in the province, more than 5,200 freshman students and nearly 2,000 others are moving into residence on campus this weekend.

At the Richmond Street gates on University Drive, construction of a new 792-bed residence is coming along. It is scheduled to open in September 2027.

“It’s a real important part of ensuring that we’re able to maintain our first-year residence guarantee that we’ve offered for three decades to students coming to Western,” said Alleyne.

Across the city at Fanshawe College, more than 1,600 students are arriving to on-campus housing.

“It’s always an exciting time of year for us,” said Erica Robertson, general manager of Fanshawe’s Residence and Conference Centre.

“It’s exciting to see all the students and all the parents who also have a lot of nerves going on. Every year is a fresh, new round of students but we have some returnees as well.”

One of those new students is 17-year-old Josh Neal of Guelph. He’s enrolled in the Golf and Club Management program.

“I’m coming a few hours from here, so it’s a little different, but it’ll be fun when we’re all settled in,” said Neal, who was asking about local golf courses to play while in the city.

“It is another step in the journey, but some people are here from my hometown, makes it a little nicer. It’s fun to meet some people and take a new step in life.”

stories.title: Canadian skyrunner still missing on Italian side of Matterhorn mountain
stories.summary: Kalie McCrystal, who friends say is a highly experienced athlete, was last spotted on Tuesday
stories.author: Eric Reguly
stories.content:
Rescue efforts in the Italian Alps for missing British Columbian mountaineering athlete Kalie McCrystal focused on tracking her movements using data from her phone’s SIM chip after helicopter searches were suspended.

There were no reports by late Sunday, European time, that the effort had determined the approximate location where she went missing on Tuesday. She was training to break the skyrunning, or mountain racing, record for ascending and descending the Matterhorn, the 4,478-metre mountain that straddles the Italian-Swiss border in the Western Alps.

A helicopter search conducted by Aosta Valley Mountain Rescue was called off after several search-and-rescue flights on Thursday failed to locate Ms. McCrystal or any evidence, such as gear that she was carrying, that may have provided a clue to her route. Since then, regular mountain guides have been on the lookout for her.

“The family is confident that everything is being done to find Kalie,” her friend Nicole Lacis, a trail runner and lawyer who lives in Vancouver, told The Globe and Mail. “They are in close contact with the mountain rescue teams.”

Ms. McCrystal was last spotted on Tuesday afternoon at a mountain shelter on the Italian side of the Matterhorn, about 650 metres below the summit. There have been no messages from her since then.

Italy’s La Stampa newspaper on Sunday said the mountain rescue team of Guardia di Finanza, which operates under the Italian economy ministry, was trying to obtain data from mobile-phone operators to “triangulate” – find the position of – her device using Italian and Swiss cellphone towers.

Rescuers who talked to Ansa, the Italian news service, said Ms. McCrystal, 38, was wearing light clothing – shorts and a jacket – that would make it hard to spot her. Live webcams showed patches of snow on the Matterhorn at 2,555 metres and almost full snow at 3,480 metres. Its summit makes it the Alps’ sixth-highest mountain.

Athletics Canada on Saturday said Ms. McCrystal was on “reconnaissance/training” ahead of her attempt to break the up-and-down skyrunning Matterhorn record.

“Kalie is an experienced skyrunner and mountaineer, with many years of experience on technical and high-altitude mountain environments,” the statement said. “She has extensive knowledge and experience of alpine terrain and previously climbed the Matterhorn.”

Ms. McCrystal’s deep background and strong finishes in skyrunning convinced the rescue team that she was not being reckless on the Matterhorn.

“She is an absolutely incredible athlete,” Ms. Lacis said. “She is very experienced on this kind of terrain, and from my understanding has done much harder routes. She is diligent and disciplined. She did not do this on a whim.

“The whole rescue team have reiterated to us several times that they do not believe Kalie was being irresponsible or reckless. They observed her through a telescope for a period of time on Tuesday and could see that she was moving carefully and, by her standards, at a fairly relaxed pace. They have stressed to us that this appears to have been a tragic accident, one which could happen to anyone in the mountains, including themselves.”

Skyrunning was pioneered in Italy in the early 1990s. It is a running, not mountain-face climbing, race that favours endurance athletes skilled enough to handle twisty, steep routes that are often treacherous. The races are run at 2,000 metres or higher with inclines of 5 per cent to 30 per cent. The distances usually covered are 20 to 50 kilometres and can take three to eight hours to complete.

Ms. McCrystal’s Aug. 7 Instagram post showed her at or near the top of the Matterhorn on a previous climb, smiling and holding onto the base of the big metal cross that commemorates the climbers who have died reaching the summit. She was wearing a green jacket, dark shorts and a black helmet.

Her post read: “Been hanging out in Cervina, Italy, for the last few days in preparation for my big goal of the season – up and down the Matterhorn in under five hours via Lion’s Ridge.”

Her last Instagram post was on Aug. 23, when she completed one of the sport’s toughest high-altitude races, the Trofeo Kima, in Lombardy in the Italian Alps.

“After 50km and 4200 metres of boulders, chains, and mud, I crossed the line in 4th in 7:59, right on my goals. Sharing the start and finish line with so many badass women was a privilege.”

Ms. McCrystal is a lawyer who specializes in international arbitration. Her Linkedin profile says she is an instructor in the school of legal studies at Capilano University, which has a campus in Squamish, B.C., where she lives. She is a graduate in law from the University of British Columbia.

Ms. McCrystal was last spotted on Tuesday afternoon at a mountain shelter on the Italian side of the Matterhorn, about 650 metres below the summit. There have been no messages from her since then.

Italy’s La Stampa newspaper on Sunday said the mountain rescue team of Guardia di Finanza, which operates under the Italian economy ministry, was trying to obtain data from mobile-phone operators to “triangulate” – find the position of – her device using Italian and Swiss cellphone towers.

Rescuers who talked to Ansa, the Italian news service, said Ms. McCrystal, 38, was wearing light clothing – shorts and a jacket – that would make it hard to spot her. Live webcams showed patches of snow on the Matterhorn at 2,555 metres and almost full snow at 3,480 metres. Its summit makes it the Alps’ sixth-highest mountain.
Athletics Canada on Saturday said Ms. McCrystal was on “reconnaissance/training” ahead of her attempt to break the up-and-down skyrunning Matterhorn record.

“Kalie is an experienced skyrunner and mountaineer, with many years of experience on technical and high-altitude mountain environments,” the statement said. “She has extensive knowledge and experience of alpine terrain and previously climbed the Matterhorn.”
Ms. McCrystal’s deep background and strong finishes in skyrunning convinced the rescue team that she was not being reckless on the Matterhorn.

“She is an absolutely incredible athlete,” Ms. Lacis said. “She is very experienced on this kind of terrain, and from my understanding has done much harder routes. She is diligent and disciplined. She did not do this on a whim.

“The whole rescue team have reiterated to us several times that they do not believe Kalie was being irresponsible or reckless. They observed her through a telescope for a period of time on Tuesday and could see that she was moving carefully and, by her standards, at a fairly relaxed pace. They have stressed to us that this appears to have been a tragic accident, one which could happen to anyone in the mountains, including themselves.”

Skyrunning was pioneered in Italy in the early 1990s. It is a running, not mountain-face climbing, race that favours endurance athletes skilled enough to handle twisty, steep routes that are often treacherous. The races are run at 2,000 metres or higher with inclines of 5 per cent to 30 per cent. The distances usually covered are 20 to 50 kilometres and can take three to eight hours to complete.

Ms. McCrystal’s Aug. 7 Instagram post showed her at or near the top of the Matterhorn on a previous climb, smiling and holding onto the base of the big metal cross that commemorates the climbers who have died reaching the summit. She was wearing a green jacket, dark shorts and a black helmet.
Her post read: “Been hanging out in Cervina, Italy, for the last few days in preparation for my big goal of the season – up and down the Matterhorn in under five hours via Lion’s Ridge.”
Her last Instagram post was on Aug. 23, when she completed one of the sport’s toughest high-altitude races, the Trofeo Kima, in Lombardy in the Italian Alps.
“After 50km and 4200 metres of boulders, chains, and mud, I crossed the line in 4th in 7:59, right on my goals. Sharing the start and finish line with so many badass women was a privilege.”

Ms. McCrystal is a lawyer who specializes in international arbitration. Her Linkedin profile says she is an instructor in the school of legal studies at Capilano University, which has a campus in Squamish, B.C., where she lives. She is a graduate in law from the University of British Columbia.

stories.title: Nova Scotia mourning woman who died in province’s severe flooding: premier
stories.summary: Environment Canada has dropped its warnings for Nova Scotia, but there is still more rain in the forecast after flooding and widespread damage was reported.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .

Nova Scotia’s premier says the province is in mourning after a woman died during the flooding that affected the province this weekend.

Nova Scotia RCMP said Sunday they had located the body of a Cleveland, N.S. woman after she went missing the previous morning. Police said they had found her vehicle parked near her residence on the far side of a flooded bridge. Her death is not believed to be suspicious, RCMP said.

“My thoughts are with her loved ones and everyone who is grieving this tragic loss,” said Premier Tim Houston on X.

The woman’s death comes as states of emergency remained in effect for three counties on Cape Breton Island Sunday morning after heavy rain washed out roads, with more in the forecast.

Environment Canada forecasted up to 120 millimetres of rain in some areas between Friday and Monday. Some regions were even forecast to see rainfall of 10 millimetres per hour.

Inverness, Victoria and Richmond counties all declared local emergencies Saturday due to severe flooding and widespread damage.

Multiple roads have been closed, the province said in its emergency alert, and conditions remained dangerous.

In Richmond County, more than 200 millimetres have been reported, with bodies of water like the River Tillard nearly touching bridges that stretch over it.

Some roads were also washed out, including near Marble Mountain in Inverness County, where a large hole could be found where the concrete gave way into the water.

Environment Canada has ended warnings for Nova Scotia, but advised on Sunday that another 10 to 20 mm of rain was possible. The national weather service did say the heaviest rain would taper off Sunday morning, though some showers could continue into Monday.

According to the weather agency, more than 100 millimetres was recorded in several parts of Cape Breton, including 130mm in Ingonish Beach and 105mm in Sydney.

Houston said Saturday afternoon he had joined Richmond MLA Trevor Boudreau earlier in the day at the command centre in Port Hawkesbury to speak with the team about the “extensive damage.”

He said on X that crews were assessing the damage, but the full extent would not be known until after the storm ends and floodwaters recede.

“Once this storm has passed, we will pull crews and equipment where needed from other areas of the province to repair roads and infrastructure as fast as we can,” he said.

Nova Scotia Emergency Management said in its own X post that as flooding was affecting roads across Cape Breton and eastern mainland Nova Scotia, people should stay off the roads unless “absolutely necessary.”

“Road conditions can change quickly, and flooded roads may be damaged or unsafe,” it said.

People are asked to check conditions before leaving, follow all road closures and barricades, don’t drive through floodwater, and turn around if drivers encounter flooding or a damaged road.

stories.title: Overdue kayaker found dead in Grand Bend
stories.summary: A 15-hour search for an overdue kayaker in Grand Bend, Ont. has ended tragically.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
A 15-hour search for an overdue kayaker in Grand Bend, Ont. has ended tragically.

OPP told CTV News that early Sunday morning, the search had concluded with the recovery of the individual who was pronounced dead.

Police first alerted the public on Saturday evening around 6 p.m., saying residents in the area will see a heavy police presence as the search continues.

Officers said the adult man was seen in a solid blue kayak wearing a yellow life jacket on Lake Huron.

The search continued through the night with the search on land, water and in the air.

The kayaker was identified as a 37-year-old man.

In an email to CTV News, Huron OPP stated they would like to thank emergency response partners and members of the public who assisted with search efforts.

stories.title: American diplomat recalls Canadian solidarity in the days after 9/11 attacks
stories.summary: The legacy of Sept. 11 is seen in the depth of the relationships between Canadians and Americans, the diplomat says
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
American diplomat Baxter Hunt recalls showing up to work at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa the morning after the 9/11 terrorist attacks and finding “a mountain of flowers” outside the building.

“It was just a day that none of us will ever forget,” said Hunt, now the U.S. consul general in Toronto. “What also stuck with me was the outpouring of support that we got from Canadians.”

This Friday marks 25 years since nearly 3,000 people in the U.S. were killed when al-Qaeda hijackers slammed planes into the World Trade Center in New York and crashed into the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

In the days that followed, Hunt witnessed many more displays of Canadian compassion and support for a grieving nation.

Three days after the attack, 80,000 people crowded Parliament Hill for a national day of mourning, according to an RCMP estimate reported by The Canadian Press that week.

‘’By their outpouring of concern, sympathy and help, the feelings and actions of Canadians have been clear,” then-prime minister Jean Chrétien told the crowd.

‘’And even as we grieve our own losses, the message they send to the American people is equally clear. Do not despair. You are not alone. We are with you. The whole world is with you.’’

Similar moments of silence took place at provincial legislatures and even in the heart of Canada’s financial sector on Bay Street. It was Canada’s first official day of mourning in three decades.

On the day of the attacks, the Newfoundland community of Gander famously took in 38 passenger planes carrying more than 6,500 travellers after officials closed U.S. airspace.

“Just an incredible showing of compassion by those people for complete strangers, who needed them at that time,” Hunt said. “There were also many, many stranded passengers who went to other locations around Canada, about 33,000, I understand.”

Hunt was quick to mention the 24 Canadians who were killed in the attacks alongside other non-Americans.

He was 38 and working as the embassy’s political-military officer on Sept. 11, 2001. American diplomats “naturally came together” with Canadian law enforcement and military officials to identify threats, he said.

“No one knew initially exactly what else might happen. And we wanted to make sure we weren’t vulnerable to other attacks,” Hunt said. “The response of Canadians at a time when we most needed it was incredible.”

Both countries standardized airport security. Allies took up air patrols around the U.S. The NATO military alliance invoked its collective security clause for the first time, sending Canadians and allied troops to fight the Taliban in Afghanistan. That war lasted for more than a dozen years and 165 Canadians – 158 soldiers and seven civilians – died in the conflict.

“It was an event that was a shift in how we perceived threats around the world, and something that happened in the homeland, which we really hadn’t seen before,” Hunt said.

“It was something that just reinforced the need for us to work together.”

Hunt spoke to The Canadian Press shortly before trade talks in Washington collapsed. Prime Minister Mark Carney accused the U.S. of launching an economic “war” on its erstwhile ally and U.S. President Donald Trump moved to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.”

Hunt said the legacy of 9/11 is seen in the depth of the relationships between Canadians and Americans throughout the ups and downs in the bilateral relationship.

“That is something that we saw big time after the 9/11 attacks. People just feeling like these are our friends and neighbours, and it is like an extended North American family. And that really came through. And that’s something that I believe is still very strong today,” he said.

“It’s great to remember that as we approach the 25th anniversary, and be grateful that we have that close, close relationship.”

The Toronto consulate is holding events this month to commemorate the anniversary.

They include an ongoing exhibition at a Toronto arts centre of pen and ink drawings by Toronto-based artist John Coburn, who was in New York after the attacks. Hunt said the exhibit includes interactive events with local college students, many of whom were born after the attacks.

On the Friday anniversary, the consulate will hold an event at the same art centre bringing together first responders and government officials to honour the victims. That event will feature Maureen Basnicki, whose husband Ken was killed at the World Trade Center.

Hunt will open the Toronto Stock Exchange that day to commemorate the city’s connections with New York. He’ll also visit a memorial walkway in St. Catharines, Ont. on Thursday.

“That is something that we saw big time after the 9/11 attacks. People just feeling like these are our friends and neighbours, and it is like an extended North American family. And that really came through. And that’s something that I believe is still very strong today,” he said.
“It’s great to remember that as we approach the 25th anniversary, and be grateful that we have that close, close relationship.”
The Toronto consulate is holding events this month to commemorate the anniversary.

They include an ongoing exhibition at a Toronto arts centre of pen and ink drawings by Toronto-based artist John Coburn, who was in New York after the attacks. Hunt said the exhibit includes interactive events with local college students, many of whom were born after the attacks.

On the Friday anniversary, the consulate will hold an event at the same art centre bringing together first responders and government officials to honour the victims. That event will feature Maureen Basnicki, whose husband Ken was killed at the World Trade Center.
Hunt will open the Toronto Stock Exchange that day to commemorate the city’s connections with New York. He’ll also visit a memorial walkway in St. Catharines, Ont. on Thursday.

stories.title: Nova Scotia state of emergency remains in effect after widespread flooding, rain forecast continues
stories.summary: Cape Breton Island and parts of the northern mainland have been battered by rainfall for several days due to a slow-moving weather system
stories.content:
Three Nova Scotia counties on Cape Breton Island continue to remain under a local state of emergency this morning.

Nova Scotia Emergency Management’s alert Saturday evening says there is severe flooding and widespread damage.

It also says multiple roads are closed and conditions remain dangerous, warning people in the affected areas not to travel unless necessary.

The Island and parts of the northern mainland have been battered by rainfall for several days due to a slow-moving weather system.

Environment Canada has kept its orange warning in place for most of the Island’s northern areas, saying there will be an additional 10 to 20 millimetres of rain.

But the national weather service also forecasts the heaviest rain to taper off this morning, with some showers expected to continue into Monday.

Premier Tim Houston said Saturday evening that he went to a command centre in Post Hawkesbury, in south Cape Breton Island, to get an update on the damage across the region.

“Crews are assessing the damage, but we won’t know the full extent until after the storm ends and the flood water recedes,” Houston said in a post to social media.

Houston said he continues to receive updates from Cape Breton officials, the provincial emergency management minister and the public works minister.

stories.title: Overdue kayaker found dead in Grand Bend
stories.summary: A 15-hour search for an overdue kayaker in Grand Bend, Ont. has ended tragically.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
A 15-hour search for an overdue kayaker in Grand Bend, Ont. has ended tragically.

OPP told CTV News that early Sunday morning, the search had concluded with the recovery of the individual who was pronounced dead.

Police first alerted the public on Saturday evening around 6 p.m., saying residents in the area will see a heavy police presence as the search continues.

Officers said the adult man was seen in a solid blue kayak wearing a yellow life jacket on Lake Huron.

The search continued through the night with the search on land, water and in the air.

The kayaker was identified as a 37-year-old man.

In an email to CTV News, Huron OPP stated they would like to thank emergency response partners and members of the public who assisted with search efforts.

stories.title: Missing London man found dead
stories.summary: A missing London man has been found dead.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A missing London man has been found dead.

Cole Rioux was reported missing by his family after he didn’t arrive at work on Aug. 28.

Rioux’s mother, Marla Rioux, posted to social media on Sunday that the 19-year-old was found dead.

“The family and I are sincerely thankful to all of you for your efforts in searching for Cole and spreading awareness,” she wrote.

She added a celebration of life will be held at a later date for those that knew him.

stories.title: A tale of two U.S. ambassadors: Hoekstra and Heyman see Canada very differently
stories.summary: A former U.S. ambassador has shown his support for Canada with a series of social media posts, as the trade war continues to escalate.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
A former U.S. ambassador to Canada is taking a strikingly different approach to cross-border relations than the current diplomat in office, as the trade war between the two countries continues to escalate.

Bruce Heyman, who served as ambassador to Canada under U.S. president Barack Obama between 2014 and 2017, has been increasingly vocal in his support for Canada. In contrast, current U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra has offended some Canadians to the point that a parliamentary petition calling for his removal has gathered more than 260,000 signatures.

Both Midwesterners, Heyman grew up in Ohio and served as a managing director of private wealth management at Goldman Sachs before Obama appointed him as U.S. ambassador to Canada. Hoekstra spent most of his childhood in Michigan and is a long-serving Republican, first as a member of Congress representing Michigan’s 2nd District from 1993 to 2011.

Ohio and Michigan are among the states most affected by the Canada-U.S. trade war. Last year, 38 per cent of all exports from Michigan and 32 per cent from Ohio went to Canada , according to data from the U.S. Department of Commerce’s International Trade Administration (ITA), with motor vehicles and parts both states’ top northbound exports.

In a series of recent posts on X, Heyman has been emphatic in his support for Canada, writing “never underestimate a Canadian,” “this American is proudly pro-Canadian,” and “love you, Canada.”

He also shared a photo of himself wearing a hat with “Lake Ontario” stitched on the front, after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename the body of water “Lake America,” and on Wednesday claimed that he’d previously been told by senior U.S. military officers that “if they were ever stuck in a foxhole under fire and they couldn’t have an American at their side they would undoubtedly want a Canadian.”

Since leaving the role of U.S. ambassador to Canada in 2017, Heyman co-founded the company Uncharted with his wife, Vicki Heyman, which connects Canadians and Americans to create a positive impact across the Canada-U.S. relationship, political engagement and philanthropy.

Heyman’s vocal support for Canada is likely good for his business. But regardless of the motivation, his public posture stands in stark contrast to that of Hoekstra, who took on the role of U.S. ambassador to Canada in April 2025.

Among the objectionable comments Hoekstra has made about Canada are his bafflement at why Canadians are angry about “51st state” comments , suggesting Canada’s response to Trump’s actions has been “nasty and mean,” and reportedly aiming an expletive-laden rant at Ontario’s trade representative .

He also reiterated Trump’s claim that the U.S. “does not need Canada” during a radio interview in Montreal, and suggested that the U.S. president’s “51st state” comments could be taken as a “term of endearment.”

More recently, Hoekstra claimed that Canada paying to construct the Gordie Howe International Bridge was a “big myth,” a comment that former prime minister Stephen Harper’s director of communications, Andrew MacDougall, branded a “punch in the face.”

The petition calling for his removal accuses the ambassador of undermining Canada-U.S. diplomatic relations and normalizing “51st state” language, and is sponsored by Green Party MP Elizabeth May.

That said, the stark difference between the two ambassadors isn’t explained by personal politics alone.

Heyman, whose current business relies on maintaining a positive relationship with Canada, served under Obama, whose administration committed to forming stronger trade ties with Canada through instructing aides to make it easier for goods and people to move between the two nations, and looking to solve a dispute over exports of Canadian softwood lumber.

Hoekstra, meanwhile, represents Trump during a dramatically different period in the bilateral relationship, characterized by tariffs and the trade war. The fallout has caused Canadians’ views of America to become increasingly negative, with a recent Angus Reid poll finding that 45 per cent of Canadians say their views on Americans are unfavourable or very unfavourable .

And it’s not just Canada that Hoekstra has had a fractured relationship with. During his time as ambassador to the Netherlands during Trump’s first term, he was forced to apologize after making false claims that the “Islamic movement” in Europe was creating “no-go zones” and burning politicians.

Meanwhile, it would be wrong to suggest that Heyman didn’t have to navigate policy differences between Canada and the U.S. during his time as ambassador. Most notable was the Keystone XL pipeline, for which Obama denied the cross-border permit in 2015, stating the project did not serve U.S. national interests .

Heyman later wrote in a book he co-authored with his wife, Vicki, that disagreements between former prime minister Stephen Harper’s government and the Obama administration over the pipeline briefly led to an “ice age in relations.”

And yet, Heyman’s pro-Canada stance has extended beyond his time in office. After Trump first imposed tariffs in March 2025, he said in an interview on Cntv that Canada had “been there for (the U.S.) in thick and thin” and that the tariffs “shouldn’t happen.”

“I just think Donald Trump must have some other issue here, and those issues are either personal with Canada, or … personally think he’s short cash,” Heyman added.

He also called the tariffs “deeply offensive to the Canadians,” and said: “I would just say to the Canadian public, there are millions of Americans that value this relationship.”

BySophie Bouquillon Staff Photojournalist

Every year,seemingly overnight, the 192-acre Exhibition Grounds transform into the spectac ular Canadian National Exhibition for 18 days. The event always reintroduces locals to some old friends— few more popular than the Wave Swinger. But few riders reflect on the attraction’s travelling entourage.

Among the 61 rides,the Wave Swinger is one of the oldest, and still one of the most in-demand.Manufactured in 1979 in Germany, the hand-painted 48-seater (currently 47) has become a staple of the midway, loved and revered by riders of all ages.In an oscillating wave-like motion, riders are flung clockwise into the cool breeze at 10.5 revolutions per minute for about two minutes, depending on the length of the line.

Rider Alicia Ferreira, 39, describes it as “not too scary” and enjoys the feeling of weightlessness, and the bird’s-eye perspective.

Behind the magic are the travelling crew members for North American Midway Entertainment who trek through 15 cities between March and November and toil for as many days as baseball players do in a regular season — 162.

The ride’s load — occupying two full tractor-trailers — travels along with its crew, and roughly 300 other vehicles as the roaming city makes it s way through North America.According to 36-year-old Bennett Kavals,North American Midway’s director of operations and personnel, t he midway is largely self-sufficient,from power generation to housing.“We can set up this product you see safely anywhere, and all we need is two days, and this magic appears …All we really need is a water source.”

And the workers, naturally. As company vice-president Scooter Koerk puts it,“the crew comes from the four winds.”

Opening in Miami in March, they snake across the U.S.Midwest with stops in Atlanta, Birmingham, Ala. and St. Louis before making their way up north to Canada in June.After starting in Brandon, Man., they visit Winnipeg, then head 1,335 kilometres west to Calgary for the Stampede. After subsequent s tops in Edmonton and Saskatoon, they finally arrive in Toronto for the CNE in late August.

For the W av e S winger crew, life on the road away from home is for the most part worth it—le ssons are learned, and both memories and money are mad e.

Crew member Shaun Mwenga, 24, says he’s trying to make the most of his twenties and most enjoys “seeing the world” and the fleeting moments of connection while operating the ride.

“I enjoy buckling up people, you can have 10 seconds of having a chat with somebody new, and that moment could change your life. You never know who you will meet.”

Mwenga moved to Calgary to study dental hygiene, and quickly realized the midway employed many temporary foreign workers from South Africa, a neighbour to his home country of Zimbabwe; he “started to build a family from there.”

One of those South Africans is 40-year-old temporary foreign worker Pietre Espin, with the midway since 2009, and the Wave Swinger for the past three years. He was initially drawn by the opportunity to travel overseas. The job lets him support his family back home in Cape Town, but his second family, his midway family, including Mwenga, is what keeps him coming back. As he puts it, “we really tight over here.”

They’re not all expats.Alexander Hawkins,a 20-year-old from Calgary who hopes to study to become an electrician or carpenter,has been on the midway for two years.His older sister Samantha had worked in ticket sales for two years and,missing her,he decided to join her.Still,he finds the distance from the rest of his family, whom he is closely connected with,to be a challenge. “I t gets really lonesome from time to time.”

Despite the periodic loneliness,the midway offers Hawkins a place to prove himself.“I always had challenges growing up with being called weak and slow. But when I’m here, I like to show that I’m not that person. Because I like to do the work even if it’s small work.”

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Toronto Island waitlist life: why one man will never give up his dream of living lakeside

Image 31Image 32Image 33

Jakob Malo, 22 and from Winnipeg, enjoys the puzzle of putting the Wave Swinger together and climbing the structure:“it’s like my ju ngle gym,I’ve always been a monkey.”Malo hopes people will look past the stigma commonly associated with the midway.“It’s a lot more lighthearted and fun than people make it out to be;we’re a family here at the end of the day and we all kind of have each other’s back.”

With five separate tour operations, known as units, North American Midway Entertainment entertain s about 17 million people a year; the CNE alone drew 1.42 million in 2025.In an hour, the Wave Swinger can accommodate 550 people,roughly the equivalent of the entire travelling staff of this unit.

Then the sun goes down, the lights go off,and CNE comes to an end, but the Wave Swinger carries on.After wrapping up their Canad ian leg in London, they “follow the sun back down south,” says Koerk, to Tulsa, Okla.

“A d ay or two after this event’s over, you’ll drive by and it’s gonna be an empty sad parking lot again,” says Kaval s.”Just like that, the lights go out and the magic’s gone for another year. And we’re off to another city to pu t smiles on other people’s faces, and we do it again and again.”

Bouquillon is a staff photographer for the Star.

stories.title: Don't want to slip and fall off the mountain? There's an app for that.
stories.summary: Calgary - When clinging to the side of a rock wall hundreds of metres in the sky, avoiding a single misstep can save your life.
stories.author: Bill Graveland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
CALGARY - When clinging to the side of a rock wall hundreds of metres in the sky, avoiding a single misstep can save your life.

Turns out there’s an app to help with that.

Ben Pearman, a rock climber since age 18, said the idea of the app came to him while his group was trying to determine the best way to climb the south face of Mount Yamnuska in southern Alberta’s Bow Valley.

“You get up there and the whole thing looks sort of like a planar surface from far away, like one big sheer cliff,” Pearman said in an interview.

“The scale just swallows you. And you’re like, ‘Oh man, it’s really easy to get lost here.’”

The sheer limestone wall of this climbing route is known as Red Shirt, and Pearman said it’s the “crown jewel” of climbing in the Rocky Mountains.

The 29-year-old is a master’s student in the University of Calgary’s Department of Computer Science. He decided to turn a climbing map into a project, creating the ThreeTopo app for climbers.

He used a drone to shoot detailed photos of the 240-metre-tall climb and created a three-dimensional digital copy of that section of the rock face.

The app examines the potential for new navigation and conveys the information to climbers. Pearman said it was also important to make it so climbers could use it one-handed when they consult it at safe points during the climb.

As an example, a climber could ask the app for information on the best way forward while at one particular spot in the climb.

The app could reply: “You’ll want to start traversing left from the anchor. Once you hit the corner, start heading upwards until you reach a bolt. As soon as you get to that bolt, you need to traverse hard left, passing a pin to reach an anchor on the face.”

In the past, said Pearman, that kind of practical information came only in the form of cryptic, decades-old typewritten notes from other climbers.

Miles Abesdris, who was in a group of experienced climbers asked to test the app, said it can take some of the scary unknowns out of trad climbing.

Trad — or traditional climbing — involves the lead climber placing temporary, removable gear into the rock. They then clip in a rope to catch a fall. The second climber comes up behind and removes the devices, leaving nothing behind.

“The first little while, (trad climbing) is somewhat horrifying, but you kind of become very comfortable there after a while,” said Abesdris, 38.

“Your hands and feet are great, but you’ve got to know where to go, right?

“There’s weaknesses in the rock. And you kind of follow the weaknesses and you kind of get a Spidey sense of where to go over the years — but sometimes you can be wrong.”

Pearman intends to make his app publicly available. He hopes other climbers will follow suit by detailing data on other popular North American routes from B.C. to Nevada, making the sport safer.

“I know a bunch of people who have had to be rescued by helicopter,” he said.

“Everyone I know has gotten off route at some time.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 6, 2026.

stories.title: American diplomat recounts Canadian solidarity with U.S. after Sept. 11 attacks
stories.summary: Ottawa - American diplomat Baxter Hunt recalls showing up to work at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa the morning after the 9/11 terrorist attacks and finding "a mountain of flowers" outside the building.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - American diplomat Baxter Hunt recalls showing up to work at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa the morning after the 9/11 terrorist attacks and finding “a mountain of flowers” outside the building.

“It was just a day that none of us will ever forget,” said Hunt, now the U.S. consul general in Toronto. “What also stuck with me was the outpouring of support that we got from Canadians.”

This Friday marks 25 years since nearly 3,000 people in the U.S. were killed when al-Qaeda hijackers slammed planes into the World Trade Center in New York and crashed into the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

In the days that followed, Hunt witnessed many more displays of Canadian compassion and support for a grieving nation.

Three days after the attack, 80,000 people crowded Parliament Hill for a national day of mourning, according to an RCMP estimate reported by The Canadian Press that week.

’‘By their outpouring of concern, sympathy and help, the feelings and actions of Canadians have been clear,” then-prime minister Jean Chrétien told the crowd.

’‘And even as we grieve our own losses, the message they send to the American people is equally clear. Do not despair. You are not alone. We are with you. The whole world is with you.’’

Similar moments of silence took place at provincial legislatures and even in the heart of Canada’s financial sector on Bay Street. It was Canada’s first official day of mourning in three decades.

On the day of the attacks, the Newfoundland community of Gander famously took in 38 passenger planes carrying more than 6,500 travellers after officials closed U.S. airspace.

“Just an incredible showing of compassion by those people for complete strangers, who needed them at that time,” Hunt said. “There were also many, many stranded passengers who went to other locations around Canada, about 33,000, I understand.”

Hunt was quick to mention the 24 Canadians who were killed in the attacks alongside other non-Americans.

People bow their heads for three minutes of silence at a memorial ceremony in Ottawa Friday Sept 14, 2001, for the victims of Tuesday’s terrorist attacks on the United States.

He was 38 and working as the embassy’s political-military officer on Sept. 11, 2001. American diplomats “naturally came together” with Canadian law enforcement and military officials to identify threats, he said.

“No one knew initially exactly what else might happen. And we wanted to make sure we weren’t vulnerable to other attacks,” Hunt said. “The response of Canadians at a time when we most needed it was incredible.”

Both countries standardized airport security. Allies took up air patrols around the U.S. The Nato military alliance invoked its collective security clause for the first time, sending Canadians and allied troops to fight the Taliban in Afghanistan. That war lasted for more than a dozen years and 165 Canadians — 158 soldiers and 7 civilians — died in the conflict.

“It was an event that was a shift in how we perceived threats around the world, and something that happened in the homeland, which we really hadn’t seen before,” Hunt said.

“It was something that just reinforced the need for us to work together.”

Hunt spoke to The Canadian Press shortly before trade talks in Washington collapsed. Prime Minister Mark Carney accused the U.S. of launching an economic “war” on its erstwhile ally and U.S. President Donald Trump moved to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.”

It’s getting harder to believe that the president is a symptom rather than the cause of what’s gone off the rails in the U.S., Susan Delacourt writes.

Hunt said the legacy of 9/11 is seen in the depth of the relationships between Canadians and Americans throughout the ups and downs in the bilateral relationship.

“That is something that we saw big time after the 9/11 attacks. People just feeling like these are our friends and neighbours, and it is like an extended North American family. And that really came through. And that’s something that I believe is still very strong today,” he said.

“It’s great to remember that as we approach the 25th anniversary, and be grateful that we have that close, close relationship.”

The Toronto consulate is holding events this month to commemorate the anniversary.

They include an ongoing exhibition at a Toronto arts centre of pen and ink drawings by Toronto-based artist John Coburn, who was in New York after the attacks. Hunt said the exhibit includes interactive events with local college students, many of whom were born after the attacks.

On the Friday anniversary, the consulate will hold an event at the same art centre bringing together first responders and government officials to honour the victims. That event will feature Maureen Basnicki, whose husband Ken was killed at the World Trade Center.

Hunt will open the Toronto Stock Exchange that day to commemorate the city’s connections with New York. He’ll also visit a memorial walkway in St. Catharines, Ont. on Thursday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 6, 2026.

stories.title: How to help your child navigate back-to-school anxiety
stories.summary: How to help your child navigate back-to-school anxiety CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Psychotherapist Lori Griffith shares tips on how families can manage nerves ahead of the first day of school
The countdown to the new school year can trigger a mix of excitement and stress.

Psychotherapist Lori Griffith, a director at the Canadian Mental Health Association (CMHA) Thames Valley, offers insight into why students and parents experience back-to-school nerves, how to validate those feelings, and when it might be time to seek professional support.
Griffith spoke with London Morning host Matt Allen.
The following has been edited for length and clarity.
Matt Allen: What are some of the emotions kids might be feeling as summer winds down?

Lori Griffith: It's completely normal for students of all ages to feel some level of anxiety about going back to school. A new teacher, new routine, social pressures, academic expectations, and uncertainty can all create stress.

The goal isn't to eliminate the anxiety. Anxiety is a normal human emotion. The goal is helping students to learn that they can cope with it. What we might see before going back to school is some butterflies before the first day, worrying if friends will be in their class, feeling nervous about a new school or teacher.
LISTEN | How to help your child:
Media Audio | London Morning :
MA: Is it just the kids who are nervous right now, or parents too?

LG: I think it's everybody. Every time you're starting a new challenge or an event, it's normal to feel a little bit anxious. The normal thing is to feel uncomfortable, but try to manage through it. As long as something's not interfering significantly with daily life, we do normally see routines and the anxiety will improve once they settle into their routine.
MA: Why do kids get so nervous heading into a new grade?

LG: I think it's the fear of the unknown. I mean, I think that's common with all of us. Also, we get this idea of this anticipatory anxiety. Often kids aren't struggling with the event itself, they're struggling with imagining the event. Maybe they're worrying all weekend about Monday, or worrying all summer about school, and thinking about every possible thing that could potentially go wrong.
MA: What are some tips for parents who are trying to psych their kids up to enter a new environment?

LG: I think it's really important to acknowledge the feeling. We're not looking to avoid or remove the feeling. We're wanting to acknowledge and then express confidence in the children and encourage gradual exposure.

As an example, if a child misses school because they're nervous, they may feel better that day, but then their brains will learn, "I survived it because I avoided it." The next time, the anxiety may come back a little bit stronger.
Instead of saying, "Don't worry, there's nothing to be nervous about," we want to say things like, "I can see you're nervous. New things can feel scary, but I know you can handle this."
MA: How can parents support their children if they don't have all the answers?

LG: One of the nice things is when we're kind of exposing ourselves to a new routine is to keep routines predictable. Children feel safer when expectations are clear. Consistent sleep schedules (sleep is one of the most important things that we can do in terms of relieving some of that worry), regular meals, and then preparing. Whether that looks like preparing on the weekend for the upcoming week, or preparing that night for the school the next day.

Focus on coping, not certainty. Parents often try to reassure away anxiety. Instead of saying that "Nothing bad will happen," try saying something to your youth or your child that says, "Whatever happens, we'll figure it out." This will teach the resilience rather than dependence on certainty.

Psychotherapist Lori Griffith shares tips on how families can manage nerves ahead of the first day of school

The countdown to the new school year can trigger a mix of excitement and stress.

Psychotherapist Lori Griffith, a director at the Canadian Mental Health Association (CMHA) Thames Valley, offers insight into why students and parents experience back-to-school nerves, how to validate those feelings, and when it might be time to seek professional support.

Griffith spoke with London Morning host Matt Allen.

The following has been edited for length and clarity.

Matt Allen: What are some of the emotions kids might be feeling as summer winds down?

Lori Griffith: It's completely normal for students of all ages to feel some level of anxiety about going back to school. A new teacher, new routine, social pressures, academic expectations, and uncertainty can all create stress.

The goal isn't to eliminate the anxiety. Anxiety is a normal human emotion. The goal is helping students to learn that they can cope with it. What we might see before going back to school is some butterflies before the first day, worrying if friends will be in their class, feeling nervous about a new school or teacher.

LISTEN | How to help your child:

Media Audio | London Morning :

MA: Is it just the kids who are nervous right now, or parents too?

LG: I think it's everybody. Every time you're starting a new challenge or an event, it's normal to feel a little bit anxious. The normal thing is to feel uncomfortable, but try to manage through it. As long as something's not interfering significantly with daily life, we do normally see routines and the anxiety will improve once they settle into their routine.

MA: Why do kids get so nervous heading into a new grade?

LG: I think it's the fear of the unknown. I mean, I think that's common with all of us. Also, we get this idea of this anticipatory anxiety. Often kids aren't struggling with the event itself, they're struggling with imagining the event. Maybe they're worrying all weekend about Monday, or worrying all summer about school, and thinking about every possible thing that could potentially go wrong.

MA: What are some tips for parents who are trying to psych their kids up to enter a new environment?

LG: I think it's really important to acknowledge the feeling. We're not looking to avoid or remove the feeling. We're wanting to acknowledge and then express confidence in the children and encourage gradual exposure.

As an example, if a child misses school because they're nervous, they may feel better that day, but then their brains will learn, "I survived it because I avoided it." The next time, the anxiety may come back a little bit stronger.

Instead of saying, "Don't worry, there's nothing to be nervous about," we want to say things like, "I can see you're nervous. New things can feel scary, but I know you can handle this."

MA: How can parents support their children if they don't have all the answers?

LG: One of the nice things is when we're kind of exposing ourselves to a new routine is to keep routines predictable. Children feel safer when expectations are clear. Consistent sleep schedules (sleep is one of the most important things that we can do in terms of relieving some of that worry), regular meals, and then preparing. Whether that looks like preparing on the weekend for the upcoming week, or preparing that night for the school the next day.

Focus on coping, not certainty. Parents often try to reassure away anxiety. Instead of saying that "Nothing bad will happen," try saying something to your youth or your child that says, "Whatever happens, we'll figure it out." This will teach the resilience rather than dependence on certainty.

MA: How do parents know if anxiety is normal or if professional help is necessary?

LG: Anxiety, it may be there for a couple weeks as they're adjusting to that schedule. When we want to look for more support is if it's persisting for more weeks, it's getting worse rather than better, it's causing significant distress, or if it's interfering with their school attendance, their sleep patterns, their friendships, family life, or other activities.

One kind of way of thinking about it is when anxiety starts running a child's life instead of simply visiting it from time to time, that's when we become more concerned.

stories.title: This survey shows if Canadians are happier compared to a year ago
stories.summary: Are things looking up for Canadians? According to a new survey, many of us across the country are feeling happier than we were a year ago.
stories.author: Elianna Lev
stories.content:
Are things looking up for Canadians? According to a new survey, many across the country are feeling happier than they were a year ago. Canadians’ happiness is up slightly from 2025, according to Leger’s Happiness Index 2026, with the national average sitting at 70.5 out of 100, compared to 68.7 in the previous year.

Out of all provinces, Quebec ranked the happiest at 74.5. Newfoundland and Labrador ranked second at 71.0, followed by New Brunswick at 70.3. Meanwhile, Ontario landed in the middle with a 69.3 index while Prince Edward Island came in last, with a 67.7 index – up slightly from 66.5 a year earlier.

Amongst the country’s largest cities, Montreal came first with an index of 72.7 out of 100, with Brampton in second place, with 71.7 – up five points from 66.7 in 2025 – and Toronto in third, with a 69.4 index, up a few points from 65.8 a year earlier.

Quebec also ranked higher when it came to optimism, with a 72.2 index, compared to 66.6 in the rest of the country. Fewer Quebecers also said they were unhappy – 22 per cent – compared to 33 per cent for the rest of the country.

Andrew Enns, Leger’s executive vice-president for central Canada, told CTVNews.CA that the spike in happiness index from this year to last could have something to do with the time of year the survey was conducted. The 2025 survey was done in March and April, while this year’s was conducted in June.

“One of the factors that might be bumping things a little bit was the fact that March, April, in Canada is a certain time of year where we’re starting in some parts of the country to get out and feel a little more free from winter,” he said.

“But for most of us, it’s still not so great. June is definitely a better time, that’s what makes us happy.” American index almost identical to Canada The survey also took the temperature on happiness south of the border, with surprising results.

Overall, Americans ranked 70.5 out of 100 on the happiness Index, which was the exact same number as Canada. However, Enns said U.S. states showed a bit more extreme results compared to Canada. “They had a few states that were higher than most provinces in Canada,” he said.

“But then they also have some states that are quite at the lower end.” The happiest states were Florida with a 75.3 index, followed by Kansas at 74.5, then New Jersey with a 74.4 index. On the bottom of the list was West Virginia with a happiness index of 62.5.

Enns said that overall, there wasn’t a great deal of differences between the two countries when it came to level of happiness and what’s driving those sentiments. What contributes to happiness? Enns said the things that contributed to happiness strongly related to our community, access to outdoor spaces, our neighbours and family.

“Money, affordability doesn’t show up as a big contributor to happiness,” he said. “Financial stress and affordability is definitely a detractor, like it can be added to the unhappy factor, but it doesn’t actually promote the happy factor of when people think about their own personal happiness.” Happiness in a municipality primarily came down to feeling safe for 46 per cent of Canadines, compared to 51 per cent Americans.

That was followed by access to nature – 40 per cent for Canadians and 27 per cent for Americans – and enjoying a good neighbourhood life, which 27 per cent of both Canadians and Americans identified with. However, when it came to being asked about barriers to happiness, the most common answers related to finances.

In Canada, 58 per cent said cost of living affected their happiness, while in the United States, the number was higher at 61 per cent. Financial pressure – cost of living, housing, debt, income and financial future - was the number one reasons behind the source of pressure for 57 per cent of Canadians and 58 per cent of Americans.

That was followed by physical health (57 per cent in Canada, 58 per cent in the U.S.) mental health (23 per cent in Canada and 26 in the U.S.) and uncertainty about the future (23 per cent in Canada versus 21 per cent in the U.S.) Methodology The research was based on a online survey filled out by 63,710 Canadians and 6,408 Americans, aged 18 and up.

The data was collected between June 9 and 29. Leger said that to ensure the sample accurately represents the population, the results were adjusted based on gender, age, and region.

stories.title: Here's what's open and closed in London this Labour Day
stories.summary: Many city services will be closed Monday, but some outdoor pools, recreation programs and attractions will be open for Labour Day.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Many city services will be closed Monday, but some outdoor pools, recreation programs and attractions will be open for Labour Day.
· Posted: Sep 06, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 10 hours ago
Here is a list of what's open and closed in London this holiday.(CBC)
Labour Day is Monday, and for many Londoners, it’s the last chance to squeeze a little more summer out of the long weekend.
Here’s what you need to know about what’s open and closed around the city.

The City of London is offering a range of free recreation activities on Monday, including swimming, arts and crafts, science workshops and basketball. Some activities require registration, while others are drop-in.
And unlike some years, Londoners still have several chances to get in an outdoor swim.
Byron, Southcrest and Silverwoods pools are open Monday, although they’re closing for the season that day. Gibbons and Stronach pools will remain open beyond the holiday.
Several wading pools will also have their final day on Labour Day, including Meredith, Silverwoods and Springbank parks.
The city’s spray pads are also open, generally from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., although the Ivey Park spray pad remains closed for the rest of the year.
If you’re looking for something beyond the pool, Storybook Gardens will be open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday. Admission is $10.70, with children under two admitted free.
Other attractions, including the London Children’s Museum at Kellogg Lane, East Park and Boler Mountain, are also open for the long weekend.
London Public Library branches will be closed Monday for Labour Day, although its digital library remains available.
If you’re planning to shop, check before you head out.
White Oaks Mall and CF Masonville Place will be closed Monday for Labour Day.
Individual stores, restaurants and grocery stores can set their own holiday hours, so it’s a good idea to check before making a trip.
Liquor and beer retailers may also have holiday closures or reduced hours.
London Transit will run on a holiday schedule Monday.
There are also several route and schedule changes taking effect Sunday, Sept. 6, so regular riders should check their route before heading out.
Banks will be closed Monday.
There will also be no regular Canada Post collection or delivery on Labour Day.
And if Monday is your usual garbage day, your collection will be pushed back one day to Tuesday, Sept. 8.
So if you're heading out Monday, check the hours first. The forecast for Monday from Environment Canada is calling for cloudy skies with a high of 23 C.

Labour Day is Monday, and for many Londoners, it’s the last chance to squeeze a little more summer out of the long weekend.

Here’s what you need to know about what’s open and closed around the city.

The City of London is offering a range of free recreation activities on Monday, including swimming, arts and crafts, science workshops and basketball. Some activities require registration, while others are drop-in.

And unlike some years, Londoners still have several chances to get in an outdoor swim.

Byron, Southcrest and Silverwoods pools are open Monday, although they’re closing for the season that day. Gibbons and Stronach pools will remain open beyond the holiday.

Several wading pools will also have their final day on Labour Day, including Meredith, Silverwoods and Springbank parks.

The city’s spray pads are also open, generally from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., although the Ivey Park spray pad remains closed for the rest of the year.

If you’re looking for something beyond the pool, Storybook Gardens will be open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday. Admission is $10.70, with children under two admitted free.

Other attractions, including the London Children’s Museum at Kellogg Lane, East Park and Boler Mountain, are also open for the long weekend.

London Public Library branches will be closed Monday for Labour Day, although its digital library remains available.

If you’re planning to shop, check before you head out.

White Oaks Mall and CF Masonville Place will be closed Monday for Labour Day.

Individual stores, restaurants and grocery stores can set their own holiday hours, so it’s a good idea to check before making a trip.

Liquor and beer retailers may also have holiday closures or reduced hours.

London Transit will run on a holiday schedule Monday.

There are also several route and schedule changes taking effect Sunday, Sept. 6, so regular riders should check their route before heading out.

Banks will be closed Monday.

There will also be no regular Canada Post collection or delivery on Labour Day.

And if Monday is your usual garbage day, your collection will be pushed back one day to Tuesday, Sept. 8.

So if you're heading out Monday, check the hours first. The forecast for Monday from Environment Canada is calling for cloudy skies with a high of 23 C.
