stories.title: SuperDogs lap up the love, 50 years after being unleashed on adoring fans
stories.summary: Vancouver - Lisa Sun recalls watching the SuperDogs at the Pacific National Exhibition in Vancouver as many times as she could as a kid, delighting in the performers' speed, skill and comic relief.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Lisa Sun recalls watching the SuperDogs at the Pacific National Exhibition in Vancouver as many times as she could as a kid, delighting in the performers’ speed, skill and comic relief.

Now it’s Sun and her three pugs, Mario, Luigi and Yoshi, who are entertaining crowds at the fair, 50 years after it hosted the first SuperDogs show.

Their role? “Definitely comedy,” Sun said.

“When they come out onstage, people know they’re not going to be the fastest.... But you know what? They have personality, they have character.”

The crowd-favourite SuperDogs bring generations together in a brief break from everyday life at Vancouver’s Pacific National Exhibition, where the show began 50 years ago in 1976. (Sept. 5, 2026)

Sun’s pugs wear sparkly pink bandanas as they perform their tricks. They twirl left and right in unison, and stand on their hind legs to give each other what she calls a “pug hug.”

The pugs are among hundreds of canines from across Canada, many of them rescues from humane societies and animal shelters, that have been part of the SuperDogs shows, which are also held at the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto.

While some trainers and their dogs travel for shows, most are local and return to their family homes each night after delighting crowds that can number in the thousands.

David Acer, a writer and host for the show in Vancouver, describes SuperDogs as “pure joy from beginning to end,” helping fans let their troubles go for a moment.

“It’s really among the only entertainment I’ve been a part of where I can look in the stands and see a five-year-old, a 20-year-old and a 70-year-old all laughing at the same thing,” he said following a SuperDogs performance on Thursday.

“I think every generation is feeling the pressure and the stress of the current climate, and this is an opportunity for them to come and not feel that together.”

SuperDogs lore tells of the show’s beginnings at the PNE in August 1976, when Herb Williams, a former teacher and advertising executive-turned entertainer, recruited a handful of dogs to perform tricks for fairgoers in a parking lot.

Fifty years later, SuperDogs holds three shows a day for audiences at the PNE and the CNE. The two fairs close on Monday.

The shows feature dogs small and large racing, catching Frisbees, leaping over hurdles, and weaving in and out of obstacles. Afterwards, the audience is invited to “pat and chat,” an opportunity to meet the dogs and their trainers.

Acer said the canine performers are all “super” in different ways.

“Some of them are super athletic, some of them are super smart, some of them are super cute, some of them are super fast,” he said.

“We actually think every dog is a super dog, so if you have a dog at time, (there’s) something that makes them super too.”

Still, certain dogs have exuded stand-out star power, landing them in the inaugural “Paws of Fame” class to mark the 50th anniversary of SuperDogs.

They include the “slowest SuperDog ever,” an English bulldog named Pot Roast who performed between 1992 and 1998, and Demolition Derby, an old English sheepdog described as “a big, lovable buffoon who introduced true comedy” to the show.

Sun’s first-generation trio of pugs, Snap, Crackle and Pop, were also among the 20 honourees, along with Flint, a collie who also served as a search-and-rescue dog with the Calgary Fire Department.

It’s gratifying “knowing how many hearts melt when they see these pug faces and how much joy they bring,” said Sun, who has worked with SuperDogs for 15 years.

Sun said the show offers a lighthearted distraction and a break from everyday worries, inspiring cheers and laughs from generations of fans.

“For that half hour you’re sitting in the audience, you’re not thinking about anything else but watching the dogs do their comedy, do their athleticism, do their Frisbee playing, do their dancing onstage, their racing relays,” she said.

“It’s such a blessing to be on the other side now,” Sun added. “Running with the dogs, ON the stage, doing the thing that I used to love to watch as a kid.”

Sun said dog owners shouldn’t underestimate their own canine companions.

“Always look at the dog in front of you,” she said. “They’re each individuals that can learn so many things.”

The website for the group Suite Melody Care, which brings young musicians into hospitals and care homes, lists Williams, who is in his 90s and lives in Ontario, as one of its directors. He made his final SuperDogs appearance in 2012.

The site says Williams and his SuperDogs entertained audiences that have included British royals and celebrities such as Joan Rivers and Luciano Pavarotti.

After the PNE and CNE close, the SuperDogs will be at fall fairs in Burns Lake, B.C.; Rock Creek, B.C.; Uxbridge, Ont.; and at a dog-focused event in Newmarket, Ont.

Ultimately, Acer said SuperDogs encourages people to love their dogs.

“If people go home after seeing a SuperDogs show and give their dog one more hug, one more treat, throw a Frisbee for them, it’s a win for everybody.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Reader to Reader: September 5, 2026
stories.summary: A Free Press reader who now lives in Germany, sends thanks to the Londoner who helped their son during an incident in 2024.
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Were you walking your dog, possibly a German shepherd, on Friday, Sept. 20, 2024 around 10 a.m. or 11 a.m. near the Dollarama in Pond Mills, close to Sir Wilfrid Laurier secondary school? Did you happen upon a swarm of about eight to 10 youth beating a hapless teen on the ground while holding his friend back and had the incredible courage to disrupt them? If this is you, or you know who this might be, we want to thank you from the bottom of our hearts. Our son suffered a concussion, but it could have been much worse without your intervention, since at least one of the perpetrators continued stomping on his head while he already was lying on the ground.

Unfortunately, it has taken this long for us to come to terms with the incident and to write this letter. We don’t know who you are and will never be able to thank you enough, but please know your brave intervention saved his life. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

K. Sugar-Holder, Germany

content_blocks.text: Were you walking your dog, possibly a German shepherd, on Friday, Sept. 20, 2024 around 10 a.m. or 11 a.m. near the Dollarama in Pond Mills, close to Sir Wilfrid Laurier secondary school? Did you happen upon a swarm of about eight to 10 youth beating a hapless teen on the ground while holding his friend back and had the incredible courage to disrupt them? If this is you, or you know who this might be, we want to thank you from the bottom of our hearts. Our son suffered a concussion, but it could have been much worse without your intervention, since at least one of the perpetrators continued stomping on his head while he already was lying on the ground.

stories.title: LFP Letters to the Editor: September 5, 2026
stories.summary: Free Press readers sound off on the topics of the day, including former London councillors, Donald Trump and Canadian Parliament.
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced his intention to address the European Parliament.

Carney recently implied Canada walked away from trade talks with the U.S. because of demands impinged on our sovereignty.

That is laudable.

However, Carney has to decide if he is prime minister of Canada or of Europe.

If Carney is prime minister of Canada, his first parliamentary talk should be in Ottawa, to the people of Canada.

Canadians need full transparency regarding recent events such as the rewriting of the original Gordie Howe Bridge agreement and the collapse of the recent trade talks. Only then can the government be held accountable. We cannot be blindly playing follow the leader.

Press conferences and social media posts should not be replacing the scrutiny of Parliament.

Gordon Smith, London

According to Statistics Canada, this city has seen its per-household income drop from near best in the country to near worst during two generations. This is not happenstance. It was the result of ineptitude. And some of it happened on their watch. Past councils, including those of Joe Fontana, thought money grows on trees. It doesn’t. It grows on the type of productive industries that these councils refused to bring into the city. One wonders if these candidates have learned their lessons and plan on making London a thriving industrial centre.

David Nielsen, London

The London and Middlesex Local Immigration Partnership asked 387 newcomers to rate their own lives and jobs. The answers point in different directions.

On life satisfaction and belonging, men and women rated themselves within half a point of each other, on a seven-point scale. That gap is there, but small.

On employment, the same people answered differently. Men were far more likely to work full-time (67.5 per cent), while women were more likely to work part-time or be unemployed and looking for work. Among women, 37.4 per cent held jobs needing no formal education, above the survey-wide average of 26.8 per cent, even though more than 60 per cent of respondents hold a university degree.

A job that wastes someone’s training is a number worth ­noticing.

Tristan Johnson, London and Middlesex Local Immigration Partnership

The U.S. national debt has now topped $40.1 trillion. It would take $117,000 from every living American to rid themselves of their national debt. If the U.S. Treasury was a business, would you invest?

What makes the current U.S. administration believe any responsible Canadian would willingly tie their horse to that wagon? It defies logic that a country paying $1 trillion a year in interest payments on their debt, would knowingly alienate themselves from their largest trading partner, ally and closest neighbour.

Although there are clearly economic implications for Canadians (at least in the short term), the position taken by Canada to reject the negotiating tactics deployed by the current U.S. administration was, unfortunately, the only plausible outcome.

Lake America? Please. Let’s treat the most recent executive order as if it has the same force and effect as it would over my signature, and give it zero airtime.

Chris Symons, London

The Mouse That Roared, by Leonard Wibberly, 1955, is the first in a series of comedic novels which chronicles the defeat of America by the Duchy of Fenwick, a tiny, fictional European nation with an “army of 20 men armed with longbows and chain mail.”

The sequel being written today will be The Sweet Guy Who Spoke Quietly, by Mark Carney, 2026, armed with nothing but his word.

The failure of the Americans to negotiate a deal with Canada, Canada of all peoples, has to be embarrassing, even for U.S. President Donald Trump.

Graeme MacLean, St. Thomas

stories.title: Her son was 'caged' for 5 years. Video of his life in isolation at this Ontario hospital left her 'absolutely, completely horrified'
stories.summary: Jake Gordon now slowly being released from seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care. His mom credits the Star's ongoing investigation for the change.
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
stories.content:
Jake Gordon walks around his tiny room in circles.

The room is about twice the length of the six-foot-three man. He’s locked inside.

There’s a mat on the floor and a toilet. Dressed in his pyjamas, he paces, tries to lie down, crouches in a corner, and occasionally looks out the window. At one point, his door is opened slightly, and a plate of food is delivered; he eats it sitting on his mat.

The surveillance footage goes on for six-and-a-half hours, offering a rare glimpse into the life of a seriously mentally ill patient being held in seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care in Penetanguishene, Ont.

Gordon, a 30-year-old Toronto man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, lived in isolation at Ontario’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital for five years. His mother, who is also his substitute decision-maker, shared the surveillance footage with the Star, believing the public needs to see what is happening inside the walls of the facility.

Diane Worden received the footage at the end of last month, the first time she had been able to see for herself her son’s living conditions. She wasn’t sure she could get through watching all of it.

“I was absolutely, completely horrified,” Worden said.

“He’s been in that teeny, tiny room, caged like an animal. And to think that’s been happening for five years. It’s sickening.”

The video is from August 2025, about a year before significant changes were made to Gordon’s care at Waypoint, leading to his release from seclusion just last month.

The hospital has always refused to divulge the number of people in long-term seclusion, but it’s understood to be at least a dozen. Aside from Gordon, it was revealed during an unrelated Ontario Review Board hearing last month that there are another 11 secluded patients in a different unit.

During his time in isolation, Gordon didn’t shower regularly, his teeth rotted, he gained weight and developed trouble walking. And he seriously injured his eye in an incident for which Worden is still seeking details.

In her opinion, her son ended up sicker than ever.

But on the heels of the Star’s coverage, Gordon started spending an increasing amount of time out of seclusion and out of restraints; he was being taken to the canteen and into the courtyard; he was seen by a dentist and an optometrist; he was being given access to music more often; and he was showering again.

And then last month, the hospital told Worden that her son was getting a new psychiatrist and they were ending his time in seclusion altogether.

“These sudden, sweeping changes are no coincidence. It is a direct result of your reporting and the pressure from advocates,” Worden said.

“Every week that goes by, something has changed; they’re just more involved with him than they’ve ever been.”

When she went to visit her son last month, he was not only now walking again, but dancing.

“He’s smiling; he tells me how beautiful I am,” Worden said. “He’s not the person he was, but he’s getting closer.”

The other patient whose seclusion is set to come to an end after five years is Andrew Azevedo, a 39-year-old man who also has treatment-resistant schizophrenia and was profiled in the Star in April . His Waypoint psychiatrist, Dr. Achal Mishra, revealed at Azevedo’s Ontario Review Board hearing on Aug. 20 that he was within days or a few weeks of being released from seclusion. The hospital has since told Azevedo’s family that the plan is to de-seclude him in mid-September.

Mishra denied that the Star’s investigation was the “impetus” for changes to his patient’s care, while acknowledging that “of course it impacted Waypoint, it was not something we would ignore.”

Waypoint’s CEO, Dr. Nadiya Sunderji, declined to comment on Gordon’s case as she said the hospital is bound by patient confidentiality requirements. She said no directive has been issued to release more patients from seclusion.

“The discontinuation of seclusion for an individual patient is a clinical decision made by health care professionals based on that patient’s individual circumstances,” Sunderji said. “Waypoint follows a least-restraint philosophy and is committed to ending the use of seclusion and restraint whenever it is safe and clinically appropriate.”

Waypoint has said that patients in seclusion continue to receive mental health treatment and are escorted out of their rooms for periods of time “when clinically appropriate and safe.” Depending on their care and safety plan, patients may have access in their rooms to items including a TV, reading materials and puzzles, as well as the ability to make phone and video calls.

Reached by the Star, the chair of the hospital’s board, Steve Parry, backed the hospital’s leadership in response to questions about the damning assessment in the Azevedo case prepared by Andrea Monteiro, who previously held senior roles in the correctional system. Sunderji had previously said the facility “categorically” disagrees with Monteiro’s opinion regarding torture.

Parry said he was “fully aligned” with Sunderji’s comments.

‘I knew nothing about Waypoint’

Jake Gordon was a quiet but happy child growing up in the West Hill neighbourhood of Scarborough. He had a “wonderful circle of friends,” his mother recalled, and loved playing hockey.

His family started noticing changes in his behaviour toward the end of high school, around 2013. He had trouble sleeping, fell out with some of his friends and couldn’t get out of bed to do his exams. He was diagnosed with social anxiety and depression, and ultimately bipolar disorder.

What followed after high school graduation was a series of hospitalizations, including at St. Michael’s Hospital following a car accident in 2015, where he was diagnosed with schizophrenia. His aggression became worse: he would have confrontations with hospital security and was frequently placed in restraints. Improvement from medication was never long-lasting, leading to a recognition that Gordon’s illness was treatment-resistant.

In between hospitalizations, he was living at home with his parents and brother. Sometimes he wouldn’t leave the house for weeks. But one night in the winter of 2018, he went outside with no coat or shoes and ended up getting into a tow truck to keep warm. He then drove away with it to get cigarettes.

His mother recalled he was apprehended by the police and taken to court, where, she said, it was recognized he was “very ill.” The case ended there without going any further; Gordon was released into his mother’s care, and she took him straight to the hospital.

Despite his challenges, Gordon kept up with his hockey practice.

“The one thing he lived for was his hockey,” Worden said. “He would take his equipment and get on the bus and go on his own. He absolutely loved it.

“When manic, he would literally be in the driveway for eight hours shooting pucks.”

After his condition deteriorated at a local hospital, the decision was made to send Gordon to Ontario Shores Centre for Mental Health Sciences in Whitby in 2020.

Gordon had a “phenomenal team” at Ontario Shores, Worden said, but he ended up assaulting another patient and a nurse, and was charged in relation to the latter. He received a conditional discharge — meaning probation and no criminal record.

In the wake of the assaults, Gordon was sent to Waypoint in January 2021. He’s been there ever since.

“I knew nothing about Waypoint,” Worden said.

She said that the team at Ontario Shores had assured her the transfer would be temporary — “That Waypoint would have the ability to change Jake’s behaviour and to manage him better.”

His life in seclusion — ‘He worsened’

Unlike other patients in prolonged seclusion at Waypoint, Gordon is not there because of involvement in the criminal justice system. He’s not been found unfit to stand trial or not criminally responsible, and he has no charges hanging over him.

He’s being held at Waypoint involuntarily under the Mental Health Act; his involuntary admission is renewed by a doctor every three months after concluding that he poses a serious risk of bodily harm to himself and others.

Involuntary admission can be indefinite. Lawyer Anita Szigeti, an expert on mental health law who is not representing Gordon and his family, said that once involuntary admission is renewed, a patient can challenge it before the Consent and Capacity Board, whose three-member panels are made up of a medical professional, lawyer and layperson.

The board must also hold a mandatory review of the patient’s case every year, where the patient can ask for orders such as a transfer to another facility, but the board tends to be quite conservative — “Rarely is substantial relief granted in favour of the patient,” Szigeti said.

Worden said she plans to start attending her son’s board hearings. She said he’s been held in seclusion since his arrival at Waypoint in 2021, with the hospital saying it’s due to a mix of aggressive behaviour, self-harming and psychotic episodes, but she said his 83,000-page clinical file shows he sometimes went weeks with no concerns being noted.

“He didn’t transition well; it was very traumatic for him to be plucked out of Ontario Shores and put into Waypoint,” Worden said. “He worsened.”

She told the Star she understands that her son has been placed in different rooms during his time in seclusion at Waypoint, and it’s not clear if the one seen on video from 2025 is typical.

The room looks somewhat like segregation cells in prisons, said former federal correctional investigator Howard Sapers.

“But in many ways, it is more spartan,” he said in an email.

A segregation cell would usually have a raised bunk, not a mat on the floor, as well as something to sit on, like a fixed bench, Sapers said.

Around the time he arrived at Waypoint, Gordon began experiencing extrapyramidal symptoms — violent involuntary movements commonly caused by antipsychotic medications.

His mother describes them as seizures, causing Gordon’s eyes to roll to the back of his head and his throat to close, making it difficult to breathe — “It’s very painful.”

She became concerned about Gordon’s well-being at Waypoint: If he was locked in seclusion, how would staff know he was having a seizure in order to quickly administer medication to bring the symptoms under control, as well as to stop Gordon from sticking his fingers in his eyes, as he was prone to do?

Staff assured her that the room was being recorded on video and that Gordon, like all patients in seclusion, was being checked on by a staff member every 15 minutes.

“Well, in 15 minutes, the seizure could be horrific,” Worden said.

In her independent assessment filed in the Azevedo case, Monteiro concluded that these 15-minute check-ins are conducted like “security rounds” in prisons, where a staff member looks into the room and may or may not engage with the patient.

Worden’s worst fear came true in August of last year when her son caused what doctors would later describe as “extensive trauma” to his eye with his fingers. Although she initially believed it was due to the seizures, Worden said it appears to have been the result of a psychotic episode, based on her review of Waypoint’s medical notes.

“There are several notes stating he was screaming throughout the day, which is entirely uncharacteristic of him,” she said.

He was taken to Georgian Bay General Hopsital that evening; Worden said she first found out about the incident the next morning from Georgian Bay, not Waypoint.

The prognosis for his eye is “guarded,” Worden said; she said Gordon could have double vision for the rest of his life.

She asked Waypoint for footage from Aug. 21, 2025, capturing the incident, as well as the 24 hours leading up to it. The hospital responded that due to the passage of time, only a portion of the footage from Aug. 21 — totalling six-and-a-half hours — had been retained, and parts of it were redacted before being given to Worden.

The incident is not captured in the footage provided. Worden is continuing to push the facility for answers.

“I am determined to find out how this horrific self-harm could have happened when staff were supposed to be monitoring him every 15 minutes,” she said.

A mom’s search for accountability

Much like the family of Andrew Azevedo, Worden was worried that the hospital might be moving too quickly when they informed her last month that her son’s seclusion was being terminated. She asked them to go slowly.

“They agreed to start with just a few hours out a day, and so far, everything seems to be going well,” she said.

She said she doesn’t believe the improvement can solely be attributed to any medication changes, given Gordon’s poor response to many different drugs in the past; she believes the effort the hospital is now putting into his care plan has made a major difference. She also believes the staff truly care for her son and may have been advocating for change from within.

He’s not the person he was, but he’s getting closer.

But there’s more work to be done. Her goal now is for her son to become well enough that he can be transferred to a facility closer to home, like going back to Ontario Shores.

“There’s no question Jake is too sick to come home,” Worden said.

And she wants to see some accountability from the hospital’s leadership and Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

“It feels like they have become so desensitized to this,” Worden said. “Thank goodness there has been all this public outcry.”

“This is undeniably a systemic crisis,” she said. “How is it that the CEO can allow this to happen at her facility? She makes like $700,000 a year.” (According to the Sunshine List, Sunderji, who has served as CEO since 2022, saw her salary increase last year from just under $400,000 to $658,000.)

Jones’s office has never responded to questions from the Star regarding seclusion at Waypoint. Under provincial law, Jones has the power to impose directives on the hospital’s board or order that inspectors conduct a review of Waypoint’s operations.

“I think she needs to answer your questions, I think she needs to be accountable to the people who have family there and tell us what’s going to happen in the future,” Worden said.

“Sylvia’s my age. What if it was one of hers? Would she allow this to happen?”

stories.title: As Donald Trump’s trade war rages, Mark Carney looks to the European Union — and it’s looking back
stories.summary: While the U.S. president makes angry social media posts and changes the name of Lake Ontario, Ottawa is trying to shift the historical southward focus of Canada’s economy.
stories.author: Allan Woods
stories.content:
Canada and Europe are having a moment. The timing could not be better.

With the Canada-U.S. trading relationship moving from aggression to open hostility, Foreign Minister Anita Anand was huddling in Ireland this week with her European counterparts.

While U.S. President Donald Trump drafts angry social media posts, Prime Minister Mark Carney is drafting a speech he’ll deliver this month to the European Parliament.

And while Washington changes the name of Lake Ontario, Ottawa is trying to shift the historical southward focus of Canada’s economy, with a key moment in that effort coming this fall.

All of this is part of carefully calibrated dance with the European Union as it and Canada move from transatlantic BFFs to something … considerably better.

“We’re sort of building this plane as we’re flying it,” said Mark Camilleri, the Brussels-based president and chief executive of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association.

“I don’t think anybody actually has a set understanding of where we’re going to land here.”

Some have championed Canada as the eventual 28th member of the European Union. But joining a bureaucratic behemoth would be a strange choice indeed for a government trying to do big things quickly and assert its sovereignty on the global stage.

Stéphane Dion, Canada’s former ambassador to the EU and France, has suggested formally joining a looser collective known as the European Political Community. He told a Senate committee in June that membership could strengthen political ties, serve as a one-stop venue for consulting fellow leaders and “consolidate our status as ‘the most European of non-European countries.’”

Both those options also risk the wrath of a United States, which has been critical of Europe and sought greater influence and control over its geographical neighbours .

But if Canada is going to emerge from the U.S. trade war economically intact and fundamentally transformed, something more tangible than symbolism or geopolitical poetry is required.

With the North American border dispute escalating and Trump’s tariff damage looming, pressure is on to reach a new depth in the relationship with Europe in time for an annual Canada-EU meeting planned for October.

“We cannot have another summit … that just confirms that we love each other,” Joost Korte, the EU’s special envoy for Canada, told a committee of the European Parliament in the spring.

“It needs to go a bit deeper … and we need to come up with concrete things. Otherwise, we’ve failed, yes, absolutely.”

Expectations are building, and Carney stoked the fire last month when he promised “intense discussions” to deepen economic and security ties with Europe.

“We can build such unparalleled access because we’re trusted, because we’re reliable, and because we have what the world needs,” he said.

This fall, the two sides hope to finalize a digital trade agreement that could touch on everything from online commerce, consumer protections and cybersecurity to the regulation of artificial intelligence.

After Canada was accepted into Europe’s defence procurement plan , there’s the possibility of deeper integration of the Canadian and European defence industries and having the Canadian Armed Forces participate more systematically in joint training missions with their European counterparts.

Officials could also announce Canada’s full participation in Erasmus Plus , a European travel-and-study program for university students.

But the whole of the emerging Canada-EU partnership is shaping up to be bigger than the sum of its parts, said Geneviève Tuts, the EU’s ambassador to Canada.

In an interview, she said there is no precedent for the new relationship that Ottawa and Brussels are forging — not in the partnership the 27-member bloc has with the United Kingdom, Norway, Switzerland or other non-member states.

“What is going to happen is quite unique. By that, I mean there is no existing integration model that we could simply mirror,” she said.

“We’re going to be creative and imaginative. There needs to be a name that best illustrates the depth of our relationship. I don’t think the word exists yet.”

Whatever it ends up being called, it looks set to respond to the calls of veteran Canada-EU observers.

“What I talk about is the need to stop looking at Europe as a transactional partner, but really look at it as a long-term partner, as a strategic partner,” said Camilleri.

“The relationship has, for a long time, been nice to have, but not a must-have. I think it’s definitely moved into that must-have territory in order to reach the objectives and the ambitions that the current government has expressed, and which seems to be what the Canadian population wants as well.”

It’s not just Canada that needs Europe as an alternative for goods normally sold south of the border.

The Russia-Ukraine war and the blockage in the Strait of Hormuz has exposed Europe’s reliance on oil and gas from uncertain parts of the world and the need to accelerate the transition to lower-emission energy sources.

Javier Moreno Sanchez, a Spanish member of the European Parliament and chair of its committee on Canada-EU relations, likened Canada on the global stage to “a good student who behaves well and, because of that, has often been overlooked.

“You forget them because they’re not a problem,” he said.

But in a more turbulent, chaotic and unpredictable world, that stability and reliability is cherished, as are Canada’s vast natural riches.

“Canada has a wealth of energy resources and of critical minerals,” Korte told European parliamentarians, explaining how he had toured the country, met with officials and determined what aspects of the Canada-EU relationship hold the most promise.

“They have the stuff that we need, and so that would be a no-brainer to co-operate much more, particularly on the critical minerals,” he said. “But of course it needs to be taken out of the ground, and then it needs to come to Europe.”

Korte noted that the Carney government, with the creation of its Major Projects Office to fast-track key infrastructure construction, was serious about doubling down on Europe. But he warned, “We need to give the guarantee that these investments will pay off.”

A key indicator of Europe’s interest in developing and securing Canada’s critical minerals will come at an investment summit in Toronto on Sept. 14 and 15. Carney has set a goal of securing $1 trillion of foreign investment.

Achim Hurrelmann, a Carleton University politics professor and co-director of the school’s Centre for European Studies, said the Canada-U.S. trade war might scare off those who would invest in Canada to secure access to U.S. markets.

“The hope that setting up a base in Canada to supply the United States has become much less realistic,” said Hurrelmann. “But that’s why there’s a much of a focus on strategic raw materials, where it’s really the European interest to secure these materials to be less dependent on China.”

Already, the European Investment Bank has shown an interest in expanding into Canada with the signing last spring of a letter of intent to explore future co-operation.

But the interest expressed by larger institutional investors is having a trickle-down effect, said Yvonne Denz, head of the Toronto-based Canadian German Chamber of Industry and Commerce.

“For a lot of these medium-sized companies in Germany that are family-owned, where there’s a family office that’s taking care of the investments, Canada is … somewhat of a safe haven,” she said.

“If you look at it from a European perspective, as a country like Germany with very few resources and neighbours close by that are not always your friendly … Canada seems very, very stable.”

The forging of closer ties between Canada and Europe is a rush toward certainty.

It is, said Denz, “a signal that even though it feels like the world is breaking up and splitting apart, you have these two blocs that are forging even closer relationships.”

“I don’t think anybody actually has a set understanding of where we’re going to land here.”

Some have championed Canada as the eventual 28th member of the European Union. But joining a bureaucratic behemoth would be a strange choice indeed for a government trying to do big things quickly and assert its sovereignty on the global stage.

Stéphane Dion, Canada’s former ambassador to the EU and France, has suggested formally joining a looser collective known as the European Political Community. He told a Senate committee in June that membership could strengthen political ties, serve as a one-stop venue for consulting fellow leaders and “consolidate our status as ‘the most European of non-European countries.’”
Both those options also risk the wrath of a United States, which has been critical of Europe and sought greater influence and control over its geographical neighbours .
But if Canada is going to emerge from the U.S. trade war economically intact and fundamentally transformed, something more tangible than symbolism or geopolitical poetry is required.

With the North American border dispute escalating and Trump’s tariff damage looming, pressure is on to reach a new depth in the relationship with Europe in time for an annual Canada-EU meeting planned for October.
“We cannot have another summit … that just confirms that we love each other,” Joost Korte, the EU’s special envoy for Canada, told a committee of the European Parliament in the spring.
“It needs to go a bit deeper … and we need to come up with concrete things. Otherwise, we’ve failed, yes, absolutely.”
Expectations are building, and Carney stoked the fire last month when he promised “intense discussions” to deepen economic and security ties with Europe.
“We can build such unparalleled access because we’re trusted, because we’re reliable, and because we have what the world needs,” he said.

This fall, the two sides hope to finalize a digital trade agreement that could touch on everything from online commerce, consumer protections and cybersecurity to the regulation of artificial intelligence.

After Canada was accepted into Europe’s defence procurement plan , there’s the possibility of deeper integration of the Canadian and European defence industries and having the Canadian Armed Forces participate more systematically in joint training missions with their European counterparts.
Officials could also announce Canada’s full participation in Erasmus Plus , a European travel-and-study program for university students.
But the whole of the emerging Canada-EU partnership is shaping up to be bigger than the sum of its parts, said Geneviève Tuts, the EU’s ambassador to Canada.

In an interview, she said there is no precedent for the new relationship that Ottawa and Brussels are forging — not in the partnership the 27-member bloc has with the United Kingdom, Norway, Switzerland or other non-member states.
“What is going to happen is quite unique. By that, I mean there is no existing integration model that we could simply mirror,” she said.
“We’re going to be creative and imaginative. There needs to be a name that best illustrates the depth of our relationship. I don’t think the word exists yet.”
Whatever it ends up being called, it looks set to respond to the calls of veteran Canada-EU observers.
“What I talk about is the need to stop looking at Europe as a transactional partner, but really look at it as a long-term partner, as a strategic partner,” said Camilleri.

“The relationship has, for a long time, been nice to have, but not a must-have. I think it’s definitely moved into that must-have territory in order to reach the objectives and the ambitions that the current government has expressed, and which seems to be what the Canadian population wants as well.”
It’s not just Canada that needs Europe as an alternative for goods normally sold south of the border.

The Russia-Ukraine war and the blockage in the Strait of Hormuz has exposed Europe’s reliance on oil and gas from uncertain parts of the world and the need to accelerate the transition to lower-emission energy sources.

Javier Moreno Sanchez, a Spanish member of the European Parliament and chair of its committee on Canada-EU relations, likened Canada on the global stage to “a good student who behaves well and, because of that, has often been overlooked.
“You forget them because they’re not a problem,” he said.
But in a more turbulent, chaotic and unpredictable world, that stability and reliability is cherished, as are Canada’s vast natural riches.

“Canada has a wealth of energy resources and of critical minerals,” Korte told European parliamentarians, explaining how he had toured the country, met with officials and determined what aspects of the Canada-EU relationship hold the most promise.

“They have the stuff that we need, and so that would be a no-brainer to co-operate much more, particularly on the critical minerals,” he said. “But of course it needs to be taken out of the ground, and then it needs to come to Europe.”

Korte noted that the Carney government, with the creation of its Major Projects Office to fast-track key infrastructure construction, was serious about doubling down on Europe. But he warned, “We need to give the guarantee that these investments will pay off.”

A key indicator of Europe’s interest in developing and securing Canada’s critical minerals will come at an investment summit in Toronto on Sept. 14 and 15. Carney has set a goal of securing $1 trillion of foreign investment.

Achim Hurrelmann, a Carleton University politics professor and co-director of the school’s Centre for European Studies, said the Canada-U.S. trade war might scare off those who would invest in Canada to secure access to U.S. markets.

“The hope that setting up a base in Canada to supply the United States has become much less realistic,” said Hurrelmann. “But that’s why there’s a much of a focus on strategic raw materials, where it’s really the European interest to secure these materials to be less dependent on China.”
Already, the European Investment Bank has shown an interest in expanding into Canada with the signing last spring of a letter of intent to explore future co-operation.
But the interest expressed by larger institutional investors is having a trickle-down effect, said Yvonne Denz, head of the Toronto-based Canadian German Chamber of Industry and Commerce.
“For a lot of these medium-sized companies in Germany that are family-owned, where there’s a family office that’s taking care of the investments, Canada is … somewhat of a safe haven,” she said.
“If you look at it from a European perspective, as a country like Germany with very few resources and neighbours close by that are not always your friendly … Canada seems very, very stable.”
The forging of closer ties between Canada and Europe is a rush toward certainty.
It is, said Denz, “a signal that even though it feels like the world is breaking up and splitting apart, you have these two blocs that are forging even closer relationships.”

stories.content:
One person is dead following a single-vehicle collision in Southwold Township.

Elgin County OPP and Middlesex-London Paramedic Service were called to John Wise Line shortly after 7:25 p.m. Friday for a report of a single-vehicle collision.

The driver was pronounced dead at the scene.

John Wise Line is closed between Begg Road and Middle River Road while the investigation continues.

stories.title: Mark Carney runs into backlash over push to build Canadian data centres
stories.summary: Carney and other government officials have also presented data centres as an opportunity to bolster Canada’s digital sovereignty.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
The data centre backlash that has gripped U.S. politics is spreading north, complicating Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to attract investment in the rapidly expanding artificial intelligence infrastructure.

In many respects, Canada is an alluring alternative for Silicon Valley firms: it has a cooler climate, abundant energy resources and plenty of open land. But a growing number of Canadian communities are looking to slam the brakes on server farm projects.

Two municipalities — Oakville, Ontario and Rocky View County, Alberta — have implemented one-year moratoriums on data centre developments. In the sparsely-populated province of Manitoba, Premier Wab Kinew vetoed a project that would have been built outside of Winnipeg, saying the drawbacks outweighed the benefits.

A huge 7.5 gigawatt proposal by Canadian entrepreneur and Shark Tank personality Kevin O’Leary has also sparked pushback, while protestors have marched against data centres proposed in Vancouver which have been championed by all levels of government.

The Canadian hesitancy mirrors the skepticism toward data centres that has led to hundreds of local bans in the U.S., as well as a statewide moratorium in New York. Supersized data centres are loud and energy-hungry, and many people are still not convinced about the benefits of AI the facilities are meant to support.

Carney and other government officials have also presented data centres as an opportunity to bolster the country’s digital sovereignty. But tech policy critics warn that efforts to store Canadians’ data domestically aren’t always a protection against U.S. influence, while the economic benefits of these projects May be more modest than some claim.

Although the number of local bans in Canada is limited for now, public polling suggests the hesitancy is more widespread. An Angus Reid Institute poll found 68% of respondents would oppose a large AI data centre near their home, while a survey by Leger found four in five respondents said they’re concerned about potential increases to electricity bills and environmental impacts.

Two of the three petitions with the most signatures gathered to submit to Canada’s House of Commons are calling for a stop to data centres. The left-wing New Democratic Party is calling for a nationwide pause.

“I don’t think their concerns are groundless, but I don’t think we can put the brakes on progress,” said Jim Balsillie, the former head of BlackBerry Ltd., who has become an outspoken advocate for Canadian technological sovereignty.

Canadian Advantage

Canada’s AI data centre expansion is still in its early stages, but it’s poised to ramp up fast. Recent research from Toronto’s York University shows there are only five operational hyperscale data centres, defined as 50 megawatts or above, but 159 more are announced or under construction. That push is also showing up in trade data: Canadian imports of U.S. goods hit a record high in June driven by a surge in the computer parts used for data centres.

The federal government argued in its AI strategy that Canada is “uniquely positioned to lead in building this infrastructure responsibly and sustainably.”

“As demand for AI compute grows, Canada’s approach will be to link new data centre development with clean energy expansion, robust environmental standards, and tangible benefits for local communities,” the document said.

Balsillie said the challenge with data centres is that, unlike other forms of capital investment, they don’t necessarily spur the same kind of economic benefits to people, while the negative spillovers can be material for communities.

“It’s a fine line between being strip-mined for low value-add, metaphorically, and capturing high value-added sovereign participation in this era of AI,” Balsillie said.

Carney’s government unveiled a framework on Thursday to help guide communities’ decisions on data centre development. It said such projects must create lasting local benefits, limit environmental impacts and ensure electricity costs are not pushed onto residents. Tech giants including Amazon.com Inc., Meta Platforms Inc. and Anthropic PBC signed on to the principles.

BCE Inc. Chief Executive Officer Mirko Bibic applauded the framework, which he said acknowledged the critical nature of AI infrastructure and the need for more domestic compute capacity.

“On the other hand, there’s an acknowledgement that while we do that, we need to engender trust amongst all stakeholders in the country — citizens, communities, investors,” Bibic said in an interview Friday on BNN Bloomberg.

Provincial governments are also trying to address concerns surrounding energy costs. British Columbia is restricting electric grid use for data centres and forcing operators to compete for access.

Energy-rich Alberta’s government has been particularly bullish about data centres and attracted the bulk of Canada’s proposals. Nonetheless, it’s stipulated operators must supply their own power. The province will be home to a $13-billion Meta data centre, set to be the largest in the country.

Even so, an analysis by the Pembina Institute suggested Albertans could see their electricity bills rise by as much as $460 per year, because the centres would be allowed to connect to the grid before their own generation comes online. The Brookings Institute found data centres create a modest amount of jobs and workers see no wage gain, while home prices tend to rise by 2-5% in communities that harbor the infrastructure.

“Canada has always been seduced by this promise of jobs, and we’ve given away a lot historically in the past in order to get jobs here. And data centres don’t really have that promise,” said Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute, a public policy think tank.

Federal and provincial officials have also pitched data centres as a necessity to bolster Canada’s sovereignty at a time when tensions are high with the U.S.

“Ontario has a choice: we can build the economy of the future and ensure Canadians’ data stays in Canada and out of President Trump’s hands, or we can get left behind and risk Canadians’ data being sent down to the U.S.,” Premier Doug Ford said in August.

But Balsillie said holding Canadians’ data domestically doesn’t necessarily protect it from the Trump administration. Under the Cloud Act, U.S. law enforcement can compel American tech companies to hand over electronic data, regardless of where it is stored.

“It’s not sovereign if you haven’t got sovereign governance,” he said.

The Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement, signed in 2020, also blocks some restrictions on cross-border information transfers.

paragraphs: The data centre backlash that has gripped U.S. politics is spreading north, complicating Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to attract investment in the rapidly expanding artificial intelligence infrastructure.

In many respects, Canada is an alluring alternative for Silicon Valley firms: it has a cooler climate, abundant energy resources and plenty of open land. But a growing number of Canadian communities are looking to slam the brakes on server farm projects.

Two municipalities — Oakville, Ontario and Rocky View County, Alberta — have implemented one-year moratoriums on data centre developments. In the sparsely-populated province of Manitoba, Premier Wab Kinew vetoed a project that would have been built outside of Winnipeg, saying the drawbacks outweighed the benefits.

A huge 7.5 gigawatt proposal by Canadian entrepreneur and Shark Tank personality Kevin O’Leary has also sparked pushback, while protestors have marched against data centres proposed in Vancouver which have been championed by all levels of government.

The Canadian hesitancy mirrors the skepticism toward data centres that has led to hundreds of local bans in the U.S., as well as a statewide moratorium in New York. Supersized data centres are loud and energy-hungry, and many people are still not convinced about the benefits of AI the facilities are meant to support.

Carney and other government officials have also presented data centres as an opportunity to bolster the country’s digital sovereignty. But tech policy critics warn that efforts to store Canadians’ data domestically aren’t always a protection against U.S. influence, while the economic benefits of these projects May be more modest than some claim.

Although the number of local bans in Canada is limited for now, public polling suggests the hesitancy is more widespread. An Angus Reid Institute poll found 68% of respondents would oppose a large AI data centre near their home, while a survey by Leger found four in five respondents said they’re concerned about potential increases to electricity bills and environmental impacts.

Two of the three petitions with the most signatures gathered to submit to Canada’s House of Commons are calling for a stop to data centres. The left-wing New Democratic Party is calling for a nationwide pause.

“I don’t think their concerns are groundless, but I don’t think we can put the brakes on progress,” said Jim Balsillie, the former head of BlackBerry Ltd., who has become an outspoken advocate for Canadian technological sovereignty.
Canadian Advantage

Canada’s AI data centre expansion is still in its early stages, but it’s poised to ramp up fast. Recent research from Toronto’s York University shows there are only five operational hyperscale data centres, defined as 50 megawatts or above, but 159 more are announced or under construction. That push is also showing up in trade data: Canadian imports of U.S. goods hit a record high in June driven by a surge in the computer parts used for data centres.
The federal government argued in its AI strategy that Canada is “uniquely positioned to lead in building this infrastructure responsibly and sustainably.”

“As demand for AI compute grows, Canada’s approach will be to link new data centre development with clean energy expansion, robust environmental standards, and tangible benefits for local communities,” the document said.

Balsillie said the challenge with data centres is that, unlike other forms of capital investment, they don’t necessarily spur the same kind of economic benefits to people, while the negative spillovers can be material for communities.
“It’s a fine line between being strip-mined for low value-add, metaphorically, and capturing high value-added sovereign participation in this era of AI,” Balsillie said.

Carney’s government unveiled a framework on Thursday to help guide communities’ decisions on data centre development. It said such projects must create lasting local benefits, limit environmental impacts and ensure electricity costs are not pushed onto residents. Tech giants including Amazon.com Inc., Meta Platforms Inc. and Anthropic PBC signed on to the principles.
BCE Inc. Chief Executive Officer Mirko Bibic applauded the framework, which he said acknowledged the critical nature of AI infrastructure and the need for more domestic compute capacity.

“On the other hand, there’s an acknowledgement that while we do that, we need to engender trust amongst all stakeholders in the country — citizens, communities, investors,” Bibic said in an interview Friday on BNN Bloomberg.
Provincial governments are also trying to address concerns surrounding energy costs. British Columbia is restricting electric grid use for data centres and forcing operators to compete for access.

Energy-rich Alberta’s government has been particularly bullish about data centres and attracted the bulk of Canada’s proposals. Nonetheless, it’s stipulated operators must supply their own power. The province will be home to a $13-billion Meta data centre, set to be the largest in the country.

Even so, an analysis by the Pembina Institute suggested Albertans could see their electricity bills rise by as much as $460 per year, because the centres would be allowed to connect to the grid before their own generation comes online. The Brookings Institute found data centres create a modest amount of jobs and workers see no wage gain, while home prices tend to rise by 2-5% in communities that harbor the infrastructure.

“Canada has always been seduced by this promise of jobs, and we’ve given away a lot historically in the past in order to get jobs here. And data centres don’t really have that promise,” said Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute, a public policy think tank.
Federal and provincial officials have also pitched data centres as a necessity to bolster Canada’s sovereignty at a time when tensions are high with the U.S.

“Ontario has a choice: we can build the economy of the future and ensure Canadians’ data stays in Canada and out of President Trump’s hands, or we can get left behind and risk Canadians’ data being sent down to the U.S.,” Premier Doug Ford said in August.

But Balsillie said holding Canadians’ data domestically doesn’t necessarily protect it from the Trump administration. Under the Cloud Act, U.S. law enforcement can compel American tech companies to hand over electronic data, regardless of where it is stored.
“It’s not sovereign if you haven’t got sovereign governance,” he said.
The Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement, signed in 2020, also blocks some restrictions on cross-border information transfers.

That complication applies to the supply chain, too. Balsillie argued that CoreWeave Inc., a New Jersey-based company, is in line to receive a portion of federal funding for “sovereign” computing infrastructure, awarded to Cohere Inc., a Canadian AI company. The government declined to comment and CoreWeave didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Cohere spokeswoman Amanda Taggart said: “Training frontier models requires highly specialized infrastructure, and at the time no Canadian vendor had the experience, timelines or chipsets required to train large language models from scratch at this scale. Those capabilities are still developing in Canada, and we want to help build them. That effort is already underway, and we look forward to sharing more soon. In the meantime, we are working with partners from across the world in order to continue our growth and build a generational AI company from Canada.”

Patrick Searle, the head of the Council of Canadian Innovators, which represents tech CEOs in the country, said in a statement that there are “active conversations ongoing between government and industry exploring how to build digital infrastructure in a way that responds to public concerns.”

“At the same time, this is increasingly an issue of economic sovereignty,” he added. “As compute becomes increasingly important to our economy, national security and competitiveness, Canada needs sufficient infrastructure and technological capacity here at home.”

stories.title: Hiker Stanislav Volo, missing for five days in B.C., is found alive
stories.summary: Sea to Sky RCMP said Volo was taken to hospital with minor injuries
stories.content:
A hiker missing for five days in mountainous terrain near Squamish, B.C., has been found alive, walking himself to safety after a massive search.

Squamish Search and Rescue shared a photo of Stanislav Volo, 43, smiling broadly and giving a thumbs-up with two overjoyed rescuers.

“After several long days of searching, we are incredibly relieved to share that Stanislav has been found alive and is safe,” the organization said in a social media post late Friday.

It said Volo walked out himself and was found on the Indian Arm forest service road.

Sea to Sky RCMP said Volo was taken to hospital with minor injuries.

The Mounties said partners in the search included RCMP Integrated Police Dog Services, Squamish Search and Rescue, RCMP Lower Mainland Emergency Response Team, RCMP Air Services and the Sea to Sky Gondola team.

Volo had last been seen getting off the Sea to Sky Gondola at 11:33 a.m. on Sunday, aiming to hike to the challenging Mount Habrich Loop.

But he had been missing since failing to catch the gondola back down that day.

The search narrowed on Tuesday after a 911 call was made from Volo’s cellphone.

While Sue Nicholson with the Squamish Search and Rescue said the call was garbled and dropped out, it led rescuers to believe that he was still in the Mount Habrich Loop area.

Volo’s sister Ola pleaded on social media this week for help from other hikers who might have crossed paths with him.

But Squamish Search and Rescue warned the public on Thursday not to enter the Habrich area on their own after noticing messages about the search were being widely shared.

On Friday, it had better news to share.

“We know so many people across Squamish, the Sea to Sky, and beyond have been following his story, sharing our posts, sending messages and hoping alongside his family,” the organization said on social media. “Today, we get to share the news we’ve all been waiting for.”

stories.title: Toronto police announce arrest in arson that damaged MP’s vehicle
stories.summary: Threatening behaviour toward politicians in general has been on the rise in recent years
stories.author: Matthew Frank
stories.content:
Toronto police have arrested and charged one suspect and are searching for another for allegedly setting multiple cars on fire outside an east Toronto MP’s home.

In the early morning on Aug. 27, a suspect allegedly poured gas on vehicles parked outside the home of Liberal MP Salma Zahid in the Scarborough area of Toronto and set two on fire, damaging a third car, police said in a Friday news release.

The level of threats and abuse faced by MPs across all parties has spiked in recent years.

Police and firefighters responded to a 1:21 a.m. call about the fires, they said. No injuries were reported.

Roshvin Crofton, 24, was arrested on Aug. 30 and faces five charges, including arson causing to property and mischief over $5,000, Toronto police said in a news release. Investigators are still searching for another suspect in the alleged arson and are looking for any information involving a black 2025 Hyundai Sonata between Aug. 23 and Aug. 27, police said.

Ms. Zahid said in a statement that she welcomes both the arrest and news that police are seeking another person connected to the case. The investigation is ongoing and there’s no information on a motive, she said.

“With the support of my colleagues and with the guidance of security professionals, I will continue my work representing the people of Scarborough Centre-Don Valley East and I look forward to returning to Ottawa when the House of Commons resumes sitting later this month,” she said.

Ms. Zahid, who represents the riding of Scarborough Centre-Don Valley East, was first elected in 2015.

It’s the second time in nearly two years that a vehicle was allegedly set ablaze in front of a home on Ms. Zahid’s street. The 2024 case, which occurred outside an address a few houses away from the MP’s, is still being investigated, police said.

Both Prime Minister Mark Carney and federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre previously condemned the alleged arson in August.

Sergeant-at-Arms Patrick McDonell previously told a House of Commons standing committee that the number of security files his office opened on threatening behaviour towards MPs climbed from eight in 2019 to 530 in 2023. Threats and harassment against federal politicians also increased by 700 per cent in the same time frame, he said in 2024.

Female MPs in particular have been targeted with abuse and death threats .

In 2022, a man approached and aggressively harassed former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland in rural Alberta, and called her a traitor who should leave the province.

Liberal MP Iqra Khalid, who represents Mississauga-Erin Mills, said in 2024 that people have spat at her and made threats against her life. Members of a right-wing extremist organization had stalked her office and shared her address, she said, as well as videotaped her as she walked around her community.

Former environment minister Catherine McKenna spoke out when she was in office about the threats and harassment she received, which led her to request additional security.

RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme has suggested the federal government draft new laws that make it easier to charge people who threaten elected officials.

Internal RCMP documents from 2024 warned protecting parliamentarians and other public figures put a “significant strain” on personnel.

RCMP estimates from 2025 said the number of threats against public officials across the country increased from approximately 1,300 in 2022 to 2,600 in 2023 and was projected to exceed 3,500 in 2024.

Both Prime Minister Mark Carney and federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre previously condemned the alleged arson in August.

Sergeant-at-Arms Patrick McDonell previously told a House of Commons standing committee that the number of security files his office opened on threatening behaviour towards MPs climbed from eight in 2019 to 530 in 2023. Threats and harassment against federal politicians also increased by 700 per cent in the same time frame, he said in 2024.
Female MPs in particular have been targeted with abuse and death threats .
In 2022, a man approached and aggressively harassed former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland in rural Alberta, and called her a traitor who should leave the province.

Liberal MP Iqra Khalid, who represents Mississauga-Erin Mills, said in 2024 that people have spat at her and made threats against her life. Members of a right-wing extremist organization had stalked her office and shared her address, she said, as well as videotaped her as she walked around her community.
Former environment minister Catherine McKenna spoke out when she was in office about the threats and harassment she received, which led her to request additional security.
RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme has suggested the federal government draft new laws that make it easier to charge people who threaten elected officials.
Internal RCMP documents from 2024 warned protecting parliamentarians and other public figures put a “significant strain” on personnel.
RCMP estimates from 2025 said the number of threats against public officials across the country increased from approximately 1,300 in 2022 to 2,600 in 2023 and was projected to exceed 3,500 in 2024.

stories.title: ‘Targeting’ and ‘intimidation’: Council candidates undeterred by razor-slashed campaign signs
stories.summary: A pair of candidates running for seats on London City Council independently contacted CTV News about threatening tactics used to destroy some of their campaign signs.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A pair of candidates running for seats on London City Council independently contacted CTV News about threatening tactics used to destroy some of their campaign signs.

Ward 13 candidate Andrew Crook kept some of his signs that were slashed to pieces using a razor blade or knife.

“Actually bringing a weapon to damage them, and especially when it’s a long chain of signs, not just one sign, but multiple signs in a row, it’s clearly somebody who’s targeting,” Crook said.

He had a total of 15 signs damaged last weekend, including several with a blade.

Although Crook’s signs humorously read “A name that demands honesty”, he says the impact to his campaign is no laughing matter.

“Fifty bucks a sign is typically what it runs, so it adds up pretty quickly,” he explained. “And that’s not to mention the stress and having to go out and (replace) it.”

Ward 12 candidate Ribal Zebian also had some of his signs slashed since the nomination period closed. “One small one was cut up, and two large signs were cut up. We have a total of 13 lost signs,” he said.

He believes the use of a blade goes beyond vandalism, and was intended to be a threat.

“It’s a form of intimidation,” he said. “The individuals who are doing this are trying to intimidate my campaign, trying to make us get (off) the ballot.”

Undeterred, both candidates remain committed to campaigning for a seat on council.

“It hurts. It hurts because these are things that in a democratic country, you would assume these things wouldn’t be happening,” Zebian added.

“This is our democracy, and ultimately, I think it’s important that we respect the people putting their names out there,” Crook said. “You don’t have to agree with me, you don’t have to support me, but don’t devastate (my) signs.”

According to Deputy City Clerk Sarah Corman, “The City of London addresses concerns and complaints related to election sign placement, size, timing, and other requirements under the Election Sign By-law. Any concerns about theft or destruction of election signs should be forwarded to the London Police Service, as vandalism or mischief falls under the Criminal Code.”

Election Day is Oct. 26.

stories.title: Town of Gander urges calm as Pete Hoekstra’s planned visit for 9/11 anniversary angers locals
stories.summary: U.S. Ambassador says he is returning on Sept. 11 to honour enduring bond with the place that famously welcomed and sheltered American passengers
stories.author: Lindsay Jones
stories.content:
A week before U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra is set to give remarks in Gander to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, the Newfoundland town that became famous for its kindness on that day addressed growing community anger about his attendance.

“We understand why people feel strongly about this,” said a statement from the town released Friday afternoon. “We are proud Canadians, and we understand the frustration and disappointment many Canadians are feeling about the current state of the relationship between Canada and the United States.”

As the terrorist attacks were unfolding on Sept. 11, 2001, 38 planes carrying thousands of passengers were diverted to Gander. The town famously stepped up, with locals opening up their homes, setting up shelters and providing meals and medication to the stranded passengers, many of whom were American. They formed lifelong bonds and connections that are emotionally depicted in the immensely popular Broadway musical Come From Away . Gander’s kindness, a symbol of co-operation between the Canada and the U.S., has also been immortalized in a new Heritage Minute , released this week.

But anti-American tension has ratcheted up in recent weeks with U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada, his order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America and the slew of trolling memes coming out of the White House. This week, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posted on social media a screenshot of a young Canadian cadet and her instructor at the end of summer training camp, mocking them with the words “this is real,” raising the ire of people across the country.

Mr. Hoekstra himself has faced fierce backlash for months, after saying earlier in the year that annexing Canada as the 51st state would be a great topic of discussion for Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mr. Trump. A House of Commons petition signed by more than 260,000 Canadians calling for his removal remains active.

Mr. Hoekstra’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Earlier this week Mr. Hoekstra said in a statement that he is returning to Gander on the 9/11 anniversary to say thank you and to honour the enduring bond.

Mr. Hoekstra is hosting a breakfast for volunteers and attending a commemoration service in Gander where he’s speaking on friendship and connection.

Plans for his attendance have triggered controversy and emotion in the community and on social media, said Mayor Percy Farwell in an interview with The Globe and Mail prior to the town’s statement.

“There is a certain delicacy to the timing this year,” he said, referring to Mr. Trump’s trade war. “This story does transcend that.”

“Administrations come and go and ambassadors come and go but at the end of the day we have a lasting relationship.”

The town explained in its statement that it followed the appropriate protocol when planning the commemoration by extending invitations to government and diplomatic representatives, adding that this doesn’t mean the town endorses “any individual, their comments or their political views.”

In his interview, Mr. Farwell asked that the focus of the commemoration be about people, the close to 3,000 people who lost their lives on 9/11 and the acts of humanity in Gander, not politics.

Meanwhile, the popular national satire publication The Beaverton had already re-written the script with a post titled “Come from Away sequel will see Newfoundlanders put the friggin’ boots to Pete Hoekstra.”

stories.title: As glaciers melt near mountains, risks multiply and Canada isn’t prepared, scientists warn
stories.summary: The Himalayan disaster that led to flooding in Nepal is a cautionary tale about the climate crisis
stories.author: Om Shanbhag
stories.content:
Six years ago, a rapidly retreating glacier in the southern Coast Mountains of British Columbia shrunk away from the base of the nearby mountainside causing millions of tonnes of rock to fall.

The Elliot Creek landslide , with a mass similar to that of all Canadian automobiles combined, landed in an alpine lake, creating a tsunami and draining the lake. The displaced water flooded a nearby fjord, destroying kilometres of salmon habitat and scouring nearby forest.

According to a 2022 study , despite detecting the resulting seismic event, its location remained unknown until forestry workers found the site two weeks later.

In the remote valleys of the Coast Mountains, the tsunami and flooding caused no structural damage or fatalities. But its root cause appears to be similar to the landslide behind the Aug. 26 floods in Nepal , which have claimed the lives of more than 1,250 people.

As the Himalayan glacier thinned and retreated, geologists believe the removal of ice could have caused the high-altitude landslide.

But in both the Himalayas and Canada, scientists don’t know where the next such event will happen.

The effects of climate change are creating evolving risks in high mountain regions, Daniel Shugar, a geomorphologist and associate professor at the University of Calgary, said.

“With glaciers, they’re changing so quickly that the hazard – and therefore the risk – is not the same now as it was five years ago or in five years’ time from now,” Prof. Shugar said.

Climate change is leading to conditions that can destabilize high-mountain rock and ice, strengthening prospects for disasters such as the Himalayan flood along the border between Nepal and China's Tibet, scientists say, while warning climate change May not be sole trigger.

Glaciers are receding and thinning at an unprecedented rate, with glaciers in Western Canada expected to largely disappear by the end of the century, according to a report released by Environment and Climate Change Canada this week.

The report expects the number and severity of floods and landslides to increase as glacier ice melts, even if carbon dioxide emissions reach net-zero. The Paris Agreement established a global goal to reach net zero by 2050.

“Even if we did turn off the taps today, we have a lot of global warming that’s already built into the system, baked in, and so we are going to see these impacts,” Prof. Shugar said.

Between 2021 and 2024, glaciers in Western Canada lost 12 per cent of their volume, melting twice as fast as they did in the last decade, according to a study co-authored by Prof. Shugar, Brian Menounos, Hakai affiliate and geography professor at the University of Northern British Columbia and others.

“It’s clear that our high mountains are changing rapidly, and it really does call for a combined systematic effort to monitor these high elevations,” Prof. Menounos said. However, risk mapping and management is often only completed after a disaster happens.

“Sadly, in many cases, we use a whack-a-mole approach,” he said.

Jeffrey Crompton, a researcher at the Geological Survey of Canada, is in the early stages of creating a monitoring system which would identify the greatest hazards and the risks they pose to people and infrastructure.

“It’s a huge problem, and we need a lot more resources than we currently have to be able to get at it,” he said.

Luck has saved many Canadians from alpine disaster, Dr. Crompton said. Despite Canada not having the same densely populated river valleys as in the Himalayas, several large landslide events in North America could have led to tragedies.

Last year in Tracy Arm, an Alaskan fjord, a landslide event , similar to the Elliot Creek event occurred. As the South Sawyer glacier lost ice, it exposed a cliff face that soon gave way, displacing enough water to cause a tsunami. Tracy Arm sees a lot of marine traffic, with tour boats and cruise ships frequently operating in the fjord. Happenstance meant few boaters were near the landslide when it happened.

Other events have also come close to tourist areas and mining communities, such as northern B.C.’s Canoe Glacier landslide in 2021, and have posed threats to infrastructure, such as highways, pipelines and power lines.

“Back to back to back, all of these very large events [are] happening, and they all kind of follow this common theme of happening in these mountainous regions where there’s rapid deglaciation,” Dr. Crompton said.

Glaciers in the Arctic are also melting at a rapid pace, increasing the threat of disaster in the region. As shipping increases through the north, the area could be the next frontier for these hazardous events, Prof. Shugar said.

“We’re starting to see really, really big [landslides], and that’s a concern, and that’s something that I think we as a scientific community, but also we as a society, need to be paying attention to as we consider development in mountain environments,” Prof. Shugar said.

Switzerland and Norway both have risk mitigation systems, which allow the two countries to monitor for hazards and keep communities safe in alpine locations and fjords, Prof. Shugar said.

“We in Canada have nothing like that,” Prof. Shugar said. “We don’t even know where the unstable slopes are, let alone knowing which ones might collapse.”
paragraphs: Six years ago, a rapidly retreating glacier in the southern Coast Mountains of British Columbia shrunk away from the base of the nearby mountainside causing millions of tonnes of rock to fall.

The Elliot Creek landslide , with a mass similar to that of all Canadian automobiles combined, landed in an alpine lake, creating a tsunami and draining the lake. The displaced water flooded a nearby fjord, destroying kilometres of salmon habitat and scouring nearby forest.
According to a 2022 study , despite detecting the resulting seismic event, its location remained unknown until forestry workers found the site two weeks later.

In the remote valleys of the Coast Mountains, the tsunami and flooding caused no structural damage or fatalities. But its root cause appears to be similar to the landslide behind the Aug. 26 floods in Nepal , which have claimed the lives of more than 1,250 people.
As the Himalayan glacier thinned and retreated, geologists believe the removal of ice could have caused the high-altitude landslide.
But in both the Himalayas and Canada, scientists don’t know where the next such event will happen.
The effects of climate change are creating evolving risks in high mountain regions, Daniel Shugar, a geomorphologist and associate professor at the University of Calgary, said.
“With glaciers, they’re changing so quickly that the hazard – and therefore the risk – is not the same now as it was five years ago or in five years’ time from now,” Prof. Shugar said.

Climate change is leading to conditions that can destabilize high-mountain rock and ice, strengthening prospects for disasters such as the Himalayan flood along the border between Nepal and China's Tibet, scientists say, while warning climate change May not be sole trigger.

Glaciers are receding and thinning at an unprecedented rate, with glaciers in Western Canada expected to largely disappear by the end of the century, according to a report released by Environment and Climate Change Canada this week.

The report expects the number and severity of floods and landslides to increase as glacier ice melts, even if carbon dioxide emissions reach net-zero. The Paris Agreement established a global goal to reach net zero by 2050.
“Even if we did turn off the taps today, we have a lot of global warming that’s already built into the system, baked in, and so we are going to see these impacts,” Prof. Shugar said.

“It’s clear that our high mountains are changing rapidly, and it really does call for a combined systematic effort to monitor these high elevations,” Prof. Menounos said. However, risk mapping and management is often only completed after a disaster happens.
“Sadly, in many cases, we use a whack-a-mole approach,” he said.
