stories.title: The Globe and Mail wins two Online Journalism Awards
stories.summary: Journalists honoured for stories about the first professional football player to come out as transgender and an experimental brain surgery
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
The Globe and Mail has won two Online Journalism Awards, one for a feature about the first professional football player to come out as transgender, and the other for a personal story about an experimental brain surgery.

Jana G. Pruden’s piece, titled Her turn to play , won in the category of Topical Reporting: Gender and Identity, Large Newsroom.

The piece profiled Maven Maurer, who as Mike Maurer was a Grey Cup winner and MMA fighter. The story gave readers an intimate view into Maven’s journey – her fears, her vulnerabilities and, ultimately, her courage.

Anna Mehler Paperny’s essay, titled Holes in my head, wires in my brain , won in the Personal Narrative category. The piece used illustration, animation and video to bring readers inside Ms. Paperny’s experience with deep brain stimulation to treat her chronic depression.

Digital storytelling editor Laura Blenkinsop and a team including Timothy Moore, Mark Medley, John Sopinski and Bryan Gee contributed to the piece.

The Globe and Mail was also named a finalist in three other categories.

The Globe’s coverage of the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., in February was nominated for Breaking News, Large Newsroom. The Globe mobilized a large team of reporters to Tumbler Ridge and in bureaus across the country after an 18-year-old shot and killed eight people, including five children at the town’s school, before killing herself. It was one of the country’s deadliest mass shootings.

Jennifer Yang, Melissa Tait and Timothy Moore were named finalists in two categories – Excellence in Science Reporting, Large Newsroom, and Feature, Large Newsroom – for The two halves of Maryam .

The piece told the story of Maryam Fatima, a baby who developed catastrophic seizures and whose doctors proposed a treatment that would destroy half her brain to save her life. The piece offered both an intimate portrait of a family’s agonizing decision and also a deeply reported look at the science behind the procedure.

The awards are run by the Online News Association and recognize excellence in digital journalism around the world. The winners will be honoured at a ceremony in New York on Oct. 1.

stories.title: Randolph College for the Performing Arts ordered to cease operations
stories.summary: A restraining order was issued against the school by the Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, ordering it to cease operations
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Randolph College for the Performing Arts, a postsecondary theatre school that lost its accreditation in February, has been issued a restraining order by the provincial government requiring the school to cease operations as a career college.

Last week, the school told The Globe and Mail that it had filed an application with the Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security to reinstate its status as a college. But on Aug. 31, the ministry issued its restraining order against Randolph for contravening the Ontario Career Colleges Act. A notice on the ministry’s website said the school can no longer advertise itself as a career college, offer vocational programs or charge fees for such programming.

Randolph, which until February had 86 students enrolled, operated as an unregistered career college after its accreditation expired on Feb. 1, according to the restraining order . When asked why the school’s accreditation had lapsed, founder George Randolph told The Globe it had switched auditing companies, “which took longer than anticipated.” (Randolph, who in 2017 formally resigned from the school after an independent investigator found that he had engaged in “unwelcome comments and physical gestures,” has served as vice-chair of the school’s board since 2019.)

The ministry said in its restraining order that the college offered and advertised unapproved vocational programs between Feb. 1 and Aug. 28, and collected tuition fees from students enrolled in the unapproved courses.

Randolph’s tuition was $13,710 per academic year for a program that condensed three academic years into two calendar years of study, for a total program cost of $41,130 per student.

Failure to comply with the actions of the restraining order could result in fines of up to $250,000.

In an e-mailed statement to The Globe on Sept. 1, Randolph, the founder, said the college is reviewing the matters raised by the ministry with legal counsel. He declined to answer specific questions about the college’s finances and personnel, citing the “ongoing regulatory process.”

Former students affected by the closing of the school have been provided two options by the ministry: They can either work with the province to find a new program to finish their studies, or they can receive a partial refund for fees paid to Randolph.

In e-mails sent to faculty and students on Aug. 31, Randolph’s board said the school would begin winding down the remaining administrative, student, employment and regulatory obligations for its diploma program.

Randolph Kids, a popular program for students aged three to 17 that included dance, acting and singing classes, has also closed. However, the children’s program will resume operations this fall under the umbrella of the Canadian Centre for Arts Education and Innovation, a new not-for-profit business incorporated in April.

On Tuesday evening, O’neil Edwards, listed on Randolph’s website as its executive director until Aug. 20, told parents at an informational Zoom meeting that the new centre’s programming will continue in the former Randolph space at 730 Bathurst Street.

In a June 12 e-mail to a parent of a Randolph College student, viewed by The Globe, ministry investigator Eric Joly said the college had not been allowed to charge or collect fees since its registration had expired on Feb. 1.

However, e-mails and bank records shared with The Globe this week show that in March, the school solicited and accepted thousands of dollars in tuition payments from students for college courses that had not yet been taught. In an Aug. 26 e-mailed statement to The Globe, the school’s founder said tuition received after Feb. 1 was related to instruction that had already been provided prior to the college’s loss of accreditation.

Lily Burden, who was scheduled to start her fourth term of Randolph instruction this fall, said her experience at the college was “wonderful” until February’s accreditation issue came to light. “The workload was a lot, but it was amazing,” she said. “I know I got at least some of an amazing education.”

Lily’s parents, Steve and Sarah Burden, who paid for their daughter’s tuition, similarly praised the program – especially for its industry connections. (Randolph alumni include Saturday Night Live cast member Veronika Slowikowska as well as actors Matt Raffy, Amaka Umeh and Paul Nolan.)

But the Burden family became concerned when the June 12 e-mail from Joly informed them they shouldn’t be paying tuition to the school. A Feb. 26 e-mail to the Burdens from Randolph’s finance administrator said it was “perfectly fine” to proceed with payment for Lily’s second year.

“That was the first notification we got from any government ministry,” Steve said about the June e-mail. Students had been informed by the school of the accreditation issue in February, Lily said, and were told that as a result, the school would pivot its course offerings to nongraded workshops.

“It’s a huge loss,” Sarah said, pointing out that between Randolph’s two unaccredited terms and its cancelled fall term, her daughter has lost a full calendar year of education. “She should be graduating next year. Now we don’t know when she’ll graduate.”

In an e-mailed statement to The Globe on Sept. 1, Randolph, the founder, said the college is reviewing the matters raised by the ministry with legal counsel. He declined to answer specific questions about the college’s finances and personnel, citing the “ongoing regulatory process.”

Former students affected by the closing of the school have been provided two options by the ministry: They can either work with the province to find a new program to finish their studies, or they can receive a partial refund for fees paid to Randolph.

In e-mails sent to faculty and students on Aug. 31, Randolph’s board said the school would begin winding down the remaining administrative, student, employment and regulatory obligations for its diploma program.

Randolph Kids, a popular program for students aged three to 17 that included dance, acting and singing classes, has also closed. However, the children’s program will resume operations this fall under the umbrella of the Canadian Centre for Arts Education and Innovation, a new not-for-profit business incorporated in April.

On Tuesday evening, O’neil Edwards, listed on Randolph’s website as its executive director until Aug. 20, told parents at an informational Zoom meeting that the new centre’s programming will continue in the former Randolph space at 730 Bathurst Street.

In a June 12 e-mail to a parent of a Randolph College student, viewed by The Globe, ministry investigator Eric Joly said the college had not been allowed to charge or collect fees since its registration had expired on Feb. 1.

However, e-mails and bank records shared with The Globe this week show that in March, the school solicited and accepted thousands of dollars in tuition payments from students for college courses that had not yet been taught. In an Aug. 26 e-mailed statement to The Globe, the school’s founder said tuition received after Feb. 1 was related to instruction that had already been provided prior to the college’s loss of accreditation.

Lily Burden, who was scheduled to start her fourth term of Randolph instruction this fall, said her experience at the college was “wonderful” until February’s accreditation issue came to light. “The workload was a lot, but it was amazing,” she said. “I know I got at least some of an amazing education.”

Lily’s parents, Steve and Sarah Burden, who paid for their daughter’s tuition, similarly praised the program – especially for its industry connections. (Randolph alumni include Saturday Night Live cast member Veronika Slowikowska as well as actors Matt Raffy, Amaka Umeh and Paul Nolan.)

But the Burden family became concerned when the June 12 e-mail from Joly informed them they shouldn’t be paying tuition to the school. A Feb. 26 e-mail to the Burdens from Randolph’s finance administrator said it was “perfectly fine” to proceed with payment for Lily’s second year.

“That was the first notification we got from any government ministry,” Steve said about the June e-mail. Students had been informed by the school of the accreditation issue in February, Lily said, and were told that as a result, the school would pivot its course offerings to nongraded workshops.

“It’s a huge loss,” Sarah said, pointing out that between Randolph’s two unaccredited terms and its cancelled fall term, her daughter has lost a full calendar year of education. “She should be graduating next year. Now we don’t know when she’ll graduate.”

stories.title: Quebec will not administer free flu shots this fall
stories.summary: Quebec was the second province after Alberta to stop providing free COVID-19 vaccines to its population last year
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha, Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Quebec will no longer administer free flu shots for its entire population this fall, a year after it stopped providing COVID-19 vaccinations at no cost.

Other provinces, when reached by The Globe and Mail, said they are still maintaining their flu shot coverage, typically offering the vaccine for free to everyone six months of age and older.

The Quebec Health Department said its decision relied on the guidance of the province’s immunization committee, an independent advisory panel also known by its French abbreviation, CIQ.

“In recent years, particularly during the pandemic, the decision was made to offer free vaccination to everyone. This year marks a change so that the vaccination program reflects the recommendations of the CIQ,” department spokesman Émile Giard said in an e-mail.

In an 11-page interim scientific opinion released in April, CIQ recommended that Quebec harmonize the criteria for its flu and COVID-19 vaccination programs.

“There is an interest in synchronizing the vaccination campaigns against COVID-19 and against influenza during the fall to increase coverage, facilitate planning and reduce costs.”

The CIQ opinion noted that the benefits of vaccination against COVID-19 “for healthy people aged 65 to 74 are more limited.”

As a result, it suggested maintaining the previous year’s policy on offering COVID-19 shots for Quebeckers 75 and older, immunocompromised people and those living in remote locations, seniors’ homes and long-term care facilities.

Marilie Beaulieu-Gravel, a spokeswoman for an association representing pharmacy owners in Quebec, also known by its French acronym Aqpp, said it is too early to know how much its members would charge for a flu shot.

Quebec was the second province after Alberta to stop providing free COVID-19 vaccines to its population last year. Alberta limited coverage to specific high-risk and vulnerable populations, in addition to health care workers after union bargaining and widespread pushback.

The two provinces scaled back after the federal government decided in January, 2025, to stop funding provinces for the purchase of COVID-19 shots.

Alberta has since defended its approach to COVID-19 coverage as a way to reduce vaccine waste, but has also cited Quebec’s analysis as part of its reasoning. Roughly eight per cent of Alberta’s population was vaccinated against COVID-19 last season. Coverage was 14 per cent in 2024-25 when it was universally available.

The Western province has been tight-lipped on its 2026-27 vaccine campaign, but further details are expected to be released in the coming weeks.

However, ON Friday, Alberta’s Ministry of Primary and Preventative Health Services confirmed it has no plan to change its flu immunization program, meaning residents will still be able to access flu shots free of charge this season.

The ministry declined to answer questions from The Globe and Mail about COVID-19 coverage.

Canada’s National Advisory Committee on Immunization recommends that the seasonal flu vaccine should be offered annually to everyone six months of age and older who does not have a medical reason to avoid it. The committee said vaccination is “particularly important” for people at high risk of flu-related complications or hospitalization, including seniors and pregnant individuals.

For COVID-19 shots, Naci strongly recommends the vaccine be offered to high-risk individuals and that adults older than 80, long-term care home residents, moderate or severely immunocompromised individuals and adults 65 to 79 with underlying medical conditions receive a second dose per year. Everyone else May receive an annual vaccine.

In Saskatchewan, influenza and COVID-19 vaccines will continue to be provided free of charge to all residents six months and older. The same is true in Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Ontario and Manitoba.

The British Columbia Ministry of Health said free flu shots will be available to all residents six months and older, but it’s unclear who will be covered for COVID-19 shots. While COVID-19 vaccines will be available this fall, eligibility and immunization locations have yet to be announced.

The government website states: “If a COVID-19 vaccine is recommended for you, you will receive a notification.”

Similarly, Nova Scotia said that details of the full respiratory vaccine program, including COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, shots, will be announced in coming weeks.

stories.title: Bombers, Riders fans clash over ‘Regina-style’ pizza in Labour Day Classic trash talk
stories.summary: The Saskatchewan Roughriders will meet the Winnipeg Blue Bombers at Mosaic Stadium on Sunday. Ahead of the game, Riders and Bombers fans are duking it out over Regina-style pizza.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Annual trash talk between the Winnipeg Blue Bombers and Saskatchewan Roughriders, among the teams and their fandoms, is building ahead of Sunday’s Labour Day Classic.

This year, it’s all about the pizza.

In a social media post Tuesday, the Bombers reiterated its three-year-old statement that, “honestly, Regina-style pizza is terrible.”

After three years “reflecting” on the various “not kind” responses the team received from Riders fans, it said its opinion remains unchanged.

“It’s still terrible. Honestly, it’s worse than we ever thought. It’s like someone took a three-week old lasagna and slapped it on a piece of dough. It’s awful, and our opinion will never change,” the team posted.

Regina-style pizza is characterized by its square slices and gratuitous servings of toppings, including vegetables and meat, that are covered by cheese and are served atop a thick layer of crust.

Marina Rubina, a Regina resident, Riders fan and content creator, said when she saw the Blue Bombers’ post, she was angry and shocked. She took the trash talk as an opportunity to post a video showing what she thought was worth showcasing in Winnipeg.

In it, after extensively researching for 14 minutes, she concluded she “still couldn’t find a reason to go” to the Manitoban city. Upon that realization, she helped herself to a slice of pizza.

“You can come to Regina just to try the pizza. (Then,) it’s already worth it to make the trip,” she said, adding she loves the city’s pizza pie.

More than 570 kilometres west of Regina, in Winnipeg, Cassie Liebrecht, a lifelong Bombers fan, told Global News she found the Blue Bombers’ pizza post “hilarious.”

“I loved seeing that. There’s always such good humour attached to it, and I love seeing the rivalries. I love amping up the rivalries especially before big games like this. It just adds to the excitement,” Liebrecht said.

She said she had never heard of Regina-style pizza before the Bombers’ post, but Liebrecht is now following the topic ahead of Sunday’s game, which she will be watching from her cabin.

Scott Charney has supported the Blue since he was a child. He said he is also a fan of any, and all, pizza – including Regina-style.

“I’m a pizza guy so I like all pizza. I’m going to eat it regardless,” Charney said.

The Labour Day Classic is set to kick off at Mosaic Stadium on Sunday at 5 p.m. local time.

4:01 DT on the Bombers: Labour Day Classic
paragraphs: Annual trash talk between the Winnipeg Blue Bombers and Saskatchewan Roughriders, among the teams and their fandoms, is building ahead of Sunday’s Labour Day Classic.
This year, it’s all about the pizza.
In a social media post Tuesday, the Bombers reiterated its three-year-old statement that, “honestly, Regina-style pizza is terrible.”
After three years “reflecting” on the various “not kind” responses the team received from Riders fans, it said its opinion remains unchanged.

“It’s still terrible. Honestly, it’s worse than we ever thought. It’s like someone took a three-week old lasagna and slapped it on a piece of dough. It’s awful, and our opinion will never change,” the team posted.
Regina-style pizza is characterized by its square slices and gratuitous servings of toppings, including vegetables and meat, that are covered by cheese and are served atop a thick layer of crust.

Marina Rubina, a Regina resident, Riders fan and content creator, said when she saw the Blue Bombers’ post, she was angry and shocked. She took the trash talk as an opportunity to post a video showing what she thought was worth showcasing in Winnipeg.
In it, after extensively researching for 14 minutes, she concluded she “still couldn’t find a reason to go” to the Manitoban city. Upon that realization, she helped herself to a slice of pizza.
“You can come to Regina just to try the pizza. (Then,) it’s already worth it to make the trip,” she said, adding she loves the city’s pizza pie.
More than 570 kilometres west of Regina, in Winnipeg, Cassie Liebrecht, a lifelong Bombers fan, told Global News she found the Blue Bombers’ pizza post “hilarious.”

“I loved seeing that. There’s always such good humour attached to it, and I love seeing the rivalries. I love amping up the rivalries especially before big games like this. It just adds to the excitement,” Liebrecht said.
She said she had never heard of Regina-style pizza before the Bombers’ post, but Liebrecht is now following the topic ahead of Sunday’s game, which she will be watching from her cabin.
Scott Charney has supported the Blue since he was a child. He said he is also a fan of any, and all, pizza – including Regina-style.
“I’m a pizza guy so I like all pizza. I’m going to eat it regardless,” Charney said.
The Labour Day Classic is set to kick off at Mosaic Stadium on Sunday at 5 p.m. local time.

The Roughriders are currently second in the CFL’s West Division, with a 7-4 record. Winnipeg is trailing with its 6-5 record, but the team is coming off a huge win against the league-leading Montreal Alouettes.

stories.title: Timeline of turmoil for B.C. Conservatives, with nine defections in three weeks
stories.summary: The B.C. Conservatives have been in a state of upheaval since former finance critic Peter Milobar quit the official Opposition caucus three weeks ago. The party has since suffered a parade of defections from legislators citing differences with Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay of strategy and ideology.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservatives have been in a state of upheaval since former finance critic Peter Milobar quit the official Opposition caucus three weeks ago. The party has since suffered a parade of defections from legislators citing differences with Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay of strategy and ideology.

Here’s a timeline of the turmoil.

Aug. 14: Milobar (Kamloops Centre) quits the caucus, citing a lack of “ideological alignment” with Findlay. Milobar, a former leadership contender and finance critic for the Opposition, had clashed with Findlay in a debate when she accused him of having a conflict of interest because Milobar’s Indigenous wife once held paid positions with the local Indigenous band.

Aug. 22: Reann Gasper (Abbotsford-Mission) resigns her seat so Findlay can run in a byelection. Gasper is appointed Findlay’s deputy chief of staff.

Aug. 24: Ian Paton (Delta South) quits the party, saying the Conservatives’ direction under Findlay no longer aligns with his beliefs and he intends to form a new party with Milobar. Milobar says at the announcement that he and Paton could be a party of two, but suggests there could be more defections.

Aug. 25: Rosalyn Bird (Prince George-Valemount) quits the Conservatives to sit as an Independent, issuing a statement warning about divisive leadership. She says legislators “should be able to firmly reject racism, antisemitism, homophobia and hatred while still having difficult and necessary conversations about immigration, Indigenous reconciliation, addiction, crime, gender, religion and the many other issues on which reasonable people sometimes disagree.”

Aug. 26: Teresa Wat (Richmond-Bridgeport) resigns to sit as an Independent on Aug. 26. She accuses Findlay of reneging on a promise to apologize over “serious and unfounded accusations” reportedly made by Findlay about Wat, calling her “CCP,” a reference to the Chinese Communist Party. Findlay calls Wat’s departure is a “betrayal of the hardworking volunteers, campaign workers and voters who helped get her elected.”

The same day, Brennan Day (Courtenay-Comox) quits the caucus, saying he no longer supports the direction of the party under Findlay. Day says he has lost confidence in the judgment, conduct and ethical standards of Findlay’s leadership and the people she surrounds herself with.

Aug. 27: Bruce Banman (Abbotsford South) quits and rallies other Conservatives to join him “regardless of political affiliation.” He says many have told him Findlay is “unelectable,” and that under her another election win by the NDP is becoming increasingly likely.

Aug. 28: Findlay says suggestions that a recording shows she illegally offered jobs to legislators, in exchange for resigning so she could stand in a byelection, are “preposterous.” Police say they were aware of the purported recording of Findlay addressing Conservative legislators that was released on social media on Thursday. Findlay later announces a caucus meeting to be followed by a news conference on Aug. 31.

Aug. 29: Premier David Eby calls a byelection in Abbotsford-Mission, with voting day set for Saturday, Sept. 26.

Aug. 30: Findlay cancels the caucus meeting and news conference.

Aug. 31: A’a: Liya Warbus (Chilliwack-Cultus Lake) quits the caucus, saying she has lost faith in Findlay’s leadership, citing the sudden cancellation of the caucus meeting and the circumstances surrounding the resignation from the legislature of Gasper to make way for Findlay to stand in a byelection.

Sept. 1: Paton says he has been asked to speak to the RCMP. He says he expects to be asked about his allegation that Findlay’s chief of staff, Chris Delaney, had said that if he stepped down as an MLA so Findlay could run in a byelection, he could be given a position as an adviser at the same salary.

Sept. 2: Legislators Donegal Wilson (Boundary-Similkameen) and Scott McInnis (Columbia River-Revelstoke) quit caucus, both citing Findlay’s reported connections to Alberta separatists as part of a series of concerns. Their departures reduce the Conservative caucus to 28; it had had 44 members after the 2024 election.

Findlay announces that Delaney has resigned as her chief of staff, and she has appointed Gasper to replace him. Findlay says she is the victim of a “co-ordinated political attack.”

Sept. 4: Rosalyn Bird, Bruce Banman and A’a:liya Warbus say in a joint statement that they’re joining the yet-to-be-named party being formed by Milobar and Paton.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 04, 2026.

stories.title: As volunteers decline, Elgin County clubs look online for recruits
stories.summary: The new directory brings 32 service clubs into one place as organizations grapple with falling volunteer participation.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
Two organizations have collaborated to establish an online directory aimed at boosting volunteerism in Elgin County service clubs as participation declines.

Service clubs across Elgin County have partnered with Volunteer Elgin, a non-profit initiative that connects people with volunteer opportunities, and the Elgin St. Thomas Community Foundation – which connects donors to charitable community campaigns – on a centralized online service club directory that “will highlight the many clubs contributing to community life and provide a simple starting point for residents who want to learn more,” a Volunteer Elgin news release said.

“We want to create a visible online presence for people who are seeking opportunities, and a place where all of the service clubs can be accessed in one spot,” said Tracy Robinson, executive director of the Elgin St. Thomas Community Foundation.

The impetus for launching the online portal came from listening to the community and hearing from service clubs struggling to recruit and retain volunteers, Robinson said.

The initiative grew out of challenges identified at an annual breakfast hosted at the Rotary Club of St. Thomas, according to the release.

Formal volunteering has declined sharply, with national data showing a 40 per cent decrease in volunteer hours between 2013 and 2023, the release said.

Robinson said service clubs are an indicator of the health of a community.

“There’s countless volunteer hours that service club members give, and if they’re struggling, then you know there’s a real problem,” she said.

The hope is that the directory will bolster service club membership so they can “continue to serve our communities,” said Carolyn Johnson, chair of Volunteer Elgin.

stories.title: ‘It’s no prank’: Residents in Middlesex County fear injury as wheel nut loosening continues
stories.summary: It is a potentially dangerous act that hasn’t let up, according to residents of a community north-west of London, Ont.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
It is a potentially dangerous act that hasn’t let up, according to residents of a community north-west of London, Ont.

Wheel nuts continue to be loosened from vehicles in Ailsa Craig, Ont.

“I’ve known four people, actually, who had their lug nuts loosened. The tires hadn’t fallen off, they heard the noise first. Thank God,” said resident Wayne Higman.

But in one case, a tire flew off while a vehicle was moving.

Tonya Nichol told CTV News London she was almost back to town after running errands when it happened last month.

“Just as I turned the corner to come into town, the tires vacated my vehicle, crossed the road and into the ditch.”

The aftermath left her truck damaged and her heart in her throat. She can’t get the thought out of her head about what might have happened if she’d been going faster.

“I had my daughter and her friend from dance in the truck at the time. It could have been three of us injured if we had been going highway speeds and it fell off then.”

Her anger took her to social media, where she discovered she wasn’t alone.

“Since then, we’ve heard at least 8 other people have been affected by it.”

CTV News also spoke to a volunteer firefighter who nearly lost her tire.

All the stories are enough to warrant concern from police and residents.

“I’m worried, it doesn’t sound safe, it puts the whole community at risk,” said Kevin Peterson.

The level of concern amplified once people began to suspect that this could potentially be related to an online challenge.”

A social media challenge has circulated online for several years, encouraging the dangerous prank.

Police forces across the province have tried to alert people to the danger.

In Ailsa Craig, O.P.P. have confirmed that two people were caught on video surveillance tampering with wheel nuts. They have not been apprehended.

Meanwhile, residents here report checking their tires before they drive until the perpetrators are caught or at least learn there is nothing funny about their actions.

“That’s no prank to pull because there’s a lot of danger, people taking lug nuts off tires,” said Higman.

“It could cost somebody their life,” added Nichol solemnly, as she reflected again on her good fortune that her tire came off at a slow speed.

stories.title: Lunenburg water conservation continues after Dares Lake dam breach
stories.summary: Water conservation efforts continued for a second day in Lunenburg, N.S., along with school and business closures, as crews worked on repairs to the Dares Lake dam.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Ella Macdonald
stories.content:
Water conservation efforts continued for a second day in Lunenburg , N.S., along with school and business closures, as crews worked to repair the Dares Lake dam.

The recently-constructed dam was breached Wednesday around 1 p.m. after a crack formed, sending water into the pump building.

Since the dam is the Town of Lunenburg’s main water supply, many businesses, industries, and restaurants were forced to close in an effort to conserve water.

Mayor Jamie Myra says the breach overflowed the lake and submerged the pump building. That meant no water was being pumped into the town’s water treatment facility.

“So eventually if that wasn’t rectified, we’d run out of water,” he said.

Closures in the town range from cafes to daycares, and larger companies like High Liner Foods, which is headquartered in Lunenburg.

“If it doesn’t get back up and running within the next 12 to 24 hours, you’re talking hundreds of thousands of dollars (in revenue) lost (in the town) over Labour Day weekend,” said Myra.

For tourists who stopped by the popular waterfront community, it was a disappointment.

“We were going to go and have lunch at the Salt Shaker. I feel bad for the businesses, they’re losing a lot of money,” said one visitor.

Myra says the dam was installed within the last year and cost the town about $1 million.

“I never ever envisioned the new dam just collapsing or giving way. That, to me, is a shocker,” he said.

As of Friday, two out of the three pumps in the building are working but not at 100 per cent, according to the mayor.

“People have been listening to the directive, people have been using less water, and the two pumps that are out working are somewhat being able to catch up to the water capacity,” he said.

“So if things keep going in the right direction, we’re hoping sooner rather than later our water utility is back up to the standards it needs to be to start delivering safe drinking water to everybody.”

Myra says the breach has now been secured and the focus remains on getting all three pumps fully operational.

He applauds the town’s efforts to fix the problem and apologizes to the businesses and students at Bluenose Academy who haven’t been able to return to class for the new school year.

“I really learned in the last 48 hours how close this community is. We haven’t had any pushback from residents (or) business owners. We all want the same end result and we’re all working together to get there,” he said.

Myra adds that anyone with property damage caused by the breach should contact his office.

Property owner Connor Veinot is keeping a close eye on the water.

What was once a small stream on his property has risen four feet and is threatening to flood his yard.

“I didn’t think it would rise that fast,” he said.

Now that the breach has been secured, he’s hopeful the water will recede. However, heavy rain in the forecast has him fearing the worst.

“Damage, erosion, undermining and stuff. Hopefully we don’t get a lot of downpour on top of it because it is a lot of force and I’m scared that it might take the bridge out behind me,” he said.

As for the cause of the damage, Myra says it’s still unclear but he’s in touch with provincial officials as they work to figure that out.

“(The dam) was a partnership between other levels of government as well. So it’ll be more than just us that are wondering what happened,” he said.

stories.title: London-area unemployment climbs to 8.5% amid tariff uncertainty
stories.summary: The region lost about 1,600 jobs in August as economists pointed to trade uncertainty and weaker hiring.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
The London region’s unemployment rate rose to 8.5 per cent in August from 8.2 per cent in July, according to Statistics Canada figures released Friday.

The London census metropolitan area includes London, St. Thomas, Strathroy and parts of Elgin and Middlesex counties.

The region’s labour force shrank by about 800 people, to 341,800 in August from 342,600 in July. Of those, 312,900 were employed in August, compared with 314,500 in July.

The rise in unemployment may be due to uncertainty surrounding trade negotiations with the United States, said David Ristovski, an economist with Signal49 Research, an economic forecasting agency formerly known as the Conference Board of Canada.

“The recent weakness that we’ve been seeing over the last six to eight months really stems from the uncertainty surrounding the ongoing trade situation with the United States, and so, that’s significantly impacting multiple sectors,” he said.

The latest jobs report comes after U.S. President Donald Trump implemented Section 338 tariffs on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between American and Canadian negotiators fell apart.

Canadian dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of comparable U.S. goods will come into effect Tuesday.

Additional tariff threats could be causing Canadian businesses to take a more cautious approach to hiring in the near term, reducing demand for labour, Ristovski said.

“That’s what we think has sort of played out in London over the last six to eight months,” he said.

Other factors, such as job seekers becoming discouraged and leaving the labour force, people leaving the city to pursue work elsewhere, or leaving the job market to pursue schooling, might also be contributing to the higher unemployment rate, Ristovski said.

“There’s also a bit of weakness in the education sector, given that there have been minimal population gains in recent months, particularly among international students,” he said.

Statistics Canada reported the London region’s population grew slightly in one month, to 541,000 from 540,500.

Ristovski expects a trade deal between Canada and the United States by Jan. 1, 2027, which he said would help London’s economy and labour market bounce back.

But there is still uncertainty on that front, he said, and if a deal isn’t reached, conditions could potentially worsen.

“That will have many negative repercussions, not only in the London region, but especially other cities and metropolitan areas in and around Southwestern Ontario,” he said.

Canada’s overall unemployment rate held steady at 6.4 per cent, while Ontario’s rose one-tenth of a percentage point to 6.9 per cent.

stories.title: Another golf push cart company is threatened by Canada's tariffs on Chinese EVs
stories.summary: An Ontario company being threatened by a massive retroactive tax bill isn't alone.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — An Ontario company that is being threatened by a massive retroactive tax bill because its golf carts were categorized by Ottawa as electric vehicles (EVs) isn’t alone.

At least one other Canadian company that also has its motorized push carts manufactured in China says it has also received a tax bill from Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) that is large enough to threaten its business.

Hanson Xie, director of operations of Markham, Ont.-based Axglo Inc., says the federal government has told his company to pay about $500,000 in back taxes for the importation of its carts. The three and four-wheeled buggies are just large enough to carry a golf bag, but have never been confused with an electric-powered sedan or sport utility vehicle.

Xie said his six-person company, which has been in the golf cart business since 2009, is profitable but doesn’t have the money to cover an unexpected bill of that size. “What type of small business has $500,000 to pay Cbsa?”

As National Post reported late last month , Xie’s tax tale is similar to JPSMGolf of Pickering, Ont., a competitor that had been hit earlier this year with a tax bill of $178,000. In both cases, the companies are facing hefty interest charges as they look for solutions.

The government has an appeal process for such matters, but companies say they must first either pay their tax bill or post a bond that is lost if they lose the appeal.

It’s unclear how many other Canadian companies that make small motorized products have also been hit with retroactive tax bills because they’ve been categorized as EVs. The domestic golf cart business has only a handful or so players, but small businesses that import and sell mobility scooters, power wheelchairs and other electric or battery-powered gadgets May also fall under the same automotive classification.

In a letter to JPSMGolf earlier this year, Cbsa confirmed its ruling that his golf carts are “undoubtedly” considered EVs because they “are conveyances used by the golfer to get their bag and associated accessories across the golf course during play.”

Finance Canada, which categorizes importers’ goods, was unavailable for comment. When contacted about the JPSMGolf case, a Cbsa spokesperson said that the department couldn’t comment on specific company cases, nor does it have the authority to deviate from the wording of surtax rulings.

But an Ottawa customs broker said he regularly deals with categorization problems. Olexiy Tyshchenko, of Ambassador Customs Brokerage, said not every product fits neatly into one of the government’s specific categories, especially when it comes to new technologies and products.

“This happens quite often,” said Tyshchenko. “I’m not surprised.”

The two Ontario golf cart companies’ retroactive tax bills stem from a 17-month window in 2024-25 where Chinese-made EVs were taxed by Ottawa at a rate of 100 per cent, following a brief trade war between the two countries. The Trudeau government applied the tariff to protect the Canadian auto industry and to stay on side with similar policies by the United States and some other Western countries.

That trade war and the surtax ended earlier this year after the Carney government reached a deal with Beijing to allow 49,000 Chinese EVs (about 3 per cent of the Canadian market) into the Canadian market at a tariff rate of 6.1 per cent. In exchange, China agreed to drop its tariffs on Canadian seafood and some key agricultural products.

stories.title: Federal Tories launch ‘Conservatives for Canada’ campaign ahead of Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said earlier this summer his caucus would be campaigning against separation
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
The federal Conservatives are launching a campaign to encourage Albertans to vote to remain in Canada in the upcoming referendum.

On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote on whether they want to remain a province or begin the process to hold a referendum on separation.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said earlier this summer his caucus would be campaigning against separation.

He tapped Parkland MP Dane Lloyd to lead that effort.

Lloyd says he spent the summer meeting with people on both sides of the issue and it’s become clear that a campaign is needed to engage Conservative supporters and ensure they vote.

MPs are set to return to Ottawa for the fall sitting of the House of Commons on Sept. 21.

stories.title: Rock the Runway, Bckyrd Fest moving from London airport to Harris Park
stories.summary: Rock the Runway and Bckyrd Fest are moving to downtown London after organizers said they were unable to develop an acceptable traffic management plan for the festivals at London International Airport.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Rock the Runway and BCKYRD Fest are moving to downtown London after organizers said they were unable to develop an acceptable traffic management plan for the festivals at London International Airport.
· Posted: Sep 04, 2026 4:22 PM EDT | Last Updated: September 4
Rock the Runway and BCKYRD Fest are moving from the London International Airport to Harris Park after failing to develop a traffic management plan for the airport site.
Jones Entertainment Group announced the change Friday afternoon, saying the festivals will now take place in downtown London on Sept. 17 and 18.
Organizers say they couldn't reach an agreement that would allow the events to go ahead while minimizing traffic disruption and keeping patrons and the surrounding community safe.

"From day one, our goal has always been to create an incredible festival experience while ensuring the safety of our patrons and the surrounding community," Jones Entertainment Group said in a media release.
"When it became clear that we could not achieve the traffic plan we felt was necessary, we made the decision to move the event."
Organizers said traffic challenges at last year's event were an important factor in the decision.

"Harris Park gives us the opportunity to deliver the same experience in a location that is accessible, right in the heart of the city and proven with the last 22 years of Rock the Park," the release said.

"We absolutely love the airport and are incredibly grateful for everything their team has done to support Rock the Runway," organizers said. "They have been outstanding partners throughout this process, and we look forward to continuing that relationship."
For ticket holders, organizers said previously purchased tickets remain valid at Harris Park, and no action is required. Parking passes for the airport will be automatically refunded.
Thursday's Rock the Runway lineup includes Limp Bizkit, Cypress Hill, JJ Wilde and The Dirty Nil.
Friday's BCKYRD Fest lineup includes Disco Lines, Loud Luxury, Bunt., Ian Asher, Dudley and Nader. For the latest information, visit Rock the Runway's social media.

stories.title: Rock the Runway changes venue weeks before festival
stories.summary: Organizers say traffic-management concerns prompted the last-minute switch, with all previously purchased tickets still valid.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
We independently select everything we recommend. Buying through us may earn us a commission, which supports our work.

This year’s Rock the Runway, the outdoor concert set to be held at London International Airport, is moving to Harris Park after organizers were unable to reach a solution to traffic problems.

In a news release Friday afternoon, Jones Entertainment Group announced the Sept. 17-18 event would move from London International Airport to Harris Park in downtown London.

“After months and multiple meetings and extensive discussions with various organizations and agencies, organizers were unable to reach an agreeable traffic management solution that would allow the event to move forward at the airport while maintaining minimal traffic disruption and keeping public and patron safety the top priority,” JEG officials wrote.

Last year’s inaugural concert drew 25,000 people for singer-songwriter Noah Kahan and became the largest concert in London’s history. But despite the success, concertgoers experienced traffic congestion and cell service problems that affected vendors and fans accessing their tickets.

Organizers had already capped attendance at 15,000 this year to address those issues.

“When it became clear that we could not achieve the traffic plan we felt was necessary, we made the decision to move the event,” officials wrote.

Nothing will change for ticket holders except the location, JEG said. All previously purchased Rock the Runway tickets, along with tickets for its second night, BCKYRD Fest, will remain valid at Harris Park.

No exchanges, updates or additional action are required from ticket holders. A new festival site map and updated arrival information will be released shortly.

All previously purchased parking passes will be automatically refunded and no action is required to request a refund.

JEG said the decision does not change its relationship with London International Airport.

“They have been outstanding partners throughout this process, and we look forward to continuing that relationship,” JEG wrote.

stories.title: Pitching in: Medical student turns health struggles into non-profit for youth facing homelessness
stories.summary: Canadian Courage Project works with foundations and organizations to provide health services for young people
stories.author: Paul Waldie
stories.content:
The organizers: Shania and Anya Bhopa

The pitch: Co-founding the Canadian Courage Project

As a child, Shania Bhopa’s health was always a concern. She had gastrointestinal problems, kidney stones and struggled with mental-health issues.

“I was just a really sick kid and I always felt like doctors never communicated to me the things I needed to know,” Ms. Bhopa, 28, said from her home in Toronto.

Her experiences led her to study communications at university, with a focus on health care. She went on to earn a doctorate from McMaster University in global health. She also spent time working on health care concerns in youth shelters and she wrote a children’s book about the “gut-brain connection.”

“I think that true human connection comes from good communication, and it really does lack in the health care system,” she said.

In 2020, she launched the Canadian Courage Project with her sister, Anya, who is a veterinarian. The non-profit works with more than a dozen foundations and organizations to provide a range of services for youth experiencing homelessness, including animal care programs, community libraries and workshops.

The project has recently partnered with Friends of Ruby, a Toronto shelter for 2SLGBTQIA+ young people. They opened the Jade Health & Wellness Room, which offers primary care, mental health, dental and wellness support services to people served by Friends of Ruby. The project has been backed by around $20,000 from Telus Health, a division of Telus Corp.

“We’re able to collaborate with family medicine, nurse practitioners, two dentists and dental hygienists, and three alternative medicine specialists,” said Ms. Bhopa. She added that current and former residents of the shelter have been involved in the programming.

Ms. Bhopa is studying to become a doctor, and her dream is to blend her interests in medicine and research. Her goal is “to spend half of my week in a clinic with my patients and then half in my lab building the interventions to help them.”

stories.title: Toronto orders Live Nation to hire engineer, fix Rogers Stadium before AC/DC show
stories.summary: Images from the venue, located near Downsview Park, show blue bleachers strewn around the site, while its grandstands appear to be partially collapsed.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
stories.content:
The City of Toronto has ordered Live Nation to fix Rogers Stadium after the outdoor music venue was battered by Wednesday’s storm, leaving swathes of its seating damaged.

Images from the venue, located near Downsview Park, show blue bleachers strewn around the site, while its grandstands appear to be partially collapsed.

Inspectors with the City of Toronto issued an order to Live Nation on Thursday to fix the stadium and retain an engineer before it is allowed to host rock legends AC/DC in mid-September.

The city said parts of the north side of the stadium structure had collapsed, while seats had been displaced and parts of the concert venue are in “condition that May pose a risk” to people’s health or safety.

A seven-part order sets out a series of conditions Live Nation must meet before it is allowed to host people in its outdoor Toronto venue.

The city told the promoter to make sure nobody can enter the damaged site and then retain an engineer to assess the damage. Live Nation has until Sept. 8 to share its findings and solutions with the city.

The order says Live Nation must then follow all the steps suggested by the engineer and update the city no later than Sept. 11 on what it’s been able to do. Reconstruction work, the city said, will require a building permit.

The order means Live Nation has 12 days, including the Labour Day long weekend, to fix the structure before AC/DC are due to play in Toronto.

A spokesperson for Live Nation said it had been working with technical teams from Toronto since the venue was first set up.

“Wednesday’s storm was a severe and significant weather event that City officials have deemed a ‘100-year storm,'” they wrote.

“The inspection, assessment and remediation of structures affected by significant weather events, like a red-level storm of this nature, is a standard process, and we remain engaged with the City as that work continues.”

It’s the latest setback for a stadium beset by issues since it opened last summer.

Live Nation said it would make adjustments after concertgoers initially complained the 50,000-person venue seemed ill-prepared to handle crowds and local officials raised noise complaints.

The venue last hosted a show on Aug. 23 for K-pop superstars BTS.

— with a file from The Canadian Press

stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
A coalition of close to 300 labour and community groups are calling on the federal and Alberta governments to halt the removal of 10 international students it says were singled out for enforcement at a protest.

The Migrant Rights Network group makes the demand in a public letter sent this week on behalf of transnational groups, including Amnesty International, Cupe Ontario and Climate Justice Saskatoon.

The network says in the letter that targeting newcomers for enforcement while they’re protesting immigration rules is a violation of the Charter right of free speech and will have a chilling effect on those wanting to speak out.

“Migrants across the country are being told that joining the next protest, picket line or public meeting could put their ability to remain in Canada at risk,” says the letter.

The letter is pinned to a recent protest in Calgary by 1,500 graduates from Portage College, a public institution based in northeastern Alberta with programs delivered through partner campuses in Calgary and Edmonton.

The network says that graduates completed programs that made them eligible for post-graduation work permits, but over the summer they were refused the permits as the federal government changed the eligibility rules on its website.

The federal government disagrees.

In an e-mail, a spokesperson for Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab said there had been no changes to eligibility criteria for the post-graduation work permit program but that the government had updated its web page in June to clarify existing requirements.

Affected students began weeks of demonstrations starting in mid-July in Edmonton and Calgary. The network says the Aug. 12 protest in Calgary is what triggered their letter.

On that day, police were called in on a complaint that protesters were blocking a sidewalk.

A spokesperson for Calgary police said in an e-mail that officers went to the scene, asked for identification from demonstrators and called the Canadian Border Services Agency with concerns.

The spokesperson added that the protesters had not committed any crimes.

The border agency said its officers were called in to check if demonstrators were non-compliant under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. It interviewed 12 of them.

Network spokesman Syed Hussan said that number was narrowed to 10 by the day’s end and that those found to be non-compliant were given exclusion orders. Exclusion orders demand the person leave Canada and not return for at least a year.

Border services, in an e-mail, said those who receive removal orders are given due process, including the ability to appeal and request judicial reviews.

“We fully agree that the freedom of peaceful assembly is a Charter-protected right. We are aware of and reviewing the letter issued today by civil society organizations,” it said Wednesday.

Hussan said the students were promised – then unfairly denied – the work permits. He said those whose study permits had expired were still within a 90-day window to renew them.

“On the immigration side, this is the wrong decision,” Hussan said.

“But what’s most dangerous is that freedom of expression is a Charter protected right. And that Charter-protected right was attacked.”

The letter also calls for the post-graduation work permits to be granted, for the actions of police and border officials that day be investigated and for clear rules not to target migrants at peaceful protests.

The network says there are more demonstrations planned for Sept. 20, including in Toronto, Vancouver and Ottawa.

Alberta Immigration Minister Joseph Schow said the rules are clear.

“Anyone who comes to Canada on a temporary status needs to return home once their permit is expired,” he said in a statement.

“That is the position of our government, and it’s not going to change.”

One of the protesters, 29-year-old Gurpreet Singh, said he’s trying to decide whether to fight his exclusion order or return to India.

In December, 2024, Singh graduated with a certificate in osteopathic therapy, which involves hands-on manipulation of joints to help reduce pain and stiffness.

He said he had to quit his job after being denied a postgraduate work permit, because he can’t work.

“I’m not asking for any kind of mercy or anything,” Singh said in an interview.

“I’m just asking [for] what we were told before coming to Canada.”

stories.title: Arbour to attend King Harald V's funeral, delaying visit to Newfoundland and Labrador
stories.summary: Ottawa - Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour will attend the state funeral of Norway's King Harald V next week.
stories.author: The Canadian Press staff The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour will attend the state funeral of Norway’s King Harald V next week.

The king died at the age of 89 on Aug. 28 and the funeral is scheduled for Sept. 9 in Oslo.

Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour stands by tall ships from seven countries at the Rendez-Vous Naval de Quebec at the Port of Quebec City on Friday, July 24, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Jacques Boissinot

The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘211 years of community’: Funding aims to protect Upper Hammonds Plains from wildfires
stories.summary: A historic African Nova Scotian community is receiving provincial funding to reduce its wildfire risk, in a bid to help preserve the area's heritage.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
A historic African Nova Scotian community is receiving provincial funding to reduce its wildfire risk , in a bid to help preserve the area’s heritage.

“What is being protected here is not only housing, it is 211 years of community,” said Hammonds Plains-Lucasville MLA Rick Burns on Friday.

Burns announced the province is committing $199,000 from its Sustainable Communities Challenge Fund to support the Upper Hammonds Plains Community Land Trust.

The trust is working on wildfire risk assessment and mitigation plans to protect individual properties and shared assets, including 85 historic homes, a church and community buildings.

“(It) just shows the reflection of the community at large, both here in Upper Hammonds Plains and throughout Hammonds Plains, to become a fire safe community and to build resilience locally,” said Burns.

Since the Tantallon wildfire that destroyed 151 homes and temporarily displaced 16,000 people in 2023, the trust has been looking at ways to reduce the wildfire risk in the Upper Hammonds Plains area.

“We were trying to figure out what can we do right now to ease people’s minds, right?” said Curtis Whiley, the trust’s founder and CEO.

“So we started to try to figure out how can we can do some education with folks to understand what they can do around their own homes.”

The trust is part of a national program called FireSmart Canada, which provides recommendations that help homeowners and communities prepare for wildfires. The provincial funding will help the community with initiatives such as home assessments, community clean-ups and remediation.

Assistant Fire Chief Richard Hayes with Halifax Fire says some of this work could include assessing properties and making sure anything flammable is kept away from structures.

“Looking at the tree areas surrounding your property and looking at what can burn and bring that fire close, that’s what we concentrate on,” he said.

“So right around the home, just making sure that there’s no combustibles.”

A Halifax Regional Municipality staff report released in July listed Upper Hammonds Plains as the third-worst community when it comes to egress issues.

The report ranked the top 100 worst communities across the municipality.

2:06 Upper Hammonds Plains community hopeful as egress and connectivity marked as high concern

Residents have been outspoken about the community’s safety concerns , especially with a growing population and developments in the neighbourhood.

He says the land trust has had productive discussions with all levels of government on improving the situation, and believes this latest investment is a positive step toward preserving the heritage of the area.

“Partners are coming together to the table to really address all of these concerns, including water infrastructure (…) emergency egress and even community connectivity, which is what we’re really advocating for,” he said.

“(It’s) going to require significant investment, right, once these studies are all completed.”

stories.title: Gander, N.L., defends invitation to U.S. ambassador Hoekstra to 9/11 commemoration
stories.summary: The Town of Gander, N.L., says its invitation to United States Ambassador Pete Hoekstra to attend a 9/11 ceremony this month was protocol, not an endorsement.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Town of Gander, N.L., says its invitation to United States Ambassador Pete Hoekstra to attend a 9/11 ceremony this month was protocol, not an endorsement.

Hoekstra is among a list of dignitaries attending the town’s commemoration of the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States.

News of his attendance prompted strong reactions online, as well as an article in satirical news site The Beaverton, titled “Come from Away sequel will see Newfoundlanders put the friggin’ boots to Pete Hoekstra.”

“Come From Away” is a hit musical about how the people of Gander fed, clothed and cared for more than 6,500 air passengers who were stranded there for days after the 9/11 attacks.

In a news release Friday, Gander’s town council said the community’s 9/11 story is about people, not politics.

The town said it understands Canadians are frustrated by ongoing tensions with the United States, but it asked residents to look beyond those differences.

“There are times when we will disagree. There are also times when we have to recognize that something is bigger than those differences,” the news release said. “For Gander, September 11 is one of those times.”

The town council followed appropriate protocols when it invited governments and diplomatic representatives to the ceremony next week, it said.

Hoekstra has caused controversy by criticizing the “elbows up” campaign against U.S. tariffs and by expressing irritation with Canadians’ response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s rhetoric about making the country the 51st state.

Earlier this week, Hoekstra said he was attending “not just on behalf of those who were stranded, but for an entire nation that remains moved by Gander’s generosity.”

“I look forward to meeting many of those who opened their hearts and homes and honouring the enduring bond built that week,” the ambassador said in an emailed statement.

Thirty-eight planes made emergency landings in Gander after the U.S. airspace closed on Sept. 11, 2001. Hijackers had just slammed planes into the World Trade Center in New York, killing nearly 3,000 people.

“We are not asking anyone to change how they feel or what they believe,” said Friday’s release from Gander’s town council.

stories.title: Bear activity shuts down popular campground in Bruce Peninsula National Park
stories.summary: A popular campground in Ontario’s Bruce Peninsula National Park will be closed over the long weekend because of increased bear activity in the area. Parks Canada says Cyprus Lake Campground will be closed through Labour Day. It also says parking access for the Grotto, one of the top tourists attractions in the region, has been […]
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A popular campground in Ontario’s Bruce Peninsula National Park will be closed over the long weekend because of increased bear activity in the area.

Parks Canada says Cyprus Lake Campground will be closed through Labour Day.

It also says parking access for the Grotto, one of the top tourists attractions in the region, has been cancelled up to Saturday.

Parks Canada says it will inform the public if the closures have to be extended as it continues to monitor bear activity.

It says reservations at other parking areas and day visits to the park remain unaffected.

Government data shows more than 490,000 people visited Bruce Peninsula National Park last year.

stories.title: 'We're taking it very personally': Republican mayor from Lake Ontario city rejects Trump's 'Lake America'
stories.summary: The mayor of a city in New York State on the shore of Lake Ontario has said his community is taking the lake's renaming "very personally."
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
The mayor of a New York State city on the shore of Lake Ontario has said his community is taking the lake’s renaming “very personally” and will not be using the new “Lake America” name.

Robert Corradino is a Republican and has been mayor of Oswego, in the Republican stronghold of Oswego County, since January 2024.

Despite the area’s political allegiance, he says his community is “trying to understand why a name that has endured for centuries would suddenly be changed” when there is “no practical, historical, or cultural need to change it.”

In an interview with National Post, Corradino said: “We can disagree with the current administration’s take about renaming Lake Ontario and still support some of its other initiatives. But we’re taking the renaming of the lake very personally in Oswego.”

The change has since been adopted by both Google and Apple Maps for users in the U.S., but Corradino has said that Oswego does not support the renaming, and won’t be altering any signage, tourism materials or official communications to reflect the new name.

“The lake provides so much for our community as well as our identity,” Corradino said, citing the economic boost from charter boats and cruise ships as well as “beautiful sunsets.”

“Lake Ontario is in the DNA of Osweganians,” he said, adding, “Everything that we are emanates from the lake.”

The mayor said that the souring relationship between Canada and the U.S., which re-escalated following the breakdown of trade negotiations last month, has hit the tourism industry in Oswego, located just an hour from the border.

“Our tourism from Canada is down substantially. We have stores, we have museums that depend on tourism, and Canadians are a big part of our tourism business,” he said.

It’s a trend that has rippled across the U.S., with recent data from Statistics Canada revealing that Canadian travel to the United States dropped by 10.6 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025.

Speaking about the direction he’d like to see Canada-U.S. relations take, Corradino added: “I would hope that our two countries, because of our long-standing relationship, could sit down in a conference room and discuss issues calmly and professionally, and work these differences out without changing the name of the lake.”

Meanwhile, other politicians in the U.S. have also condemned Trump’s executive order , including former U.S. secretary of state Hillary Clinton, who simply wrote, “It’s Lake Ontario,” in a post on X, and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who said , “The American people don’t want to rename Lake Ontario Lake America.”

On the Canadian side, Carney responded to Trump’s actions shortly after the executive order was signed, explaining on social media that “the name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big’.”

He added that the name is more than 400 years old and predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence.

“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” he wrote. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a new Lake Ontario sign in Winona, Ont., to remind Trump “it’s Lake Ontario, now and forever.”

In a video posted on X, the Ontario premier said, “You May have heard that President Trump is trying to rename this lake all because he doesn’t like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves.”

Ford continued: “Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. And long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario. But just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we have set up a sign to remind them, it’s Lake Ontario now and forever.”

Ford’s comments on the lake’s longstanding name were echoed in a press release issued by Corradino on Tuesday, in which he was quoted as saying: “Lake Ontario has carried its name for hundreds of years. It is a name rooted in history, geography, and the shared identity of the communities that surround it…The name Lake Ontario comes from a Huron Indigenous people’s word that means lake of shining waters. The province of Ontario took its name from the lake in 1867, over two hundred years after the name first appeared on the maps of European explorers.”

He added: “The city of Oswego will continue using the name that reflects our history and honors the generations who have lived, worked, and built their lives along its shores.”

stories.title: Rock the Runway and Bckyrd Fest moving to Harris Park
stories.summary: have been moved to Harris Park.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
have been moved to Harris Park.

The Jones Entertainment Group (JEG) said after months and multiple meetings, this decision was made to allow the event to move forward without traffic issues that were experienced at the 2025 event.

“Given the traffic challenges experienced last year, it was especially important to us that we had a plan in place that would provide a smooth, safe, and positive experience for everyone attending the festival, as well as the surrounding community,” said the group.

They said moving to Harris Park gives them the confidence needed.

“From day one, our goal has always been to create an incredible festival experience while ensuring the safety of our patrons and the surrounding community,” they added.

“When it became clear that we could not achieve the traffic plan we felt was necessary, we made the decision to move the event. Harris Park gives us the opportunity to deliver the same experience in a location that is accessible, right in the heart of the city and proven with the last 22 years with Rock the Park.”

JEG said that this location move does not change its relationship with London International Airport.

“They have been outstanding partners throughout this process, and we look forward to continuing that relationship.”

Nothing changes for ticketholders; other than the location you must go to for the event. No exchanges, updates, or further action is required.

Previously bought parking passes will be automatically refunded.

The events take place Sept. 17 and 18 at Harris Park.

stories.title: What to know as London’s first centre-running BRT lanes are set to open
stories.summary: Route 90 will begin using the new centre lanes Sunday, giving riders and drivers their first look at how the system will work.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
London drivers on Wellington may not agree given the current traffic headaches, but construction of the southern bus rapid transit link has reached a milestone – with buses beginning to run in some completed centre lanes. LFP’s Jack Moulton reports.

Beginning Sunday, London Transit’s Express Route 90, which runs from Masonville Place to White Oaks mall, will begin using a roughly one-kilometre stretch of completed centre-running bus rapid transit lanes on Wellington between Simcoe Street, just south of Horton Street, and Grand Avenue, where it will merge back into mixed traffic.

The idea is to get Londoners used to what will be the city’s first use of centre-running bus lanes, said London’s director of construction Jennie Dann. The lanes will make up much of the Wellington Gateway and part of the East Link BRT routes.

Dann said centre-running lanes are a preferred BRT design around the world because they reduce interactions with other vehicles, including parked ones.

“It’s a small piece in our larger rapid transit program, but it’s an important step because it gives us a chance to see how the new road design is going to work with buses, drivers, pedestrians, cyclists, all using the corridor,” she said.

“Just as importantly, it gives Londoners a chance to get used to it . . . let’s start using it and see how people respond, and if we need to make any adjustments.”

The city has already begun trialling its BRT “contraflow lane” on King Street by similarly redirecting one bus route. While it left some drivers confused and concerned , Dann said it hasn’t caused major issues.

The biggest change for drivers brought about by the new centre lanes and medians will be restrictions on left turns to and from some driveways and smaller streets, Dann said.

Drivers intending to turn left from Wellington onto a side street, or left onto Wellington from one, will instead have to proceed to the nearest signalized intersection that allows U-turns and wait for an advanced left-turn signal to complete the turn.

City hall responds as merchants group sounds alarm over Wellington BRT work

London traffic congestion ranking improves – what’s behind the shift?

“Which is actually a good thing on a busy arterial like Wellington Road – instead of people making unprotected turning movements mid-block, we’re sending them up to the next signalized intersection,” she said. “It’s actually, in a lot of ways, safer.”

The express bus, which makes only a handful of stops, will stop at the Wellington and South Street station instead of its usual Grand Avenue stop.

Riders will board and disembark from protected platforms in the middle of the road and will have to wait for the normal walk signal at the intersection to cross.

All other Route 90 stops will remain at their normal curbside locations. Routes 1 and 13, which also travel on Wellington, will continue using existing curbside stops.

“We’re going to start practising using that transition, and then allow the buses to stop at the South Street stop, get some transit users used to using that median shelter, and then they’ll continue over the (Clark’s) bridge and then at Grand Avenue they’ll merge back into mixed traffic,” Dann said.

“As we do complete more sections of centre-running that are ready to go, we’re going to start to expand using existing express routes.”

Dann said work on widening Clark’s bridge over the Thames is complete.

The third phase of the Wellington Gateway between Wilkins Street and Harlech Gate has only landscaping work left, while the section from Harlech Gate to Exeter Road still needs shelter work and landscaping.

Traffic headaches at Wellington and Commissioners Road will continue into next year, however, Dann said, adding she hopes major work on Wellington between Commissioners and Wilkins will wrap up this year.

At the same time, work is beginning on Wellington from Watson Street to Whetter Avenue, including straightening the S-curve through that stretch and installing a new sewer trunk.

Dann said the expanded sewer is large enough for her to walk through and will be buried three storeys deep.

“That’s going to take us probably through to mid-2027. At that point, we should be pretty much out of the Commissioners intersection, and then we’re going to start with . . . moving south towards Base Line,” she said.

“The main goal of that is to keep access to the hospital as open as we can throughout the construction of both these contracts.”

The Wellington Gateway is expected to begin operations in 2029.

On the East Link BRT, Dann said sections of both Highbury Avenue north of the rail overpass and Oxford Street East are nearly complete and awaiting a top coat of asphalt this fall.

The on-campus station at Fanshawe College is finished and ready for the school year.

Work on widening Highbury’s rail overpass has shifted to the east side and will likely be completed next fall, she said.

Crews hope to finish the stretch of Dundas Street west of Highbury by early next year after the road was completely closed for deep sewer upgrades.

Construction at the Dundas and Highbury intersection will begin once Dundas reopens and is also expected to last until next fall, around the time full service on the East Link is expected to begin.

stories.title: N.B. regulator to review complaints about noise and odours near potato chips factory
stories.summary: The 17 residents say the Covered Bridge Potato Chips Ltd. plant brings overwhelming smells, constant noise and more traffic to their once-quiet neighbourhood.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .

A group of residents who live near a potato chip factory in a New Brunswick town are moving forward with their case against the company.

The 17 residents say the Covered Bridge Potato Chips Ltd. plant brings overwhelming smells, constant noise and more traffic to their once-quiet neighbourhood.

Each resident filed a claim with provincial farming regulator alleging the plant was causing significant and ongoing disruption to their lives.

The company’s lawyer, Sheila Mecking, has asked the province’s Farm Practices Review Board to settle the case, arguing that the company is an agricultural operator under provincial legislation.

The New Brunswick Farm Practices Review Board says it will consider whether it has jurisdiction to settle the complaints against the popular chip-making company.

The residents’ lawyer Basile Chiasson wants to pursue the case in court and argues the board doesn’t have jurisdiction.

The regulator’s chair Maurice Maillet said on Friday that the board, made up of five people who work in agriculture, will consider the arguments and come to a decision in the near future.

Chiasson said he expects the board to pave the way for the residents to take legal action at the Court of King’s Bench.

Last year, Covered Bridge converted its storage warehouse in Woodstock into a chip-processing factory, after its previous facility in another town burned down.

Some residents have said they hope Covered Bridge, which sells its chips across North America, leaves Woodstock entirely.
