stories.title: Changes to Canada's climate now 'irreversible,' federal report says
stories.summary: Ottawa - A new government report says the impacts of climate change in Canada are now largely irreversible and average temperatures are expected to rise by at least 3.5 C by the end of the century.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The impacts of climate change in Canada are now largely irreversible and average temperatures are expected to rise by at least 3.5 C by the end of the century, a new government report warns.

The report, published Thursday, is the second released by Environment and Climate Change Canada examining changes to Canada’s climate. It was authored by nearly two dozen government and climate science experts.

It says that even if the world reaches net-zero emissions by 2075 — which would mean any greenhouse gases would be captured by nature or technology — the effects in Canada will be stark.

The report says those effects include a nearly 50 per cent increase in the area burned by wildfires and glaciers in Western Canada losing more than 75 per cent of their mass.

“The most surprising thing is the contrast between what the report says that we can expect for our future climate, and the level of action that the federal government and other governments in Canada are taking,” said Ryan Ness, adaptation research director at the Canadian Climate Institute.

With the climate policies now in place around the world, average temperatures in Canada are expected to rise five degrees by the year 2100, with a 50 per cent chance that winter temperatures will increase by more than 10 C in much of Nunavut.

“That’s a lot of climate change that we have to adapt to and we’re not ready for it,” Ness said.

“We’re already seeing how vulnerable we are to the climate-driven disasters that we’ve experienced over the last few years. It’s only going to get worse, and yet the pace of action on adaptation is not high.”

Ness said adaptation should include things like retrofitting homes with more fireproof material and building firebreaks and flood walls around communities.

In a report issued last year on Canada’s national climate adaptation strategy, Canadian environment commissioner Jerry DeMarco said Ottawa’s efforts to prepare the country for the impacts of climate change had stumbled out of the gate.

DeMarco’s report concluded the strategy was not effectively designed and did not prioritize Canada’s climate change risks, and that departments relied instead on existing priorities and consultations.

DeMarco cited the short-term health impacts of wildfire smoke, estimated to cost between $410 million and $1.8 billion annually between 2013 and 2018. He also remarked on the spike in Lyme disease cases from 144 in 2009 to 2,525 in 2022 — an increase of more than 1,500 per cent.

A progress report on the climate adaptation strategy released by Ottawa last month said there are hundreds of new flood-mapping projects underway to better identify flood-prone areas.

It also acknowledged that 94 per cent of people living in high-risk areas don’t yet know their home is susceptible to floods.

The new report released Thursday says droughts and flash floods will become more frequent and severe as temperatures rise.

“Canada’s latest state of the climate report is a stark warning of what Canadians will face if governments fail to tackle the climate crisis with the urgency it requires,” said Julia Levin, associate director of national climate at Environmental Defence.

“This report should be a call to action. What the future looks like for our children depends on the policy choices being made today. The worst impacts of climate change are far from inevitable.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney has been accused of backsliding on climate policy for the better part of the last year.

He eliminated the consumer carbon price in March 2025, on his first day in office. While he promised a strengthened industrial carbon pricing system, he was accused of weakening that system through an agreement with Alberta in May that has ramifications for every other province and territory.

His government is also moving to repeal the electric vehicle sales mandate – Ottawa has promised stronger tailpipe standards but those are still years away – and to cancel the oil and gas emissions cap. Carney’s government also has delayed new methane regulations in Alberta.

Carney has said federal climate policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau was too expensive and divisive and “not sustainable over the long term.”

In response to Thursday’s report, the office of Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is still committed to reaching net-zero by 2050.

“To protect Canadians from the impacts of climate change and severe weather, the federal government has committed more than $2.1 billion to implement the National Adaptation Strategy and support a wide range of adaptation-related activities,” said Chris Zhou, Dabrusin’s director of communications.

“Our government is moving with urgency to fight climate change, while working together to build the energy security, industrial capacity, and strategic autonomy that will define this century for Canada.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 4, 2026.

stories.title: $13.8 million in illicit tobacco and nicotine products seized at southern Ontario border crossings in August
stories.summary: Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) officers at land ports of entry across southern Ontario seized more than $13.8 million worth of illicit tobacco and nicotine products in August
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) officers at land ports of entry across southern Ontario seized more than $13.8 million worth of illicit tobacco and nicotine products in August, with most of the interceptions involving large commercial shipments entering from the United States.

According to Cbsa, the seizures prevented illegal tobacco and nicotine products from entering the Canadian market and disrupted a source of revenue linked to organized crime.

According to the agency, proceeds from the illicit tobacco trade are often used to support and expand other criminal activities in Canada and abroad.

The Cbsa said it continues to work closely with law enforcement partners to identify and intercept contraband at the border, limiting opportunities for criminal organizations to profit from illegal trade.

Among the largest seizures reported during the month were two separate interceptions of loose-leaf tobacco at the Blue Water Bridge in Point Edward, Ont.

Aug. 20: Border services officers at the Blue Water Bridge seized 14,964 kg of loose-leaf tobacco, valued at $2,765,969

Aug. 17: At the Ambassador Bridge, Cbsa officers seized 1,781,000 cigarettes, valued at $333,189

Aug. 14: At the Blue Water Bridge, border services officers seized 15,222 kg of loose-leaf tobacco, valued at $2,809,921

Aug. 11: Border services officers at the Blue Water Bridge seized 2,796 kg of nicotine pouches, valued at $2,983,499

Aug. 6: At the Peace Bridge, Cbsa officers seized 3,000 kg of waterpipe tobacco, valued at $299,820

Aug. 2: At the Queenston Bridge, border services officers seized 7,658 kg of nicotine and tobacco products, valued at $2,704,524

The Cbsa said officers in the southern Ontario Region have seized more than $52.2 million worth of tobacco and nicotine products since Jan. 1, 2026.

According to Cbsa, the seizures prevented illegal tobacco and nicotine products from entering the Canadian market and disrupted a source of revenue linked to organized crime.
According to the agency, proceeds from the illicit tobacco trade are often used to support and expand other criminal activities in Canada and abroad.

The Cbsa said it continues to work closely with law enforcement partners to identify and intercept contraband at the border, limiting opportunities for criminal organizations to profit from illegal trade.
Among the largest seizures reported during the month were two separate interceptions of loose-leaf tobacco at the Blue Water Bridge in Point Edward, Ont.

stories.title: Prehistoric Yukon 'cheetahs' were fish eaters, not really cheetahs at all: study
stories.summary: Slender, agile cheetahs that roamed the Yukon 30,000 years ago were not technically cheetahs at all, but relatives of the puma that adapted to mostly eat fish instead of antelopes in a harsh northern climate, new research shows.
stories.author: Marissa Birnie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Slender, agile cheetahs that roamed the Yukon 30,000 years ago were not technically cheetahs at all, but relatives of the puma that adapted to mostly eat fish instead of antelopes in a harsh northern climate, new research shows.

A study published in the journal Current Biology analyzed fossils found in the Yukon and Wyoming in the United States belonging to Miracinonyx trumani, also known as the “American cheetah.”

With their gracefully slim bodies and long legs, the now-extinct cats appeared to resemble African cheetahs.

But the researchers found the cats were actually closer relatives of the puma, having diverged from the puma lineage around 2.6 million years ago as growing grasslands and cooling temperatures drove diversification in many North American mammals.

Grant Zazula, a paleontologist for the Yukon government and one of the study’s co-authors, said the species’ identification in the territory was interesting because the pronghorn antelope hunted by their southern counterparts never existed there.

The researchers wanted to find out what the Yukon cats were eating instead, so they sent the fossils for analysis. The results showed a chemical signature that matched other fish-eating predators like grizzly bears, Zazula said.

In fact, the Yukon cats adapted to eat mostly fish, a unique preference compared to the more diverse diet favoured by their southern kin.

“We’ve never seen a cat behave like this before,” Zazula said in an interview Thursday.

He said the cats likely made the change to adapt to their new environment after travelling farther north into a Yukon that was vastly different 30,000 years ago.

Gone were the boreal forests with their spruce trees and animals such as moose found in modern-day Yukon. Instead, the cats would have faced tree-barren grasslands and walked alongside woolly mammoths, wild horses, bison and other large mammals.

“Because there were so many of these big herbivorous animals on the landscape, we had lots of carnivores that were eating them,” Zazula said. The other predators included lions, sabretooth cats, wolves and grizzly bears.

The Yukon cheetahs would have had to find their niche in a competitive and unforgiving environment, Zazula added.

Luckily, the region’s rivers were rich with salmon and the cats could eat fish carcasses along the banks or have their pick from fish-packed spawning grounds.

Their distinct diet was likely key to their survival in the north, Zazula said.

“In order to live and be successful in the Yukon during the Ice Age, it had to figure out its way to live. And that fishing niche wasn’t occupied,” he said.

The Yukon environment also had an impact on the cats’ genetics, the researchers found. Two of the genes that regulate circadian rhythm — essentially the body’s internal alarm clock that reacts to changes in brightness — were non-functional in the cats.

It could be because the animals had to adapt to seasonal extremes of sunlight and darkness because of their high-altitude homes, or the cats could have been nocturnal.

The cats eventually went extinct after they couldn’t adapt to ecosystem changes at the end of the Ice Age.

But Zazula said their hardiness in adapting to their Yukon environment had parallels to the people who now live there.

“Everybody that moves to the Yukon has to figure out a different way to live if you’re not from here,” he said. ”(The cats) made their way, they figured it out by adapting to new resources and new environmental conditions. It became something unique — the Yukon cheetah.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Snowbirds take to the skies one last time in original planes at Toronto CNE this weekend
stories.summary: This year marks the Snowbirds' 55th outing at the CNE and their final one at the annual end-of-summer event until at least the early 2030s.
stories.author: Dilshad Burman
stories.content:
After more than six decades in service, the original CT-114 Tutor jets used in the Canadian Forces Snowbirds aerial acrobatic squadron will be retiring this year.

That means their appearance at the Canadian National Exhibition (CNE) in Toronto this year will be the last performance at the annual Canadian International Air Show (CIAS) featuring the classic aircrafts.

“This season concludes our time with the venerable CT-114 Tutor… it’s a Canadair limited CL-41, designed, engineered, built in Canada, just in Montreal, in Catrierville,” explained Major Maciej Hatta, team lead, Canadian Forces Snowbirds.

“They all came off the production line between 1963 and 1965, so they are showing a bit of their age but they’re still maintained to robust airworthiness standards.”

Since 1971, the Snowbirds have performed approximately 2,700 times in the Tutor jets and are a staple at national events and celebrations.

This year marks the Snowbirds’ 55th outing at the CNE and their final one at the annual end-of-summer event until at least the early 2030s. The squadron, based in Moose Jaw, is being grounded until new planes replace the fleet.

“The plans are to return with a different aircraft, hopefully sooner rather than later and be back in full force in the near future,” said Hatta.

The Snowbirds final performance in the CT-114 Tutor jets will be at the Grey Cup in Calgary on Nov. 15.

The federal government says the modern CT-157 Siskin II aircraft will take over for the CT-114 Tutor jets, but there is no current timeline for when replacement will be completed.

The CIAS features 15 acts in total, with the Snowbirds performance being the grand finale. The show runs on Saturday, Sunday and Monday from 12 p.m. to 3:40 p.m.

The performers in order of appearance are:

12 p.m. – CF-18

12:14 p.m. – Northern Stars

12:35 p.m. – CP-140 Aurora

12:46 p.m. – Mike and Sam Tryggvason – “Showcat”

12:59 p.m. – Marco Rusconi P-51

1:15 p.m. – Luke Penner – Extra 300

1:31 p.m. – Edenvale Classic Aircraft Foundation – Fleet Cornell

1:38 p.m. – Trevor Rafferty – Christen Eagle

1:54 p.m. – CH-146 Griffon – SAR

2:09 p.m. – Dan Fortin – Nanchang CJ6

2:30 p.m. – USAF F-35A Demo Team

2:50 p.m. – CF Snowbirds

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Sentencing delayed again for man behind Ditch-2 wildfire
stories.summary: Jason Halkett will have to wait at least a few more weeks to learn what type of sentence he will serve for starting the Ditch-2 wildfire last year after pleading guilty in April.
stories.author: Grace Miller
stories.content:
By Grace Miller Global News

Posted September 4, 2026 10:28 am

Updated September 4, 2026 11:12 am

A La Ronge man who sparked a massive wildfire north of Prince Albert last summer has had his sentencing date in court rescheduled a fourth consecutive time.

Jason Halkett will have to wait a few more weeks at least to learn what type of sentence he will serve for starting the Ditch-2 wildfire last year after pleading guilty in April.

The Ditch-2 wildfire was one of the many devastating fires of last year’s record-setting season, reaching 200, 000 hectares burned.

At the Montreal Lake Cree Nation Band Office, Halkett waited until 1 p.m. to hear that his sentencing would be postponed due to a lengthy court docket.

Crown Counsel Robyn Ermine and defense lawyer Evan Streiloff have said they are putting forward contested sentencing submissions

Halkett was arrested in August of last year months after the fire was first sparked in the Weyakwin area in May 2025.

The fire damaged structures and forced the evacuation of several communities.

Halkett has been remanded back into custody and is expected to be back in court September 17.

He could face up to a maximum of 14 years in prison.
paragraphs: By Grace Miller Global News
Posted September 4, 2026 10:28 am
Updated September 4, 2026 11:12 am
A La Ronge man who sparked a massive wildfire north of Prince Albert last summer has had his sentencing date in court rescheduled a fourth consecutive time.
Jason Halkett will have to wait a few more weeks at least to learn what type of sentence he will serve for starting the Ditch-2 wildfire last year after pleading guilty in April.
The Ditch-2 wildfire was one of the many devastating fires of last year’s record-setting season, reaching 200, 000 hectares burned.
At the Montreal Lake Cree Nation Band Office, Halkett waited until 1 p.m. to hear that his sentencing would be postponed due to a lengthy court docket.
Crown Counsel Robyn Ermine and defense lawyer Evan Streiloff have said they are putting forward contested sentencing submissions
Halkett was arrested in August of last year months after the fire was first sparked in the Weyakwin area in May 2025.
The fire damaged structures and forced the evacuation of several communities.
Halkett has been remanded back into custody and is expected to be back in court September 17.
He could face up to a maximum of 14 years in prison.

stories.title: Weapons, cellphones, drugs among $112K in contraband seized at N.B. prison
stories.summary: Seized items included handmade alcohol, edged weapons, vaping devices, cellphones, a USB key, and a USB card reader.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Correctional Service Canada (CSC) says it’s stepping up measures to prevent contraband from entering its prisons, and has recently seized packages at a maximum security institution in New Brunswick containing handmade alcohol, edged weapons, and cell phones.

The items were seized on Aug. 31 at Atlantic Institution in Renous, N.B., and also included hashish, tobacco, shatter (cannabis concentrate), vaping devices, a USB key, and a USB card reader.

In a Friday news release, CSC says the total estimated value of the items is $112,150.

To prevent drugs from entering institutions, CSC says it uses tools such as ion scanners and drug-detector dogs to search buildings, property, inmates, and visitors.

The federal agency has also set up an anonymous tip line at 1‑866‑780‑3784 for reporting contraband and activities at federal institutions.

“These activities May be related to drug use or trafficking that May threaten the safety and security of visitors, inmates, and staff members working at CSC institutions,” CSC said.

stories.title: Economy sheds 42,000 jobs, unemployment rate steady in August, says StatCan
stories.summary: StatCan said there was little change in the private sector and self-employment in August, but the public sector shed 20,000 positions in its third straight month of losses.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
The previously hot labour market stalled out to end the summer with a loss of 42,000 jobs in August, Statistics Canada said Friday.

The unemployment rate held steady at 6.4 per cent last month, the agency said.

August’s losses fell short of economists’ expectations for a gain of 15,000 positions.

2:01 Business Matters: Canada could lose 90,000 jobs due to new U.S. tariffs

It puts an end to a hot streak for the labour market that saw 181,000 jobs added from April through July. The unemployment rate had dropped by half a percentage point over the previous three months.

StatCan said there was little change in the private sector and self-employment in August, but the public sector shed 20,000 positions in its third straight month of losses.

The business, building and other support services sector led declines, followed by public administration, natural resources and utilities.

The manufacturing industry has been hit hard by U.S. tariffs but the sector proved to be a surprise pocket of strength in August with a gain of 22,000 jobs.

August’s job figures only partially capture impacts from a new wave of 50 per cent tariffs on about $28 billion worth of Canadian goods applied by the United States mid-month.

StatCan said the layoff rate – the proportion of people who were unemployed as the result of a layoff between July and August – was 0.8 per cent in August. That rate stood at one per cent a year ago and averaged 0.9 per cent for the same months in the three years before the COVID-19 pandemic.

2:19 Canadian premiers show united front as trade talks with US collapse

For industries reliant on export demand from the United States, StatCan said the layoff rate was marginally higher over the past 12 months when compared with other sectors.

The annual increase in average hourly wages cooled to two per cent in August, the agency said, down from 2.8 per cent in July and 3.3 per cent in June. The last time the annual wage increase was that low was November 2017.

Young workers aged 15 to 24 faced 19,000 job losses in August. Despite a tough end to the season, StatCan said this past summer jobs market was statistically better for youth than last year.

On average, the jobless rate for students returning to school in the fall stood at 15.9 per cent from May to August this year – two percentage points lower than the same period in 2025.

stories.title: Woman granted almost half of father's $1.8 million estate by judge after being cut out of will
stories.summary: Her dad left almost everything to her brother because he said she estranged herself from him
stories.author: Susan Lazaruk
stories.content:
A woman cut out of her father’s will because they were estranged has been awarded almost half of his estate by the B.C. Supreme Court.

The 2022 will of Daniel Dancey “did not make adequate, just and equitable provision for the proper maintenance and support” of Kristin Enes, according to Justice Judith Hoffman.

“His reasons for disinheriting her are not defensible,” she ruled.

Dancey’s son, Jeffery Dancey, opposed changing the will, which left almost all of the $1.8 million estate to him, maintaining his father had reason to leave nothing to his sister.

He also told the court that his father wanted him to inherit the estate because he lived in the basement of the house and helped him around the house.

Hoffman found that Jeffery Dancey was entitled to 55 per cent of the estate and Enes 45 per cent.

“Jeffery’s moral claim to the estate, in comparison to Kristin’s claim, is slightly enhanced due to the care he provided to Dan in the last years of his life,” she said in the decision.

The ruling outlined factors used to assess whether the deceased parent has a moral obligation to independent children. According to precedents, these include the relationship between parent and child, including “abandonment, neglect and estrangement by one or the other” and the reason for disinheriting a child, she said.

Others include the size of the estate, what each child contributed to the estate, the claimant’s reasonable expectations, standard of living, financial need, character and the needs of other beneficiaries.

“Misconduct can justify a disinheritance, but only when it is directed at the will maker and is relatively severe,” Hoffman wrote, citing a 2010 B.C. decision.

Court heard there were two periods of estrangement, which came after Enes allowed her mother to live with her after she separated from Dancey and, more recently, after Enes separated from her husband.

It heard Dancey was estranged from others in his life and that he had evicted his son from his basement suite at one point.

Enes testified that she had reconciled with her father in 2023, a year after the will was written, a view disputed by her brother.

Hoffman said she found Enes the more credible and reliable witness.

“Even if they had not reconciled, the weight of the evidence supports the conclusion that the estrangement was not caused by Kristin and, therefore, cannot constitute just cause to disinherit her.”

“The evidence demonstrates that the estrangement originated with Dan and his disappointment in Kristin’s divorce … not a valid and rational reason to disinherit her,” she ruled.

Hoffman said Enes is a single mother of three with a mortgage and her financial circumstances are “precarious” and “this factor weighs in favour of a variation.”

She acknowledged Jeffery Dancey made more contributions to the estate than Enes, but “not so overwhelming as to negate Dan’s moral obligation to provide for Kristin.”

The brother maintained his financial circumstances were worse than his sister’s because he does not own property and that he will have to move out of his father’s house if the estate were split.

He said he didn’t work because he chose instead to look after his father, who was suffering seizures in the years before he died.

But Hoffman found it was his choice to forgo more reliable forms of income and that his financial need “does not translate into a higher moral claim to the estate than Kristin.”

stories.title: Fixed mortgages rates rise, Toronto returns to office and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Sept. 4
stories.summary: Plus, this week’s lowest fixed and variable mortgage rates in Canada
stories.author: Moira Wyton
stories.content:
This week: What a steady interest rate and the trade war mean for your mortgage, and Toronto returns to the office. Plus, a city gets creative with multiplexes, and one property worth a look.

Despite nearly a year of steady key rates in Canada, uncertainty is the only thing potential buyers and mortgage shoppers can count on right now. The Bank of Canada this week held the benchmark at 2.25 per cent yet again, because, as Erica Alini reports , the latest exchange of tariffs with the U.S. has only heightened the two risks it’s balancing: inflation and a potential major economic slowdown.

“So far, that has meant stability for variable mortgage rates, which tends to move in tandem with the Bank of Canada’s policy rate,” Erica writes, but it’s not good news for every rate. “On the other hand, investors’ concerns about U.S. debt, inflation and the U.S.-Iran war are among the reasons for the recent global run-up in bond yields, which influence fixed-rate mortgages.”

Now you’d be hard pressed to find a fixed rate below the 4-per-cent mark, and as Rachelle Younglai reports , that’s already keeping buyers on the sidelines. Toronto home sales fell in August after five months of rebound, showing that the trade war May cancel out any confidence the steady rate decisions give buyers. Our coverage of the BoC’s decision has all the details, and here’s Erica’s guide to how Canada’s countertariffs might hit your wallet .

Has traffic seemed worse lately, or is your train to work really getting more crowded? If you’re in Toronto, it’s not just your imagination. Return-to-office mandates are bringing workers back to the downtown core – sometimes much to their chagrin – and transforming the urban economy in the process.

The reversal has been fast and shocking, as Jason Kirby, Rachelle Younglai and Vanmala Subramaniam report. Many of Toronto’s tallest towers are filled to the brim when, as recently as 15 months ago, blocks of their floors sat empty. Companies landlords once courted with steep discounts and perks are now competing for leases, turning corporate real-estate back into a landlord’s market.

But with many workers frustrated by long commute times and no desk space when they do come in, the return to office hasn’t been all smooth sailing. Read the team’s deep dive into how in-office mandates are reshaping Toronto’s downtown, and how employees are feeling about it.

Rates shown are the lowest available for each term/type and category (insured vs. uninsured) as of market close on Thursday, Sept. 3 .

Looking for a home that’s anything but cookie-cutter? Much-needed “missing middle” housing is starting to look a little different in Calgary, thanks to changing land-use policies that leave designers room to get creative.

After the city allowed densification on lots previously zoned for just one or two dwellings, about 5,000 standard row houses popped up in two years. As Ximena Gonzalez reports, that zoning’s requirements for height, footprint and setback can make the designs seem repetitive, and they’ve changed the face of some Calgary neighbourhoods.

But after the city rescinded that policy, designers told Ximena they’re taking advantage of other recent land-use classifications that offer the flexibility to build livable multi-family dwellings with character. From a window-filled design that spared mature trees to a low-rise building geared at seniors and students, these Calgary projects are breaking the mould .

If you – and your lower back – are tired of working from a kitchen stool or the couch, here’s a potential solution that won’t make your desk an eyesore. “ Cloffices ” are on the rise as people who work from home try to keep some semblance of work-life separation in smaller spaces.

But are they creative or claustrophobic? While working in a closet might make some feel like Harry Potter in his cupboard under the stairs, designers and people with cloffices told Matthew Hague the set-ups – if done right – are far from depressing. From folding desks in the pantry to built-in units that combine workspaces and storage, here are their expert tips and tricks to make a cloffice work .

55 Cochrane Dr., Brockville, Ont. – Full gallery here

Civil engineer Samuel Keefer built this Georgian home four years before selecting the plans for the Parliament Buildings in Ottawa, but you don’t have to be as technically minded as he was to appreciate the heritage details. Woodfield Manor – also sometimes called Butterfield Manor, after later owner George Butterfield – has been carefully restored to its original 1855 glory. And while not every heritage feature survived, those that remain continue to tell the home’s story.

Five marble fireplaces adorn the 6,000 square feet of living space, where the antique pine floors have been refurbished and ceilings soar high over original woodwork. Owners Debbie and Peter Lafrance thoughtfully reimagined the home as a hub for entertaining, adding modern features like a custom chef’s kitchen with large windows and heated black-and-white porcelain tiles in the entrance. But if you look closely, you’ll still see plenty of reminders of an earlier way of life, like the servant’s bell or the hitching post for horses outside.

The couple also spent long hours creating and mending a covered patio, in-ground pool, conservatory with motorized windows and a widow’s walk to enjoy the views of the Gananoque and the Thousand Islands area they’re both originally from. Atop the roof, the widow’s walk offers a perfect view of ships coming in and out of the harbour, and when sunset hits or bugs come out, they enjoyed taking cover in the conservatory with a glass of wine.

What do you think is the asking price for the property?

stories.title: Jann Arden to appear at pro-Canada concert ahead of Alberta separation vote
stories.summary: Jann Arden is set to join a cohort of Alberta performers for a free concert promoting national unity ahead of the province's fall referendum on quitting Canada.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted September 4, 2026 8:16 am

Jann Arden is set to join a cohort of Alberta performers for a free concert promoting national unity ahead of the province’s fall referendum on quitting Canada.

The Forever Canadian campaign says its “Calgary Concert for Unity” is to be held Sept. 20 at The Confluence Historic Site, also known as Fort Calgary.

Folk musicians Celeigh Cardinal, Reuben Bullock and John Wort Hannam, and jazz singer Caity Gyorgy are also set to perform.

A campaign news release says Alberta’s place is within Confederation and encourages people to gather as “loud and proud Canadians.”

The referendum on Oct. 19 is to ask Albertans, among other things, whether they wish to remain part of Canada or hold a second, binding vote on separating.

Those in favour of separation say Alberta doesn’t need Ottawa and is more than able to go it alone, while those opposed say Canada can work and that leaving could threaten Indigenous treaty rights.

stories.title: Pedestrian dies of injuries after collision in northwest London Wednesday night
stories.summary: London police say they are investigating a fatal crash involving a vehicle and a pedestrian Wednesday night in the city's northwest end.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London police say they are investigating a fatal crash involving a vehicle and a pedestrian Wednesday night in the city's northwest end.
· Posted: Sep 04, 2026 8:12 AM EDT | Last Updated: September 4
London police are investigating the crash and asking anyone who may have seen it or recorded it to come forward.(CBC)
London police say a pedestrian has died of their injuries after being struck by a vehicle late Wednesday night in the city's northwest end.

stories.title: Full lineup released for 2026 Forest City Film Festival
stories.summary: The cameras are rolling and London’s film community is taking centre stage.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
The cameras are rolling and London’s film community is taking centre stage.

“Tonight we’re announcing a variety of titles of films that we’re going to be screening at our festival in October,” said Matthew Downs with Forest City Film Festival. “They’re films that come from both here in southwestern Ontario and films from around the world.”

The 11th annual Forest City Film Festival will take place from October 15th to the 25th, celebrating community, culture, and cinema.

“There are so many creative people here doing stuff on a world level it would blow your mind,” said Rob McCallum, directory of ‘Faking Filmnation’. “Film fest is a great way to come check it out and celebrate it.”

Organizers said this year’s festival features a record-breaking 141 films.

“I spend the year watching out for films,” said Downs.

Executive Director of the festival, Ethan Hickey said this year will be like no other.

“We have the biggest films we’ve ever had this year,” said Hickey. “Also some really great locally made regional films.”

McCallum said there’s something for everyone in London’s film scene.

“Whether it’s loneliness, finding that hopeless love, or a cool documentary about saturday morning cartoons like ‘Faking Filmnation’ it doesn’t matter what it is,” said McCallum. “It’s a chance for London to come together on its own terms away from the big city of Toronto, Vancouver, or Montreal.”

Producer of ‘The Cage’, Ali Shareef said he wanted to create an action-packed film.

“It’s about a former gangster who becomes a vigilante and goes on to hunt the organization he was once apart of,” said Shareef. “That’s the whole concept of the story.”

Downs said while it’s hard to pick a favourite film, one in particular stands out.

“‘Club Kid’ is my number one thing that I’ve seen all year but there’s so many things it’s really hard to pick,” said Downs. “It’s like picking a favourite child.”

Showtimes and locations can be found on the festival’s website.

stories.title: What you need to know about insurance after major Ontario storm
stories.summary: Navigating insurance can be overwhelming as southern Ontario residents pick up the pieces after a destructive storm passed through on Wednesday.
stories.author: Ritika Dubey
stories.content:
By Ritika Dubey The Canadian Press

Posted September 4, 2026 8:04 am

Navigating insurance can be overwhelming as southern Ontario residents pick up the pieces after a destructive storm passed through on Wednesday.

Matt Hands, vice-president of insurance at Ratehub.CA, says to start by checking your insurance policy and figuring out whether your home or vehicle is covered for damages caused by the storm.

Hands says most standard home insurance policies should cover wind- and hail-related damages, but they May not cover flooding.

stories.title: Lawsuits, controversies and familiar faces fuel crowded Ward 3 election race
stories.summary: Incumbent Peter Cuddy faces five challengers in a race shaped by past disputes and competing visions for the ward.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
Lawsuits between candidates, anger management classes and town hall confrontations – Ward 3 is shaping up to have one of the more intriguing civic election races ahead of the October vote.

First-term incumbent Peter Cuddy is seeking another four-year mandate but he faces opposition from several prominent figures, including his Thames Valley District school board trustee successor Leroy Osbourne, video producer and content creator Ben Durham, and political consultant Zak Rahim, who had a legal dispute with Cuddy in late 2024.

“I’m a little surprised that there are so many candidates. But again, I welcome everybody to the race. And if there’s a better candidate, they can win – they should win,” Cuddy told The Free Press Thursday.

“But if they’re going to represent Ward 3, then they have to do the things that I’ve done. You’ve got to get out and work hard and work hard for the residents every day.”

The first-term councillor faced dual missteps in early 2025, including being removed from the library board for repeated absences. Most notably, CTV London reported on videos showing Rahim serving Cuddy legal papers in November 2024. Cuddy is recorded on video repeatedly cursing and lashing out at Rahim.

Cuddy, who previously apologized for the incident and signed up for anger management classes, says the legal issue was resolved. The integrity commissioner looked into the matter and found he had acted inappropriately, but did not recommend further sanctions, Cuddy said.

Speaking Thursday, Cuddy said he loves the job – particularly resolving constituent issues in the community. He points to his tabling of a proposed bylaw in 2024 to protect tenants from bad faith “renovictions” as one example.

The proposed bylaw targeting the improper use of a type of eviction notice that requires tenants to vacate their unit for extensive repairs or renovations was unanimously approved.

Nominations close with 110 candidates in London civic election

Will London voters consider 'strong mayor' powers in this fall's civic election?

Cuddy said his priorities are cutting red tape at city hall, addressing homelessness and keeping property taxes low. He argues large increases over the current city council term have put the city in a good fiscal position to avoid further hikes.

“I will not support a property tax hike again, like we did last time. Our budget’s in good condition, our reserve funds are good – we don’t have to do that again,” Cuddy said.

Cuddy said he holds no ill will or animosity toward Rahim and wishes him the best during the campaign.

Rahim acknowledged the past incident, but told The Free Press he is “not concerned about the past” or his opponents.

He believes he brings a unique perspective to city hall. He points to his experience with city hall processes as a consultant and volunteer work as an ambulance responder, where he has seen the addictions and homelessness crisis up close.

“I think Londoners really want some change, they want new, fresh blood and new ideas at city council,” Rahim said. “As a young person, I believe I represent that as well.”

His platform is based on four pillars: better roads and transit; greater public accountability; respecting taxpayers, including reversing the council pay raise; and housing, specifically greater protections for renters.

“I’ve been seeing the homelessness crisis grow on our street in real time, and I think as a city, we’re not taking enough action to protect renters, keeping them in their homes and protecting them,” Rahim said.

Durham was the first registered candidate for Ward 3, signing up on the day nominations opened for the Oct. 26 election.

He made headlines in September 2025 when he documented Ward 4 Coun. Susan Stevenson preventing him from recording one of her town hall meetings in a viral video viewed millions of times. The integrity commissioner has since cleared Stevenson of wrongdoing in the matter.

Not long after registering, Durham posted what he described as a “tongue-in-cheek” meme to Reddit referencing the controversy, saying he planned to allow recordings of his town hall meetings.

He said his overall platform includes better city communications, including through town halls.

“I’ve heard at the doors, people would like to be more engaged, but they don’t know what is happening within their communities or within London as a whole,” he said.

Durham’s other three campaign pillars include homelessness, fiscal responsibility and “smarter traffic and safer streets,” which includes better construction co-ordination and traffic calming – two issues he said he has repeatedly heard about while canvassing by electric bike.

On homelessness, Durham said that, if elected, he would like to seek a position on the board of the Association of Municipalities of Ontario and advocate for more sustainable homelessness and addictions funding from the province.

As for the competitiveness of the race, Durham said he is focused solely on his campaign, putting on “blinders” when it comes to other candidates and races.

Also in the race is Leroy Osbourne, who succeeded Cuddy as Thames Valley District school board trustee representing wards 2 through 6 in 2022. The board was placed under provincial supervision last year, stripping trustees, including Osbourne, of their powers.

Osbourne did not respond to a request for comment from The Free Press before publication. His platform released Wednesday focuses on three areas: housing and home ownership, infrastructure, and transit and traffic.

“The city can’t fix everything on its own. There are struggles here where we need more help from senior levels of government,” he wrote. “I think there are proven and better ways to go about what is in front of us.”

Osbourne’s platform promotes ideas used in other cities, such as predictive software for identifying infrastructure repairs, a rent-to-own program for prospective homeowners and on-demand minibuses to connect residents of several Ward 3 neighbourhoods to bus routes, including bus rapid transit.

Also running for council in Ward 3 are Harkirat Kaur and Riya Philip. A candidates debate for the ward, organized by the Urban League of London, is scheduled for Oct. 1.

stories.title: A Brockville home steeped in history
stories.summary: Woodfield Manor was built in 1855 for railway engineer Samuel Keefer
stories.author: Hannah Alper
stories.content:
55 Cochrane Dr., Brockville, Ont.

Asking Price: $2,239,000

Taxes: $12,860 (2025)

Lot Size: 0.82 acres

Agents: Natalie Sobhie, Re/Max Boardwalk Realty Ltd., Brokerage

When Debbie Lafrance and her husband, Peter, walked through the Brockville home they would eventually buy in 2021 – the peak of COVID-19 bidding wars – its Georgian grandeur was there. It just needed to be uncovered.

The couple is originally from Gananoque and the Thousand Islands area – where the Woodfield Manor, 55 Cochrane Dr., sits – and they were looking for a place to retire. The curved driveway, the marble fireplaces, the light streaming through the windows and the in-ground pool appealed to Ms. Lafrance, who loves to swim in the summer.

“By the end of the weekend, we were putting in an offer,” said Ms. Lafrance.

The Georgian-style home is steeped in history. Built in 1855 for Samuel Keefer – the civil and railway engineer behind the Brockville & Ottawa Railway and the city’s railway tunnel – the estate later belonged to George Butterfield, whose family donated part of the grounds to create the close-by Butterfield Park. This is why the home is sometimes called Butterfield Manor, depending on who you talk to. Walking in, realtor Natalie Sobhie said, you can feel there’s a story behind it. The five marble fireplaces, soaring ceilings, and original woodwork have survived, as have reminders of an earlier way of life. There is a self-contained secondary suite with its own driveway and separate address that once belonged to the butler. There’s a bell for the servant. And outside, a hitching post where horses once waited by the stables.

But some parts of the home had not aged gracefully.

“The staircase when we moved in was all finished with pink carpet and peach tile, probably from the eighties,” Ms. Lafrance laughs. Rather than gutting and renovating the historic house, they set out to restore it to its original grandeur. With long hours dedicated to creating and mending a covered patio, an in-ground pool, a conservatory and a widow’s walk, she and her husband put in the work to make the house feel like a home.

“We said, ‘Okay, what can we save? What can we restore? What can we put back to its original?’” Ms. Lafrance said. “And then we worked from there.”

While the original stone façade and Georgian proportions were preserved, the couple thoughtfully reimagined the almost 6,000-square-foot home. They had the original pine floors refinished and added a custom chef’s kitchen, with a Dacor gas range and a waterfall island. Heated black-and-white porcelain flooring was installed in the entrance hall beneath a dramatic 16-light chandelier.

Ms. Lafrance designed the kitchen with entertaining in mind. In addition to the high-end appliances, large windows flood the room with natural light. A door opens onto the outdoor patio space.

One of the couple’s favourite parts of the home is the widow’s walk that adorns the rooftop. It’s the ideal spot to see the boats coming in and out of the harbour.

Ms. Lafrance also loves the light-filled conservatory, which has been equipped with motorized windows. It has become a hub for visiting friends and family. At sunset, the covered conservatory brings in the view and leaves out the bugs.

“It’s a room where you can sit there and watch the sunsets with a glass of wine,” said Ms. Lafrance.

stories.title: Two offers for B.C. ranch-style home due for an update
stories.summary: Three-bedroom home on a large lot in Tsawwassen was built in 1981, but has ‘good bones,’ listing agent says
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
748 Juniper Place, Tsawwassen, B.C.

Asking price: $1,499,000 (June 15)

Selling price: $1,400,000 (Aug. 10)

Taxes: $5,885.29 (2025)

Days on market: 56

Listing agent: Dwayne Launt, Oakwyn Realty

This ranch-style home sits on a large 6,727-square-foot lot in Tsawwassen’s Forest by the Bay neighbourhood, on a quiet street among well-maintained homes.

Built in 1981, and in original condition, the three-bedroom home with 2½ bathrooms has “good bones,” listing agent Dwayne Launt said. But it needs extensive updates, including replacement of carpeted and [tiled] floors, a new kitchen and new bathrooms.

The nearly 3,000-square-foot, one-level house with attached garage was well maintained by the previous owners and could easily be lived in without updates, he added. The landscaping is mature, lush and low maintenance. The property is in a suburban area and not considered easily walkable to the shops.

The sellers had power of attorney for their parents and no one was living in the home when it was listed, Mr. Launt said. That made it easy to show to the many people who viewed it.

“There were lots and lots of showings – lots of young families and folks looking towards getting out of a multilevel home and into a rancher,” he said. “Everything is on one level, and everything was working perfectly. You could easily live there without doing a single thing. But young families are looking for a more modern look. A lot of people don’t want to do the updates.”

The sellers received two offers, but the first offer collapsed. The sellers accepted the second offer.

“We felt the price was in line,” Mr. Launt said. “And because it’s an estate sale, they wanted to move on.”

“Everyone wants hardwood floors and new cabinets. Once you get into stuff like that, it can cost a lot of money,” the listing agent said.

“But this had a big lot, a great layout, and it was in a great neighbourhood.”

The sale completed on Sept. 4.

stories.title: Cleanup continues after destructive Ontario thunderstorms, hail
stories.summary: The number of southern Ontario homes and businesses remaining in the dark is much lower today as crews worked to restore power after destructive thunderstorms this week.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted September 4, 2026 7:49 am

The number of southern Ontario homes and businesses remaining in the dark is much lower today as crews worked to restore power after destructive thunderstorms this week.

Dangerous thunderstorms and high winds ripped out trees, tore down power lines and flooded major streets as more than 100 millimetres of rain fell in some areas Wednesday.

Toronto fire officials reported just shy of 1,500 calls over a 24-hour period, which they said was their second-highest call volume in a day, after the 2013 ice storm.

City manager Paul Johnson called it a “100-year storm” that caused widespread destruction in Toronto and the surrounding areas.

Among the most damaged structures was the 50,000-capacity Rogers Stadium in Toronto’s north end, where bleachers were ripped out by high winds that also left behind partially collapsed grandstands.

The Northern Tornadoes Project says the damage in Toronto appears to have been caused by downbursts.

stories.title: Crash involving motorcycle, passenger vehicle closes intersection near Aylmer
stories.summary: Motorists are being advised to avoid the area and use alternate routes while the road closures remain in effect.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A crash between a motorcycle and a passenger vehicle has forced the closure of John Wise Line and Imperial Road in Malahide, south of Aylmer.

John Wise Line is closed between Rogers Road and Hacienda Road. Imperial Road is closed between Van Patter Line and Calton Line, while crews respond to the scene.

No further information about the number of people involved or the extent of any injuries was immediately available.

Motorists are being advised to avoid the area and use alternate routes while the road closures remain in effect.

stories.title: Only 1 person charged after RCMP dismantle Canada’s largest super lab
stories.summary: Gaganpreet Singh Randhawa pleaded guilty in B.C. Supreme Court to several drug-trafficking and firearms-related charges.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
An enormous drug seizure at a rural property near Falkland in 2024 is back in the spotlight after a guilty plea in B.C. Supreme Court on Wednesday.

Gaganpreet Singh Randhawa pleaded guilty in B.C. Supreme Court to several drug-trafficking and firearms-related charges.

Randhawa is the only person to have been charged in connection with the massive operation so far.

“It’s just you know unbelievable to think that this one guy is running all of that and that the police were able to obtain a search warrant based on the information that they had, and that only one guy was the only name that came up and involved in this,” said Bryan Tepper, Conservative MLA for Surrey-Panorama and shadow minister for the solicitor general.

Tepper, who is also a retired RCMP officer himself, fears that those at the bottom of criminal organizations are being prosecuted while those who are running and financing them remain untouched.

“It’s almost a low hanging fruit that we have to, we got to charge somebody. That guy was there,” Tepper said.

Rob Dhanu, a former federal crown prosecutor, said those at the top of these kinds of organizations insulate themselves.

“So just like a CEO is not going to be in the trenches of the business that they’re involved in, those at the very top level have individuals at the mid-level and lower-level who are setting up the operation, they’re producing the drugs, they’re distributing the drugs,” Dhanu said.

“With Mr. Randhawa, what we likely have here is someone who is doing the dirty work and was likely at the mid to lower level of the organization, which is much easier for police to investigate and then to successfully arrest.”

Dhanu added that these types of investigations are challenging and can take years.

“We’re talking about investigators that would be numbered in the dozens who are trying to coordinate their efforts. There’s surveillance. There’s individuals getting warrants out there. There’s individuals who are on the back end, filtering through all the reports and putting them all together in a manner that makes sense,” Dhanu said.

“While drugs fall under federal policing,” Tepper said, “the province plays a part too and needs to boost court resources so that more people are held accountable.

“We’re not administering the courts the way we should be. You know, we do have the responsibility to do administration of justice,” Tepper said.

RCMP say the investigation into this case is ongoing but so far no other arrests have been made.

“The police are still going to see this as a success because it’s very, very rare for an entire organization, all the tiers, to be dismantled,” Dhanu said.

“So the fact that they’ve taken down this massive lab, they prevented all these drugs from hitting the streets. That’s still a success.”

Randhawa will be back in court in early 2027 for sentencing.

stories.title: The lingering importance of public spaces
stories.summary: Parks are not just the leftover gaps between buildings, but a place for citizens to encounter one another
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
This summer, the Esplanade Tranquille in Montreal was full of people lingering in the shade, relaxing on benches under maple trees and watching the crowd. A nearby café spilled out onto the square. People stopped without having anywhere particular to go.

People are always lingering there. Completed in 2022, Esplanade Tranquille occupies a former parking lot. In winter, a refrigerated rink fills the square with skaters. The space forms part of the Quartier des spectacles, Montreal’s long-running effort to make downtown a place to spend time rather than simply a place to pass through. The nearby café provides changing facilities, cool drinks in summer and, in winter, hot chocolate and blankets.

Canada has spent decades treating public space as the leftover gaps between buildings, but that is changing. Montreal, Edmonton and Toronto have recently shown that governments can make parks that become part of daily life in a city.

That task is becoming both harder, and more important, as public space is seen by some as a source of danger, and society becomes more atomized.

Public places are where citizens encounter one another. The Canadian urbanist Ken Greenberg has argued that shared public space helps “make democracy work” in diverse societies.

That May sound grand for a park or square; it is not. People who live in the same city increasingly occupy separate worlds. They May live in different neighbourhoods, work in different places, and socialize on their phones. Public space gives people a place to meet across lines of geography, background and class.

Toronto has gained such a place with this summer’s expansion of Biidaasige Park on its waterfront. The expanded park surrounds the naturalized Don River with wetlands, beautifully designed gardens, public art and places to get close to the water. (It lacks only a café.)

Montreal has been building social places for years. In Plateau Mont-Royal, Place des Fleurs-de-Macadam creates a friendly hangout: benches, lush perennial gardens, a water feature.

Edmonton offers another example. Under City Architect Carol Bélanger, the city produced a remarkable succession of civic buildings and public spaces. Its new downtown O-day’min Park has transformed former parking lots into a 1.8-hectare public landscape.

The parks themselves are only part of the story. Their success also tells us something about how governments should work.

In Toronto, the agency Waterfront Toronto has an explicit agenda to “lead with landscape.” In 2007, it ran a design competition for the billion-dollar project of reshaping the mouth of the Don River.

The landscape architects Michael Van Valkenburgh Associates won with a bold scheme to bring back vanished wetlands in an expanded system of parks. This would serve as flood protection and allow building homes for thousands of people. It worked: Along a rebuilt river, today people are fishing, kayaking and simply hanging out.

Waterfront Toronto uses design competitions and other tools to choose designers for the quality of their ideas. It does not treat the lowest price as the definition of value. And the organization has people and processes, including a design review panel, that allow it to follow through.

Montreal has developed similar expertise through its Bureau du design, which helps city departments manage the procurement of major public projects. And Edmonton has done something similar through its city architect’s office. Since Mr. Belanger took his role in 2009, he has responded to former mayor Stephen Mandel’s demand for “no more crap.” The city has produced fine libraries, recreation centres and parks by some of Canada’s top designers.

Someone inside government has to care about design, to understand it, and keep caring about a place after it is built. Usually, parks and public buildings suffer from a lack of vision. There is no coherent idea and there is no one in charge.

Today, Canadian cities face enormous pressure to build housing. But they also need to build – and to rebuild and care for – the spaces in between.

Montreal, Edmonton and Waterfront Toronto have shown how this can be done. The question is whether others will treat their successes as exceptions or learn from them.

stories.title: Copper thieves emboldened by demolitions along Wellington for BRT construction
stories.summary: The owner of a small commercial plaza believes the demolition of buildings on either side of his property to accommodate widening Wellington Road for Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) lanes has emboldened thieves and vandals to target his building.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
The owner of a small commercial plaza believes the demolition of buildings on either side of his property to accommodate widening Wellington Road for Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) lanes has emboldened thieves and vandals to target his building.

On Monday morning, Pramod Kukadia was notified by a tenant of the yellow-brick plaza that the air conditioning in their unit wasn’t working.

A repair crew discovered that two roof-top commercial Hvac units had been destroyed by thieves for what Kukadia estimates was less than a hundred dollars worth of copper components.

Buying two new units and installing them with a crane could cost over $50,000.

“These units are tens of thousands of dollars to replace, (and) the two tenants won’t have any air conditioning for a short period of time,” he tells CTV News.

During the night, the copper thieves used a maintenance ladder mounted to the side of the plaza to get on the roof.

“There’s a gate on it with a lock, but they cut the lock off,” explains a disheartened Kukadia. “Some of my (Hvac contractors) told me that there were other units (damaged) nearby as well. So it’s probably a group of people.”

In preparation for widening the road, the City of London acquired and subsequently demolished a stretch of houses and commercial buildings on either side of the plaza at 100 Wellington Rd.

However, because the plaza building is sufficiently setback from the curb, it wasn’t acquired by city hall.

“There’s nobody around here watching at night now, so it’s kind of free wheeling for (thieves),” Kukadia argued.

He says recently a daycare in his plaza had its playground equipment stolen by thieves who cut through a chain link fence.

Problems with graffiti have also grown worse since the neighbouring buildings along the east side of Wellington were razed.

Kukadia previously owned Curry’s restaurant next door before it was acquired by the city and demolished.

He’s now taking costly steps to protect his plaza, “We’ve got security coming in every night, multiple times a night. We’ve installed some cameras and sensors up on the roof so if anybody goes up we will be notified right away.”

Construction of the final section of BRT along Wellington Road, between Watson Street and Base Line Road, officially began on Sept. 2.

“There’s nobody around here watching at night now, so it’s kind of free wheeling for (thieves),” Kukadia argued.
He says recently a daycare in his plaza had its playground equipment stolen by thieves who cut through a chain link fence.
Problems with graffiti have also grown worse since the neighbouring buildings along the east side of Wellington were razed.
Kukadia previously owned Curry’s restaurant next door before it was acquired by the city and demolished.

He’s now taking costly steps to protect his plaza, “We’ve got security coming in every night, multiple times a night. We’ve installed some cameras and sensors up on the roof so if anybody goes up we will be notified right away.”
Construction of the final section of BRT along Wellington Road, between Watson Street and Base Line Road, officially began on Sept. 2.

content_blocks.text: The owner of a small commercial plaza believes the demolition of buildings on either side of his property to accommodate widening Wellington Road for Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) lanes has emboldened thieves and vandals to target his building.
On Monday morning, Pramod Kukadia was notified by a tenant of the yellow-brick plaza that the air conditioning in their unit wasn’t working.
A repair crew discovered that two roof-top commercial Hvac units had been destroyed by thieves for what Kukadia estimates was less than a hundred dollars worth of copper components.
Buying two new units and installing them with a crane could cost over $50,000.
“These units are tens of thousands of dollars to replace, (and) the two tenants won’t have any air conditioning for a short period of time,” he tells CTV News.
During the night, the copper thieves used a maintenance ladder mounted to the side of the plaza to get on the roof.

“There’s a gate on it with a lock, but they cut the lock off,” explains a disheartened Kukadia. “Some of my (Hvac contractors) told me that there were other units (damaged) nearby as well. So it’s probably a group of people.”

stories.title: Business Brief: Behind the back-to-office numbers
stories.summary: Downtown Toronto’s towers are rapidly filling up
stories.author: Jason Kirby
stories.content:
Good morning. Labour Day is approaching, which means back to the grind for a lot of people – and increasingly, back to the office instead of working from home. We’ll unpack how return-to-office mandates are helping revive downtown Toronto’s office market, and its economy.

Mining: Iron ore giant Vale is shelving the planned IPO of its base-metals unit as the Brazilian government presses the company to retain control of its assets, sources say.

Trains: Ottawa will spend $4.7-billion to manufacture and maintain hundreds of Via Rail passenger cars at Ontario and Quebec facilities, eschewing imports from the United States.

Tech: Open AI, Anthropic and other major AI firms agreed to a new federal framework for data-centre development as local objection to the centres mounts.

Programming note

There will be no newsletter on Monday, Sept. 7 as the team takes a break for Labour Day. However, our website will be staffed throughout the long weekend so please

. We’ll be back in your inbox on Tuesday. Enjoy your long weekend.

Hi, I’m Jason Kirby, an economics reporter with The Globe.

If you’ve spent time in downtown Toronto lately, you’ll have noticed the area has got a lot of its buzz back after a prolonged pandemic slump. Restaurants and coffee shops are bustling again, as is the underground path network that links the city’s skyscrapers.

Behind the shimmering glass facades of those buildings, there’s been tremendous change over the past year, with many of the largest, premium towers swinging from a glut of empty space to the tightest commercial real estate market in years.

My colleagues and I dug into the numbers. Real estate reporter Rachelle Younglai and labour reporter Vanmala Subramaniam joined me in writing our Saturday long read to understand what’s happening in the world of work.

The race for space

Back in May, 2024, The Globe tapped commercial real estate firm CoStar Group to crunch the vacancy and availability numbers on the 47 large office towers in downtown Toronto. One in three buildings were sitting one-fifth empty, and several were only half full.

We revisited those same buildings with CoStar again, and most of that empty space has been grabbed by companies – especially banks – scrambling to find enough room for their employees. As real estate advisers and others repeatedly told us, the power balance has swung hard from a market in which tenants could set the terms to a landlord’s market.

The memo heard across Bay Street

Another power dynamic has flipped – the one between employers and workers – and it directly explains everything we’re seeing.

As far back as 2022 and 2023, there were grumblings among businesses and bank executives about the Zoom economy, and about all of us office drones attending meetings in dress shirts and pajama bottoms. The banks called on their employees to spend two to three days in the office, but the uptake was slow.

Then in May last year, Royal Bank of Canada sent a memo informing its employees they’d need to be back at their desks four days a week, starting that September. Other banks and businesses quickly followed suit.

By then, unemployment rates were on the rise, job vacancy numbers had plummeted, and forces including the Canada-U.S. trade war and the rise of artificial intelligence were leaving workers uneasy about their job security.

But the downtown rebound isn’t all stick and no carrot. Return-to-office mandates created a critical mass of people downtown on a regular basis, providing a gravitational draw for other workers. And as several younger employees told us, there’s career value to being seen in the office – even if it means shelling out money again for lunches and commuting.

Not all office markets are alike

Not all cities have seen the same rebound. Vacancy rates in large office buildings in Vancouver and Montreal have levelled off, but are still higher than before the pandemic. By the vacancy metric, Calgary’s core has recovered to pre-pandemic levels, but the city was already dealing with a glut of empty space in 2019.

Even in the broader Toronto area and nearby smaller cities, office vacancies remain elevated.

But to the extent that any other parts of the country want to take their cue from Toronto, Hogtown’s downtown experience shows there’s a path back to something akin to the economic vibrancy cities offered before the pandemic.

Canada’s new $20 bill features a vertical portrait of King Charles, an image of the Canadian National Vimy Memorial and unique security properties, Ian Bailey writes . It’ll enter circulation in February.

“The food industry is more than just feeding Canadians – it’s an economic engine with still so much room to grow. To see that level of commitment was really exciting.” — James Donaldson, chief executive officer at BC Food & Beverage

Industry associations in B.C. and Manitoba have pitched the construction of regional food terminals that would lessen reliance on American trade. Their proposals follow the rollout of Ottawa’s National Food Security Strategy, which pledged $3-billion over a decade to enhance domestic processing and grocery competition, Mariya Postelnyak and Susan Krashinsky Robertson report .

Earnings: Ski-Doo maker BRP Inc. raised its financial forecast for the year, while apparel maker Lululemon’s outlook continued to deteriorate .

CPTPP: The 12-country Trans-Pacific trade pact is serving as Canada’s insurance policy against Donald Trump’s economic coercion, Rita Trichur writes .

Basketball: Kawhi Leonard’s pending return to the Toronto Raptors reflects well on MLSE, which refused to indulge his uncle’s outlandish demands, argues Andrew Willis .

Global markets were mixed ahead of key U.S. payrolls data and August jobs numbers on this side of the border.

Wall Street futures were muted with the Dow pointing lower, while TSX futures were little changed.

Overseas, the pan-European STOXX 600 was up 0.02 per cent in morning trading. Britain’s FTSE 100 slipped 0.05 per cent, Germany’s DAX climbed 0.11 per cent and France’s CAC 40 declined 0.05 per cent.

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei closed 1.26 per cent higher, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 1.74 per cent.

The Canadian dollar traded at 72.45 U.S. cents.

stories.title: Warm temperatures, improving conditions expected for southern Ontario Friday
stories.summary: The chance of showers and thunderstorms continues across southern Ontario Friday, but conditions are expected to improve through the afternoon, according to CTV London meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
The chance of showers and thunderstorms continues across southern Ontario Friday, but conditions are expected to improve through the afternoon, according to CTV London meteorologist Julie Atchison.

“The risk for showers will drop off as we head into the late afternoon,” Atchison said.

A few showers are expected Friday morning as a stationary boundary continues to bring rain and thunderstorms to the region. Rain could linger around the noon hour in London before conditions shift to a mix of sun and cloud.

Temperatures will reach 26 C in the afternoon, feeling closer to 31 with the humidex.

A 40 per cent chance of light showers is expected Saturday, but the rain is not expected to last long.

Sunday is expected to bring full sunshine, while Monday will see a mix of sun and cloud with a high of 25 C.

The weather will remain pleasant Tuesday, with a mix of sun and cloud and a high of 25 C. The risk of scattered showers and thunderstorms returns Wednesday and Thursday.
