stories.title: New poll finds Toronto viewed as one of Canada’s least safe cities
stories.summary: The study tested 15 cities and found Toronto ranks second‑lowest on net safety at –18, ahead only of Winnipeg at –28.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Lucas Casaletto

Posted September 3, 2026 5:58 am.

Toronto is facing the largest safety‑reputation penalty of any major Canadian city, according to a new national public‑perception study that suggests the country’s biggest urban centre is viewed as far less safe than its crime‑severity data would indicate.

A new Liaison Strategies survey , released Thursday, finds 57 per cent of Canadians consider Toronto somewhat or very unsafe, compared with 39 per cent who say it is safe.

Only Winnipeg fares worse, with 59 per cent calling it unsafe. The results also concluded that Toronto’s negative rating has also worsened over time — up five points from 52 per cent in 2017.

The study looked at 15 Canadian cities and found Toronto ranks second‑lowest in net safety, at –18, ahead only of Winnipeg at –28.

But when you look at official Crime Severity Index (CSI) data, Toronto sits much lower on the national list, meaning its crime severity is not among the worst. That contrast creates what researchers call Canada’s largest “reputational penalty”; the gap between Toronto’s relatively moderate crime‑severity ranking and the far more negative way Canadians perceive the city’s safety.

Liaison says the gap is politically and economically significant: only 12 per cent of respondents say crime statistics are the main factor shaping their impression of city safety. Instead, perceptions are driven by news coverage, personal experience, word of mouth, and national image.

Among the cities tested, negative perceptions cluster around the country’s largest urban centres:

Winnipeg — 59 per cent unsafe

Toronto — 57 per cent unsafe

Vancouver — 52 per cent unsafe

Edmonton — 50 per cent unsafe

Saskatoon — 45 per cent unsafe

Montreal — 41 per cent unsafe

Regina — 37 per cent unsafe

Calgary — 35 per cent unsafe

At the other end of the spectrum, Quebec City (+57), Ottawa (+56) and Charlottetown (+51) lead the country in net safety.

David Valentin, Principal at Liaison Strategies, says Toronto’s perception gap is the defining feature of the study.

“Toronto has a public‑safety reputation problem. It is not just that 57 per cent of Canadians call Toronto unsafe. It is that Toronto is being perceived almost the same way as Winnipeg, even though the official crime‑severity picture is not the same.”

Valentin says Winnipeg’s perception aligns with its crime‑severity data, while Toronto’s does not — creating the largest reputational penalty among all cities tested.

“Residents, visitors, investors, students, and businesses do not respond only to police‑reported crime statistics. They also respond to what they think a city feels like.”

stories.title: Bank of Canada set to unveil redesigned $20 bill featuring King Charles
stories.summary: Royal Canadian Mint has produced coins featuring King Charles since 2023
stories.author: The Canadian Press staff
stories.content:
For the first time in more than 70 years, a new monarch will appear on Canada’s $20 bill.

The Bank of Canada unveiled the new banknote on Thursday during a ceremony in Ottawa.

The bill features a linework image of King Charles III executed by Canadian engraver Jorge Rodrigo Peral based on a 2024 photograph taken by Andrew Parsons, a British photographer, for the currency. The King’s portrait is displayed vertically on the bill.

Charles became King after the 2022 death of his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, whose time on the $20 banknote has now exceeded the length of her record-breaking 70-year reign. Work on the new banknote began on the day of King Charles’ coronation, May 6, 2023, according to a Bank of Canada official speaking on background ahead of the unveiling.

The Bank of Canada has unveiled the design for the country's newest $20 note, which features King Charles III for the first time.

The Canadian Press

The back of the bill features an image of the Canadian National Vimy Memorial in France. About 3,600 Canadians died at the Battle of Vimy Ridge in 1917 during the First World War.

Circulation of the new $20 bill is scheduled to begin next February.

It’s the second vertical banknote produced by the Bank of Canada after the $10 note, which features Viola Desmond, a civil-rights pioneer and businesswoman from Nova Scotia. It was unveiled in 2018.

Since 1937, when King George VI first appeared on the $20 banknote early in his reign, all of Canada’s $20 bills have featured likenesses of Canada’s monarchs.

As an eight-year-old princess, the future Queen Elizabeth was first featured on the Bank of Canada’s inaugural $20 banknote in 1935, before her portrait was replaced by her father’s. She returned to the $20 bill in 1954, after ascending to the throne in 1952.

“Her image became one of the most recognizable on our currency for generations of Canadians. Today, this tradition continues with His Majesty King Charles III, who is appearing on a Canadian banknote for the first time,” Governor-General Louise Arbour told the unveiling ceremony on Thursday.

Ms. Arbour said Canadian banknotes are more than just a form of payment.

“They reflect our history, our realities and the significant achievements of our collective journey,” she said. “Our currency affirms our sovereignty and our determination to define ourselves in the eyes of the world on our terms.”

Tiff Macklem, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, said at Thursday’s unveiling that the bill will feature new security features to prevent counterfeiting.

These include a purple security stripe that appears to spin and transform when the bill is moved. The stripe, which is difficult to reproduce, has been used elsewhere in the world but is making its debut in Canada with the new $20 banknote.

“Our new $20 note is both visually stunning and more secure than ever,” Mr. Macklem said.

Ahead of the bill’s rollout in 2027, the bank will hold discussions with law enforcement agencies and financial institutions to raise awareness of its security features, Mr. Macklem said.

Of the Vimy Ridge imagery on the banknote, Mr. Macklem noted that his grandfather, also named Tiff, was a lieutenant in the Canadian military who served as a liaison officer during the battle.

“Fortunately – as evidenced by my standing here before you – my grandfather returned home to Canada. Many did not,” he said.

He noted that the Vimy Memorial, which he personally saw during a visit to France earlier this summer, is a symbol of sacrifice.

“The soaring pillars and solemn sculptures honour those who gave their lives to protect freedom, peace and democracy,” he said.

stories.title: Guerrero Jr. looks like himself again as Blue Jays win big over Guardians
stories.summary: Finally, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. got under one and hit it a long way. Beside home plate at Progressive Field, Guerrero Jr. stood and watched as the ball soared down the left-field line. It stayed fair, clearing the wall by a wide margin, and Guerrero Jr. could begin his first home run trot in nearly a month. More […]
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Finally, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. got under one and hit it a long way.

Beside home plate at Progressive Field, Guerrero Jr. stood and watched as the ball soared down the left-field line. It stayed fair, clearing the wall by a wide margin, and Guerrero Jr. could begin his first home run trot in nearly a month.

More importantly, the three-run homer gave the Blue Jays a 6-0 lead and some reason for optimism as they push for the playoffs. That swing — one of three big ones for Guerrero Jr. Wednesday — helped the Blue Jays beat the Guardians 11-0 and climb back to within 1.5 games of Cleveland in the American League wild-card standings.

“That was nice,” said manager John Schneider. “I’ve been behind him the entire year and will continue to be, but I think that was a little bit of a deep breath for him and a deep breath for everyone. Hopefully he can stay right there.”

Dylan Cease lowered his season ERA to 2.25 with six innings of scoreless baseball, and Josh Smith added a solo home run in the eighth as the Blue Jays improved to 69-71 on the season, but this game was all about Guerrero Jr.

In a season of many lows for the 27-year-old, this game was a high point. To this point, the production just hasn’t been there — and ultimately, he’s accountable for those results. Within the last week, he’s heard boos at Rogers Centre.

Still, that doesn’t mean it’s been easy for Guerrero Jr. Midway through the season, he tried to work his way out of the slump, taking upwards of 300 swings per day. Later, he opted for rest, skipping the All-Star Game to help with lingering back and hamstring soreness.

All the while, the questions about his performance intensified. That’s part of the job at this level — but in ways it’s a new challenge for Guerrero Jr., who has never struggled like this before. Along the way, he’s had to learn new ways to handle these struggles.

“He talks to his teammates about it,” Schneider said recently. “He’s open about it.”

And the way Schneider sees it, the more Guerrero Jr. talks to his teammates about it, the better. They’re all pulling for him. They all respect him. Lean into it.

“And Vlad’s good at lying,” Schneider continued. “He’s good at saying, ‘No, I’m good.’ And you have to keep asking and break down that wall a little bit.”

Once you do?

“He’s way more honest with me and the guys than probably he leads on to the media,” Schneider said. “But yeah, he’s frustrated for sure. (And) he’s more aware of it probably than you guys know.”

If so, the swings Guerrero Jr. took Wednesday must have offered him plenty of relief. Along with the no-doubt home run, he contributed an RBI double that nearly left the park, as well as an opposite-field RBI single.

While Guerrero Jr. declined to speak to writers after the game, Schneider expressed confidence that a game like this could provide some momentum for his first baseman.

“You never know where the mental game takes you in this long season, you know?” Schneider said Wednesday. “Mentally, you have to be tough, and mentally, you have to focus on what’s important in the moment. And I think Vlad’s doing a good job right now of working on that.”

It was the first three-hit game since July 25 for Guerrero Jr., who drove in five, a season best. It’s hard to quantify, but he looked like himself again.

Meanwhile, it was with games like this in mind that Cease chose to sign in Toronto, and he enjoyed his first taste of September baseball with his new team.

“It felt great,” the right-hander said. “I’m not really trying to think about all that when I pitch. I’m just going out and trying to execute, but yeah, the result definitely makes us happy.”

While Cease could have pitched deeper into the game if needed, the Blue Jays removed him after 83 pitches. Not only has he thrown 156.1 innings already, the Blue Jays hope he’ll be pitching many more.

“I’m probably still learning how to manage workloads and all that, but that’s why we’ve got Max (Scherzer) here who’s done it for 25 years,” Cease said. “You’ve just got to ask him how to do it.”

Most importantly, the Blue Jays won, setting up a massive series finale on Thursday between Tanner Bibee and Jose Soriano. At this point in the season, it’s about the team rather than any individual player.

But it’s impossible not to dream about the kind of difference Guerrero Jr. can make if he can stay locked in for a few more weeks. A night like this reminds everyone of the immense potential he still offers.

“Whatever has happened isn’t important,” Schneider said. “And what’s going to happen is the most important. So I think Vlad having a firm grasp on that is really, really big for him and really big for us.”

stories.title: Saab intensifies pitch to sell Gripen jets to Canada, promising assortment of benefits
stories.summary: Behind the scenes, Swedish defence company is pulling out all the stops to secure major order and deepen ties
stories.author: Gavin John
stories.content:
In the final-assembly hall for the Saab Gripen fighter jet in the Swedish city of Linkoping, the flags of Saab’s eight customer countries hang above the production line. A ninth spot holds a white banner reading, in red capital letters, Reserved.

Asked whether it was for Canada, a Saab official smiled, shrugged and said nothing.

Behind the scenes, though, Saab is pulling out all the stops in order to put Canada’s name on the banner.

At a recent briefing at Saab’s Linkoping headquarters that included The Globe and Mail, company officials laid out a range of benefits that Canada can expect should it go ahead with a major order for Gripen jets.

Saab had already promised a Canadian assembly line for the Gripen but had yet to detail the scope of that promise. The company is proposing to build the fighter jets in Canada from parts to finished aircraft, across a network of roughly 10 prime partners and some 250 suppliers in several provinces.

Canada would be the first start-to-finish Gripen production line outside Sweden, provided the order is large enough to justify it, Saab officials say. Canada has also been invited by Saab and the Swedish government to join Sweden’s next combat-aircraft program in the future, if the Gripen is selected.

It’s not clear at what stage and how detailed talks are between Saab and the federal government. The company’s promises come amid a growing trade rift between Canada and the U.S., traditionally this country’s largest military supplier. And Ottawa is still determining whether to forge ahead with a deal to buy additional U.S.-made F-35 fighter jets.

Saab’s previously announced partners include Bombardier, CAE, IMP Aerospace & Defence, Arcfield Canada and Cohere.

Beyond that, a document viewed by The Globe showed plans for half a dozen “Saab innovation hubs” across Canada for R&D, AI, cybersecurity and Arctic innovation.

Saab, which manufactures the JAS 39E Gripen, lost a competitive bid in 2022, when Canada, looking to replace its aging fleet of F-18s, chose U.S.-based Lockheed Martin to buy 88 F-35s.

The deal locked in the purchase of the first 16 planes, which are now in production, but when American tariffs were first introduced a year and a half ago, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered a review of the contract for the remaining 72 planes.

After trade talks collapsed late last month, Canada announced that it would fight U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest levies with countertariffs that are set to take effect next week.

The F-35 review, and any potential decision on the Gripen, are now caught up in the intensifying trade war, with Washington reportedly demanding that Canada complete the full F-35 buy while calls mount for the federal government to cancel the rest of the order.

At the same time, Saab continues its comprehensive multiyear campaign to woo Canada with no assurances that it will bear fruit.

In an interview, Saab CEO Micael Johansson put the decision in larger terms. “Canada has to decide, [does it] want the sovereign aerospace industry and is that important to them? That’s the first decision,” he said. “And then if they take that decision, Sweden and Saab is the best choice.”

He does not expect the F-35 to disappear; Canada has 16 under contract and has paid long-lead costs on 14 more. “I don’t think Canada will give up F-35 completely,” he said. “I have no clue how many.”

Mr. Johansson insists that Saab is not asking Canada to choose between suppliers. “We’re not trying to replace F-35. That’s a Canadian sovereign decision to go F-35,” he said. And a minute later: “It’s not replacing F-35. It’s both.”

A spokesperson for the office of Industry Ministry Mélanie Joly said in a statement that the minister has been in constant contact with Saab, as well as Lockheed Martin. “Her objective remains to create good-paying jobs for Canadians, especially at a time where Canada’s manufacturing sector is dealing with the impacts of the trade war,” said Gabrielle Landry, deputy director of media relations.

Mr. Carney vowed last spring that “the days of our military sending 70 cents of every dollar to the United States are over” and has already made moves to diversify its purchases, including Canada’s continuing negotiations with Saab for a separate program: six GlobalEye early-warning aircraft.

Mr. Johansson said in the recent interview that a term sheet for the GlobalEye was due to be signed by the end of August.

The Defence Investment Agency, the federal body negotiating the purchase, said in a statement that, “The term sheet has not been signed.” The statement added that “Canada has been in constant and productive discussions with Saab regarding the GlobalEye” and that “these negotiations are not related to trade discussions between Canada and the U.S.”

The company’s ambitions, however, are much larger than that, and include the sale of at least 40 Gripen fighters, which Saab says is the number it would need to make building the aircraft in Canada viable. Saab says it needs a third final-assembly line, in addition to those in Sweden and Brazil, for its Gripen E fighter to meet demand.

Canada can maintain sovereign control over the aircraft’s military software, Saab says, and keep a classified program office in Montreal under Canadian control.

Saab officials offered a breakdown of estimated regional benefits. A document dividing production of both Gripen and GlobalEye by region shows that 50 per cent will go to Quebec, 26 per cent to Ontario, 14 per cent to the West and 10 per cent to Atlantic Canada.

Slightly less than half the work would be production and mechanics; the rest would be research and development, and program management.

In addition to establishing groundwork on the supply side, Saab has also moved to try to overcome one of the biggest hurdles. The Gripen’s one American part is its most important: the F414 engine, made by General Electric. Its export is governed by the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or Itar, the U.S. rules that allow Washington to approve, restrict or refuse the export of American military technology and dictate where it is repaired.

“Every contract that we secure is also backed by a licence from the U.S.,” Mr. Johansson said. So far, it has held: “It’s never been a problem, GE supporting us tremendously, and GE is also supporting doing things in Canada.”

On July 22, GE Aerospace and Canadian company Magellan Aerospace signed a memorandum of understanding to overhaul the engines in Mississauga if Canada buys the Gripen, so the engines would be fixed in Ontario rather than shipped to the United States. The hedge was negotiated by Saab and GE, its American supplier; Ottawa has said nothing publicly about seeking such assurances itself.

The office of Stephen Fuhr, the Secretary of State for Defence Procurement, said in a statement that it “regularly engage[s] with defence-industry representatives including from Saab.”

However, it noted: “Engagement does not constitute the launch of a procurement process, a commitment to procure or an assessment against requirements.” The F-35 procurement, the statement said, “is currently under review,” and the DIA “does not comment on the receipt of solicited or unsolicited proposals from industry.”

Asked whether it was for Canada, a Saab official smiled, shrugged and said nothing.
Behind the scenes, though, Saab is pulling out all the stops in order to put Canada’s name on the banner.

At a recent briefing at Saab’s Linkoping headquarters that included The Globe and Mail, company officials laid out a range of benefits that Canada can expect should it go ahead with a major order for Gripen jets.

Saab had already promised a Canadian assembly line for the Gripen but had yet to detail the scope of that promise. The company is proposing to build the fighter jets in Canada from parts to finished aircraft, across a network of roughly 10 prime partners and some 250 suppliers in several provinces.

Canada would be the first start-to-finish Gripen production line outside Sweden, provided the order is large enough to justify it, Saab officials say. Canada has also been invited by Saab and the Swedish government to join Sweden’s next combat-aircraft program in the future, if the Gripen is selected.

It’s not clear at what stage and how detailed talks are between Saab and the federal government. The company’s promises come amid a growing trade rift between Canada and the U.S., traditionally this country’s largest military supplier. And Ottawa is still determining whether to forge ahead with a deal to buy additional U.S.-made F-35 fighter jets.
Saab’s previously announced partners include Bombardier, CAE, IMP Aerospace & Defence, Arcfield Canada and Cohere.
Beyond that, a document viewed by The Globe showed plans for half a dozen “Saab innovation hubs” across Canada for R&D, AI, cybersecurity and Arctic innovation.
Saab, which manufactures the JAS 39E Gripen, lost a competitive bid in 2022, when Canada, looking to replace its aging fleet of F-18s, chose U.S.-based Lockheed Martin to buy 88 F-35s.

The deal locked in the purchase of the first 16 planes, which are now in production, but when American tariffs were first introduced a year and a half ago, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered a review of the contract for the remaining 72 planes.
After trade talks collapsed late last month, Canada announced that it would fight U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest levies with countertariffs that are set to take effect next week.

The F-35 review, and any potential decision on the Gripen, are now caught up in the intensifying trade war, with Washington reportedly demanding that Canada complete the full F-35 buy while calls mount for the federal government to cancel the rest of the order.
At the same time, Saab continues its comprehensive multiyear campaign to woo Canada with no assurances that it will bear fruit.

In an interview, Saab CEO Micael Johansson put the decision in larger terms. “Canada has to decide, [does it] want the sovereign aerospace industry and is that important to them? That’s the first decision,” he said. “And then if they take that decision, Sweden and Saab is the best choice.”

He does not expect the F-35 to disappear; Canada has 16 under contract and has paid long-lead costs on 14 more. “I don’t think Canada will give up F-35 completely,” he said. “I have no clue how many.”

Mr. Johansson insists that Saab is not asking Canada to choose between suppliers. “We’re not trying to replace F-35. That’s a Canadian sovereign decision to go F-35,” he said. And a minute later: “It’s not replacing F-35. It’s both.”

A spokesperson for the office of Industry Ministry Mélanie Joly said in a statement that the minister has been in constant contact with Saab, as well as Lockheed Martin. “Her objective remains to create good-paying jobs for Canadians, especially at a time where Canada’s manufacturing sector is dealing with the impacts of the trade war,” said Gabrielle Landry, deputy director of media relations.

Mr. Carney vowed last spring that “the days of our military sending 70 cents of every dollar to the United States are over” and has already made moves to diversify its purchases, including Canada’s continuing negotiations with Saab for a separate program: six GlobalEye early-warning aircraft.
Mr. Johansson said in the recent interview that a term sheet for the GlobalEye was due to be signed by the end of August.

The Defence Investment Agency, the federal body negotiating the purchase, said in a statement that, “The term sheet has not been signed.” The statement added that “Canada has been in constant and productive discussions with Saab regarding the GlobalEye” and that “these negotiations are not related to trade discussions between Canada and the U.S.”

The company’s ambitions, however, are much larger than that, and include the sale of at least 40 Gripen fighters, which Saab says is the number it would need to make building the aircraft in Canada viable. Saab says it needs a third final-assembly line, in addition to those in Sweden and Brazil, for its Gripen E fighter to meet demand.
Canada can maintain sovereign control over the aircraft’s military software, Saab says, and keep a classified program office in Montreal under Canadian control.

Saab officials offered a breakdown of estimated regional benefits. A document dividing production of both Gripen and GlobalEye by region shows that 50 per cent will go to Quebec, 26 per cent to Ontario, 14 per cent to the West and 10 per cent to Atlantic Canada.
Slightly less than half the work would be production and mechanics; the rest would be research and development, and program management.

In addition to establishing groundwork on the supply side, Saab has also moved to try to overcome one of the biggest hurdles. The Gripen’s one American part is its most important: the F414 engine, made by General Electric. Its export is governed by the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or Itar, the U.S. rules that allow Washington to approve, restrict or refuse the export of American military technology and dictate where it is repaired.

“Every contract that we secure is also backed by a licence from the U.S.,” Mr. Johansson said. So far, it has held: “It’s never been a problem, GE supporting us tremendously, and GE is also supporting doing things in Canada.”

On July 22, GE Aerospace and Canadian company Magellan Aerospace signed a memorandum of understanding to overhaul the engines in Mississauga if Canada buys the Gripen, so the engines would be fixed in Ontario rather than shipped to the United States. The hedge was negotiated by Saab and GE, its American supplier; Ottawa has said nothing publicly about seeking such assurances itself.
The office of Stephen Fuhr, the Secretary of State for Defence Procurement, said in a statement that it “regularly engage[s] with defence-industry representatives including from Saab.”

However, it noted: “Engagement does not constitute the launch of a procurement process, a commitment to procure or an assessment against requirements.” The F-35 procurement, the statement said, “is currently under review,” and the DIA “does not comment on the receipt of solicited or unsolicited proposals from industry.”

stories.title: Virtual classrooms organized in Canada offer lifeline to girls under Taliban rule
stories.summary: On a recent summer Friday, nearly a dozen students logged on for their online literature class. It was a group of mostly young women joining from different parts of Afghanistan, eagerly waiting for their turn to discuss a story they had read the week before.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
On a recent summer Friday, nearly a dozen students logged on for their online literature class. It was a group of mostly young women joining from different parts of Afghanistan, eagerly waiting for their turn to discuss a story they had read the week before.

Before the Taliban’s return to power five years ago, the women were studying in high school or university, hoping education would give them a better future. Some had just obtained their undergraduate degrees. But their plans were put on hold when, like millions of other Afghan girls, they were barred from going to school.

Once a week, the group gathers in a Google Meet room for a 90-minute class hosted by Toronto-based poet and educator Hazrat Wahriz. In this lesson attended by a reporter, they discussed a short story about a teenage boy’s journey fleeing the Taliban.

The story’s author, Shams Erfan, joined the virtual class from Toronto and listened attentively throughout the session. Then he had a few words for the women.

“I hope you continue ... writing, critiquing, reading, protesting, attending online classes,” he said in Persian.

“These activities are a fight,” he continued, ”a fight against the Taliban ideology that is trying to remove you all.”

Since 2021, the Taliban regime has been excluding women from every aspect of public life by imposing what international human rights groups call a system of “gender apartheid.” It has issued sweeping edicts to restrict women’s right to work, education and freedom of movement.

In a report published last month, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization estimated that 2.4 million Afghan girls have been barred from secondary education, a number that could increase to four million by 2030.

The Taliban also banned education for girls and women during its first rule in the late 1990s, before the regime was toppled in 2001 by a U.S-led international coalition in response to the 9/11 attacks.

Canadian troops spent 13 years in the country as part of a Nato stabilization mission. More than 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces personnel were deployed to Afghanistan from 2001 to 2014.

Girls and women returned to classrooms in 2001, and Canadian military and aid organizations invested heavily in women’s education and empowerment projects over the years.

But the Taliban waged a bloody insurgency that paved their way back to power in 2021. Soon after seizing Kabul, the regime renewed its ban on women’s education.

As the ban continues, virtual and underground schools operating from overseas — including the one founded by Wahriz in Toronto — have become a lifeline for many.

In addition to online literature, photography and critical thinking courses, Wahriz’s non-profit, the Network of Community Schools for Girls in Afghanistan, runs a web of secret schools across the country.

“Our first school was established in one of the faraway provinces of Afghanistan and since then, we gradually expanded our activities,” he said

More than 1,600 girls are now being taught in his underground classrooms by female teachers turning their own homes into learning centres, he said.

Under current rules, girls are only allowed to go to school up to Grade 6, meaning those attending secondary and higher education are violating the Taliban’s strict religious code. If caught, they could face severe punishment including physical violence and imprisonment.

Despite those risks, Wahriz said, girls are showing up in classrooms every day to learn math, physics, chemistry and history in a fight against the “darkness.”

“We are challenging that darkness just by our existence,” he said.

Wahriz said funding for the network mostly comes from “kind-hearted” people he knows, including his Canadian friends and an organization based in the United Kingdom.

The teachers are paid US$100 a month when funding is available, he said.

“They are dedicated, committed enough not to expect every month to get paid, but are sure that whenever we find something, they get paid,” Wahriz said.

He said even though his efforts are like a “small drop in the desert” given the magnitude of the crisis, he is optimistic because others are also doing the same.

“Drop by drop, it becomes a sea,” he said, referring to a Persian proverb.

A number of similar organizations in other countries are also working to bypass the Taliban ban on girls’ education.

Women’s rights was a central issue during the 2020 peace talks between the Taliban and the former U.S.-supported Afghan government.

Taliban negotiators repeatedly said they would no longer oppose women’s right to education and employment, but “within the framework of Islamic law,” a vague promise they immediately broke after seizing power. They have since issued more than 100 edicts targeting women, according to the United Nations.

The group’s top leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and his chief justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani are now wanted by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity in their treatment of women and girls.

The Canadian government said it has been backing efforts to expand education opportunities for all Afghans, including girls and women, for over two decades, and has provided more than $143 million to fund education and health-care programs in the past five years while avoiding any investments through the Taliban.

“Canada strongly condemns the ongoing repression, systematic human rights abuses and erosion of fundamental freedoms under Taliban rule in Afghanistan, and is deeply concerned by the worsening humanitarian situation,” Global Affairs Canada spokesperson Brittany Fletcher said in a statement.

For Murwarid Ziayee, the devastating impact of the ban on women’s education was a “painful” experience.

She was in her last semester of law school when the Taliban took power in 1996 and closed the doors of Kabul University to female students. But she didn’t give up on her dreams, she said.

Ziayee self-studied, learned English and computer skills, and even found a job at an underground non-profit that helped educate women at the time. She was able to complete her studies and obtain her degree after the Taliban were overthrown in 2001.

Ziayee, now the senior director of Calgary-based Right to Learn in Afghanistan, said she is trying to do her part to help girls and women who have once again been banned from school.

“It’s better to be in front seat and have the wheel and move forward and do what can be done,” she said in interview.

The non-profit, formerly known as Canadian Women for Women in Afghanistan, was founded in 1998 and has been working to empower women through education ever since.

Ziayee said more than 700 students, mostly in Afghanistan, are attending the organization’s virtual school and 92 per cent of them are girls.

The first cohort will graduate from high school next year, she said. “Once you provide these girls with the education ... the doors to many opportunities will open for them.”

She said students from Grade 7 to Grade 9 study the former government’s curriculum before taking Canadian and internationally accredited courses during the three years of high school.

Once the students graduate, they obtain internationally accepted diplomas so they can apply for post-secondary education abroad. Most of the funding comes from the federal government or individual Canadians, while people living in other countries also support some students.

But even though many other organizations are involved, they cannot fulfil a state’s job to provide education, Ziayee said.

“The gap is huge and that’s why we are obviously impatiently waiting and praying and advocating for the day that things change in Afghanistan,” Ziayee said.

Until then, Ziayee said the group wants to see the international community step up to fund alternative ways to support more Afghan women and girls “who are left behind and waiting for opportunities to be enrolled.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

Sharif Hassan, The Canadian Press

“They are dedicated, committed enough not to expect every month to get paid, but are sure that whenever we find something, they get paid,” Wahriz said.

“Drop by drop, it becomes a sea,” he said, referring to a Persian proverb.
A number of similar organizations in other countries are also working to bypass the Taliban ban on girls’ education.
Women’s rights was a central issue during the 2020 peace talks between the Taliban and the former U.S.-supported Afghan government.

Taliban negotiators repeatedly said they would no longer oppose women’s right to education and employment, but “within the framework of Islamic law,” a vague promise they immediately broke after seizing power. The group’s top leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and his chief justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani are now wanted by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity in their treatment of women and girls.

“Canada strongly condemns the ongoing repression, systematic human rights abuses and erosion of fundamental freedoms under Taliban rule in Afghanistan, and is deeply concerned by the worsening humanitarian situation,” Global Affairs Canada spokesperson Brittany Fletcher said in a statement.

“It’s better to be in front seat and have the wheel and move forward and do what can be done,” she said in interview.
The non-profit, formerly known as Canadian Women for Women in Afghanistan, was founded in 1998 and has been working to empower women through education ever since.
Ziayee said more than 700 students, mostly in Afghanistan, are attending the organization’s virtual school and 92 per cent of them are girls.
The first cohort will graduate from high school next year, she said. “Once you provide these girls with the education ... the doors to many opportunities will open for them.”
She said students from Grade 7 to Grade 9 study the former government’s curriculum before taking Canadian and internationally accredited courses during the three years of high school.

Once the students graduate, they obtain internationally accepted diplomas so they can apply for post-secondary education abroad. Most of the funding comes from the federal government or individual Canadians, while people living in other countries also support some students.
But even though many other organizations are involved, they cannot fulfil a state’s job to provide education, Ziayee said.
“The gap is huge and that’s why we are obviously impatiently waiting and praying and advocating for the day that things change in Afghanistan,” Ziayee said.

“I hope you continue ... writing, critiquing, reading, protesting, attending online classes,” he said in Persian.

stories.title: A pediatric emergency physician on the risks of e-scooters
stories.summary: Fractures, head and brain injuries among most common e-scooter injuries
stories.author: The Decibel Staff, Sherrill Sutherland
stories.content:
The popularity of e-scooters on Canadian roads has exploded in recent years. But new data from health officials and the Canadian Paediatric Society shows that the risks of e-scooters can lead to hospitalization and death. Has policy and regulation kept up with how readily available the transportation has become?

Dr. Daniel Rosenfield , pediatric emergency physician at SickKids Hospital in Toronto and chair of the Injury Prevention Committee for the Canadian Paediatric Society, joins The Decibel to talk about the trauma cases he’s seen first-hand, why e-scooters can be deadly and how to balance regulation with medical safety.

Questions? Comments? Ideas? E-mail us at thedecibel@globeandmail.com

stories.title: Toronto home sales fall in August, ending five-month rebound
stories.summary: Activity slowed in a month when trade talks with the U.S. collapsed, injecting more uncertainty into the market
stories.author: Rachelle Younglai
stories.content:
Toronto home sales fell in August, ending a five-month rebound in activity, as the U.S.-Canada trade war intensified and gave some potential homebuyers reason to pause.

The city and surrounding area saw 5,484 property transactions last month, according to the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board. That was 1.3 per cent lower than July, 28 per cent below the 10-year average for August, and the first monthly sales decline since February.

Activity slowed in a month when trade talks with the United States collapsed, injecting more uncertainty into the market.

Although mortgage rates remained somewhat steady last month, the board said would-be buyers are worried that borrowing costs will rise.

“The main hold-back for many households has been concerns around trade with the United States and the potential for higher inflation and borrowing costs in the future,” Trreb chief information officer Jason Mercer said in a statement.

The average interest rate on a five-year fixed mortgage stayed at 4.8 per cent after trade negotiations fell apart in August, according to rate comparison website Ratehub.CA .

“If the trade war persists, weakening economic sentiment could weigh on sales activity even if mortgage rates remain relatively stable,” Jamie David, Ratehub’s vice-president of marketing and mortgages, said in a statement.

Ms. David s aid worsening trade problems could put the housing market’s recovery back on hold, similar to what occurred when the U.S. introduced the first round of tariffs last year.

The Toronto region is the country’s largest real estate market. Its activity has helped bolster national sales over the past few months.

From July to August, the Toronto region’s home price index fell 0.1 per cent to $931,200. Compared with a year ago, the typical home price was down 4.5 per cent.

The steepest year-over-year declines happened to the north of the city of Toronto in York Region, where the home price index fell 6.2 per cent.

In comparison, the city of Toronto’s home price index declined by 3.7 per cent. In Halton, a wealthier area to the west of the city, the typical home price was down 3 per cent.

Condos across the Toronto region continued to lose the most value, falling 7.1 per cent year-over-year. In comparison, detached houses in the Toronto region decreased by 4.5 per cent.

stories.title: Storm Stayed's new owners share their vision as London brewery changes hands
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 3, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 3
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 3, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 3
4EST Brewery bought the Old South staple with goal of keeping popular beers, menu items and community
The new owners of Storm Stayed Brewing Co. say they plan to preserve much of what made the Old South brewery a community fixture as they begin a new chapter for the business.
Storm Stayed, located on Wharncliffe Road, has been purchased by 4EST Brewery, a local company founded by Colin Gunn and Myles Rombough.
The pair started 4EST nine years ago as students at Western University. What began as a passion project brewing beer in Rombough's garage eventually became an online retail business.
For the past two years, Storm Stayed has also been brewing 4EST's beer under a contract arrangement.
Gunn said the relationship gave the pair a close look at the brewery and its operation.
"We actually started brewing our beer at Storm Stayed almost two years ago now. We're also in the Lcbo, so we needed a good consistent brewer and we found that in Storm Stayed."
When the opportunity came to purchase the brewery, Gunn said, it seemed like the right way to take 4EST to the next level.

"It became apparent that we would want to open a brewery one day and this opportunity came along to take over or bring under our umbrella a brewery that already was operating, had a proven track record, great product and a community presence."
Although the new owners are still working out exactly what changes they want to make, they say customers can expect plenty of familiar things when the taproom reopens this weekend.
That includes popular Storm Stayed beers such as its Hazy IPA, Sunburst New England Pale Ale, Irish Red and Nitro Stout.
Rombough said the brewery's community events, including markets held in its parking lot, will also continue.
"We really want to get a grasp on everything Storm Stayed has done," he said.
"Looking at it from the outside perspective, we know the things we love ... they make great beer, the community is obviously a big part of their business and that's a big part of ours as well."
Gunn said the brewery's regular customers shouldn't expect the change in ownership to mean their favourite beers disappear.
"The craft beer nerds out there can be rest assured that they're still going to be able to have their favourite beer, it just will be under new ownership," he said.
"And the 4EST brands that they know and love will stay around, but there will also be more of them."
Storm Stayed's former co-owner, Justin Belanger, could not be reached for comment before publication.
In a Facebook post announcing the change in ownership, Belanger said he was proud of how the brewery had grown and of the community staple it had become over the past decade.
For Gunn and Rombough, taking over an established brewery comes at a challenging time for the craft beer industry.

Beer consumption has been declining, while breweries are also facing higher production costs following the pandemic and inflation. U.S. tariffs have added further pressure to the cost of some materials.
While 4EST has not been directly affected by tariffs, Gunn said the company is seeing higher costs for materials such as aluminum.
The new owners say those challenges make quality and the overall customer experience increasingly important.
"As the volume of people drinking goes down, the quality of the product needs to go up in order to justify it," Gunn said.
"If someone's only going to enjoy one or two beers tonight, they should be really good beers."
The company is also looking at ways to appeal to people who are drinking less or not drinking alcohol at all, including non-alcoholic and lower-alcohol beers.
Gunn said the goal is to make a visit to the brewery worthwhile even for customers who aren't going out as often.

"We're excited to not only provide a really high-quality product but also create an atmosphere where if it's not in the budget to go out often, we want to make it something that you really enjoy, and you get a lot of value out of and a lot of fun out of."
As for the Storm Stayed name, Rombough said the new owners haven't decided whether they'll keep it or eventually rebrand the brewery.
That decision will come in the months ahead.
For now, the pair are focused on taking over the brewery while preserving the parts of Storm Stayed that customers already know.
"We're just super excited for our next chapter," Rombough said.

| CBC News | Posted: September 3, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 3

4EST Brewery bought the Old South staple with goal of keeping popular beers, menu items and community

The new owners of Storm Stayed Brewing Co. say they plan to preserve much of what made the Old South brewery a community fixture as they begin a new chapter for the business.

Storm Stayed, located on Wharncliffe Road, has been purchased by 4EST Brewery, a local company founded by Colin Gunn and Myles Rombough.

The pair started 4EST nine years ago as students at Western University. What began as a passion project brewing beer in Rombough's garage eventually became an online retail business.

For the past two years, Storm Stayed has also been brewing 4EST's beer under a contract arrangement.

Gunn said the relationship gave the pair a close look at the brewery and its operation.

"We actually started brewing our beer at Storm Stayed almost two years ago now. We're also in the Lcbo, so we needed a good consistent brewer and we found that in Storm Stayed."

When the opportunity came to purchase the brewery, Gunn said, it seemed like the right way to take 4EST to the next level.

"It became apparent that we would want to open a brewery one day and this opportunity came along to take over or bring under our umbrella a brewery that already was operating, had a proven track record, great product and a community presence."

Although the new owners are still working out exactly what changes they want to make, they say customers can expect plenty of familiar things when the taproom reopens this weekend.

That includes popular Storm Stayed beers such as its Hazy IPA, Sunburst New England Pale Ale, Irish Red and Nitro Stout.

Rombough said the brewery's community events, including markets held in its parking lot, will also continue.

"We really want to get a grasp on everything Storm Stayed has done," he said.

"Looking at it from the outside perspective, we know the things we love ... they make great beer, the community is obviously a big part of their business and that's a big part of ours as well."

Gunn said the brewery's regular customers shouldn't expect the change in ownership to mean their favourite beers disappear.

"The craft beer nerds out there can be rest assured that they're still going to be able to have their favourite beer, it just will be under new ownership," he said.

"And the 4EST brands that they know and love will stay around, but there will also be more of them."

Storm Stayed's former co-owner, Justin Belanger, could not be reached for comment before publication.

In a Facebook post announcing the change in ownership, Belanger said he was proud of how the brewery had grown and of the community staple it had become over the past decade.

For Gunn and Rombough, taking over an established brewery comes at a challenging time for the craft beer industry.

Beer consumption has been declining, while breweries are also facing higher production costs following the pandemic and inflation. U.S. tariffs have added further pressure to the cost of some materials.

While 4EST has not been directly affected by tariffs, Gunn said the company is seeing higher costs for materials such as aluminum.

The new owners say those challenges make quality and the overall customer experience increasingly important.

"As the volume of people drinking goes down, the quality of the product needs to go up in order to justify it," Gunn said.

"If someone's only going to enjoy one or two beers tonight, they should be really good beers."

The company is also looking at ways to appeal to people who are drinking less or not drinking alcohol at all, including non-alcoholic and lower-alcohol beers.

Gunn said the goal is to make a visit to the brewery worthwhile even for customers who aren't going out as often.

"We're excited to not only provide a really high-quality product but also create an atmosphere where if it's not in the budget to go out often, we want to make it something that you really enjoy, and you get a lot of value out of and a lot of fun out of."

As for the Storm Stayed name, Rombough said the new owners haven't decided whether they'll keep it or eventually rebrand the brewery.

That decision will come in the months ahead.

For now, the pair are focused on taking over the brewery while preserving the parts of Storm Stayed that customers already know.

"We're just super excited for our next chapter," Rombough said.

stories.title: This advisor tried working in New York’s fashion industry before moving to Toronto and landing in finance
stories.summary: Micha Choi started in administration at a Bay Street mutual fund before working her way up to become an advisor
stories.author: Brenda Bouw
stories.content:
In the Behind the Advice series , Globe Advisor asks advisors about their relationship with money from a young age, the lessons they’ve learned over the years, and how those experiences shape the advice they give clients. Behind the Advice is also a podcast: You can find episodes from all four seasons here . Stay tuned for Season Five coming in late September.

Micha Choi, vice-president and portfolio manager for Guardian Capital Advisors, talks about learning to budget by doing bookkeeping for her immigrant parents’ small businesses, how she got into finance and why she thinks Mrs. Doubtfire would make a good advisor:

Describe your upbringing and how it influenced your views about money.

I grew up in Seoul, Korea during the 1980s when it was a poor country. Before my younger brother was born, my parents and I lived in a very tiny room with no heating, kitchen or bathroom.

Then Korea went through a significant economic boom. My parents started taking out loans, investing in buildings (which we moved into) and taking on tenants. My dad used to stop me in the middle of a bustling Seoul street to watch people buy and sell goods, or what he described as ‘watching money move.’ That’s when I first started to think about money and the economy.

When did you come to Canada, and what was that experience like?

When I was 13, my dad read an article saying Vancouver was closest to heaven, so he sold the buildings in Korea and we moved to Langley, B.C., a suburb of Vancouver. They chose Langley because they said there were very few immigrants there and thought it would force me to learn English faster.

Because they didn’t speak English, my parents couldn’t find work in Canada, so they ended up running small businesses, starting with a sandwich shop and later a coin laundry before expanding into other businesses.

As a teenager, along with peeling potatoes, making salads and sandwiches, folding laundry and cleaning lint out of dryers, my dad made me do the bookkeeping for each business. That’s when I first learned about budgeting: how much money you bring in and how much you spend.

What did you want to be growing up and how did you get into financial services?

I am obsessed with reading, writing and books, so I wanted to be a writer or do something in the book industry. But because English wasn’t my first language, I gave up that idea.

After getting an economics degree at the University of British Columbia, I decided to get into fashion and became a fashion buyer. I moved to New York City, but after six months I decided the city wasn’t for me, so I moved to Toronto. Since no fashion job would cover the rent, I decided to work in finance. Using my business degree, I found a job as an administrator at a mutual fund company, which is how I got started in this industry.

What’s the biggest money mistake you’ve made and what did you learn from it?

In my third year of university, my parents gave me a credit card. I used it to lease a Mini Cooper, and they helped me with the payments. I planned to pay them back. Years later, my dad told me he struggled to make payments when he lost his business during the financial crisis. I felt bad. To this day, I do not finance vehicles. I buy used cars and pay with cash. I also never use credit to buy things I can’t afford.

What’s the hardest piece of money advice for you to follow?

A few years ago, a client gave me a copy of Die With Zero by Bill Perkins. The book talks about how so many people work longer than necessary and end up dying having enjoyed life less, or waiting too long to give back to others. Now I share this book and the concept with many clients contemplating retirement.

While I’m still in the mid-point of my career, it’s something I’m a lot more mindful of. I also want my clients to know they don’t always have to be so frugal and can enjoy life more.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve received in your career?

When you make a mistake, take responsibility. Owning up to your own mistakes and faults can be powerful in the world where everyone else is trying to ‘fake it until you make it.’

What advice do you have for someone who wants to enter your business?

First ask yourself why you want to do this. A lot of young people in our industry come from families with parents or relatives in the business and they think it looks cool, but it’s not for everyone. It requires a lot of focus and hard work.

Also, read as much as you can about market history, economic booms and busts, and human behaviour, because at the end of the day it’s a people business.

Which famous person or fictional character would make a great financial advisor, and why?

Mrs. Doubtfire [the fictional British nanny persona from the 1993 movie starring Robin Williams, adapted from the 1987 novel Madame Doubtfire] , because he/she would do anything to take care of their family. That’s what a good advisor does for their clients – takes care of them. Also, Mrs. Doubtfire is a good communicator who can distill a complex idea into something understandable, which is what advisors should do.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

stories.title: Ottawa spending $4.7B on new made-in-Canada Via Rail passenger cars
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government is spending $4.7 billion to build 313 new passenger cars for Via Rail.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Thunder BAY — Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a $4.7 billion contract to build 313 new passenger cars for Via Rail on Thursday.

Carney made the announcement at the Alstom plant in Thunder Bay, Ont., where the cars will be built.

“Our rail cars on our long-distance and remote routes are more than 70 years old. They were built when the NHL had six teams. Goalies wouldn’t wear masks. The Leafs would win the (Stanley) Cup,” Carney said.

“Those old cars have served our country well, but they’re long overdue for retirement. It’s time to build new ones, to build them here at home.”

Carney emphasized the fact that the new cars are being built in Canada.

“For the first time in four decades, those cars will be produced and assembled and maintained in our country. Cars that used to be built in the United States will be built right here in Thunder Bay at Alstom, by the best workers in the world,” Carney said.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon called the investment the single largest in Via Rail’s history and said the project will lead to 700 new jobs.

“This is a truly Canadian project. Canadian supply chains, workers, and it’s a renewed investment in that passenger rail service that connects us all,” MacKinnon told The Canadian Press following the announcement.

He said the first new car should be delivered in 2031.

In the 2024 federal budget, the previous Liberal government announced new funding for VIA Rail to replace its aging fleet on routes outside the Québec City-Windsor Corridor.

MacKinnon said the procurement process has been ongoing since then and the work is “long overdue.”

“That we’ll be able to replace it with Canadian-made equipment is an unbelievably good bonus,” he said.

Via Rail last imported passenger cars in August 2025 through a 2018 contract with Siemens Canada to replace locomotives and cars in the Windsor-Quebec City fleet, the company told The Canadian Press.

The cars and locomotives were manufactured at Siemens’ facility in Sacramento, California.

The contract is for nine different types of passenger cars: 78 sleepers, 58 coaches, 38 panorama cars, 29 baggage cars, 26 accessible sleepers, 25 dome cars, 20 dining cars, 20 prestige sleepers and 19 berth cars.

A spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office said the average age of passenger cars along Via’s long distance and remote routes is 77 years.

In July, the government announced plans to spend $1.6 billion to replace 45 of Via Rail’s aging locomotives and another $357 million to build a new assembly plant and maintenance facility.

The locomotive contract was awarded to Stadler, a Swiss company which will use its facility in Valencia, Spain to design and manufacture much of the fleet. The government said 36 of the 45 locomotives will be completed in Canada.

Those new trains are also expected to be delivered in 2031.

At the time of the announcement, the federal government said the new locomotives would improve Via Rail’s reliability and on-time performance, which Canada’s auditor general found had dropped to a dismal 30 per cent in the first three months of 2025.

Conservative transport critic Dan Albas said in a media statement that Conservatives have pushed the Carney government to ensure taxpayer dollars support Canadian workers and industries using Canadian sourced materials.

“We expect that the Liberals will have put in place safeguards in the contracts to ensure these rail cars are built on time and on budget,” said Albas. “As the auditor general has reported, the fundamental issue is Via Rail’s reliability. Having new passenger cars does not address this.”

Albas also said the Conservatives call on the government to “stop paying Via Rail executive bonuses and address the deterioration of service.”

“While the Liberals are good at spending taxpayer money, they are not good at fixing problems,” he said.

MacKinnon said Via Rail will run the contract management, adding there are safeguards in place.

Addressing concerns about Via’s reliability, MacKinnon said the Crown corporation will be under new leadership soon.

“There are things they don’t control, meaning they run on someone else’s tracks, and that’s a very hard obstacle to get over, although I’m also hoping that we can get to a better running arrangement with CN,” he said.

“But on the things that Via can control, customer service, reliability, we have set high expectations for the things they can control, and I don’t think I’ve made any secret of either my impatience or concern for some of these problems to get resolved.”

After the announcement, Carney met with pop star Bryan Adams, who was scheduled to perform in Thunder Bay on Wednesday and Thursday. The pair went to a bakery to try a local pastry before visiting the Terry Fox National Historic Monument.

Carney later toured the Thunder Bay Fire Management facility.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray in Ottawa.

stories.title: The key to winning the Canada-U.S. trade war is not retaliating, says think tank
stories.summary: A free-market think tank is calling on Canadian policymakers to turn the other cheek as the United States ramps up its cross-border tariffs.
stories.author: Rahim Mohamed
stories.content:
Ottawa — A free-market think tank is calling on Canadian policymakers to turn the other cheek as the United States ramps up its cross-border tariffs.

“When you’re in a trade impasse like the one we’re in with the U.S., what works is being able to outlast the other guy,” said Vincent Geloso, a senior economist at the Montreal Economic Institute and the author of a new research note on the ineffectiveness of counter-tariffs.

“Eventually, there’ll be an opportunity to act at the right time in the right way,” said Geloso.

The Carney government has been scrambling to respond to U.S. President Donald Trump’s use of Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to put 50 per cent tariffs on a host of Canadian goods. The tariffs took effect on Aug. 22, after last-minute trade talks collapsed.

But Geloso says that Carney would be smart to learn from Canada’s response to the U.S.’s first use of the Tariff Act during the Great Depression.

“In the ’30s we did counter-tariffs. We actually did two rounds of retaliation, (both) of which did absolutely nothing,” said Geloso.

The U.S. raised tariffs by an average of 20 per cent on more than 800 Canadian products under the 1930 Tariff Act, prompting retaliation from Liberal prime minister Mackenzie King and his Conservative successor R.B. Bennett. Bennett was especially aggressive in his response, putting matching counter-tariffs on roughly 30 per cent of U.S. exports to Canada.

Geloso says that these measures had no perceptible effect on the American economy or the direction of U.S. trade policy. However, they did substantial harm to Canada’s economy.

He estimates that falling prices for goods Canada sold to other countries caused about half of Canada’s losses during the Great Depression, with counter-tariffs being a key driver of this effect.

Geloso said that what ultimately resolved the impasse was a change in government in the U.S., with Democrat Franklin Delano Roosevelt winning a massive mandate in the 1932 presidential election. He added that Roosevelt demonstrated his commitment to open markets by naming free-trade evangelist Cordell Hull his first secretary of state.

“Naming Cordell Hull in that position was about as radical of a pro-free trade signal (Roosevelt) could have sent at the time,” said Geloso.

The Roosevelt government quickly restored cross-border trade relations, signing a reciprocal trade agreement with Canada in 1935.

Geloso admits that the situation is somewhat different this time around, with Canada facing punitive, targeted cross-border tariffs, rather than ones the U.S. has broadly applied to all its trade partners. Section 338 has never before been invoked in the Tariff Act’s 96-year history.

However, he says this doesn’t change the fundamental dynamics of the Canada-U.S. relationship.

“What worked then is what will work now, and that’s being patient,” said Geloso.

Geloso said he supported Carney’s decision to walk away from negotiations but said the prime minister needs to avoid being goaded into a tit-for-tat tariff war that Canada cannot win.

“(Carney) can either play the jingoist card or the adult card,” said Geloso. “And the adult card would be to exercise patience and wait for the other guy to tire himself out of the shenanigans he’s doing.”

Geloso said that, for the time being, Carney should focus on implementing measures that mitigate the immediate damage of the tariffs and make Canada’s economy more resilient, such as reducing red tape for businesses.

stories.title: Bank of Canada unveils new $20 bill featuring King Charles
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada has unveiled a new bill today featuring an image of King Charles.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — King Charles III is now the fourth monarch to appear on a Canadian banknote after the Bank of Canada unveiled the final design for a new $20 bill that will go into circulation early next year.

This is the first Canadian banknote to feature Charles, whose image replaces that of the late Queen Elizabeth II.

The central bank was directed by former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government back in 2023 to feature the King in its next redesign process.

Bank of Canada officials said Thursday the design process cost $6 million and each note will cost an additional $0.05 to print because of a raft of new security features, bringing the cost up to $0.35 per bill.

“Bank note security is critical for Canadian consumers and businesses and for the integrity of our currency system,” Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said at an unveiling event in Ottawa on Thursday.

Macklem said the security features are part of the central bank’s “relentless fight against counterfeiting.”

A first-of-its-kind security strip, positioned below the King’s portrait, shifts as the note moves and has elements that appear to be 3D. Dark bands on the petals of a poppy appear to spin, a maple leaf changes from light to dark, and a series of small 20s shift to become maple leaves as the note is tilted back and forth.

Bank of Canada officials said they plan to do outreach in the coming months to ensure that retailers and law enforcement are aware of the changes.

Four online content creators were invited to Thursday’s event and paid to produce videos raising awareness of the new bills. The Bank of Canada said its budget for that pilot project is $25,000.

Things like vending machines and ATMs that accept or dispense cash, along with some online applications that authenticate cash, will need to be upgraded. Bank officials said advance images of the new notes are being provided to ensure the transition is smooth.

Both the current $20 bill and the new note feature an image of Canada’s National Vimy Memorial in France, a monument to all Canadians who fought in the First World War.

Macklem said the tribute is particularly meaningful to him because his grandfather, who was also named Tiff Macklem, fought in the war and was injured in the Battle of Passchendaele. The central banker said he visited the memorial earlier this summer.

“The memorial is also a symbol for Canadian sovereignty on the world stage. The Battle of Vimy Ridge is widely viewed as a coming-of-age moment in Canada’s development,” he said.

The new bill also features design elements chosen in consultation with Indigenous Peoples. A small window on the lower part of the note contains culturally significant plants, including cedar, sweetgrass, wild strawberries and Arctic cotton.

All 13 provincial and territorial flowers are also included in the design, with the names of each province and territory set in small type.

Both the old and new bills have accessibility features, including a series of raised dots, which were developed with groups like the Canadian National Institute for the Blind.

The new bills are made of the same polymer as the previous round of banknotes, but each design is now going to be vertical rather than horizontal. The $10 vertical notes are already in circulation with an image of human rights activist Viola Desmond on the front.

The next bank note to be redesigned is the $5 bill, which will feature an image of Terry Fox and is expected to be released in 2028.

The King ascended to the throne in September 2022 after the death of his 96-year-old mother, who reigned for 70 years. Her image first appeared on the Bank of Canada’s $20 note in 1935 when she was eight-year-old Princess Elizabeth.

The reigning monarch has been featured on Canadian bills since 1935.

The Royal Canadian Mint has produced coins featuring King Charles since 2023.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

Sarah Ritchie, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadian paper cup and bowl maker sees growing local demand amid tariffs
stories.summary: A Canadian paper cup and bowl manufacturer is seeing growing demand from foodservice customers across the country as tariffs prompt coffee chains and fast-food restaurants to seek out more Canadian-made take-out packaging.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
A Canadian paper cup and bowl manufacturer is seeing growing demand from foodservice customers across the country as tariffs prompt coffee chains and fast-food restaurants to seek out more Canadian-made take-out packaging.

Eco Guardian Inc., which makes compostable and recyclable cups and bowls in Aurora, Ont., is one of a number of Canadian manufacturers poised to expand domestic business amid the escalating trade war between Canada and the U.S.

The company has received so many requests from potential new customers in the past two weeks that even if only half turn into orders it will be extremely busy, Eco Guardian founder and CEO Anil Abrol said in an interview.

“This has fast-tracked our growth,” said Abrol. “We’re bringing the equipment on faster and building up our capacity.”

The situation highlights the effect of the trade war on Canadian manufacturers, with some companies emerging as potential beneficiaries.

However, the slate of so-called tariff winners May be small, and could shift as the trade tussle unfolds.

Eco Guardian recently opened its new facility north of Toronto with the capacity to produce more than a billion paper cups a year.

The company was in talks with a U.S. manufacturer of paperboard when the first round of tariff threats hit last year, prompting the company to change course and source its raw material from Asia and Europe instead.

That shift means the company makes its products in Canada without U.S.-origin inputs, shielding it from Canadian retaliatory tariffs and making its cups and bowls more attractive to the domestic foodservice industry.

Despite becoming more appealing to Canadian restaurants and cafes, Eco Guardian has dealt with challenges in the U.S. due to tariffs.

“There’s a 50 per cent tariff that started,” Abrol said. “My team told me there’s one container which they have shipped … the container value might be $25,000 (and) there’s a tariff of $14,000.”

One of the company’s machines, which was producing paper packaging exclusively for a U.S. customer, was switched off this week and will be converted to a new customer’s product, he said.

However, Eco Guardian has managed to maintain sales to the U.S. customer by distributing a similar product made in Asia rather than made in Canada, he said.

While Eco Guardian manufactures paper cups and bowls in Ontario, it also distributes compostable and recyclable packaging including fibre plates, clamshells and cutlery made overseas.

“Our supply from Asia will continue to them,” Abrol said. “We will not suffer any sales loss.”

Still, the company’s plan to grow its U.S. market share is on pause.

“We May see our exports to U.S.A. reducing a bit or not increasing the way we have planned it,” he said. “But the Canadian large customers for whom we built this factory … we’ll be able to service them Canadian-made products without any exposure to either Sept. 8th (tariffs) or anything which might be looming ahead.”

The company is also positioned to benefit from an ongoing anti-dumping investigation by the Canada Border Services Agency involving Chinese-made paper cups and containers, Abrol said.

If the Cbsa finds the paper packaging — used to serve hot or cold take-out drinks and food — is being sold at unfair prices in Canada, the packaging could face large duties.

Those potential anti-dumping duties could send the price of paper cups and containers from China skyrocketing.

“Some of the large customers … especially some of their distributors who are buying it directly from Asia … they’re in panic mode,” Abrol said. “And that’s why we’re in discussions with them.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Lambton County alerts staff to prepare for arrival of AI data centres
stories.summary: The mayor of Sarnia is pushing Lambton County to set a clear platform for the anticipated arrival of AI Data Centres.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
The mayor of Sarnia is pushing Lambton County to set a clear platform for the anticipated arrival of AI Data Centres.

“Right now, we’re flying blind, without radar,” said Mike Bradley in an interview with CTV News London.

Bradley is calling for staff to review the potential impact of data centres on water, power, the environment and municipal infrastructure.

On the other side of the coin, he wants a better understanding of how the centres could create, and potentially cost jobs.

“And I think that’s why we’re all grappling with jobs versus the other impacts that could actually cut jobs in our communities. That’s what this is all about, just let’s understand what we’re dealing with, which is a difficult question,” he conceded.

Lambton County is already part of the rapidly evolving data centre push, including an AI advanced manufacturing education site at Lambton College.

Additionally, this past spring, MPP Bob Bailey was quoted in various local media suggesting that representatives from a data centre had reached out to him directly.

But with large volumes of water, and several hundred megawatts of power needed to supply a large data centre, opposition exists.

However, at the county council level, Bradley’s motion received unanimous support without comment.

“And I’m not arguing the merits either way,” he stated. “I just think we need a better understanding of what we can do, what we should do, and what we shouldn’t do.”

There are examples for Lambton County to look to across the country.

In one case, Bell Canada Enterprises (BCE), the owner of CTV, is preparing to build a $1.7 billion data centre in Saskatchewan.

BCE contends it will generate $12 billion in economic value and create more 1600 permanent, construction and spinoff jobs.

Yet, the project faces opposition from environmentalists and nearby residents.

It is a scenario likely to repeat in Lambton once a data centre is announced, but Bradley argues having a plan will give Lambton the edge.

“We May be innovative and do some different things that others are not doing with AI data centres. It’s evolving very quickly, this part of the economy.”

Council has directed staff to have the report completed by early 2027.
