stories.title: Winnipeg woman saves father and child from drowning: WPS
stories.summary: Winnipeg police said the child entered the Red River first and started to drown, prompting their father to follow her. A bystander saved both.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Jayclyn Morrissette is a Winnipeg woman police are crediting for saving a father and his child from drowning in the Red River.

The child entered the Red River near St. John’s Park on Aug. 24 and began to drown, prompting the father to jump in and try to save them, according to the Winnipeg Police Service’s (WPS) news release.

Morrissette told Global News she jumped off the park bench she was sitting on when she saw the child, adding that she intervened after noticing the father – who entered the river before her – was starting to sink.

“I knew that I was about to save two people. My first thought was to get him (the father) first, since he’s closer. So, I threw everything out of my pockets and then I jumped in,” she recalled.

She described rescuing the father as “difficult” because he was struggling and trying to hold onto her, pulling her into the water. Her neighbour, who was nearby and on the phone with 911, helped pull Morrissette and the man out of the water.

Her attention then shifted to the man’s child, who Morrissette said was further in the water than their father, and “no longer moving” while face down in the water.

After reaching the child, the woman headed back toward the shoreline, police said.

Morrissette held the child on her chest as she helped them expel the water from their lungs. After returning to shore, she said others started trying to help the child, but did not know how to do CPR. She went back to help the family.

“I had kept performing it until I no longer could, my arms had given out. At that point of picking up the father and swimming back-and-forth, my arms could only handle so much,” she said. Her neighbour took over until the police arrived.

“I remained calm and just did what I thought anybody should do.”

Winnipeg police said her actions that day demonstrated “remarkable courage and selflessness.”

North district WPS officers arrived at the scene shortly before 7 p.m. and took over efforts to save the unconscious child. The child was taken to hospital in critical condition but has since stabilized and is expected to make a full recovery.

Police credited the bystander who swooped into action “for saving both the lives of the child and parent during this incident.”

Morrissette said she started to feel some of the emotional effects of her life-saving park visit when she saw her daughter and spoke with her mom at home.

“I still feel like what I did wasn’t that heroic. Anybody would do that. I would hope anybody would do that,” she said.

“I would only hope that if my child was in the same situation someone would do that too.”

The release reminded parents to supervise their children around water and to exercise caution when visiting parks and waterways.

stories.title: Rabies vaccine operation targets raccoons and skunks in Montreal parks
stories.summary: Workers will be spreading sweet-smelling baits containing a rabies vaccine through Montreal's parks in the coming weeks to head off an outbreak of the deadly disease.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted September 2, 2026 12:51 pm

Teams of workers will be spreading sweet-smelling baits containing a rabies vaccine through Montreal’s parks in the coming weeks in the hopes of heading off an outbreak of the deadly disease.

The provincial environment department said last month that it is leading an effort to distribute some 815,000 baits throughout the Estrie, Montérégie and Centre-du-Québec regions to the south and east of the city, as well as in nine Montreal-area parks.

The baits will be spread by hand and each one looks like a small piece of green ravioli in a packet.

The province has recorded 171 raccoon rabies cases since the beginning of the year, including two cases in cats.

There have also been seven cases of bat rabies, one of which was detected in Montreal in late July.

People are being asked to avoid handling the baits, and should wear gloves or use a shovel if they are forced to move one.

They should also wash their hands after touching one of the baits.

stories.title: Lake Ontario renamed 'Lake America' for U.S. users of Apple Maps
stories.summary: Move follows Google's similar change, even as majority of Americans remain opposed to changing the name of Lake Ontario.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Apple has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America on the web version of its Apple Maps, but only for U.S. users of the service.

The decision by the tech giant took place on Tuesday, the same day John Ternus officially took over as CEO, succeeding Tim Cook, who had led the company for 15 years.

It follows a move by Google’s parent company, Alphabet, to change the name of the lake on its Google Maps, also for U.S. users.

“These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now,” Google said in a statement announcing its change. “People using Maps in the U.S. will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the U.S. and Canada will see both names.”

U.S. President Donald ‌Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to rename the lake, which was given its original title, Ontari:io , millennia ago by Indigenous people and means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.” European settlers in the 1600s started using the word, which also became the official name of the adjoining province in 1867.

In an ‌interview on Fox Business’ Mornings with Maria program on Monday, U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Trump had reached out to Apple directly, “so I’m sure that we May be seeing that change coming up soon to Lake America.”

This comes even as a new poll finds that almost two-thirds of Americans oppose the renaming.

The Ipsos poll reported that 63 per cent of Americans were against the new name, with only 14 per cent in favour and another 21 per cent unsure. Democrats and independents were most likely to be opposed (84 and 65 per cent respectively) but even among Republican voters, just 33 per cent were in favour and 43 per cent against.

The Google change caused confusion and consternation in Canada, as maps on sites run by Hydro One, Metrolinx, Infrastructure Ontario, the Lcbo and others all displayed the American name over the weekend.

However, Ontario government agencies have restored Lake Ontario to their websites, with Metrolinx telling National Post on Monday that “the issue has since been resolved, and our maps once again show Lake Ontario.”

The international boundary running between the U.S. and Canada means that about 52 per cent of the surface area of Lake Ontario is in Canada, with the remainder in New York State. However, Trump has pointed out that, due to the varying depth of the water, more of Lake Ontario by volume is on the American side.

The naming issue mirrors that of the Gulf of Mexico, which Trump ordered to be renamed the Gulf of America early last year. Both Google and Apple subsequently revised their map apps to reflect the change for U.S. users.

paragraphs: Apple has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America on the web version of its Apple Maps, but only for U.S. users of the service.
The decision by the tech giant took place on Tuesday, the same day John Ternus officially took over as CEO, succeeding Tim Cook, who had led the company for 15 years.
It follows a move by Google’s parent company, Alphabet, to change the name of the lake on its Google Maps, also for U.S. users.

“These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now,” Google said in a statement announcing its change. “People using Maps in the U.S. will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the U.S. and Canada will see both names.”

U.S. President Donald ‌Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to rename the lake, which was given its original title, Ontari:io , millennia ago by Indigenous people and means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.” European settlers in the 1600s started using the word, which also became the official name of the adjoining province in 1867.

In an ‌interview on Fox Business’ Mornings with Maria program on Monday, U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Trump had reached out to Apple directly, “so I’m sure that we May be seeing that change coming up soon to Lake America.”
This comes even as a new poll finds that almost two-thirds of Americans oppose the renaming.

The Ipsos poll reported that 63 per cent of Americans were against the new name, with only 14 per cent in favour and another 21 per cent unsure. Democrats and independents were most likely to be opposed (84 and 65 per cent respectively) but even among Republican voters, just 33 per cent were in favour and 43 per cent against.

The Google change caused confusion and consternation in Canada, as maps on sites run by Hydro One, Metrolinx, Infrastructure Ontario, the Lcbo and others all displayed the American name over the weekend.

stories.title: Group prepares push for referendum on proposed downtown arena in Saskatoon
stories.summary: Saskatoon residents May soon get their say on the proposed downtown arena, a project that could become the largest in the city's history.
stories.author: Chris Carr
stories.content:
Saskatoon residents May soon get their say on the proposed downtown arena, a project that could become the largest in the city’s history.

Ken Wood, a retired arena manager, announced on Aug. 21 his plans to organize an effort to force a referendum on the proposed $1.2 billion Downtown Event and Entertainment District. At the same time, he launched voteondeed.CA , where people can find details on the petition to force that referendum.

“Right now, we’re concentrating on volunteers. We’re thinking that is going to be key, getting out there, door to door,” said Wood, former CEO of Credit Union Centre.

Wood said nearly 100 people are offering to canvass. Once they start, they will have 90 days to collect signatures from 10 per cent of eligible voters to force a referendum.

Based on information from the City of Saskatoon, the threshold for meeting this requirement is 26,615 valid signatures. Should the group gather the required signatures, the petition would need to be presented to the city clerk within 90 days after the first signature is collected. A referendum would then need to happen within nine months.

Wood said his group is still working with legal on how the ballot question would be worded.

While the question would be hypothetically structured, Saskatoon Mayor Cynthia Block sees the real question facing the community as something beyond a simplistic, binary ‘should the city proceed or not with the project.’

“We will be making a significant investment in one of two things: taking care of the infrastructure we already own, which will be expensive, or investing in new infrastructure that we will own,” said Block.

Wood sees that as a false argument. He believes renovations at SaskTel Centre could be made much cheaper than some are saying.

“People, when looking at SaskTel, when they are looking at the renovation, they are looking at bringing it up to NHL standards. To me, that’s a non-starter,” said Wood.

Wood said renovations at the existing facility could be done for much cheaper than that.

But Block believes Saskatoon requires a venue with a higher roof to accommodate acts that would otherwise end up in other cities.

“To me, one of the really big questions should be … are we going to invest in aging infrastructure that will not serve the future in the way that modern cities are able to serve and what does that do to our competitive edge?” said Block, noting the city’s responsibility to maintain infrastructure.

“The roof of the building has to be higher, or we can’t attract a lot of the events that a lot of cities are going to be able to attract, including, probably, Regina.”

Wood said we could know as soon as next week when the petition will be launched.

In July, the provincial government said it would match federal funding up to a third of the eligible project costs. So far, there has been no funding commitment to the project from the federal government.

Block said the direction of council has always been that the cost will not impact property taxes.

“If that were ever to change, that would come back to council and there would be a full public discussion at that time. And I am not anticipating that for a number of reasons,” Block said.

Wood said cost is an issue that has come up repeatedly with people he has spoken with.

“People are very concerned about the financial viability of this project. It’s [would be] 100 percent government-financed. And there is no case of a major arena being built like this in North America and being fully funded by government,” said Wood.

Back in June, the city of Saskatoon signed a Memorandum of Understanding to explore a possible partnership with Muskeg Lake Cree Nation.

Earlier this year, city council rejected a proposal from administration to enter into an agreement with U.S.-based Oak View Group 360 to manage the arena.

stories.title: Clinical trial patient says ketamine treatment for bipolar depression changed his life
stories.summary: Toronto — Greg Rennie says his bipolar depression was an eight out of 10 when he went in for his first ketamine infusion in April 2025.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Hannah Alberga, The Canadian Press

Posted September 2, 2026 12:16 pm.

Last Updated September 2, 2026 1:53 pm.

Toronto — Greg Rennie says his bipolar depression was an eight out of 10 when he went in for his first ketamine infusion in April 2025.

He ranked it a zero out of 10 right afterward.

Rennie, who has had bipolar depression for almost 30 years, was one of the 68 participants in a University Health Network clinical trial evaluating the safety and effectiveness of repeated ketamine infusions for people with bipolar depression.

The 61-year-old was hooked up to an IV in a UHN hospital room. About 10 minutes after they turned on the ketamine he recalls feeling like he was floating, dissociated from his body, like he was in outer space. He began to envision himself in a dark room where at times light would shine through.

“I realized what it was showing me is that this is your depression. That I’m in this black box,” he said.

“It did change my life in the way that it made me realize how dark the depression is and that a lot of the time I live within this black room.”

Rennie wasn’t the only one who found his symptoms improved.

The clinical trial, published in Jama Psychiatry Wednesday, found the treatment reduced depressive symptoms for more than 35 per cent of participants, who received two 40-minute ketamine infusions over two weeks.

That’s compared with fewer than 12 per cent in the control group receiving a benzodiazepine medication as a comparison.

Psychiatrist and senior author Dr. Joshua Rosenblat said the ketamine infusions also didn’t trigger mania, psychosis or suicidality.

“That’s one of the most important takeaways, that it didn’t trigger mania, which is what a lot of people were concerned about,” Rosenblat said.

“What we found was that with each subsequent dose there were more and more benefits,” Rosenblat said.

People with bipolar depression have often been excluded from ketamine treatment due to the risk of bringing on a “switch” from depression to mania, said Dr. Jennifer Swainson, a psychiatrist in Edmonton who was not involved in the study.

“This randomized controlled trial suggests that this is not a significant concern, not more so than we May see with the course of the illness itself,” Swainson said.

Ketamine, an anesthetic used for decades to block pain during surgery, has been offered in small doses to treat severe depression, and other psychiatric disorders, over the past 20 years.

There is a need for a treatment that works for bipolar depression, as about one in three do not respond to standard treatments and many medications make people feel worse, Rosenblat said. Approximately three per cent of people in Canada will experience bipolar disorder, according to the federal government’s latest statistics.

There have been concerns about the risk of ketamine treatment leading to addiction in the wake of Matthew Perry’s overdose death. The former “Friends” star was receiving legitimate ketamine infusion treatments for depression but turned to a dealer for supplying him with illicit doses, according to court filings.

However, research shows that most people using ketamine for depression are not at high risk of abusing it or developing an addiction, Swainson said. Toronto — Greg Rennie says his bipolar depression was an eight out of 10 when he went in for his first ketamine infusion in April 2025.
He ranked it a zero out of 10 right afterward.

Rennie, who has had bipolar depression for almost 30 years, was one of the 68 participants in a University Health Network clinical trial evaluating the safety and effectiveness of repeated ketamine infusions for people with bipolar depression.

The 61-year-old was hooked up to an IV in a UHN hospital room. About 10 minutes after they turned on the ketamine he recalls feeling like he was floating, dissociated from his body, like he was in outer space. He began to envision himself in a dark room where at times light would shine through.
“I realized what it was showing me is that this is your depression. That I’m in this black box,” he said.
“It did change my life in the way that it made me realize how dark the depression is and that a lot of the time I live within this black room.”
Rennie wasn’t the only one who found his symptoms improved.

The clinical trial, published in Jama Psychiatry Wednesday, found the treatment reduced depressive symptoms for more than 35 per cent of participants, who received two 40-minute ketamine infusions over two weeks.
That’s compared with fewer than 12 per cent in the control group receiving a benzodiazepine medication as a comparison.
Psychiatrist and senior author Dr. Joshua Rosenblat said the ketamine infusions also didn’t trigger mania, psychosis or suicidality.
“That’s one of the most important takeaways, that it didn’t trigger mania, which is what a lot of people were concerned about,” Rosenblat said.
“What we found was that with each subsequent dose there were more and more benefits,” Rosenblat said.

People with bipolar depression have often been excluded from ketamine treatment due to the risk of bringing on a “switch” from depression to mania, said Dr. Jennifer Swainson, a psychiatrist in Edmonton who was not involved in the study.
“This randomized controlled trial suggests that this is not a significant concern, not more so than we May see with the course of the illness itself,” Swainson said.
Ketamine, an anesthetic used for decades to block pain during surgery, has been offered in small doses to treat severe depression, and other psychiatric disorders, over the past 20 years.

There is a need for a treatment that works for bipolar depression, as about one in three do not respond to standard treatments and many medications make people feel worse, Rosenblat said. Approximately three per cent of people in Canada will experience bipolar disorder, according to the federal government’s latest statistics.

There have been concerns about the risk of ketamine treatment leading to addiction in the wake of Matthew Perry’s overdose death. The former “Friends” star was receiving legitimate ketamine infusion treatments for depression but turned to a dealer for supplying him with illicit doses, according to court filings.

However, research shows that most people using ketamine for depression are not at high risk of abusing it or developing an addiction, Swainson said. In her experience of treating patients with ketamine for depression, she said many reported a neutral opinion or even a dislike of the drug’s effects, but kept using it as prescribed because it helped.

The barrier to ketamine treatment becoming more widely accessible is it’s not covered by most provincial health insurance. Some clinics cover the cost of a limited number of sessions or suggest patients join clinical trials like this one to get access to it. There are also private community clinics that offer treatment that can cost $4,200 for a full cycle of six treatments.
The study found patients’ symptoms returned after they stopped the infusions, suggesting they would need maintenance sessions to keep up the antidepressant effects.
That’s what Rennie has done. He was referred to a private clinic, where he gets infusions every couple months, for $500 for a session.
“That’s the sad part of it,” said Rennie, who believes the therapy should be covered and available across Canada. “I think that has to change.”

stories.title: Élections Québec says it's too late to print voter documents in English
stories.summary: The unilingual documents have prompted an outcry from advocacy groups representing anglophones in Quebec, who say they are creating an unnecessary barrier for voters.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Élections Québec says it is too late to make changes to the unilingual French documents it is mailing to voters ahead of the Oct. 5 election despite facing backlash from the anglophone community.

The provincial elections authority was reacting to comments made by Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette, who said she is in discussions with Élections Québec to determine the next steps.

“We will see what our obligations are,” Fréchette said.

The unilingual documents have prompted an outcry from advocacy groups representing anglophones in Quebec, who say they are creating an unnecessary barrier for voters.

Kelly Burke, Commissioner of Official Languages of Canada, also told The Canadian Press in a statement that her office has already started reviewing two complaints regarding Élections Québec’s decision.

Élections Québec said on Tuesday it could not print the documents in both French and English, as it has done in the past, to comply with language legislation that makes French the sole language of communication for public institutions.

The printed documents include a QR code to the Élections Québec website, where information is available in English.

The legislation, adopted in 2022, allows some people to continue receiving services in English. Anglophones who qualify and Indigenous people can contact the agency to request English information, though it says the campaign period is too short to send physical documents.

The agency added that it asked the commissioner of the French language to make an exception for the election, but to no avail.

A lobby group representing anglophones in the province has asked the government and Élections Québec to reverse the decision.

In an email, the commissioner said the law applies to Élections Québec as it is treated as a government organization. It said some exceptions can be made, though “these exceptions do not permit the systematic dissemination of communications in a language other than French.”

The government’s language policy specifies that “institutional bilingualism is incompatible with the Charter (of the French language),” and the commissioner “does not have the authority to create exceptions to the Charter,” it added.

The provincial ministry responsible for the French language did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

One constitutional lawyer says there could be grounds to contest the law, commonly known as Bill 96, as a result of this year’s electoral policy. An English school board has already challenged the constitutionality of the law, and the case could make its way to the Supreme Court.

Karine Millaire, a law professor at Université de Montréal, said the law appears to discriminate against anglophones and allophones and impacts their right to vote.

She said those who cannot read French are facing additional barriers to access voter information, including how to register, rather than receiving communications in the language they understand.

“It’s a law that was so, so broad and far-reaching — it was a massive piece of legislation — that we’ll continue to see constitutional challenges as cases like these arise,” she said.

Citizens or interest groups could even challenge the outcome of an election if they believe there were irregularities that impacted results, she said, especially since Élections Québec requested to be exempt from the law.

“They themselves believed — and this is no small matter from a legal standpoint — that they should not act in this way and that they should educate all voters in the same way,” she said. “So that’s certainly no trivial matter.”

Party leaders were also asked to comment on the issue on the campaign trail.

“It is what it is,” said Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard, acknowledging Élection Québec is an independent agency. Though he shares voter concerns about access to voting, he said there is “not much (he) can do right now.”

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre-Plamondon maintained that he opposes institutional bilingualism, but compared voting information to the legal system where Quebecers can access justice in either official language.

“When it comes down to fundamental rights, like voting, there needs to be a mechanism through which anglophones can get information in English,” he said, adding that the Coalition Avenir Québec government’s legislation was “sometimes not planned adequately.”

Québec solidaire’s parliamentary leader, Ruba Ghazal, said she is especially worried for seniors who May not have internet access or understand digital platforms.

“We won’t protect the French language by penalizing citizens,” she said. “They have a right to clear information to participate in democracy.”

Voters should receive information cards by the end of the week of Sept. 14, ahead of the election on Oct. 5, according to Élections Québec.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 2, 2026.

stories.title: B.C. government confirms gas revenue forecast errors worth $1.46B
stories.summary: Energy Minister Adrian Dix said the most significant error, a 44-cent overstatement in the forecasted per-gigajoule price of natural gas this fiscal year, was a "serious mistake."
stories.author: Brenna Owen
stories.content:
Errors including botched currency conversions led the British Columbia government to overstate its forecasted natural gas revenues by about $1.46 billion over five fiscal years, officials confirmed on Tuesday.

Energy Minister Adrian Dix said the most significant error, a 44-cent overstatement in the forecasted per-gigajoule price of natural gas this fiscal year, was a “serious mistake.”

But he said the errors affect the province’s forecasting, not its actual revenues, which can vary in a given year. Price fluctuations, including the spike and subsequent decline linked to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, have led the province to both underestimate and overestimate its revenues over the years, Dix said.

“That part is a normal part. What isn’t a part of it is human error that we’re acknowledging today and correcting in the budget,” he told reporters in Vancouver.

Senior staff with the ministries of energy and finance told a technical briefing earlier Tuesday that the errors had been independently verified and corrections would be included in the province’s quarterly fiscal report expected later this month.

The briefing heard the impact on B.C.’s deficit — last pegged at $7.7 billion for fiscal year 2025-2026 — would be made clear with the release of that report.

The most substantial of the errors made by Energy Ministry staff related to U.S.-Canadian dollar conversions, when a formula was incorrectly applied across a spreadsheet.

The province’s forecasting is based on private-sector estimates of natural gas prices, which are provided in Canadian or U.S. dollars.

Dix said the error involved an incorrect assumption that figures were shown in U.S. dollars, when in fact they were Canadian dollars. The numbers were “again translated into Canadian dollars, leading to an overstatement of revenue,” he said.

2:14 Will budget error cost BC billions in natural gas revenue?

The briefing heard correcting that error resulted in a price decrease of 44 cents per gigajoule of natural gas in B.C.’s forecasting for 2026-2027.

Budget 2026 shows incorrect forecasted prices per gigajoule ranging from $2.34 to $4.83 at plant inlet, referring to gas that hasn’t yet been processed.

“We’re making changes to the way the process happens to ensure that such errors do not occur in the future,” Dix said.

The Opposition B.C. Conservatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but last week, their finance critic Gavin Dew called for the auditor general to examine the flawed revenue forecasts, after they were originally reported by Business in Vancouver.

“This isn’t just an accounting error. It’s a credibility problem,” Dew said in a statement, while Opposition Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay said B.C. could not afford budgets “built on wishful thinking.”

The information in Tuesday’s technical briefing was provided on background, meaning it was not for attribution to an individual.

A second error involving the conversion of energy units amounted to a five-cent decrease in the forecasted price.

Two other errors stemming from the use of data from 2025 instead of this year’s figures resulted in a decrease in the plant inlet price of 1 cent per gigajoule, while adding 3 cents to the outlet price.

Combined, correcting the errors amounted to an average annual decrease in expected revenues of $292 million from this fiscal year to the one starting in 2030.

The impact for the current fiscal year is $306 million, reducing forecasted revenue by about 24 per cent, from $1.297 billion to $991 million.

The Energy Ministry is working with experts to improve its quality assurance process in forecasting moving forward, staff told the briefing.

The briefing heard Treaty 8 First Nations in northeastern B.C. had alerted government officials to what they believed to be an error in the province’s accounting of processing and transportation costs for natural gas in June.

Staff said the province reviewed its calculations and confirmed those costs were appropriately incorporated into its forecasting, but in July uncovered the series of errors related to the conversion of currency units of natural gas.

The errors come as the province works on an updated framework for collecting natural gas royalties that’s set to come into force on Jan. 1, with the goal of returning 50 per cent of profits after accounting for companies’ production costs.

Staff at the briefing acknowledged concerns among Treaty 8 First Nations that the framework won’t hit that target and said further information would be available this fall.

Dix said officials were confident they were “on the right track.”

He said the goal was to establish a new royalty framework that’s “fair for the taxpayers and the owners of the resources,” including First Nations.

It must also strike a balance with the industry, he said.

“We have to make sure (there’s) a good return for the people so that we can help pay for things that are really important to me, like health care and education, ON the one hand, and you’ve got to ensure that we have an industry that’s in the province.”

stories.title: Website takes bets on London mayoral race, even though Canadians can't legally wager
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 3:48 PM | Last Updated: 17 hours ago
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 3:48 PM | Last Updated: 17 hours ago
Expert says election betting websites could affect voter behaviour
The available choices for mayor shown on the screen include incumbent Josh Morgan, along with candidates Susan Stevenson, Kirsten Krose and John Feher.

But the options on the list aren't part of a ballot to be marked with an 'X' by voters. Instead, the names are options for bettors willing to wager on who will be London's next mayor, with more than $6,000 already in the pot.

The betting options are posted at Polymarket.com, a U.S.-based prediction-market website. Such sites offer bets on outcomes as varied as whether Bitcoin will rise or fall and which celebrity couples will get married (or separated).
Prediction markets allow users to wager on so-called binary outcomes—yes or no propositions.
In addition to London's mayoral race, Polymarket offers odds on who will be the next mayor in other Ontario cities, including Windsor, Toronto and Stratford.
Media Video |

At first glance, Polymarket bets look similar to the wagering menu of a sports betting website but actually work very differently. The main difference is that users aren't betting against the house or a bookmaker, which uses handicappers to set the odds of each outcome.

Instead, Polymarket users are betting against other users backing the opposite side of their bet. The odds of the bets are expressed as shares of each contract, which pays for a specific outcome. The contracts are priced between one cent and one dollar, with a dollar as the approximate payout, less a handling fee.

For example, a contract for incumbent Josh Morgan to win the mayoral race—again with the payout at about a dollar—costs 64 cents, based on odds posted Wednesday. In other words, a bettor would risk 64 cents and collects just under a buck if Morgan wins.
A contract to win a dollar if Susan Stevenson wins would cost 15 cents.
The bets can be scaled upward. For example, a contract to win $1,000 if Morgan is re-elected would cost the bettor $640.
Also, prediction market contacts can be sold before the outcome happens, with a price determined by the market of that particular event.

anadian regulators h ave approved limited prediction-market trading on three types of outcomes: economic indicators, financial markets and climate trends. Prediction market bets on sports, elections or pop culture aren't allowed.

Also, only two prediction market websites have been approved for users in Canada: Wealthsimple and Interactive Brokers Canada. Canadians can't technically open a Polymarket account, although many get around those rules using a virtual private network (VPN) to conceal their location.

So, how is Polymarket able to offer odds for London's mayors race, along with mayoral races in Windsor, Stratford, Waterloo and Toronto? Because the site has users in other jurisdictions in which such bets aren't restricted by regulators.
Canada's regulatory approach to bar prediction-market betting on elections is a sound one, said Brock University professor of finance Ernest Biktimirov.

He sees a number of problems with betting on elections, including the potential for insider trading, when people working on a political campaign, or the candidates themselves, use non-public information about the race to turn a profit.

"It's a thin market," said Biktimirov, referring to the relatively small amount of prediction-market bets placed on a local elections in smaller cities. "In big races like Toronto, it's much more difficult to move the prices. When it comes to local elections, the number of people trading is smaller and one person with a large amount of money, they can move the prices of this contact."

Insider trading on prediction markets in political races has been an issue in the United States. The prediction market site Kalshi barred three political candidates from using the site, alleging that they bet on their own races. One of the allegations involved a Senate seat.
Another problem is that voters might view the posted odds as akin to a poll which aims to provide an accurate indicator of where the candidates' support stands.
Noah Vanderhoeven, a political science professor at Western University, said prediction markets have the potential to affect voter behaviour.
"The risk would be someone places a lot of money behind one position ... and that's not necessarily representative of what the polling is and that could affect people's decision making," he said.
Voters in Ontario municipal races, including London, cast their votes on Oct. 26.

| CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 3:48 PM | Last Updated: 17 hours ago

Expert says election betting websites could affect voter behaviour

The available choices for mayor shown on the screen include incumbent Josh Morgan, along with candidates Susan Stevenson, Kirsten Krose and John Feher.

But the options on the list aren't part of a ballot to be marked with an 'X' by voters. Instead, the names are options for bettors willing to wager on who will be London's next mayor, with more than $6,000 already in the pot.

The betting options are posted at Polymarket.com, a U.S.-based prediction-market website. Such sites offer bets on outcomes as varied as whether Bitcoin will rise or fall and which celebrity couples will get married (or separated).

Prediction markets allow users to wager on so-called binary outcomes—yes or no propositions.

In addition to London's mayoral race, Polymarket offers odds on who will be the next mayor in other Ontario cities, including Windsor, Toronto and Stratford.

Media Video |

At first glance, Polymarket bets look similar to the wagering menu of a sports betting website but actually work very differently. The main difference is that users aren't betting against the house or a bookmaker, which uses handicappers to set the odds of each outcome.

Instead, Polymarket users are betting against other users backing the opposite side of their bet. The odds of the bets are expressed as shares of each contract, which pays for a specific outcome. The contracts are priced between one cent and one dollar, with a dollar as the approximate payout, less a handling fee.

For example, a contract for incumbent Josh Morgan to win the mayoral race—again with the payout at about a dollar—costs 64 cents, based on odds posted Wednesday. In other words, a bettor would risk 64 cents and collects just under a buck if Morgan wins.

A contract to win a dollar if Susan Stevenson wins would cost 15 cents.

The bets can be scaled upward. For example, a contract to win $1,000 if Morgan is re-elected would cost the bettor $640.

Also, prediction market contacts can be sold before the outcome happens, with a price determined by the market of that particular event.

anadian regulators h ave approved limited prediction-market trading on three types of outcomes: economic indicators, financial markets and climate trends. Prediction market bets on sports, elections or pop culture aren't allowed.

Also, only two prediction market websites have been approved for users in Canada: Wealthsimple and Interactive Brokers Canada. Canadians can't technically open a Polymarket account, although many get around those rules using a virtual private network (VPN) to conceal their location.

So, how is Polymarket able to offer odds for London's mayors race, along with mayoral races in Windsor, Stratford, Waterloo and Toronto? Because the site has users in other jurisdictions in which such bets aren't restricted by regulators.

Canada's regulatory approach to bar prediction-market betting on elections is a sound one, said Brock University professor of finance Ernest Biktimirov.

He sees a number of problems with betting on elections, including the potential for insider trading, when people working on a political campaign, or the candidates themselves, use non-public information about the race to turn a profit.

"It's a thin market," said Biktimirov, referring to the relatively small amount of prediction-market bets placed on a local elections in smaller cities. "In big races like Toronto, it's much more difficult to move the prices. When it comes to local elections, the number of people trading is smaller and one person with a large amount of money, they can move the prices of this contact."

Insider trading on prediction markets in political races has been an issue in the United States. The prediction market site Kalshi barred three political candidates from using the site, alleging that they bet on their own races. One of the allegations involved a Senate seat.

Another problem is that voters might view the posted odds as akin to a poll which aims to provide an accurate indicator of where the candidates' support stands.

Noah Vanderhoeven, a political science professor at Western University, said prediction markets have the potential to affect voter behaviour.

"The risk would be someone places a lot of money behind one position ... and that's not necessarily representative of what the polling is and that could affect people's decision making," he said.

Voters in Ontario municipal races, including London, cast their votes on Oct. 26.

stories.title: $3.9M in skilled trades funding to help women, domestic violence survivors: Ontario
stories.summary: Ontario says it's spending nearly $3.9 million across four training projects intended to help women, including survivors of domestic violence, train for in-demand skilled trade careers.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario says it’s spending nearly $3.9 million across four training projects intended to help women, including survivors of domestic violence, train for in-demand skilled trade careers.

More than half of that Skills Development Fund money is earmarked for Women’s Crisis Services of Waterloo Region to help 42 women who are survivors of gender-based violence train to be carpenters and machine mechanics, among other trades.

stories.title: Healing in the Public Eye: Medical tattoos mark next step in Peloza’s health journey after chemotherapy
stories.summary: Councillor Elizabeth Peloza is providing a health update in her ongoing series about her cancer journey called Healing in the Public Eye.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Coun. Elizabeth Peloza is providing a health update in her ongoing series about her cancer journey called Healing in the Public Eye.

Tonight, she shares her milestone completing chemotherapy, and the start of radiation treatments.

“It was a great day, I was never so excited to be having toxic chemicals put in me,” Elizabeth Peloza recalls about her final chemotherapy treatment.

Peloza has been sharing her breast cancer journey with CTV News in a special series called Healing in the Public Eye.

Recently, Peloza sat down to share her thoughts about reaching the milestone in her treatment.

“I got to ring the bell that signals the end of chemo,” she said about the tradition of ringing a brass bell inside the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre at the London Health Sciences Centre.

“When anyone in that space rings the bell, the auditorium echoes with people clapping,” Peloza explains. “Everyone is celebrating with you because they are in that same place themselves or with a loved one.”

She’s was also excited for the removal of a peripherally inserted central catheter, known as a Picc line, that delivered the chemotherapy drugs close to her heart.

Running a finger over the small scar on the inside of her arm she explains, “I can now sleep comfortably, not worry about putting clothes on and catching it, and I can shower without having to bag it up.”

However, ringing the bell and removing the Picc line isn’t the end of Peloza’s cancer treatments.

“Everyone’s journey can include different things and can be in a different order,” she explains. “For me, it was the surgery first, then chemo, and now I’m going into radiation. For me, it’ll be 19 rounds of radiation.”

Early in her radiation treatments, she’s mentally preparing for side effects.

“I’ve been told it could feel like a sunburn, and then you keep going tanning every day,” Peloza said.

She’s aware that patients can experience fatigue at various times during the treatments.

However, each radiation treatment is much quicker than chemotherapy.

“Radiation is super fast,” she explains. “The bed is already precisely set-up to your exact measurements (regarding) where they need to place you for treatment. You hop on the bed, it takes a couple minutes, and then off you go with your day.”

Previously, chemotherapy treatments would require up to six hours at the cancer centre.

“They put three really small dots on my body, which are a permanent tattoo that they use to align the machine when I go in for radiation treatment,” she explains.

Asked if those were her first tattoos, she laughs.

“I was never cool enough to have a tattoo, so now I’ve got my first, second, and third tattoo all at the same time,” Peloza said.

She’s unsure whether to keep the tiny tattoos after her breast cancer journey is over.

“They’ll be a reminder. But the (surgery) scars are another reminder whenever I look down.”

stories.title: Workers find historic human remains in Manitoban RM: RCMP
stories.summary: A road maintenance crew found the human remains last week, according to the Manitoba RCMP, who said carbon dating and testing is being arranged.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Carbon dating is underway after road workers found human remains in RM of Wallace-Woodworth, Man., police said.

Last Wednesday, crews found two pieces of a human skull and a bone on Road 57 North while cleaning ditches in the aftermath of recent flooding, according to a news release from the Manitoba RCMP. It says at that point, work stopped and the police were called.

Officers with the Virden RCMP received a report from the crew around 2:15 p.m. on Aug. 26 and established a perimeter around the area where the remains were found, just east of Road 148 West, police said.

The next morning, a forensic anthropologist and her team were called to the site. They found a partial skull, right shin bone and lower left femur, the RCMP said. The Manitoba Historic Resources Branch also searched the area.

“The remains are consistent with those of a historical or archaeological nature,” police added, noting that carbon dating and testing is being arranged for some of the remains.

stories.title: Toronto police deem fire at commercial building suspicious
stories.summary: Just after 3 a.m., firefighters and police were called to Finch Avenue East and Willowdale Avenue for reports of a fire at a commercial building.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
stories.content:
Toronto police are investigating a fire in North York as suspicious after they rushed to the scene in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

Just after 3 a.m., firefighters and police were called to Finch Avenue East and Willowdale Avenue for reports of a fire at a commercial building.

Firefighters quickly put out the fire, officials said, with no injuries reported.

Toronto police said they wouldn’t attend the scene to offer an update Wednesday morning, but confirmed the fire was considered suspicious.

They offered no details about their nascent investigation.

Roads in the area were closed as firefighters got the blaze under control and assessed that the building was stable.

stories.title: Vancouver-area home sales drop almost 5% in August amid lag: board
stories.summary: Greater Vancouver Realtors says there were 1,869 home sales last month, which was 20.7 per cent below the 10-year seasonal average.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted September 2, 2026 11:24 am

Home sales in the Vancouver region dropped 4.6 per cent last month compared with a year ago, continuing a lag since May that is expected to persist through the end of 2026.

Greater Vancouver Realtors says there were 1,869 home sales last month, which was 20.7 per cent below the 10-year seasonal average.

Andrew Lis, the board’s chief economist and vice-president of data analytics, says inventory levels have receded from their 2025 heights, and paired with slower-than-usual sales, this has caused prices “to drift downwards across all market segments.”

The composite benchmark price for all types of residential properties in Vancouver was $1,081,900, a 5.6 per cent decline from August 2025 and a 0.6 per cent dip from July 2026.

There were 4,100 new listings on the market last month, down three per cent year-over-year and 1.3 per cent lower than the 10-year average.

Meanwhile, total inventory fell 2.7 per cent annually to 15,798, which was 26.2 per cent above the long-term average.

stories.title: University of Waterloo student arrested in U.S. espionage case
stories.summary: Chinese national accused of taking pictures of aircraft, airport facilities in Toronto, Chicago
stories.author: Matthew Frank, Colin Freeze
stories.content:
American authorities say they suspect that an Ontario university student had been spying for an unknown person in China by taking photos of aircraft and airport facilities in Toronto and Chicago.

On Aug. 23, U.S. Customs and Border Patrol officers arrested the student, Weiheng Zeng, a Chinese citizen born in 2004, while he attempted to cross the Ambassador Bridge and travel to Detroit, a criminal complaint filed by the FBI states.

Mr. Zeng, an undergraduate at the University of Waterloo who lives in Cambridge, Ont., is being detained in Detroit, where he has been charged with one count of making false statements.

However, in an interview with The Globe and Mail Wednesday in Mr. Zeng’s family’s home in Cambridge, his twin sister, Meixuan Wang, disputed the allegations as far-fetched. She described her brother as a “really nerdy, silly guy,” who is obsessed with airplanes and has autism spectrum disorder.

“If he’s a spy, I’m Trump’s dad,” said Ms. Wang, who also uses the name Jade.

None of the allegations against Mr. Zeng have been tested in court.

Defence lawyer Celeste Kinney, a public defender who represented Mr. Zeng in court after his arrest, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Ms. Wang told The Globe on Wednesday that the family is looking for a lawyer in the U.S. to represent her brother.

An unnamed spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Ottawa said in an e-mail that it “firmly opposes hyping up the so-called ‘China spy threat’ and the baseless speculations and smears against China.”

Speaking to The Globe on behalf of her family, Ms. Wang said she read the Federal Bureau of Investigation complaint and that it came as a surprise because her brother – known as “Billy” – always shared many details of his life with her.

She said her brother’s autism spectrum disorder can cause people to regard him differently. He May not have realized the trouble he was in when he spoke to U.S. federal agents at the border, Ms. Wang said.

“He doesn’t look at your eyes when he’s speaking with you. He’s not really confident; he doesn’t recognize your emotions,” she said.

Ms. Wang said her family came to Canada from the southwestern Chinese city of Chengdu during the pandemic, when she and her brother were high-school students. Last month, they both celebrated getting their Canadian permanent residency status. She said her brother was studying global business and digital arts at the University of Waterloo but wanted to be a pilot.

Ms. Wang showed The Globe a copy of her brother’s Yellow Zone pass to the London Ontario Air Show from two weeks ago, where he was among thousands of spectators watching U.S. F-22 Raptors take flight.

Shortly after that air show, she said, she got in the family car with her brother, so he could drive her back to a Chicago art school, where she was studying ceramics.

When they tried crossing into the U.S. on Aug. 23, U.S. border guards singled them out for inspection, Ms. Wang said. He was arrested and she said she was held for a full day for questioning by U.S. Customs and the FBI before being let go.

“They said: ‘Does your brother work for the Chinese government? I said, ‘Oh no, of course not,’” she told The Globe.

The Fbi’s investigation was triggered after surveillance footage from April 21 showed Mr. Zeng taking pictures of aircraft and facilities at Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport, which he is alleged to have taken for a Chinese contact, according to the criminal complaint.

Karen Tride, spokesperson for The Chicago Department of Aviation, which manages the airport, declined to comment on the incident.

The footage also allegedly showed that he drove a van with Ontario licence plates into a FedEx employee parking lot near the airport. At the time, FedEx employees spotted Mr. Zeng in the company’s parking lot taking pictures, walking the fence line and attempting to open locked trailers, the criminal complaint states.

FedEX didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Zeng was also seen climbing a parked forklift to take more pictures, and he later acknowledged doing so, the document says. It also says that U.S. law enforcement officials were able to tie the van to Mr. Zeng.

On the day of his arrest, Mr. Zeng allegedly drove the same van to the Ambassador Bridge, with two passengers including his sister inside, and told U.S. border officials that he was travelling for a one-day trip to Chicago.

Since the vehicle had been flagged after the April 21 incident, U.S. border officials and the FBI held Mr. Zeng and interviewed him multiple times, the criminal complaint states. It alleges that his story changed in each interview.

Mr. Zeng initially told investigators that he was taking photos for his hobby and for a flight-radar website, according to the complaint.

U.S. officials searched his phone and allegedly found pictures of multiple military aircraft. Investigators also found pictures of Mr. Zeng holding rifle-style firearms and wearing tactical clothing, the FBI alleges. Mr. Zeng told U.S. officials that the weapon was an airsoft gun, the complaint states.

By the third interview, Mr. Zeng allegedly told investigators that a Chinese contact, who sent him an image of a badge with a picture of Tiananmen Square and a Chinese five-star symbol, had communicated with him online since November, 2024, and offered to pay Mr. Zeng money for the photos of specific planes and tail numbers at the Chicago airport.

Mr. Zeng also allegedly said in a sworn statement that he believed that the contact was a member of the Chinese Communist Party and wanted the photos for “research,” the complaint states.

“Zeng claimed that he thought it was ‘cool,’” referring to communicating with the Chinese contact, the complaint states, “and wanted ‘to have the opportunity to work with someone like [agents] at the FBI.’”

Mr. Zeng allegedly told investigators that in October, 2025, the same Chinese contact allegedly directed him to take pictures of the inside of a FedEx facility at Toronto Pearson International Airport. The complaint states that he told the FBI that he only got photos of the building’s exterior.

He also allegedly said that he trespassed earlier that year but was turned away by a FedEx employee, the complaint says.

The airport didn’t respond to a request for comment.

When asked about the investigation, Eric Balsam, spokesperson for the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, said the RCMP is “better positioned” to answer questions about Mr. Zeng.

RCMP spokesperson Camille Boily-Lavoie said the force is aware of the incident but didn’t comment further, directing questions to U.S. authorities.

University of Waterloo spokesperson Anne Galang said in an e-mail the university doesn’t “normally comment on ongoing criminal investigations.”

According to the FBI, Mr. Zeng said he was coached on how to beat surveillance in Canada by using his Chinese-made Huawei cellphone.

“The SIM card, which was from China Telecom, allowed Zeng to by-pass Canadian cellular networks and connect directly with the Chinese provider network to send text messages,” the complaint states.

Mr. Zeng allegedly said he was told to never use his Huawei phone in the United States and was instructed to replace his SIM cards and destroy the old ones “which he did by burning it with a lighter” every four to five months.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Alyse Wu argued in a Detroit court on Aug. 26 that Mr. Zeng should continue to be detained to prevent him from leaving the area.

“He is a foreign resident and a foreign citizen. According to what is alleged in the complaint, his only known tie to this district appears to be using it as a crossing point to enter our country for what appears to be espionage-type activities,” she said at a hearing that day in a Detroit courtroom.

Documents filed in U.S. district court say Mr. Zeng also appeared before a judge on Tuesday in Detroit.

stories.title: Sports Notes: Buczkowski wins cycling world title, Knights head west, Mustangs football ready for opener, Majors finish 2nd
stories.summary: Brent Lale takes a look at local sports from the past few days and into the weekend.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The London Knights are heading west

The bus departed for the airport Wednesday afternoon as the boys are off to Victoria, B.C. for a pair of exhibition games in a series titled “Clash of the Kingdoms.”

The series on Friday and Saturday is the first regular interleague pre-season meeting between WHL and OHL clubs outside of the Memorial Cup since 2010.

The Knights will take 25 skaters and three goalies on the road for the games which will be played at the Save-On-Foods Memorial Centre.

“I’ve been to Victoria once before and played in the rink once, and it’s a pretty cool barn and it’s a pretty cool place to be,” said Knights forward Brady Wassilyn.

“Taking the ferry over and just being with all the boys, you know, getting to go on the bus to the airport, being in the airport with everybody is so much fun.”

Wassilyn remembers arriving in London mid-season and believes a few days away can work wonders.

“When I first got here we had a two game road trip and I think that’s what brings the boys together as being on the road together,” he added.

London will arrive Wednesday evening, and immediately after the game Saturday will take a red-eye flight back home.

Buczkowski wins world junior cycling gold

Eve Buczkowski of Talbotville, Ont. is bringing the rainbow jersey back to Canada.

Buczkowski became the first Canadian since Maggie Coles-Lyster in 2017 to win the Junior Women’s Points Race at the 2026 UCI Junior Track World Championships in Limburg, Belgium.

“I’m really proud because it was a result that I wasn’t necessarily expecting, but I knew that it was possible,” said the 17-year old.

“Being able to come out and really just show that I am, I guess, the confident rider that I always wanted to be”.

She explained her strategy which allowed her maximum points at the Velodrome.

“Through the qualifier, I realized that taking easy laps and lapping the field was the not necessarily the quickest, but the easiest way for me to get the maximum amount of points,” she said.

“Going into the final, I used the same plan of taking easy laps. When I took my lap, It put me at the top of the leaderboard and I was able to hold that position until the final sprint where I sprinted to solidify the win”. London Majors stumble down stretch, open playoffs Friday

After leading the Canadian Baseball League standings for a large portion of the 2026 season, the London Majors picked their worst time to have a losing streak.

Needing just one victory in the final four games, London (31-17) lost all of them which cost them the pennant, and the top seed entering the playoffs.

Their recent losses were Hamilton’s gain, as the Cardinals surged to take top spot in the standings.

Tuesday night, the Welland Jackfish beat the Majors 11-3 in the completion of a suspended game which wrapped up the 48-game regular season. Hamilton, London and Welland all finished with identical records.

Franchise history was made at Labatt Park when Maikol Escotto hit a two-run home run for the Majors, giving him 16 on the season, the most ever by a London player.

After eight months on the job, Michael Faulds is finally ready to coach his first regular season football game for the Western Mustangs.

Western will open its season at Alumni Stadium Sunday night against the York Lions (1-0).

“We’ve got a lot of first-time starters, which is exciting, but also a little nerve wracking at the same time. There will be a lot of new faces for the London community and the Western community to get used to, but a lot of marquee names that people are going to get familiar with pretty quickly.”

With new starter Jerome Rancourt at quarterback, the Mustangs will take on the Lions who won their opener against Carleton.

stories.title: Hilroy says sorry for leaving Newfoundland, Cape Breton off notebooks’ Canadian map
stories.summary: A spokesperson for Hilroy's parent company, Acco Brands, says the inaccurate map was the result of a printing error.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
Hilroy has apologized for leaving Newfoundland and Cape Breton off the Canadian map on its glossy notebooks, after the mistake led to backlash online.

Hilroy’s pastel-coloured paper exercise books are well known across the country for the map of Canada on their covers. But the map on Hilroy’s glossy covered notebooks are missing a few parts of the country.

In a post to its Facebook page Tuesday, the company said its team has always been proud of the map, “which is exactly why getting it wrong stings.”

The inaccurate map was the result of a production error, the post said. The company has stopped distributing the books and is fixing the cover artwork.

“That’s our mistake, and we’re sorry,” it said. “To everyone who spotted it: you’re right and thank you for telling us.”

Hilroy’s parent company, Acco Brands, said Wednesday that the faulty books have been on shelves since last year. However, it seems customers only recently noticed the errors. The mishap has generated discussion on social media, prompting posts from Newfoundlanders and Nova Scotians expressing their dismay.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham posted a brief but blunt response on Facebook.

“You can leave Newfoundland off an exercise book, but you can’t erase us,” he wrote Wednesday. “Hilroy will never take away our identity, our history, or our place on the map.”

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said the incomplete map was “unacceptable.”

“I’ve asked the minister of education to send the makers of Hilroy scribblers a map of Nova Scotia that includes Cape Breton and Newfoundland,” Houston said, also in Facebook post.

The mistaken map also appears to be missing Haida Gwaii, an archipelago off the coast of British Columbia. An Acco Brands spokesperson said the company is aware and addressing the omission is part of its “correction plan.”

Sean Cadigan, a history professor at Memorial University in St. John’s, N.L., said Newfoundland did not join Canada until 1949, and it has been left out of maps and descriptions of the country before. It can be a sensitive issue on the island, he said.

“When there are big tours and people say they’re touring Canada, Canada often stops somewhere in Nova Scotia,” Cadigan said in an interview Wednesday.

“I think that’s just probably an old habit that often predates Newfoundland’s joining Confederation,” he added. “Obviously, people here want to emphasize, of course, since 1949, we’re part of Canada.”

Cadigan said the map was an “an embarrassing mistake” for Hilroy.

“I wouldn’t read it as any intent to slight,” he said.

stories.title: Apple changes Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ for U.S. users of Maps app
stories.summary: Google rolled out the change over the weekend, citing Trump’s order
stories.author: Shannon Proudfoot
stories.content:
Apple Aapl-Q has relabelled Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for U.S. users of its Maps app, following competitor Google days after President Donald Trump ordered a new name for the body of water amid his escalating trade war with Canada.

As of Wednesday morning, Apple Maps displayed “Lake America” for U.S. users looking at the lake that sits between the state of New York and Canada’s Ontario province. Users outside of the U.S. still saw the Lake Ontario name.

Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. Earlier this week, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told Fox that Trump had reached out to the company “directly” about the change.

Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario. What does it actually change?

The President declared the new “Lake America” name last week — marking one of the latest provocations during his trade war with Canada that is now hiking tariffs on both sides of the border. His executive order on Friday directed the Interior Department to update the lake’s name in the U.S. geographic naming service.

Google Maps rolled out the change over the weekend, citing Trump’s order and its already-established practice of using names assigned by the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (or Gnis).

“People using Maps in the U.S. will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the U.S. and Canada will see both names,” Google said in a brief statement on Saturday, reiterating that such updates “follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”

Trump cannot force Canada to also change the name of Lake Ontario. And America’s northern neighbors quickly panned the idea.

“It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever,” Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote on social media Friday.

Prime Minister Mark Carney also rejected the move last week, invoking the lake’s Indigenous roots and noting that the name predates both the Canadian Confederation and U.S. Declaration of Independence.

This isn’t the first time Trump has moved to rename water spanning beyond U.S. borders. Last year, Trump ordered that the Gulf of Mexico be renamed the Gulf of America — and both Apple and Google later updated the name on their maps in the U.S.

But not all map providers have followed suit. MapQuest, in particular, has declared it won’t be changing Lake Ontario’s label — and gave users the option to name the lake “whatever you want” through a separate online tool. Both the Lake Ontario and Gulf of Mexico names still appear as default on its platform.

MapQuest, owned by California company System1, has reported a surge of downloads recently. On Wednesday, MapQuest topped the charts of free apps with new downloads in both the U.S. and Canada on Apple’s App Store.

content_blocks.text: Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. Earlier this week, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told Fox that Trump had reached out to the company “directly” about the change.

content_blocks.text: Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario. What does it actually change?

content_blocks.text: The President declared the new “Lake America” name last week — marking one of the latest provocations during his trade war with Canada that is now hiking tariffs on both sides of the border. His executive order on Friday directed the Interior Department to update the lake’s name in the U.S. geographic naming service.

His executive order on Friday directed the Interior Department to update the lake’s name in the U.S. geographic naming service.

content_blocks.text: Google Maps rolled out the change over the weekend, citing Trump’s order and its already-established practice of using names assigned by the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (or Gnis).
content_blocks.html: Google Maps rolled out the change over the weekend, citing Trump’s order and its already-established practice of using names assigned by the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (or GNIS).

content_blocks.text: “People using Maps in the U.S. will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the U.S. and Canada will see both names,” Google said in a brief statement on Saturday, reiterating that such updates “follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”

content_blocks.text: Trump cannot force Canada to also change the name of Lake Ontario. And America’s northern neighbors quickly panned the idea.

content_blocks.text: “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever,” Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote on social media Friday.

content_blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney also rejected the move last week, invoking the lake’s Indigenous roots and noting that the name predates both the Canadian Confederation and U.S. Declaration of Independence.

content_blocks.text: This isn’t the first time Trump has moved to rename water spanning beyond U.S. borders. Last year, Trump ordered that the Gulf of Mexico be renamed the Gulf of America — and both Apple and Google later updated the name on their maps in the U.S.

MapQuest, in particular, has declared it won’t be changing Lake Ontario’s label — and gave users the option to name the lake “whatever you want” through a separate online tool. Both the Lake Ontario and Gulf of Mexico names still appear as default on its platform.

stories.title: London Knights move game radio broadcasts to Classic Rock 98.1
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 2:42 PM | Last Updated: 5 hours ago
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 2:42 PM | Last Updated: 5 hours ago
Mike Stubbs, the longtime voice of the Knights, will continue the play-by-play coverage
London Knights games will have a new home on the radio this season.

The Knights announced Wednesday that Blackburn Media Inc. and Brand One Digital will become the team's exclusive local radio and streaming media partners. The move ends a decade-long partnership with Corus radio station AM980.
Classic Rock 98.1 FM will broadcast all evening home and away games during the upcoming Ontario Hockey League season, along with pre-game coverage, intermissions and post-game highlights.
Mike Stubbs, who has called Knights games for about 29 years, will continue as the team's play-by-play voice.
"This is incredible," Stubbs told CBC News. "You don't ever want to stop and step off that ride."

Stubbs said the move from AM radio to the FM band will provide a different listening experience, while Blackburn's plans for podcasts, digital content and a new Knights app could make coverage more accessible to fans.
"I think fans are going to be able to find coverage however they like to find coverage," he said.
Knights vice president and general manager Mark Hunter said the organization is proud to enter a new era of broadcast and digital media with Blackburn Media Inc.

“We are excited to work with a locally-owned company and to continue the great tradition of delivering London Knights hockey to our fans in London and the surrounding area," Hunter said in a news release.
Games will also be streamed through the station's website and the iHeartRadio app. A new London Knights radio app is expected to launch in 2027.
Stubbs said fans can expect the same enthusiasm and coverage they've come to expect from Knights broadcasts when the team takes to the new airwaves.
"I just love what I'm able to do," he said. "I'm lucky, and I'm excited."
The Knights have not yet announced the full broadcast schedule or who will provide colour commentary alongside Stubbs.

stories.title: Couche-Tard reports slowing U.S. sales growth as it pushes ahead with takeover of Poland’s Zabka
stories.summary: ‘Progress in a business like ours is measured over years, not quarters,’ CEO Alex Miller told analysts on a call
stories.author: Nicolas Van Praet
stories.content:
Canadian convenience store operator Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc. ATD-T tallied a fifth straight quarter of same-store sales growth in the United States over the summer, maintaining positive momentum in its biggest market as it works to expand its footprint in Europe with an US$8.7-billion deal for Polish retailer Zabka Group SA.

The Laval, Que.-based company, which owns the Circle K chain, on Tuesday published results for the first quarter of the company’s fiscal 2027, which ended July 19. It included a 1.7-per-cent year-over-year increase in merchandise sales at comparable U.S. stores. Energy drinks and nicotine products performed particularly well, and the company is taking market share from rivals in key segments, it said.

The sales increase in the U.S. wasn’t as strong as in previous quarters. Analysts had warned that a sequential slowdown was coming based on the recent performance of some competitors, such as ARKO and Murphy USA.

“Progress in a business like ours is measured over years, not quarters,” Couche-Tard chief executive officer Alex Miller told analysts on a call Wednesday morning. “We’re encouraged by the start to fiscal 2027, and we’re seeing evidence that our strategy is resonating with customers and strengthening the business.”

Over all, net profit came in at US$828.5-million or US$0.90 per diluted share on total revenue of US$21.7-billion for the period, improving on the US$782.5-million during the same quarter last year, Couche-Tard said in a release after market close. The company reports in U.S. dollars.

On an adjusted basis, net earnings were US$827-million or US$0.90 per share. That’s roughly in line with the US$0.89 analysts were expecting. The company sold less gasoline over all but boosted its fuel gross margin in the U.S. and Canada.

After a solid trajectory of profit growth over the past two decades, Couche-Tard’s business has come under pressure more recently as consumers slash their spending to deal with higher levels of debt as well as inflation. Global conflict, including in the Middle East, has added to those worries and industry observers are analyzing whether it will lead to any lasting change in consumer behaviour.

Mr. Miller and his team are trying to make Circle K’s offerings more attractive in response, launching meal deals priced from US$3 to US$6 in the United States and offering rebates on gasoline on certain days in a bid to build customer loyalty. The company has said it expects it can generate year-over-year adjusted earnings-per-share growth of 10 per cent or more from fiscal 2026 through 2030.

While the 15-per-cent EPS growth for the latest quarter is higher than that, the deceleration of U.S. merchandise same-store sales growth “may raise questions” about the health of the American consumer, Stifel analyst Martin Landry said in a research note. Still, the company is outperforming many of its rivals in this environment, according to Desjardins analyst Chris Li.

Mr. Miller said consumers continue to spend but they’re being more targeted and intentional in their spending choices. One big change is that items located in the centre of stores, such as salty snacks, are falling in popularity, a fact Mr. Miller attributes in part to the growth of GLP-1 weight management drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy.

Couche-Tard announced in late July that it is making a multibillion-dollar takeover play for Poland’s Zabka, widening its footprint in Europe with a major push in one of the continent’s fastest-growing economies. Owners of about 57 per cent of Zabka stock are backing the deal and have signed agreements to tender their shares, Couche-Tard said.

The purchase still needs approval by European, Polish and Romanian regulators, including clearance by the European Commission under the European Union’s Foreign Subsidies Regulation.

It would be the Canadian company’s biggest acquisition to date, further cementing its position in a key part of the world against global rival 7-Eleven. It would also be a unique acquisition as Couche-Tard takes control of a dominant, technology-powered retailer that could transform the way Circle K operates in other countries. Couche-Tard could scale up Zabka’s AI-driven shopping application, for example, or use Zabka’s experience with cashier-less stores to roll out more autonomous sites in North America.

Couche-Tard has since launched a voluntary tender offer for Zabka at a price of 32 Polish zloty or about US$8.48 a share. That’s a premium of about 9.4 per cent from Zabka’s closing stock price the day before the offer was announced.

Analyst Janusz Pieta at mBank is among those who have argued that Couche-Tard’s offer is too low, raising the possibility that there could be shareholder pressure for better terms. But Couche-Tard’s chief financial officer Filipe Da Silva told The Globe and Mail it’s “already very attractive.”

stories.title: Bank of Canada holds key rate at 2.25 per cent once again
stories.summary: Monetary policymakers at the Bank of Canada use the policy rate to keep a lid on inflation and support economic growth when prices are contained.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
The Bank of Canada held its benchmark interest rate steady again on Wednesday as new U.S. tariffs and the ongoing war in Iran cloud the central bank’s outlook.

The Bank of Canada’s policy rate remains at 2.25 per cent after a seventh straight hold. The move was widely expected by economists.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said in prepared remarks that the persistence of the Middle East conflict has increased inflationary risks as global energy prices continue to float higher.

0:41 Bank of Canada concerned over private credit risks

A re-escalation in the trade dispute with the United States meanwhile threatens Canada’s burgeoning economic rebound, he said. That renewed uncertainty might lead businesses to delay investment and hiring decisions until the trade picture crystalizes.

“Monetary policy cannot offset the effects of tariffs or influence global energy prices. What we can do is ensure global developments don’t jeopardize price stability in Canada,” Macklem said.

Monetary policymakers at the Bank of Canada use the policy rate to keep a lid on inflation and support economic growth when prices are contained.

Inflation rose to three per cent in July after the Iran war drove a volatile period for gas prices over the spring and summer.

Economic growth, meanwhile, has shown signs of rebounding after stagnating for much of the last year. The economy surged with 3.3 per cent annualized growth in the second quarter, though few analysts expect that same pace continued into the current quarter.

The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods on Aug. 22. Macklem said the Bank of Canada doesn’t expect a “large direct impact” on the economy from the new duties, though targeted sectors could be hit hard.

Canada is planning a slate of retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods starting Sept. 8.

1:46 Canadians weigh in on Carney government’s response to U.S. tariffs

Heading into the latest wave of tariffs, Macklem said exports were on the rise and there were signs businesses were adapting to trade restrictions.

“Overall, the data reaffirm our view of a broadening recovery,” he said.

Because the economy was evolving broadly in line with the bank’s forecasts, governing council opted to keep the policy rate unchanged, Macklem said.

But he said there could be future adjustments depending on where the economy and inflation go from here.

“Governing council will assess the sustainability of the economic rebound and the outlook for inflation, and is prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed,” Macklem said.
