stories.title: Tiff 2026: The 15 buzziest movies you can’t miss at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival
stories.summary: The Globe’s most anticipated films include a Palme d’Or winner, Korea’s submission at the Academy Awards and a satirical Brian Mulroney documentary
stories.author: Barry Hertz, Johanna Schneller, Brad Wheeler, Radheyan Simonpillai
stories.content:
Even though corporate mergers, the threat of AI and myriad other crises loom in the background of the film industry, the promise of a new edition of the Toronto International Film Festival tends to erase any doom and gloom for the time being.

But with almost 300 titles to choose from at the 51st annual edition of TIFF, ticket-buyers need all the help they can get to know where to focus their attention and which movies to keep on their radar after the festival ends. To that end, The Globe and Mail has been busy digging through this year’s slate to bring you our most anticipated TIFF 2026 prospects.

An absurdist comedy pitched as the abandoned love child of Nathan Fielder, John Wilson, and alt-comedy pioneers Tim & Eric (whose company Abso Lutely Productions helped birth this vision into the world), the second feature from experimental comic Matt Barats promises to simultaneously enthrall and bewilder Midnight Madness audiences.

Japanese director Takashi Miike has made more movies than you’ve likely had meals, so his batting average can be a bit wobbly. But this spiritual sequel to Abel Ferrara’s 1992 cult classic (which itself was followed up by the narratively unrelated 2009 Werner Herzog film Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans ) has the potential to deliver the best kind of gonzo Miike cinema, akin to his Dead or Alive trilogy. Following a tough Tokyo cop (Shun Oguri) as he hunts down a crazed killer alongside FBI agent (Lily James), the film promises more neon than the eye could possibly handle.

Arriving in Toronto after winning the Palme d’Or in Cannes this spring, Cristian Mungiu’s morality play might be the most effective drama of the festival . Like the Romanian director’s Graduation , R.M.N. , and 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days (the latter of which won Cannes’ Palme d’Or in 2007), Fjord is a thorny look at societal taboos and the splintering of the family unit. But the director takes a more stomach-twisting approach than even his most loyal admirers are used to, aided by excellent performances from Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve.

September, 1989, National Theatre, London. Daniel-Day Lewis, mid- Hamlet , breaks down in tears and leaves the stage, never to return. Enter Ian Charleson, the Scottish actor famous for playing the priest “running for God” in Chariots of Fire . Unbeknownst to everyone except his director, Charleson is dying of AIDS-related complications, yet he delivers a handful of incandescent performances, confronting mortality in character and in life.

When he dies in January, 1990, eight weeks after his final performance, his obituary includes his real cause of death, the first British celebrity to do so. I have huge hopes that a film about a moment this indelible will be incredible, especially with Andrew Scott, an acclaimed Hamlet himself, playing Charleson, and Olivia Colman as a doctor desperate to beat back the raging HIV epidemic.

With her 2022 film Slash/Back , the Igloolik-born director Nyla Innuksuk delivered a miracle: a rollicking, ambitious, teen-girl sci-fi, shot entirely in Pangnirtung, Nunavut, with largely non-professional actors on a ungirut (shoestring) budget.

With In the Heart of the South , Innuksuk turns her camera on another alien landscape: the Toronto art world. Anna Lambe ( North of North ) stars as Yura, an up-and-comer whose latest piece recalls a traumatic story from her Inuk youth. But things begin to unravel when someone from that story, her friend Sesi (Zorga Qaunaq), roars back into her life. Innuksuk is sharply insightful about the way Canada’s South perceives – and co-opts – its North, but she embeds her observations organically in character and story. This one looks like smart, twisty fun.

“Go in there, read, sing, kill.” That’s the mandate for Misty Green (Rosalind Eleazar), an Emmy-winning actress who blew up her career, but may have a second chance. That is, if this audition goes well, and she can overcome her own stubborn independence, and deal with her unpredictable brother (Daniel Kaluuya) and problematic ex (Adam Driver) – not to mention the racism, sexism and classism that Hollywood pretends it doesn’t have.

I’ve just realized that all three of my picks this year are about outsiders struggling to make art in worlds that don’t welcome them. It’s crucial to see that in films, because they are still a potent deliverer of our cultural mythologies. Chris Rock – who wrote, produced and stars here, as well as directed – appears to have made it to the top. I can’t wait to see what raw truths he exposes about all it takes to get there.

So much of the excitement around Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is predicated on what it is not. As in, it’s not Blade . Or rather, it’s not the Blade movie that star Mahershala Ali and writer and director Bassam Tariq were set to make for Marvel, before that reboot fell apart. The duo walked away from that disaster and made what looks like the furthest thing from a Marvel movie: an intimate and melancholic crime thriller that cites Islamic scripture in its title. Ali stars as a hitman struggling to raise kids on his own after his wife’s sudden death. He gets to wield a blade. That’s really all we wanted.

It’s been eight years since Lee Chang-dong’s last movie (2018’s Burning ) and another eight years since the one before that (2010’s Poetry ). I’d like to think Korea’s master dramatist has been giving us the time to recuperate. His films have been soul-shaking portraits of people coping with unimaginable loss, unbearable guilt or unspeakable anger – sometimes all at once.

Chang-dong’s latest, which is Korea’s submission for the international prize at the Academy Awards, is about the intense, close-quarters relationship between two couples, one a pair of documentary filmmakers, and the other their subject. That’s a vague premise, I know. But I didn’t need to be told any of that to be sold.

Last year’s TIFF had Chandler Levack’s sophomore film, the semi-autobiographical Mile End Kicks , in which she mined her own past life as a Toronto freelance arts and culture writer who moves to Montreal and finds herself in the era before #MeToo. This year, Alexandra Pechman, another former freelance writer, whose byline appeared in the pages of Vogue and The New York Times, is premiering Magazine at the festival.

Her movie looks back at the same era but at a New Yorker-like magazine. Two movies don’t make a trend, but I’m interested in seeing this become one. I’m curious to see my contemporaries revisit a moment I sort of witnessed and open my eyes to the things I missed.

Director Ira Sachs’s story about a New York artist dying of AIDS in the 1980s is a story close to the director’s own heart, as the filmmaker himself moved to New York during the peak of the AIDS crisis in the late 1980s. The Man I Love , starring Rami Malek, is a portrait of a man still driven to create – in this case, to perform the lead in an adaptation of a piece by Quebec playwright Michel Tremblay – in spite of a terminal diagnosis. Sachs, who last directed 2023’s Passages , has a deft hand with intimacy, longing and loss. The Man I Love promises to centre the artist, not his illness, while never forgetting the crisis that devastated so many like Malek’s character in real life.

The double-barrelled threat of climate change and a hot real estate market meet in Piedmont in this documentary that looks at the past, present and unsure future of three winemaking families in the region. The Northern Italian area is a stunning backdrop to a narrative that looks at whether the next generation of Piedmontese winemakers are willing to inherit the family business, or if they would rather accept a tempting offer from a foreign real estate investor to relieve them of an uncertain future.

Our Lady Peace may not be the nineties Canadian alt-rock band with the biggest hits, the most memorable singles or the most staying power. But don’t tell any of that to the titular OLP superfan Gail. Directed by Michael Maxxis, the documentary follows Gail as she, in turn, follows the band across the country on their 30th anniversary tour. Gail is middle-aged, unapologetic in her devotion to the band and, interestingly, American, making this film not only a compelling cultural curiosity, but a timely case study in the unifying cross-border power of Cancon.

Documentarian Sean Menard, who previously explored made-in-Canada phenomena Vince Carter (2017’s The Carter Effect ) and MuchMusic (2023’s 299 Queen Street West ) now delivers a portrait of iconic marathoner Terry Fox. I do hope the title is not a riff on Forrest Gump ’s “run, Forrest, run” meme.

In case anyone wonders which A-list drummers may have been considered as fill-ins for the late Neil Peart on the current comeback tour by Canadian prog-rockers Rush, this rock doc features performance sequences with Stewart Copeland, Danny Carey, Chad Smith and Gavin Harrison sitting in with the band’s Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson.

Do not complain after the festival that you didn’t go to a screening of Matthew Rankin’s far-out, satirical documentary on Canada’s 18th prime minister. As Brian Mulroney said to John Turner, you had an option.

The duo walked away from that disaster and made what looks like the furthest thing from a Marvel movie: an intimate and melancholic crime thriller that cites Islamic scripture in its title. Ali stars as a hitman struggling to raise kids on his own after his wife’s sudden death. He gets to wield a blade. That’s really all we wanted.

It’s been eight years since Lee Chang-dong’s last movie (2018’s Burning ) and another eight years since the one before that (2010’s Poetry ). I’d like to think Korea’s master dramatist has been giving us the time to recuperate. His films have been soul-shaking portraits of people coping with unimaginable loss, unbearable guilt or unspeakable anger – sometimes all at once.

Chang-dong’s latest, which is Korea’s submission for the international prize at the Academy Awards, is about the intense, close-quarters relationship between two couples, one a pair of documentary filmmakers, and the other their subject. That’s a vague premise, I know. But I didn’t need to be told any of that to be sold.

Last year’s TIFF had Chandler Levack’s sophomore film, the semi-autobiographical Mile End Kicks , in which she mined her own past life as a Toronto freelance arts and culture writer who moves to Montreal and finds herself in the era before #MeToo. This year, Alexandra Pechman, another former freelance writer, whose byline appeared in the pages of Vogue and The New York Times, is premiering Magazine at the festival.

Her movie looks back at the same era but at a New Yorker-like magazine. Two movies don’t make a trend, but I’m interested in seeing this become one. I’m curious to see my contemporaries revisit a moment I sort of witnessed and open my eyes to the things I missed.

Director Ira Sachs’s story about a New York artist dying of AIDS in the 1980s is a story close to the director’s own heart, as the filmmaker himself moved to New York during the peak of the AIDS crisis in the late 1980s. The Man I Love , starring Rami Malek, is a portrait of a man still driven to create – in this case, to perform the lead in an adaptation of a piece by Quebec playwright Michel Tremblay – in spite of a terminal diagnosis. Sachs, who last directed 2023’s Passages , has a deft hand with intimacy, longing and loss. The Man I Love promises to centre the artist, not his illness, while never forgetting the crisis that devastated so many like Malek’s character in real life.

The double-barrelled threat of climate change and a hot real estate market meet in Piedmont in this documentary that looks at the past, present and unsure future of three winemaking families in the region. The Northern Italian area is a stunning backdrop to a narrative that looks at whether the next generation of Piedmontese winemakers are willing to inherit the family business, or if they would rather accept a tempting offer from a foreign real estate investor to relieve them of an uncertain future.

Our Lady Peace may not be the nineties Canadian alt-rock band with the biggest hits, the most memorable singles or the most staying power. But don’t tell any of that to the titular OLP superfan Gail. Directed by Michael Maxxis, the documentary follows Gail as she, in turn, follows the band across the country on their 30th anniversary tour. Gail is middle-aged, unapologetic in her devotion to the band and, interestingly, American, making this film not only a compelling cultural curiosity, but a timely case study in the unifying cross-border power of Cancon.

Documentarian Sean Menard, who previously explored made-in-Canada phenomena Vince Carter (2017’s The Carter Effect ) and MuchMusic (2023’s 299 Queen Street West ) now delivers a portrait of iconic marathoner Terry Fox. I do hope the title is not a riff on Forrest Gump ’s “run, Forrest, run” meme.

In case anyone wonders which A-list drummers may have been considered as fill-ins for the late Neil Peart on the current comeback tour by Canadian prog-rockers Rush, this rock doc features performance sequences with Stewart Copeland, Danny Carey, Chad Smith and Gavin Harrison sitting in with the band’s Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson.

Do not complain after the festival that you didn’t go to a screening of Matthew Rankin’s far-out, satirical documentary on Canada’s 18th prime minister. As Brian Mulroney said to John Turner, you had an option.

content_blocks.text: Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo
content_blocks.html: Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo

content_blocks.text: Japanese director Takashi Miike has made more movies than you’ve likely had meals, so his batting average can be a bit wobbly. But this spiritual sequel to Abel Ferrara’s 1992 cult classic (which itself was followed up by the narratively unrelated 2009 Werner Herzog film Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans ) has the potential to deliver the best kind of gonzo Miike cinema, akin to his Dead or Alive trilogy. Following a tough Tokyo cop (Shun Oguri) as he hunts down a crazed killer alongside FBI agent (Lily James), the film promises more neon than the eye could possibly handle.

content_blocks.html: Fjord

content_blocks.text: Arriving in Toronto after winning the Palme d’Or in Cannes this spring, Cristian Mungiu’s morality play might be the most effective drama of the festival . Like the Romanian director’s Graduation , R.M.N. , and 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days (the latter of which won Cannes’ Palme d’Or in 2007), Fjord is a thorny look at societal taboos and the splintering of the family unit. But the director takes a more stomach-twisting approach than even his most loyal admirers are used to, aided by excellent performances from Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve.

content_blocks.text: September, 1989, National Theatre, London. Daniel-Day Lewis, mid- Hamlet , breaks down in tears and leaves the stage, never to return. Enter Ian Charleson, the Scottish actor famous for playing the priest “running for God” in Chariots of Fire . Unbeknownst to everyone except his director, Charleson is dying of AIDS-related complications, yet he delivers a handful of incandescent performances, confronting mortality in character and in life.

content_blocks.text: When he dies in January, 1990, eight weeks after his final performance, his obituary includes his real cause of death, the first British celebrity to do so. I have huge hopes that a film about a moment this indelible will be incredible, especially with Andrew Scott, an acclaimed Hamlet himself, playing Charleson, and Olivia Colman as a doctor desperate to beat back the raging HIV epidemic.

content_blocks.text: With her 2022 film Slash/Back , the Igloolik-born director Nyla Innuksuk delivered a miracle: a rollicking, ambitious, teen-girl sci-fi, shot entirely in Pangnirtung, Nunavut, with largely non-professional actors on a ungirut (shoestring) budget.
content_blocks.html: With her 2022 film Slash/Back, the Igloolik-born director Nyla Innuksuk delivered a miracle: a rollicking, ambitious, teen-girl sci-fi, shot entirely in Pangnirtung, Nunavut, with largely non-professional actors on a ungirut (shoestring) budget.

content_blocks.text: With In the Heart of the South , Innuksuk turns her camera on another alien landscape: the Toronto art world. Anna Lambe ( North of North ) stars as Yura, an up-and-comer whose latest piece recalls a traumatic story from her Inuk youth. But things begin to unravel when someone from that story, her friend Sesi (Zorga Qaunaq), roars back into her life. Innuksuk is sharply insightful about the way Canada’s South perceives – and co-opts – its North, but she embeds her observations organically in character and story. This one looks like smart, twisty fun.

content_blocks.text: “Go in there, read, sing, kill.” That’s the mandate for Misty Green (Rosalind Eleazar), an Emmy-winning actress who blew up her career, but may have a second chance. That is, if this audition goes well, and she can overcome her own stubborn independence, and deal with her unpredictable brother (Daniel Kaluuya) and problematic ex (Adam Driver) – not to mention the racism, sexism and classism that Hollywood pretends it doesn’t have.

It’s crucial to see that in films, because they are still a potent deliverer of our cultural mythologies. Chris Rock – who wrote, produced and stars here, as well as directed – appears to have made it to the top. I can’t wait to see what raw truths he exposes about all it takes to get there.

stories.title: Inside the world’s most accessible circus at Toronto’s CNE
stories.summary: A performance championing disabled artists and accessibility features broadens spectators’ horizons
stories.author: Graham Isador, Photography by Laura Proctor
stories.content:
Omnium Circus is widely considered one of the world’s most accessible stage shows. This week, its flagship act I’M POSSIBLE is on at the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto.

With access accommodations built into the performance and several disabled entertainers championed on each bill, the show is a celebration of access culture and a space where audiences with disabilities are both welcomed and encouraged.

“Our access is integral to the production, as opposed to a retrofitted afterthought,” said Lisa B. Lewis , the Omnium founder. To make I’M POSSIBLE accessible to all audience members, the circus features sensory-first design (think house lights on at a low level), ASL translation, audio description devices and captioning when available.

On a practical level, that allows patrons with disabilities to engage with the show in a setting that feels more comfortable than a traditional circus. The venue and the entertainers can also introduce the concept of accessible performance to people who may not have engaged with it before.

“What Omnium does is different because we focus on the things that unite all of us and the human spirit that we all share, rather than focusing on just physical things that make us different,” said Ms. Lewis.

Attendees can expect acrobatics, music, and a few whimsical surprises at the show. Headlining the performances in Toronto is deaf ringmaster Malik Paris . Before joining the circus, Mr. Paris had worked as an actor and performance artist, but Omnium was a new opportunity to share his talents.

“This is the first time I’ve ever been in a leading role in a performance piece, especially one that tours all over,” Mr. Paris told The Globe via e-mail.

“Even though I am the first Deaf ringmaster, it doesn’t feel like a ‘first,’ it feels like a ‘finally.’ I’ve been here the whole time, but now, finally, I’m able to show the world what Deaf performers like me can do.”

Since its first live show in 2021, the organization has performed for more than 143,000 spectators across the United States.

The Canadian debut features one local performer, juggler and free-standing ladder acrobat: Abebe Erigete. While Mr. Erigete does not have a disability, the Omnium team believes his talent and story speak to the overall values of the company.

“Abebe trained in circus arts in Ethiopia, and has performed all over the world. One of his goals is to create a circus and dance show exploring the struggles of migration,” said Dan Lyon, the show’s Canadian producer and a trustee with the Circus Historical Society . “Abebe fits perfectly with the ethos of Omnium, which celebrates the achievements of talented people from all backgrounds.”

The feedback from patrons, both with and without disabilities, has been overwhelmingly positive, Ms. Lewis and Mr. Paris said.

They’ve received numerous letters from parents expressing thanks for the show, sharing stories about how Omnium has offered a safe environment for their kids to engage with new artistic practices and encouraging them to think differently about disability in general.

“In the middle of the circus, after seeing one of our artists flip his wheelchair over his head, a young [wheelchair user] screamed out, ‘Mom, I told you I could do more than the doctor said I could!’” said Ms. Lewis.

That kind of response is a major reason why the creative team wanted to make a different kind of circus. It’s a magical environment where people can open their minds to new ideas.

“[Omnium] allows audiences to experience the circus in a way that meets them where they are, which is so neat,” wrote Mr. Paris.

“And for many kids and families, this may be their first exposure to ASL, as well as a fully bilingual show like this. That kind of representation is much-needed across the entertainment industry.”

They’ve received numerous letters from parents expressing thanks for the show, sharing stories about how Omnium has offered a safe environment for their kids to engage with new artistic practices and encouraging them to think differently about disability in general.

“In the middle of the circus, after seeing one of our artists flip his wheelchair over his head, a young [wheelchair user] screamed out, ‘Mom, I told you I could do more than the doctor said I could!’” said Ms. Lewis.
That kind of response is a major reason why the creative team wanted to make a different kind of circus. It’s a magical environment where people can open their minds to new ideas.
“[Omnium] allows audiences to experience the circus in a way that meets them where they are, which is so neat,” wrote Mr. Paris.
“And for many kids and families, this may be their first exposure to ASL, as well as a fully bilingual show like this. That kind of representation is much-needed across the entertainment industry.”

stories.title: Canadian Tire and Tim Hortons launch partnership to boost loyalty programs
stories.summary: Toronto — Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd. and Tim Hortons are hoping to perk up their customer bases by linking their loyalty programs.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
TORONTO — Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd. and Tim Hortons are hoping to perk up their customer bases by linking their loyalty programs.

Under a partnership launched between the home goods retailer and café giant Wednesday, customers who link their Triangle and Tims Rewards accounts will earn between two and five per cent in Canadian Tire money in addition to Tims points on select Tims purchases.

The arrangement is meant to draw Tims customers to Canadian Tire and vice versa.

Right now, 53 per cent of Triangle Rewards customers are enrolled in both loyalty programs. Canadian Tire has about 12 million Triangle Rewards members and 1,600 locations across its banners. Tims counts eight million loyalty program users and 4,000 restaurants in Canada.

By uniting, “both Triangle Rewards will grow and Tim Hortons reward members will grow,” Darryl Jenkins, Canadian Tire’s executive vice-president and chief development officer, said in an interview.

How much Canadian Tire money shoppers earn will depend on whether they use a Triangle credit card to pay and what they buy.

Canadian Tire money can be redeemed for savings on purchases at the retailer as well as its other banners, including SportChek, Mark’s and Party City. Tims points can be used to purchase food and beverages at the chain.

The arrangement came about organically, Jenkins and Hope Bagozzi, Tims’ chief marketing officer, said.

Canadian Tire and Tims executives sit on many of the same boards, often network with one another and their companies sponsor many of the same events, so it made sense for them to explore if they could boost the reach of their loyalty programs together.

“Wouldn’t it be great to add more value together?” was the thinking, Bagozzi recalled.

But Liza Amlani, principal and co-founder of the Retail Strategy Group, suspects “this is less about customer delight and more about two legacy brands scrambling for incremental share in an oversaturated loyalty market.”

“Canadians are already juggling too many programs, and unless the value proposition is simple, transparent and genuinely rewarding, this risks becoming just another corporate tie-up that benefits the brands more than the shoppers,” she said in an email when the partnership was teased last September.

Canadian Tire first announced the partnership almost a year ago but waited until Wednesday to launch it and reveal how it will work.

The year in between both milestones was spent ensuring the mechanics of the partnership will work on a technical level.

Jenkins said it was by chance that it’s launching “at a really interesting time” — just after the U.S. hit Canada with a fresh round of tariffs and as Canada prepares to implement its own round of retaliatory levies in September.

“We certainly didn’t plan it this way,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 2, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX:CTC.A, TSX:QSR)

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Williams strikes out 13, leads Guardians to 6-1 win over Blue Jays
stories.summary: Williams struck out the side in the seventh and fanned five of his last six. It was his 10th double-digit strikeout game this season.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Gavin Williams struck out a career-high 13 and allowed just two singles in seven innings, leading the Cleveland Guardians to a 6-1 win on Tuesday night over the Toronto Blue Jays in a matchup of teams in the thick of the AL wild-card race.

Patrick Bailey, rookie Angel Genao and Angel Martinez all hit two-run homers for the Guardians, who are 11-4 since Aug. 12. Cleveland came in with a slim lead for the third wild-card spot.

Williams (13-7) began September by dominating the Blue Jays, allowing one unearned run. The right-hander, who was coming off a shaky outing last week, didn’t give up a hit until the fourth.

Williams struck out the side in the seventh and fanned five of his last six. It was his 10th double-digit strikeout game this season.

Hunter Gaddis and Matt Festa pitched an inning apiece to finish the three-hitter.

Bailey put the Guardians up 2-1 in the fifth with his eighth homer. Martinez led off with a walk, and one out later, Bailey drove a 3-1 pitch from Spencer Arighetti (7-8) into the left-field bleachers.

Pinch-hitting for fellow rookie Travis Bazzana in the seventh, Genao made it 4-1 with a 426-foot blast over the wall in left. Martinez opened with a single before Genao connected for his second homer since debuting on Aug. 5.

Martinez hit his 14th homer in the eighth.

Toronto got some help in scoring its only run off Williams in the fifth.

Rookie Kazuma Okamoto singled and went to third when Guardians catcher Bailey threw wildly into center on a steal. Williams then uncorked a wild pitch, allowing Okamoto to come home.

stories.title: Canada gave contracts to Iran VP’s son while investigating role in regime missile program
stories.summary: The RCMP and Canadian military were among the agencies that hired companies run by Edmonton resident 'Sal Ghafouri,' a Global News investigation has found.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
The Canadian government awarded millions worth of contracts to the son of Iran’s former vice-president, despite an ongoing investigation into allegations he helped the Islamic Republic evade sanctions and develop missile systems, documents obtained by Global News reveal.

Since founding two companies in Alberta, an Edmonton resident named “Sal Ghafouri” has received more than $2 million in federal and provincial contracts, including from the RCMP and Department of National Defence, public records show.

The 45-year-old was part of an official Canadian trade mission to Latin America, received a federal business grant and was invited to “propose legislation” to the Alberta government at consultations backed by the province’s economic development minister.

But according to newly released records, Ghafouri is actually Mohammad Reza Ghafouri Fard, an Iranian who has been the subject of a long-running Canadian investigation into his alleged work for Iran’s military and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The son of Hassan Ghafouri Fard, an Iranian politician who served as the country’s vice president, Ghafouri was “involved in the research and development of Iranian military technologies,” according to a recently declassified Canadian Security Intelligence Service report.

Before immigrating to Canada in 2013 and going into business as “Sal,” Ghafouri allegedly helped develop a guided anti-aircraft missile system and a jamming tool to “confront American aircraft” for the Iranian military and Revolutionary Guard, or IRGC.

He was also part of a “covert procurement structure” that used a front company in Southeast Asia to purchase components that were needed for Iranian military projects, CSIS alleged in its report detailing his alleged past work for the regime forces.

The allegations concern the four years CSIS alleges Ghafouri worked as an engineer at Iranian company Rabi Kosar, which the report said sold its products to SA Iran, a satellite of the Iranian Ministry of Defence, which in turn provided them to the military and IRGC.

Ghafouri “admitted to active participation in procurement activities that benefited the Iranian military, including the IRGC,” the CSIS Security Screening Branch wrote in its Jan. 13, 2023 report on Ghafouri.

The procurement network was needed because the materials were not available to Iran due to sanctions, but “Ghafouri Fard clearly indicated that he did not care that these activities were prohibited,” CSIS added.

After moving to Alberta through the government’s skilled worker program, Ghafouri returned to Iran in 2015 and met twice with members of Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security, or MOIS, the CSIS report also said.

“During Mr. Ghafouri Fard’s first meeting with the MOIS, he provided details of his employment in Canada,” according to the CSIS report, marked “secret” but recently made public in court.

“He was asked if he travelled to the U.S. and whether he had contacts with either Canadian or American intelligence services,” added the report, which noted he was a permanent resident of Canada at the time he met the MOIS.

“During the second meeting, he was given detailed instructions and warnings, as they related to police or intelligence services approaching him while living in Canada,” it said.

“He was advised to never travel to the U.S., as he would be of interest to the Federal Bureau of Investigation due to his involvement with Rabi Kosar,” it said, adding he thanked the Iranian agents for the “heads up.”

The report, which CSIS shared with immigration investigators more than three years ago, noted that “one of the functions of the MOIS outside of Iran is to acquire technology for Iran’s military industry.”

Canada launched a crackdown on Iranian regime officials living in the country in 2022 and has been attempting to deport them along with others who have aided Tehran as it has repressed its citizens and sponsored terrorist groups.

But the Ghafouri case stands out for the seriousness of the allegations about his suspected role in Iranian weapons proliferation, the length of time it has taken the government to act and his extensive contract work for Canadian agencies.

“This is yet another example of the way Canada has failed to take seriously the threat,” said Iranian-Canadian human rights activist Kaveh Shahrooz, who reviewed the CSIS report on Ghafouri for Global News.

“Our politicians pay a lot of lip service to countering the Iranian regime’s nefarious influence in Canada. But cases like this show that we fail to conduct even the most basic due diligence on those with strong, direct ties to Iran’s regime.”

CSIS declined to comment. It shared its security screening report on Ghafouri with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, which also declined to comment.

In May 2026, the immigration department informed Ghafouri it was launching proceedings to deny him from obtaining citizenship on the grounds that he is a “threat to the security of Canada.”

Ghafouri did not respond to questions. His lawyer, Bjorna Shkurti, said she could not comment because the matter was before the court.

“What I can say is that my client has lived in Canada for over a decade and has undergone multiple security screenings, both as a temporary resident and as a permanent resident,” she said.

“He strongly disputes the allegations made against him and intends to pursue all available legal avenues until the matter is fully resolved.”

None of the federal government agencies that gave contracts to Ghafouri’s companies responded to requests for comment by deadline.

But records show that while Ghafouri was flagged by immigration investigators for national security reasons in 2017, he nonetheless went on to win government procurement contracts, including two worth more than $1.5-million from the Canadian military.

Even after CSIS completed its security screening report in 2023 and sent it to immigration authorities handling his case, Ghafouri’s companies continued to benefit from federal money.

In 2024, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada awarded Melanite Group a $15,000 grant “to adopt new technologies.” Six months later, the company won another contract from the Canadian Armed Forces.

The case suggests that Canadian agencies are not talking to each other, said University of Ottawa political science Prof. Thomas Juneau, who specializes in Iran and national security and reviewed the CSIS report for Global News.

“To some degree, these processes and silos are necessary if we want the system to be fair and not arbitrary,” he said. “But the system just goes to the other extreme.”

“I mean, it’s absurd,” he said.

Juneau said he had interviewed three dozen Iranian-Canadians for a forthcoming book on transnational repression .

Military service is compulsory in Iran, but the children of high-level regime members can get a pass, if they are studying at Western universities. Ghafouri wrote on his Canadian immigration forms that he was exempted from army duty.

Instead, he came to Canada in 2005 to earn his master’s degree in engineering at Dalhousie University in Halifax. He dropped out after just one week, citing a family emergency, according to thousands of pages of documents on his case released to Global News.

The records show he returned to Iran, where his father was a conservative Member of Parliament and former vice-president to Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, a leader of the 1979 Iranian revolution that brought fundamentalist clerics to power.

Ghafouri told CSIS he “deeply respects his father but recognizes that they differ ideologically,” the report said. He said his father was “not a hardliner,” but Juneau said that while reformists, moderates and hardliners differed on policies, “it remains that they’re all regime loyalists.”

Upon arriving home from Nova Scotia, Ghafouri went to work as an engineer at Rabi Kosar, a company devoted exclusively to research and development projects for Iran’s military, according to the CSIS report.

His first project was a system called Shahin, also known as Hawk, according to a CSIS report, which described it as a medium-range anti-missile system developed by the U.S. army.

In 2010, Iran unveiled its first domestically built air defence system, which it boasted was better than Hawk and equipped with Shahin missiles with a 150-kilometre range, CSIS noted in its report.

The Iranian army called it Mersad, and said it was a “completely indigenized system developed by the Iranian experts and technicians to promote the country’s combat power.”

Ghafouri’s next project was an electronic warfare project called RAAD, which used radio signals to jam enemies’ communication capabilities, he told CSIS in an interview, the report said.

The IRGC air force unveiled RAAD in 2012 and said it was “designed to confront American aircraft at a distance of up to 50 kilometers, through the use of associated missiles,” CSIS wrote.

His third project was called SINA, a direction-finding system with military applications that could locate ships in the Persian Gulf and determine their direction of travel, according to CSIS.

The CSIS report said that while Ghafouri claimed he did not deal directly with the Iranian military or IRGC, he was in contact with SA Iran, which the intelligence agency said was “a satellite company of the Iranian Ministry of Defence (MoD).”

“The MoD would then provide the products to the military or IRGC. Mr. Ghafouri Fard maintained contact with an SA Iran buyer, to ensure that these projects would be suitable for military use and that the purchased equipment met military standards,” CSIS wrote.

A company called SAIRAN is sanctioned by the U.S. for its role in developing Iranian missiles and Shahed drones that Russia uses in Ukraine. The U.K. sanctioned SAIRAN in 2020 for manufacturing electronic components for Iran’s weapons systems.

Eighteen months into his job at Rabi Kosar, Ghafouri was reassigned to a new role as a project manager at the company office that illicitly imported components needed for its military projects, CSIS said in its report.

“Working with engineers to identify which specific parts were needed, he would provide the requirements to a Malaysian-based contact, who in turn would source their requirements from third-party countries, to include the United States,” it said.

Using the Rabi Kosar procurement network, Ghafouri launched his own company, Sima Technologies, in Iran in 2009, but the business failed, the CSIS report said.

CSIS said he joined two demonstrations organized by Iran’s Green Movement, which was protesting the 2009 re-election of president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad.

But he then returned to Canada in 2013 as a permanent resident and, after a period of unemployment, worked as a research assistant at the University of Alberta, according to his resume.

He then founded Melanite Group, which lists government “procurement” as one of its services, and says its clients included the governments of Canada, B.C., Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario, as well as the International Atomic Energy Agency.

In 2018, Ghafouri incorporated a second company, Radian Group Ltd., which also received government contracts. He is the only director of both firms, which share a common address and phone number, according to Alberta corporate records.

He registered the companies as Mohammad Reza Ghafouri Fard, which is the name on his Iranian passport. But on government contracts, he used the name Sal Ghafouri. On his immigration application, he wrote that Salman was his nickname.

Documents viewed by Global News show that Melanite and Radian won multiple contracts to procure materials for federal agencies — among them, the RCMP, which hired Ghafouri to purchase a borescope imaging device.

The defence department also hired him to supply “snow vehicle parts” to CFB-Shilo in Manitoba, where Canadian, U.S. and allied troops are trained. He got another military contract to procure six vehicle lifts in Halifax.

The Correctional Service of Canada awarded Melanite a $100,000 contract in 2019, while in 2021 the company won a $380,000 contract from Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada.

Melanite not only received government contracts, but also filed complaints when it was not awarded them. In 2019, the company alleged it was improperly disqualified from a military contract, while in 2021 it alleged “irregularities” in the bidding process.

Originally a “one-man show,” Melanite has grown “into a team of several employees, consultants, and contractors,” according to documents filed in Federal Court.

“Since its inception, it has proudly served all levels of government in Canada by supplying equipment and services to organizations such as universities, municipalities, and provincial and federal departments.”

Melanite’s most recent contract was in 2024, when it was granted a $50,000 job from the Canadian Forces to supply “road motor vehicles” to Borden, Ont., the location of the military’s largest training base.

The 'hardship' of not having citizenship

Four years after moving to Canada, Ghafouri submitted an application form for Canadian citizenship. But records show his file was suspended within months at the request of the Canada Border Service Agency intelligence unit, which raised national security concerns.

A year after submitting his application, Ghafouri turned for help to his local Liberal MP, whose office made repeated inquiries with immigration officials on his behalf, even after being told the delay was due to “security verifications.”

He went next to Ralph Goodale, then the Minister of Public Safety, whose staff were also repeatedly advised that “security checks are ongoing,” according to immigration records.

Ghafouri then wrote to the director of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, claiming in a letter that he had never been involved in any “military or political matter in Canada or abroad.”

He expressed his “dissatisfaction” with the security screening process and threatened legal action. His next move was a complaint to the National Security and Intelligence Review Agency.

Behind the scenes, national security officials were investigating Ghafouri, documents show, and in 2021, they determined there might be grounds to refuse him citizenship on security grounds.

The Canada Border Services Agency, meanwhile, did its own investigation and decided to launch deportation proceedings against him “due to his employment activities while in Iran.”

The CBSA withdrew the case last November, “due to an inability to use the required evidence,” according to government documents.

The documents do not specify whether the evidence in question was from CSIS. The CBSA declined to comment on the matter.

Ghafouri is now pursuing legal action against the immigration department, alleging the handling of his citizenship application has caused him “hardship and prejudice.”

He said the delays had forced him to miss a memorial service for his father, who passed away in 2023. He was also unable to join Canadian government trade missions, he said.

He has asked the court to award him $5,000 to $25,000 for his troubles.

In materials filed in court, Ghafouri said he had answered CSIS’s questions “in a truthful and forthright manner,” had made significant contributions to Canada and was not a security threat.

Government agencies would not have contracted his services or invited him on overseas trade missions if he was a threat, according to his court submissions.

“It’s hard to see, if there were real security concerns, how he would be permitted to engage in such business activities,” his lawyer argued.

“We have built our family, professional and community endeavors in Edmonton, Canada,” Ghafouri wrote. “And the uncertainty and delays associated with the processing of the citizenship applications and whether we will be able to stay in Canada permanently has placed a big toil on our family.”

stories.title: Carney's 'hydronym' moment is behind a cheeky campaign to raise awareness about Lake Ontario
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 3
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 3
Proceeds from apparel sales to support awareness, environmental advocacy for Great Lake
Media | This Lake Ontario water keeper wants YOU to wear your hydronyms
A new fundraising campaign builds off Prime Minister Mark Carney's use of the word "hydronym" to raise awareness and environmental protections for Lake Ontario.

London, Ont., apparel company Branded By Collins has created T-shirts emblazoned with the phrase, "My hydronyms are Lake & Ontario." A portion of the sales proceeds go to Swim Drink Fish Canada, a Toronto-based, national charity that connects people with the lake, and works to keep it safe and clean.
"This is an opportunity where for the first time in a generation, we're seeing people talk about Lake Ontario and take pride in it," said Gregary Ford, the charity's vice-president and waterkeeper.

The idea came about after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America, as the two countries traded social media jabs over trade talks that broke down last month.

Carney responded to Trump's renaming idea with a social media statement , which read in part, "We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always."

Hydronym is the proper name for a body of water. The internet was abuzz with Carney's use of the word. Many people, including Swim Drink Fish Canada's Ford, who lives in Dundas in Hamilton on the lake's Western tip, admitted they had to search for its meaning.

"I did have to look it up just with everybody else, and I'm a bit embarrassed to admit that because I work in water," he said. "But it is a beautiful and wonderfully nerdy word that I think captured people's attention to the idea of a name and what it represents."

Lake Ontario — one of the five Great Lakes — is between Ontario and New York. Its name comes from the Huron-Wendat word "oniatarí:io," which means "lake of shining waters." The province, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
Carney said on social media that the name is more than 400 years old, and predates Canada and the U.S. as countries.
Political leaders in both countries have condemned Trump's executive order.
On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a sign in Winona that said "Lake Ontario, now and always." Some U.S. politicians, both Republicans and Democrats, have also denounced the renaming.
Branded By Collins created the T-shirts after the public relations firm Curious Public reached out to managing partner Steve Ryall with the idea.

"Funny enough, I was riding a bicycle in Toronto, going right by Lake Ontario, when I got the phone call, so it was interesting timing," Ryall said. "It's fun to be a part of something like this. We’re definitely proud Canadians, so we're excited to support the initiative."
He said the majority of the company's customers are in Canada, so it hasn't directly been impacted by U.S. tariffs, but added that many people buying the products have been affected.

"Everybody's affected by it one way or another. And so hopefully [the trade situation] goes well for everybody involved, and things settle down between the two countries soon because I think it's an important relationship on so many levels."

"hydronym" campaign started out with just hats, but has since grown to T-shirts, sweaters and hoodies that come in black, red and white. Ten dollars from the sale of each item, ranging from $30 to $50, go to the non-profit. Its efforts include sharing real-time water quality data and advocating for the lake.
Gregary Ford said he works closely with the

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the New York State Department of Environment and Conservation. He admitted an executive order makes things challenging on a day-to-day basis because U.S. federal employees have to refer to it as Lake America, but he said has received support from his American counterparts.

However, Ford said, the tensions have reignited Canadian pride and more people are interested in learning about the lake's Indigenous origins, its connection to the other Great Lakes and how Lake Ontario can better be protected.

"This is obviously a deflection from trade negotiations and ongoing discourse between federal leaders on both sides of the border, but it's also an opportunity to feel proud about our heritage in water and our history with Indigenous place naming," said Ford.
"People are learning more not just about new terms like hydronyms, but also new concepts and ways of bettering our relationship with the lake that is in our backyard."
Ford said the lake is under stress from a variety of sources, including climate change, invasive species, microplastics and others, so this campaign is one way to encourage action.

| CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 3

Proceeds from apparel sales to support awareness, environmental advocacy for Great Lake

Media | This Lake Ontario water keeper wants YOU to wear your hydronyms

A new fundraising campaign builds off Prime Minister Mark Carney's use of the word "hydronym" to raise awareness and environmental protections for Lake Ontario.

London, Ont., apparel company Branded By Collins has created T-shirts emblazoned with the phrase, "My hydronyms are Lake & Ontario." A portion of the sales proceeds go to Swim Drink Fish Canada, a Toronto-based, national charity that connects people with the lake, and works to keep it safe and clean.

"This is an opportunity where for the first time in a generation, we're seeing people talk about Lake Ontario and take pride in it," said Gregary Ford, the charity's vice-president and waterkeeper.

The idea came about after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America, as the two countries traded social media jabs over trade talks that broke down last month.

Carney responded to Trump's renaming idea with a social media statement , which read in part, "We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always."

Hydronym is the proper name for a body of water. The internet was abuzz with Carney's use of the word. Many people, including Swim Drink Fish Canada's Ford, who lives in Dundas in Hamilton on the lake's Western tip, admitted they had to search for its meaning.

"I did have to look it up just with everybody else, and I'm a bit embarrassed to admit that because I work in water," he said. "But it is a beautiful and wonderfully nerdy word that I think captured people's attention to the idea of a name and what it represents."

Lake Ontario — one of the five Great Lakes — is between Ontario and New York. Its name comes from the Huron-Wendat word "oniatarí:io," which means "lake of shining waters." The province, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.

Carney said on social media that the name is more than 400 years old, and predates Canada and the U.S. as countries.

Political leaders in both countries have condemned Trump's executive order.

On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a sign in Winona that said "Lake Ontario, now and always." Some U.S. politicians, both Republicans and Democrats, have also denounced the renaming.

Branded By Collins created the T-shirts after the public relations firm Curious Public reached out to managing partner Steve Ryall with the idea.

"Funny enough, I was riding a bicycle in Toronto, going right by Lake Ontario, when I got the phone call, so it was interesting timing," Ryall said. "It's fun to be a part of something like this. We’re definitely proud Canadians, so we're excited to support the initiative."

He said the majority of the company's customers are in Canada, so it hasn't directly been impacted by U.S. tariffs, but added that many people buying the products have been affected.

"Everybody's affected by it one way or another. And so hopefully [the trade situation] goes well for everybody involved, and things settle down between the two countries soon because I think it's an important relationship on so many levels."

"hydronym" campaign started out with just hats, but has since grown to T-shirts, sweaters and hoodies that come in black, red and white. Ten dollars from the sale of each item, ranging from $30 to $50, go to the non-profit. Its efforts include sharing real-time water quality data and advocating for the lake.

Gregary Ford said he works closely with the

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the New York State Department of Environment and Conservation. He admitted an executive order makes things challenging on a day-to-day basis because U.S. federal employees have to refer to it as Lake America, but he said has received support from his American counterparts.

However, Ford said, the tensions have reignited Canadian pride and more people are interested in learning about the lake's Indigenous origins, its connection to the other Great Lakes and how Lake Ontario can better be protected.

"This is obviously a deflection from trade negotiations and ongoing discourse between federal leaders on both sides of the border, but it's also an opportunity to feel proud about our heritage in water and our history with Indigenous place naming," said Ford.

"People are learning more not just about new terms like hydronyms, but also new concepts and ways of bettering our relationship with the lake that is in our backyard."

Ford said the lake is under stress from a variety of sources, including climate change, invasive species, microplastics and others, so this campaign is one way to encourage action.

stories.title: ‘Trump bump’ could help Ford in Ontario by-elections, observers say
stories.summary: Premier sees sagging approval jump in wake of trade-war rhetoric, as voters in three ridings go to polls
stories.author: Jeff Gray, Laura Stone
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford ’s Progressive Conservatives are using his recent round of fighting words with U.S. President Donald Trump as a selling point going into three provincial by-elections on Thursday, a strategy his opponents say is an attempt to deflect from a series of recent controversies.

Voters are going to the polls in three late summer by-elections, in Hamilton East-Stoney Creek, York-Simcoe and Scarborough Southwest. The votes are being held less than two weeks after trade talks with the U.S. collapsed and Mr. Ford said Mr. Trump could “kiss my ass,” with the President responding in kind on social media and even ordering a new name for Lake Ontario.

Election signs in the east Toronto riding of Scarborough Southwest for PC candidate Noor Tarun feature a yellow sticker that reads: “Stand up to Trump.” The focus on Washington mimics Mr. Ford’s approach in his victorious 2025 general election.

But this time it follows months of polls showing sagging approval ratings amid a series of issues, such as the Premier’s aborted purchase of $28.9-million private jet and the expensing of more than $120,000 for hotel rooms by his cabinet ministers and MPPs.

A recent poll from Liaison Strategies suggested that Mr. Ford’s approval rating has rebounded. The phone survey of 1,500 Ontarians, conducted Aug. 23 to 24, showed Mr. Ford’s approval rating at 36 per cent, up from a low of 24 per cent in July. The poll is considered accurate within plus or minus 2.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. David Valentin, principal at Liaison Strategies, said the biggest boost for the PCs is happening in the north, southwest and southcentral regions of Ontario, which includes Hamilton.

“The fact that we’re back onto economic issues, away from scandals and expenses – especially in the closing week of the by-election – is going to make a big shift,” Mr. Valentin said, adding that Mr. Ford is “channelling the anger that people are feeling.”

In Hamilton East-Stoney Creek, candidates are vying to replace PC cabinet minister Neil Lumsden, who retired in August. Carrying the banner there for Mr. Ford is Jeff Beattie, a greenhouse and garden centre owner and one-term Hamilton city councillor.

The NDP are running former long-time MPP Monique Taylor, who left her provincial seat in nearby Hamilton Mountain in February, 2025, for an unsuccessful run at federal politics. The Liberal candidate, Heino Doessing, placed second to Mr. Lumsden in last year’s election – losing by about 4,000 votes.

In York-Simcoe, north of Toronto, voters will choose a replacement for departing cabinet minister Caroline Mulroney, in a riding she won handily in 2025 that has long been held by the PCs. Seven candidates are running, including Naomi Davison for the Liberals, Susan Lahey for the PCs and Bobby Nikmard for the NDP.

Scarborough Southwest, which has been held by a Liberal or New Democrat since 2003, was vacated in February by former NDP deputy leader Doly Begum, who defected to run for the federal Liberals and won a by-election in her riding earlier this year. The provincial Liberal candidate Ahsanul Hafiz narrowly won a bitter nomination battle, beating former Beaches-East York MP Nate Erskine-Smith. The NDP candidate is community advocate Fatima Shaban.

In an interview, Opposition NDP Leader Marit Stiles said she would spend the final days with door-knocking teams in Scarborough and Hamilton, where she said her party is locked in two-way races with the PCs. She said she was not hearing about any “Trump bump” of support for Mr. Ford at the doors.

In Scarborough, people are frustrated with wait times in hospitals and short-staffing in schools, Ms. Stiles said. And in Hamilton, voters want Mr. Ford to act on pledges made in last year’s campaign to help tariff-affected workers, not trade barbs with the President or purchase private jets.

“You can throw around all the insults, but a year and a half ago, you told us you were going to deliver these things for us, and we don’t see them,” Ms. Stiles said.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser, speaking by phone while canvassing in Hamilton on Tuesday, said by-elections often revolve around local issues, rather than leaders. But he acknowledged that the “Trump bump” may have helped Mr. Ford.

The PCs are cautiously optimistic about retaining their seats in Hamilton East-Stoney Creek and York-Simcoe – while acknowledging that Hamilton is the bigger fight. (Regardless of what happens, Mr. Ford will escape with the large majority he won in 2025 intact: The PCs currently hold 77 of 124 seats at Queen’s Park.)

Laryssa Waler, Mr. Ford’s former executive director of communications who is now a managing partner at public affairs firm Henley Strategies, said the PC Party has been pouring resources into Hamilton.

“All three candidates have good local name recognition and are stars in their own right,” she said. “But I think the Conservatives have the tailwinds behind them on all the trade stuff. A town like Hamilton wants to see their Premier standing up to Donald Trump and really likes that fighter in him.”

Liberal strategist Marcel Wieder said Mr. Ford has benefitted politically from the latest spat with Mr. Trump.

“Donald Trump threw Doug Ford a lifeline. Instead of talking about jets, hotel bills, health care, and affordability, Ford gets to wrap himself up in Captain Ontario,” he said.

Mr. Wieder said the Liberals are highly competitive in Scarborough Southwest, with the NDP as their main opponents. But he said some Liberal votes may bleed to the PCs, leaving the NDP victorious. In Hamilton, he said, the race could go three ways.

Erin Morrison, a former senior NDP staffer and vice-president of Texture Communications, said the trade fight means has made it harder for Ms. Stiles to get her message out. “He needed a channel changer, and he really got one in the name of Donald Trump.”

But Ms. Morrison said voters in Hamilton especially are upset about Mr. Ford’s controversies this spring, giving the NDP a “strong chance” to flip the seat. She said Scarborough is also a tight a two-way race between the NDP and the PCs.

stories.title: What’s behind the implosion of the B.C. Conservatives
stories.summary: Official opposition party is down a third of its MLAs since the last provincial election
stories.author: The Decibel Staff, Sherrill Sutherland, Gary Mason
stories.content:
It’s been a turbulent time for the official opposition of the British Columbia provincial legislature, the B.C. Conservative party. After seeing a surge in popularity leading up to the 2024 provincial election, they’ve now lost a third of their sitting members . Seven MLAs have left since mid-August alone.

Today, Globe national affairs columnist Gary Mason is on the show. He’ll explain the party’s surprising implosion, how they lost their surge in popularity and what lessons there are for politics in the province and beyond.

stories.title: Major changes coming to 24 Sussex Dr., famed architect Moshe Safdie says
stories.summary: Safdie, who will lead the jury selecting a proposal for the building’s restoration, envisions a much broader role for the prime minister’s residence
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
The acclaimed Canadian architect who will lead the jury that decides the future of 24 Sussex Dr. says significant change is coming for the official prime ministerial residence, which has sat vacant for 11 years because of its dilapidated condition.

Moshe Safdie , who has designed buildings ranging from the National Gallery in Ottawa to Terminal One at Pearson International Airport over his long career, said in an interview Tuesday that he envisions greatly expanded usefulness for the building that has been home to nine Canadian prime ministers, from Louis St. Laurent to Stephen Harper, since 1951.

Mr. Harper is the most recent prime minister to have lived in the home, which had fallen into such disrepair that Justin Trudeau declined to move in with his family in 2015. Instead, the Trudeaus lived in Rideau Cottage on the grounds of Rideau Hall, and Prime Minister Mark Carney has followed suit.

Speaking to The Globe and Mail over video chat, Mr. Safdie, 88, was asked to what degree the home, built between 1866 and 1868 as a private residence and later procured by the government for prime ministers’ use, could remain as it is.

“Even if you decided to reproduce the building in whole, you would be doing things to the site that will change it from just being what Sussex was in the past,” Mr. Safdie said.

“Change is coming and I think change is inevitable,” he continued. “This building, one hopes, is there for a long, long time, and needs to accommodate more than what Sussex had in the past.”

At the very least, Mr. Safdie said there is a need for a separate building on the site to accommodate social events held by the prime minister.

He said the goal is “not a restoration of a historic building per se,” but rather, finding a way for the site to serve multiple purposes, including housing prime ministers and their families, providing ceremonial spaces and hosting social functions.

Mr. Safdie is the founding principal of Safdie Architects. The Israeli, Canadian and American citizen has left his mark around the world. Early on, he designed Habitat 67 in Montreal, followed by such buildings as Jewel Changi Airport in Singapore, Vancouver Library Square and the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts.

He will not shape the overhaul of 24 Sussex himself, but rather is leading a jury assembled by the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada to select a proposal for the project. Mr. Carney announced the process in June on the front steps of 24 Sussex, with Mr. Safdie at his side.

Mr. Safdie said the Prime Minister personally reached out to offer him the role. “I said it would be an honour, that I think it’s a very significant project,” the architect said.

He said that since he has lived in Canada, he has met every serving Canadian prime minister, but never inside the house. As part of the design process, he said, he went through 24 Sussex in its current, “gutted” state.

The house had showed signs of physical decay from the 1990s onward; a 1995 break-in, during Jean Chrétien’s occupancy, also raised concerns about security risks. But successive governments, wary of the political risk that might come with costly renovations, held off on dealing with the issues, which ranged from mould and asbestos to rodent infestations. In 2023, the National Capital Commission gutted the building, removing its furnishings and finishes.

“It’s architecturally not a significant historic building,” Mr. Safdie said. “It has the patina of history and the history of its recent use by prime ministers.”

Still, he spoke with respect and affection about what 24 Sussex represents to Canada.

“I would encourage architects to look at this as a significant element in the identity of Canada and the capital,” he said. “In other words, this is a building that should work well and efficiently in all of the things we associate with its function.

“At the same time, this building has to rise above that to become – and I think that it’s important to think of it as – a timeless design, not something that would fall away and feel dated.”

The competition is seeking a team to design and build the restored 24 Sussex, meaning architects, developers and builders will work together to advance the winning proposal. The Rideau Hall Foundation in Ottawa is raising $50-million toward the project’s costs. Mr. Carney has said the federal government will cover the cost of security.

Mr. Safdie said he is being compensated on an hourly basis by the RAIC for his role, but added, “I would happily do it pro bono.”

Asked about advice to those preparing bids now, the architect said it’s important for “good chemistry” to exist among the teams committed to the project.

“The formulation of the teams is of significance in terms of being able to work with someone that encourages you and inspires you because they appreciate the gravitas of the assignment,” he said.

Mr. Safdie also said he is confident that the project can be executed on budget because the proposals must include a financial breakdown, and the builder will be part of the process.

“In design-build, you receive a design with the price attached, and the contractor-developer is committing to build it for that price,” he explained.

“One of the interesting issues will be there will be some variation in prices. This is not a competition where the lowest price automatically wins. Price is a factor but not the only one and so that just adds to the complexity of the selection process, but the design-build has a much better track record of being completed on time because the contractor’s input is already a part of the design process.”

Mr. Safdie said he loves the location of 24 Sussex, overlooking the Ottawa River, with its dramatic views.

“In terms of the design of the building, it should grow out of the specifics of that site in this city, in Canada,” he said. “It should be inspired by what’s specific to the building.”

stories.title: Canadian families still waiting for answers one week after Nepal disaster
stories.summary: Neeral Patel sent well-wishes to her cousin on his birthday last Wednesday, but she never heard back.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Neeral Patel sent well-wishes to her cousin on his birthday last Wednesday, but she never heard back.

Her cousin Ishan Patel was in Nepal at the time, not far from the border with China, where a devastating flash flood ripped through the valley that same day.

She’s calling for a wider international response to help in rescue efforts as the days tick by with no word on her cousin or the three family members he was travelling with.

“We want to give a lot of hope. But with each passing day, it’s just getting chipped away, and time is of the essence,” said Patel, who lives in Toronto.

Ishan Patel was travelling with his wife, Akanksha Patel, both dual Canadian-U. S. citizens, along with his mother, Shilpa Patel, and father-in-law, Umesh Patel, who are Canadian, she said.

The four were on a long-planned pilgrimage to Mount Kaliash ahead of Ishan Patel starting a new job as an orthopedic surgeon, after finishing his fellowship in July, said Neeral Patel.

“It was kind of the big holy beginnings to his new career.”

The flooding on Aug. 26 killed at least 1,204 people and left more than 4,200 missing after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.

Nepal’s Foreign Ministry said 324 foreign nationals have been rescued, while about 590 from 39 countries remain unaccounted for.

Ottawa had said 30 Canadians and permanent residents were among the missing. Later Wednesday, it reported that one Canadian citizen was safe, and the tally was changed to 29.

“The individual was unreachable due to communication outages and established contact yesterday,” Anita Anand, Canada’s foreign affairs minister, said in a statement.

In Kathmandu, police have buried dozens of unidentified bodies in trenches because there are too many to keep or identify individually.

The scale of the disaster is hampering rescue efforts, as landslides and destroyed roads have cut off remote areas.

Rescuers were also racing to reach hundreds of hydropower workers trapped in tunnels.

With so many still unaccounted for, Neeral Patel said family members have been left scouring the internet, looking on Nepal police sites and missing identity sites to see if the names of any relatives come up.

She said two family members have also travelled to Kathmandu to look in hospitals and anywhere else they can find answers, but the roads up to the flood-hit area are closed.

Making the wait even harder is that they know where to search, she said, because her cousin’s phone pinged from a spot a short distance from Hotel Kailash, where they had breakfast last Wednesday.

“This is why we’re urging everyone to please, in the right area, search as much as you can, because we’re coming up to a week’s time and still no news,” she said.

Anand said search teams in China and Nepal are using a range of specialized tools and technologies including drones, helicopters, search dogs and other advanced equipment as the ground search continues.

She added that Canada would send more than 18,000 emergency items from Canadian Red Cross stockpiles, including blankets and buckets, to the area in addition to the $5 million Ottawa has already pledged in humanitarian aid.

“We have a 10-person team on the ground in Nepal. I am in continuous touch with my colleague, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, and we will leave no stone unturned to help Canadians in need.”

Patel said Global Affairs told her family about the team being sent but they’re still holding out hope for a bigger response.

“There should be a global effort, everyone work together to try to bring our family members home.”

stories.title: Ottawa artist cancels Boston exhibit after 50 per cent tariff hits Canadian art
stories.summary: An Ottawa artist was forced to cancel an exhibit in Boston after the latest round of tariffs expanded to include Canadian artwork.
stories.author: Sabrina Bedford
stories.content:
Michael Harrington, an Ottawa-based visual artist , recently announced he had to cancel an upcoming exhibition in Boston after learning the American government implemented a 50 per cent tariff on Canadian art.

Harrington, who has been a full-time artist for nearly 30 years, said the tariffs have effectively eliminated the ability for Canadian artists to exhibit or sell to American clients.

“It’s disastrous to lose that market the way it’s being lost. It’s not good,” he said Sept. 1.

On Aug. 22, the United States imposed additional tariffs of 50 per cent on almost $30 billion worth of Canadian products, about five per cent of Canada’s annual exports to that country.

Included in the extensive list was original Canadian art, such as paintings, drawings, pastels and collages, original prints and lithographs, sculptures and jewelry.

Historically, works of art could move across the border without being taxed, and selling to American clients was a relatively smooth process, Harrington said.

He added it was hard to quantify exactly how the tariffs will impact his livelihood, because his art is sold through art dealers, international art fairs, and exhibitions and he doesn’t always know where his pieces land. But Americans are among his customer base, and losing access to one of the world’s biggest markets will only hurt him and other Canadian artists at a time when the industry is already struggling.

Artists have been hard-hit in recent months as the U.S.-Iran conflict has caused a fear of inflation, he said, and many people have cut back on discretionary spending – with art being one of the first things to go.

“The art market is very vulnerable,” he said.

“This year has been one of my worst already, which was why I was hoping to expand in the United States just to have more customer opportunities.”

The Canadian Artists’ Representation/Le Front des artistes canadiens (Carfac), the national voice of Canada’s professional visual artists, said it was “deeply concerned” about the impact these new tariffs will have on Canadian art and artists.

“Canadian artists are independent workers and entrepreneurs,” Jenna Faye Powell, Interim National Executive Director of Carfac National, said in a statement.

“Unlike large businesses and corporations, individual artists don’t have the financial resources to absorb new costs associated with these tariffs. There are tangible, immediate steps we are asking the federal government to take to ensure that artists are supported through this trade dispute. Artists cannot be an afterthought in Canada’s response.”

Some of those steps include pursuing an immediate exemption for original Canadian artworks from tariffs, providing targeted financial relief to artists, galleries, Indigenous-owned businesses and cultural organizations, and establishing an emergency support and stabilization program for visual arts organizations and businesses affected.

The federal government has introduced several financial-relief packages and counter-tariff strategies for certain sectors facing the impact of tariffs, but not yet for artists.

Harrington suggested one way the government could help would be to eliminate HST on sales of original art, not just during the trade dispute but permanently.

“If we took tax off of art, that could be a huge bonus for artists as well. I would love to see that.”

Carfac said the tariffs and the resulting instability and financial burden will “no doubt fall disproportionately on artists, arts not-for-profits, and small businesses including commercial galleries,” and called on Canadians to support local artists not only in times of uncertainty or crisis.

“We need to see buying Canadian art and supporting Canadian artists as an investment in Canada, always.”
