stories.title: Bank of Canada set to make 6th interest rate decision of the year
stories.summary: Ottawa — The Bank of Canada is set to make its sixth interest rate decision of the year this morning.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

Posted September 2, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 2, 2026 3:43 pm.

Ottawa — The Bank of Canada stuck to the sidelines Wednesday as governor Tiff Macklem suggested the re-escalating trade war with the United States is not the only risk monetary policymakers are monitoring.

The central bank left its policy rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent for a seventh consecutive decision. The move was widely expected by economists.

The bank has been watching to see whether cost pressures from the war in Iran could spread into other pockets of the consumer basket.

Inflationary risks have only become sharper since the bank’s last decision in July, Macklem said Wednesday, with global oil prices still persistently high and no end in sight for the Middle East conflict.

The economy meanwhile had been rebounding ahead of new U.S. tariffs hitting a range of Canadian goods as of Aug. 22. Canada is planning a round of retaliatory tariffs on Sept. 8 and the United States has threatened further escalation.

Macklem suggested that the new duties would weigh on fourth-quarter growth and hit targeted sectors hard, but he does not foresee a “large direct impact” on the wider economy.

Because the economy was evolving broadly in line with the bank’s forecasts, governing council opted to keep the policy rate unchanged, Macklem said.

“Monetary policy cannot offset the effects of tariffs or influence global energy prices. What we can do is ensure global developments don’t jeopardize price stability in Canada,” he said.

Macklem was tight-lipped in a press conference with reporters after the decision about whether the bank is more concerned about inflation or growth risks in the midst of an uncertain outlook.

He said the inflationary risks from Canada’s counter-tariffs are “fairly modest” and that the global energy shock remains the biggest tailwind to higher prices.

Inflation was a full percentage point above the Bank of Canada’s two per cent target at three per cent in July, which Macklem said is too high for the bank’s comfort.

He said the Bank of Canada’s rate decisions are still guided by its inflation forecast, which will be updated at the next rate announcement on Oct. 28.

Frances Donald, chief economist at RBC, said Macklem “put a stake in the ground” by emphasizing the risks of higher inflation.

In doing so, he pushed back against expectations from most analysts that the central bank’s messaging would focus on threats to growth from a re-escalating trade war with the United States.

Donald said that, all things considered, Macklem is likely more worried about inflation reigniting than a hit to the economy. But that doesn’t necessarily imply rates are set to move higher.

“We have a tendency to think about central banks as having this binary — hawkish or dovish. Are they hiking or are they cutting?” Donald said.

“But what was interesting more to me today was how governor Macklem was prioritizing the multiple risks in play.”

Macklem said most of the things that will insulate the economy from tariff threats — like diversifying Canadian exports to new markets — are not in the Bank of Canada’s purview. Much of that work needs to be done by governments and the private sector, he said.

Before the latest U.S. tariffs came into effect, exports were starting to rise again. While Macklem warned that new trade restrictions could see business confidence hampered again, he also expressed some optimism about firms’ ability to cope with an uncertain status quo.

“Businesses have been adapting to an environment with more uncertainty, higher tariffs … they’re finding ways to do business,” Macklem said.

“That has put the Canadian economy on better footing going into this latest new wave of U.S. tariffs,” he said.

Donald said that momentum gives the Bank of Canada time to gauge how the trade war and inflationary pressures are working their way through the economy before acting.

It also allows the central bank to see what stimulus the federal government has in store in its fall budget, which could reduce the need for a monetary policy response.

“What Canada needs most is very targeted support to the people, sectors, and regions who need it most, and the Bank of Canada cannot provide that, just given the bluntness of their tools. This is a role for fiscal policy,” Donald said.

Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients that the central bank will likely need to see further signs of improvement in the unemployment rate or economic growth before raising the policy rate.

But given that global oil prices have shown little signs of easing, he said a rate hike at the bank’s final meeting of the year in December is now on the table.

Ottawa — The Bank of Canada stuck to the sidelines Wednesday as governor Tiff Macklem suggested the re-escalating trade war with the United States is not the only risk monetary policymakers are monitoring.
The central bank left its policy rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent for a seventh consecutive decision. The move was widely expected by economists.
The bank has been watching to see whether cost pressures from the war in Iran could spread into other pockets of the consumer basket.

Inflationary risks have only become sharper since the bank’s last decision in July, Macklem said Wednesday, with global oil prices still persistently high and no end in sight for the Middle East conflict.

The economy meanwhile had been rebounding ahead of new U.S. tariffs hitting a range of Canadian goods as of Aug. 22. Canada is planning a round of retaliatory tariffs on Sept. 8 and the United States has threatened further escalation.
Macklem suggested that the new duties would weigh on fourth-quarter growth and hit targeted sectors hard, but he does not foresee a “large direct impact” on the wider economy.
Because the economy was evolving broadly in line with the bank’s forecasts, governing council opted to keep the policy rate unchanged, Macklem said.
“Monetary policy cannot offset the effects of tariffs or influence global energy prices. What we can do is ensure global developments don’t jeopardize price stability in Canada,” he said.
Macklem was tight-lipped in a press conference with reporters after the decision about whether the bank is more concerned about inflation or growth risks in the midst of an uncertain outlook.
He said the inflationary risks from Canada’s counter-tariffs are “fairly modest” and that the global energy shock remains the biggest tailwind to higher prices.
Inflation was a full percentage point above the Bank of Canada’s two per cent target at three per cent in July, which Macklem said is too high for the bank’s comfort.
He said the Bank of Canada’s rate decisions are still guided by its inflation forecast, which will be updated at the next rate announcement on Oct. 28.
Frances Donald, chief economist at RBC, said Macklem “put a stake in the ground” by emphasizing the risks of higher inflation.
In doing so, he pushed back against expectations from most analysts that the central bank’s messaging would focus on threats to growth from a re-escalating trade war with the United States.
Donald said that, all things considered, Macklem is likely more worried about inflation reigniting than a hit to the economy. But that doesn’t necessarily imply rates are set to move higher.
“We have a tendency to think about central banks as having this binary — hawkish or dovish. Are they hiking or are they cutting?” Donald said.
“But what was interesting more to me today was how governor Macklem was prioritizing the multiple risks in play.”

Macklem said most of the things that will insulate the economy from tariff threats — like diversifying Canadian exports to new markets — are not in the Bank of Canada’s purview. Much of that work needs to be done by governments and the private sector, he said.

Before the latest U.S. tariffs came into effect, exports were starting to rise again. While Macklem warned that new trade restrictions could see business confidence hampered again, he also expressed some optimism about firms’ ability to cope with an uncertain status quo.
“Businesses have been adapting to an environment with more uncertainty, higher tariffs … they’re finding ways to do business,” Macklem said.
“That has put the Canadian economy on better footing going into this latest new wave of U.S. tariffs,” he said.
Donald said that momentum gives the Bank of Canada time to gauge how the trade war and inflationary pressures are working their way through the economy before acting.
It also allows the central bank to see what stimulus the federal government has in store in its fall budget, which could reduce the need for a monetary policy response.

“What Canada needs most is very targeted support to the people, sectors, and regions who need it most, and the Bank of Canada cannot provide that, just given the bluntness of their tools. This is a role for fiscal policy,” Donald said.

Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients that the central bank will likely need to see further signs of improvement in the unemployment rate or economic growth before raising the policy rate.
But given that global oil prices have shown little signs of easing, he said a rate hike at the bank’s final meeting of the year in December is now on the table.
Financial markets had three quarter-point hikes baked into their forecasts by mid-2027 as of Wednesday at noon — including one before the end of 2026 — according to Lseg Data & Analytics.
Odds of a hold at the Bank of Canada’s next decision in October stood at more than 92 per cent.
Donald noted that some of the need to respond to inflation risks is already being done through higher bond yields.
Global bond yields have been rising in recent weeks largely in response to concerns over U.S. debt and inflation.
The five-year Government of Canada bond yield hit its highest point in more than two years on Wednesday as markets repriced on expectations for rate hikes.

Because that yield informs key commercial lending rates and fixed-rate mortgages in the housing market, Donald said some of the tightening that would be accomplished by a policy rate hike is already underway.

stories.title: He passed three extensive security checks in Canada. Now, a fourth has stalled his citizenship for 18 months
stories.summary: Throughout his nine years in Canada, the Egyptian man has gone through — and passed — three extensive security checks by multiple federal agencies.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
How many security screenings are needed to ensure a migrant is not a security threat to Canada?

Throughout his nine years in Canada, Ottawa resident Khaled Mohamed has gone through — and passed — three extensive security checks by multiple federal agencies, including one for a job to handle sensitive personal data at the Immigration Department.

Yet, he’s faced with a fourth vetting, this time for his citizenship application, which has already been in the system for 18 months — pending security clearance.

“I respect Canada’s national security requirements,” said Mohamed, 55, a former lawyer and MP in Egypt, who fled political persecution and arrived here for asylum in 2017 by way of Qatar.

“I never imagined that an immigration journey could involve almost a decade of repeated administrative and security-related processes concerning the same individual, involving years of government work and resources, despite successive favourable assessments.”

While Mohamed has no issue with Canada’s repeated security checks, he hopes officials could at least expedite it for those who have already gone through it and been cleared multiple times. With the system already overwhelmed by backlogs, processing delays due to security screenings are causing tremendous stress on applicants.

Mohamed said his drawn-out citizenship processing delay has cost him job opportunities and the repeat screening has exhausted him, leaving him stressed and on doctor-prescribed medication.

Time-consuming security screenings for temporary or permanent resident applications have been on

Immigration security screening has garnered growing public attention in the last few years as the number of immigration applications skyrocketed after the pandemic, leading to an explosion of files flagged for inadmissibility and security concerns.

While critics question whether the process is rigorous enough, advocates complain that it takes too long and is holding back the lives of migrants , whether they are here for asylum, to study or work, or in the process of becoming permanent residents or citizens.

Canada’s immigration screening program is managed by the Immigration Department, Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) and Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis). Immigration officials refer applicants to the Cbsa and Csis if they have concerns over an individual’s potential involvement in war crimes, crimes against humanity or organized crimes, or being a threat to national security.

The two organizations conduct independent investigations and report back to the Immigration Department, which ultimately decides if the applicant is admissible.

According to Csis, the number of immigration security screening requests it receives increased from 356,200 in 2019 to a peak of 538,100 in 2024, before it dropped to 438,600 last year after Ottawa reduced immigration intakes. The border agency said its current caseload includes 69,800 applications for temporary residence, 31,300 for permanent residence and 73,400 for refugee claims.

The Immigration Department estimated that it would take 64.8 months to complete all security screenings for permanent residence and 30.3 months for temporary residence, based on output and the number of cases in the system as of the end of November.

Toronto immigration lawyer Max Berger said the stakes are high in citizenship applications because once a person becomes a citizen, it’s difficult to strip it. However, he said the screening process has been plagued by a lack of resources and transparency, causing extensive delays and leaving people in uncertainty.

He said multiple security screenings are not necessary unless new information emerges that suggests a person was involved in nefarious activities in their home country that officials weren’t aware of before.

“Obviously, that should dictate a fresh investigation,” said Berger, co-president of the Canadian Immigration Lawyers Association. “It causes delays and backup in the system, and endless headaches for clients ... The previous comprehensive security screenings should be adequate. Otherwise, you’re saying that they were worthless and we have to start again.”

Mohamed is no stranger to the security screening process, which includes interviews and thorough documentations.

He practised law for more than two decades and was a law-school professor before he ran for public office after the fall of President Hosni Mubarak in 2011. He was a member of the Freedom and Justice Party and briefly served as an MP in the Egyptian parliament, which was dissolved in a military coup in 2013, forcing him to flee.

After spending four years in limbo in Qatar, Mohamed came to Canada with his wife and three daughters in August 2017, made a refugee claim and underwent his first security screening. All adult asylum seekers must pass a mandatory front-end security screening by the border and intelligence agencies before their claims are forwarded to the refugee board.

He was cleared and granted protection in Canada after almost two years, in July 2019. He immediately applied for permanent residence, but again was flagged for security checks by the very same agencies.

It took him more than three years to be cleared by the little-known Centre of Expertise in Security Cases, an internal specialized unit within the Immigration Department tasked with admissibility decisions. He became a permanent resident in February 2023.

In its report, the centre examined Mohamed’s role in the Freedom and Justice Party and its relationship with the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood, a designated terrorist organization in Egypt, in connection to the protests that led to the fall of Mubarak’s regime. It also weighed his circumstances and assessed if he violated any of the provisions on security and subversion of a government in Canadian immigration law.

The report said neither had the Freedom and Justice Party subverted the Egyptian government by force nor was it an organization that has participated in or will participate in terrorism. As a result, Mohamed was found not to be “a risk to Canadian security due to his former membership and participation in the Freedom and Justice Party.”

After completing a college program to be a paralegal here, Mohamed applied for jobs at the Immigration Department and had to go through the standard federal personnel security screening process. He got his 10-year “reliability status” granted within two months and started working for the department as a program assistant in 2024.

While an immigration employee, he applied for his Canadian citizenship. He was let go last year due to federal budget cuts and now drives an Uber for a living in part because he can’t afford the professional fees to work as a paralegal.

Mohamed said officials have not asked for additional documents, information, travel history, employment history or other materials for the security screening of his citizenship application. The only thing requested was new fingerprints due to the expiry of his criminality check.

The Immigration Department declined to address how the vetting processes vary for asylum seekers, applicants for temporary and permanent residence and citizenship candidates in order to “protect the integrity” of the security screening programs.

Gaps in Canada’s security screening have been in the spotlight in recent years. A father and son from Egypt with alleged ties with terrorist group Isis were granted permanent residence and became citizens, and were later charged with plotting a violent Toronto terrorist attack in 2024. Senior officials and ex-officials of the Iranian regime have been found in Canada despite Ottawa’s official ban in 2022 .

Last year, a government report to Parliament said the Immigration Department between April 2016 and October 2025 initiated nine citizenship investigations into individuals suspected of involvement in war crimes, crimes against humanity and/or genocide.

Do prior security checks get remembered?

The Immigration Department said it referred Mohamed’s application for security screening in March 2025 as part of a routine program requirement applied consistently across citizenship applications against anyone aged 15.5 years and older. It said Mohamed’s security clearance is ongoing.

The department said it “recognizes the patience applicants demonstrate and the trust they place in Canada’s immigration system. We understand that waiting for a decision can be a significant source of stress and uncertainty.”

Mohamed said every security screening puts him under tremendous stress and his doctor has put him on Escitalopram, a prescription antidepressant, since 2021. He said the current delay in his citizenship processing has already cost him a potential job at Global Affairs Canada and a job offer as a legal adviser in Qatar. (The former required Canadian citizenship while the latter involved travel and Mohamed can’t get an Egyptian or Canadian passport.)

“I don’t know what I can do,” said Mohamed, who has not travelled since arriving here in 2017. “Citizenship is a freedom. Right now I am not belonging to any country. I’m not arguing that security screening should only occur once. But previous governmental (security) assessments should at least form part of the institutional memory.”

(The former required Canadian citizenship while the latter involved travel and Mohamed can’t get an Egyptian or Canadian passport.)

“I don’t know what I can do,” said Mohamed, who has not travelled since arriving here in 2017. “Citizenship is a freedom. Right now I am not belonging to any country. I’m not arguing that security screening should only occur once. But previous governmental (security) assessments should at least form part of the institutional memory.”

stories.title: Ice investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (September 2, 2026) – The London Police Service (LPS) is releasing information to keep the public informed, and to identify any potential additional victims, as part of an ongoing child exploitation investigation involving a London man.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
General Releases

LONDON, ON (September 2, 2026) – The London Police Service (LPS) is releasing information to keep the public informed, and to identify any potential additional victims, as part of an ongoing child exploitation investigation involving a London man.

On July 26, 2026, Kyle Vanderheiden, 39, of London was arrested by members of the LPS Internet Child Exploitation Unit (ICE) and charged with the following offences:

Two counts of printing, publishing or possessing for the purpose of publishing child sexual abuse and exploitation material

Telecommunications agreement to commit specific criminal offences with another under or believed to be under 16 years

Possession of child sexual abuse and exploitation material

Obtaining sexual services for consideration from a person under 18 years of age

Luring a person under 18 years of age by means of telecommunication

Making sexually explicit material available to a person under 18 years of age or believed to be under 18 years of age; and,

Importing, selling or distributing child sexual abuse material.

On August 21, 2026, Vanderheiden was released from custody by the court after a contested bail hearing, and is subject to the following bail conditions:

To reside with surety in London, Ontario and remain in or on the property of their residence at all times

To not be in the company of or communicate, directly or indirectly, by any physical, electronic or other means with anyone under the age of 18 years

To not be within 10 metres of any school, community centres, daycares, swimming pools, parks or anywhere children are known to be or frequent except for required court appearances; and,

To not possess any weapons.

Vanderheiden is scheduled to re-appear in London court on October 1, 2026.

A photograph of Vanderheiden is being released in support of public awareness and the continuing investigation.

Investigators believe there may be people who have information relevant to the investigation or who believe they may have had contact with Vanderheiden in similar circumstances. Police are asking anyone with information, including potential additional victims, to contact investigators.

Police are also asking anyone who believes Vanderheiden may be breaching a condition of his release to contact police and avoid placing themselves at risk. In an emergency, call 9-1-1.

The LPS recognizes that coming forward in matters involving sexual violence can be difficult and support is available. Information and links to local support services are available on the LPS website.

Anyone with information related to this investigation, including anyone who believes they may have experienced similar conduct, is asked to contact the London Police Service Internet Child Exploitation Unit at 519-661-5670. Anonymous information can also be provided to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477) or through London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

For media inquiries, contact:

stories.title: This international student in Canada protested a work permit refusal. Now, he and 9 others face ejection from the country
stories.summary: Advocates say they are alarmed by the pushback of immigration authorities against migrants trying to exercise their right to protest.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
For weeks this summer, Gurpreet Singh had joined other international students for a round-the-clock protest in Calgary over the bulk refusals of their postgraduation work permits by the Immigration Department .

With protest signs erected on the lawn, the students took turns demonstrating across from their alma mater, the Canadian Institute of Osteopathic Therapy (Ciot), where they graduated from the private college’s joint programs licensed by its public partner, Portage College.

Singh didn’t anticipate their peaceful demonstration would bring out the Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) and land him — and nine other students — an exclusion order that forces them to leave the country and bans them from returning.

“They did it to sabotage our protest,” said the 29-year-old man, who came here from India on a study permit in 2023 and was refused a work permit in early July because graduates from “non-credit” programs like Ciot-Portage’s are no longer eligible under the rules updated a month earlier by the Immigration Department.

“They are successful in stopping our protest because all the students are afraid now. Nobody is coming out. Everyone is scared Cbsa officers would be out there waiting for them.”

Advocates say they are alarmed by the pushback of immigration authorities against migrants trying to exercise their right to protest.

International graduates protest near the Canadian Institute of Osteopathic Therapy in Calgary after hundreds of them had their work permit applications refused.

On Wednesday, they delivered an op en letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, demanding an independent investigation into the incident and clear rules to ensure protest won’t trigger immigration enforcement.

It also urges authorities to withdraw the exclusion orders against 10 of the students.

“Freedom of expression and peaceful assembly are fundamental Charter-protected rights,” said the letter, endorsed by more than 250 civil liberties, human rights, labour, faith, environmental, migrant, refugee and community groups across the country.

“They do not belong only to Canadian citizens or permanent residents. Migrants must be able to speak out, organize and protest without those activities becoming a pathway to immigration enforcement.”

The border agency said it was contacted by Calgary Police Service on Aug. 12, requesting a status check on four individuals at a student protest. Upon confirmation that two of the people were non-compliant with their immigration status, Cbsa arrived at the scene and conducted further investigation.

In total, 20 individuals had their status verified, with 12 individuals identified as being “possibly inadmissible” and being asked to attend followup interviews. Advocates said 10 of them have since been issued exclusion orders.

“Inland investigations are an important tool to identify those who should not be in the country and are critical to ensuring compliance with the law,” the Cbsa said in an email. “Foreign nationals admitted into Canada are not able to work or study unless authorized and are expected to depart Canada at the end of their authorized period of stay.”

The agency said it’s aware of and reviewing the open letter and its demands, and that “the freedom of peaceful assembly is a Charter-protected right.”

Syed Hussan of the Migrant Rights Network said border agents are used to raid targeted places such as malls, schools and shelters for immigration enforcement but these operations have become less frequent in recent years.

“What happened on Aug. 12th is incredibly dangerous,” said Hussan, whose organization led the advocacy effort for the Ciot-Portage students.

“It hearkens to the use of (U.S. President) Trump-style targeting of people for speaking up for their rights. It’s completely outside the rules. A protest where you are speaking up for justice should be a place where you get justice, not immigration enforcement.”

In an email, Alberta’s Jobs and Immigration Minister Joseph Schow said anyone who comes to Canada on temporary status needs to return home once their permit is expired.

“That is the position of our government, and it’s not going to change,” said Schow, adding that the province supports police and border officials in law enforcement.

Hussan said about 1,500 international graduates from the Ciot-Portage programs were denied work permits after the Immigration Department quietly tweaked the rules in June.

The affected students, he said, had been informed when they enrolled in these programs that they would be eligible for a work permit upon graduation. Portage College also told CBC News last month that it’s the school’s understanding that students enrolled in non-credit public-private partnership programs prior to May 15, 2024 would qualify, “consistent with the information available at the time and the way these applications had historically been administered.”

“The term non-credit had never appeared in any immigration publication” as a criteria for postgraduation work permit, said Hussan.

International graduates have recently started ongoing protests near the Canadian Institute of Osteopathic Therapy in Calgary.

Singh, who has a bachelor’s degree in English literature from India, said he first studied organizational management at the joint Cambrian-Hanson College partnership program in Brampton before moving to Calgary. He graduated from the administrative professional certificate program at Ciot in December 2024 and applied for a postgraduation work permit.

He said the refusal came as a shock after an 18-month wait, while he continued working at a gas station and later at a concrete plant, ON maintained status. He quit working immediately after he lost his work authorization on July 9.

“I completed my study and they only displayed the non-credit criteria on its website months later,” said Singh, whose parents spent a total $36,000 on his tuition fees in Canada. “It’s just not fair.”

He said he had a pending challenge of the work permit refusal before the Federal Court and was weighing his options during the 90-day grace period to restore his temporary status when Cbsa issued him the exclusion order. Many refused students had been accepted by other schools and applied for a new study permit to successfully extend their status, he added.

“I didn’t have time to do that and now I can’t do anything and must leave Canada,” lamented Singh, who has used up his savings on legal fees and is surviving on community support through crowdfunding . He is required to report to Cbsa once every two weeks and confirm his exit.

The Immigration Department said there have been no changes to the eligibility criteria for post-graduation work permit, and officials only updated its webpage to “clarify” the rules related to non-credit programs of study.

“Canada supports the right to peaceful protest, freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” it said in an email. It didn’t address the students’ and advocacy groups’ demands.

Julia Sande, a lawyer with Amnesty International Canada, said she was appalled by the Cbsa’s crackdown at the student protest in Calgary, warning that targeting peaceful protests strikes fear and makes people think twice about speaking out.

“It’s intimidation, pure and simple,” said Sande, whose organization endorses the open letter to Carney, Diab, Anandasangaree and Smith.

“Things like freedom of speech, peaceful assembly and the right to protest extend to everyone in Canada. I cannot see how this is seen as relevant or justified to be checking people’s immigration status. It has no bearing on whether they’re allowed to protest.”

stories.title: Alberta separatist ties hasten implosion of Canada’s B.C. Conservative Party as 9 MLAs have now resigned in a month
stories.summary: Alberta separatist ties among senior staff lead B.C. MLAs Donegal Wilson and Scott McInnis to resign, making nine caucus departures in a month.
stories.author: Emma McIntosh
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservative Party continued to unravel as two more members stepped down from its caucus Wednesday, citing ties between senior staffers and the Alberta separatist movement .

The hires by party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay “raise serious questions about her judgement,” MLA Donegal Wilson said in a statement.

“I never imagined things could go this wrong, this quickly,” Wilson’s statement said.

Hours after Wilson’s exit, MLA Scott McInnis also announced he was leaving the party, pointing to “serious ethical questions” around Findlay’s senior staff. He also said reported connections between Findlay staffers and Alberta separatism “added to those concerns,” saying the issue is contentious in his riding, which borders Alberta.

Both Wilson and McInnis pointed to lists of other concerns about Findlay’s leadership of the party, which she won in May. They are the eighth and ninth MLAs to leave the Conservative caucus in the past month, and will both sit as independents. Findlay’s office did not answer questions from the Star.

Wilson and McInnis’s departures come the day after the Star reported two staff with ties to the Republican Party of Alberta (RPA) had recently joined the senior ranks of the B.C. Conservative Party. The RPA is a provincial party that has campaigned for Alberta to separate from Canada.

Apollo Chung was executive director of the separatist Alberta Republican Party before moving to the B.C. Conservatives.

The first hire was Apollo Chung, a longtime B.C. political operative who has previously worked as executive director of the RPA. A Star investigation published earlier this month found that Chung was among a group of four donors who gave thousands to the Republican Party of Alberta in 2025 while apparently living in B.C., seemingly in violation of Elections Alberta’s campaign finance rules. Chung has not responded to requests for comment from the Star.

He was director of operations for the B.C. Conservative Party until last week, when Findlay announced he had been fired.

Findlay did not give a reason for the firing, which came after alleged audio recordings surfaced online of a Findlay staffer talking about using political work to enrich themselves. A Canadian Press report said the audio was allegedly of Chung. The Star cannot independently verify the authenticity of the recordings.

The second hire is Jake Bregolisse, who has ties to B.C. and Alberta, and previously worked for Sovereign North Strategies, a political consulting firm co-directed by Republican Party of Alberta (RPA) leader Cameron Davies, according to two sources for the Star story earlier this week . Bregolisse is now Findlay’s director of legislative affairs and strategic planning.

Someone named Jacob Bregolisse also donated $5,000, the maximum amount allowed by law, to the RPA in 2025. Another name on the list of maximum donors in 2025 was Apollo Chung.

Sovereign North Strategies was the parent company of a polling firm that a recent Star investigation found had released a poll finding record support for the RPA but that did not disclose the firm’s ties to the party leader.

Sovereign North was also involved in a recent B.C. political kerfuffle: in April, Elections BC levied a $4,500 fine against provincial party BC United for commissioning a website that was critical of Findlay’s predecessor John Rustad, and attempting to make it look like the work of disgruntled Conservatives. Sovereign North helped make the website, the election watchdog found, though it did not levy any penalties against the company.

Bregolisse and the party have not answered questions from the Star about his hiring.

When Findlay won the race to lead the Conservative Party in May, she pledged it to “faith, family and freedom,” a common political slogan also used by the RPA. She has said she would maintain an economic relationship with Alberta, should it decide to separate, though her office previously told the Star she believes in federalism and is a “Canadian, born and bred.”

McInnis said he believes the party under Findlay cannot attract the centrist voters it would need to win an election. “This is a recipe for failure,” he said in the statement.

With files from Alex Boyd

Apollo Chung was executive director of the separatist Alberta Republican Party before moving to the B.C. Conservatives.

The first hire was Apollo Chung, a longtime B.C. political operative who has previously worked as executive director of the RPA. A Star investigation published earlier this month found that Chung was among a group of four donors who gave thousands to the Republican Party of Alberta in 2025 while apparently living in B.C., seemingly in violation of Elections Alberta’s campaign finance rules. Chung has not responded to requests for comment from the Star.
He was director of operations for the B.C. Conservative Party until last week, when Findlay announced he had been fired.

Findlay did not give a reason for the firing, which came after alleged audio recordings surfaced online of a Findlay staffer talking about using political work to enrich themselves. A Canadian Press report said the audio was allegedly of Chung. The Star cannot independently verify the authenticity of the recordings.

The second hire is Jake Bregolisse, who has ties to B.C. and Alberta, and previously worked for Sovereign North Strategies, a political consulting firm co-directed by Republican Party of Alberta (RPA) leader Cameron Davies, according to two sources for the Star story earlier this week . Bregolisse is now Findlay’s director of legislative affairs and strategic planning.
Someone named Jacob Bregolisse also donated $5,000, the maximum amount allowed by law, to the RPA in 2025. Another name on the list of maximum donors in 2025 was Apollo Chung.

Sovereign North Strategies was the parent company of a polling firm that a recent Star investigation found had released a poll finding record support for the RPA but that did not disclose the firm’s ties to the party leader.

Sovereign North was also involved in a recent B.C. political kerfuffle: in April, Elections BC levied a $4,500 fine against provincial party BC United for commissioning a website that was critical of Findlay’s predecessor John Rustad, and attempting to make it look like the work of disgruntled Conservatives. Sovereign North helped make the website, the election watchdog found, though it did not levy any penalties against the company.
Bregolisse and the party have not answered questions from the Star about his hiring.

When Findlay won the race to lead the Conservative Party in May, she pledged it to “faith, family and freedom,” a common political slogan also used by the RPA. She has said she would maintain an economic relationship with Alberta, should it decide to separate, though her office previously told the Star she believes in federalism and is a “Canadian, born and bred.”
McInnis said he believes the party under Findlay cannot attract the centrist voters it would need to win an election. “This is a recipe for failure,” he said in the statement.

stories.title: Driving in heavy rain can be dangerous. Here’s how to navigate roads safely
stories.summary: Driving out in a storm can greatly increase your risk of collision. An expert shares how to do it safely.
stories.author: Kevin Jiang
stories.content:
With the GTA getting slammed by a severe thunderstorm Wednesday, navigating Toronto traffic can become even more perilous than usual.

Experts say such heavy downpour can lower visibility and put your vehicle at risk of hydroplaning or collisions in general — but there are simple ways to stay safe.

“Regardless of how (bad it’s raining) or which kind of weather there is, the number one key factor is planning ahead,” Naureen Raziq, the director of communications and an instructor at Toronto’s Globe Driving Academy, told the Star.

“People only associate dangerous conditions or safety when it comes to a rainy day — but this is something that should be followed every day that you are on the road,” she said.

Here are her main tips for safe driving.

For Raziq, it’s key that drivers plan ahead and map out their routes before departure — especially during bad weather. During heavy rain, for example, drivers should learn of areas more prone to flooding and avoid those roads.

“A lot of driving has to be done mentally beforehand by planning ahead, even if you’re doing a civilian route,” she said. “I always look to see how long it’s going to be and what the road looks like, because it can change from day to day. It May be construction is going on, but it (wasn’t) going on yesterday.”

Make sure you know of the weather conditions at your destination and along your route, and plan accordingly, she continued. If it is raining, make sure to leave earlier as you can expect traffic conditions to be worse than usual.

No matter the weather conditions, drivers should always perform a circle check before heading out, Raziq explained. This means circling around the vehicle looking for any signs of damage or malfunction.

“You always walk around the vehicle to make sure there’s no leakage coming under the vehicle or the tires are okay,” she said. “There’s no scratches that happened maybe overnight, especially if the car is parked on a main road. Maybe something can be broken overnight.

“Try to do that before you even get into the vehicle, to not face any potential issues when you go driving on the road.”

The most common mistake when it comes to driving in the rain that Raziq has encountered is not having functional windshield wipers.

“People don’t get that checked regularly,” she said. “Only on a day when it’s actually raining is when they will use it — and when it’s not working, that’s one of the things that leads to collisions.”

Make sure they’re working properly and not worn out before you hit the road. If they need replacing, do it immediately instead of waiting for the next rain or snow storm.

It’s crucial your tires have around the recommended air pressure of 30 or 32 PSI, and that they can maintain enough friction with the ground to provide traction.

All-season tires are usually sufficient for driving in the rain, Raziq said — just make sure the treads aren’t too worn down. She often sees drivers using off-market tires that, while they match the make and model of the vehicle, are of inferior quality with poor traction that can lead to collisions.

I’d like to help with long drives and I’m starting to dream of the road’s freedom, writes Cathrin Bradbury. My family is not entirely on board.

In heavy rain, it’s important to turn your fog lights on — another frequent mistake Raziq sees drivers making. These lights shine a low and flat beam close to the ground, cutting through low-visibility conditions and making it easier to see.

Do not turn on your high beam headlights, as the light could reflect off falling rain and make visibility worse, according to Transport Canada .

Make sure the area in front of your dashboard is well ventilated, like with air conditioning, to avoid fog build-up in the window, Raziq said. Air conditioning serves to whisk away moisture in the air, helping keep your window clear.

“Sometimes when you have the air conditioning on, you have it pointed at your feet or face. Just make sure to also have it on at the front dashboard” to de-fog your window, she said.

When driving under ideal conditions, drivers should maintain three-to-five seconds of distance from the car in front. In wet and slippery conditions, this changes to five to seven seconds of distance, Raziq explained, as tires May have a harder time getting traction when braking on wet surfaces.

Additionally, drivers should drive slower and look ahead for coming traffic impediments — ideally looking “three traffic lights ahead” if possible when driving on busy city streets.

Range, charging time and heating can change for EVs, depending on the weather. EVs tend to lose a significant amount of range in cold

Hydroplaning happens when your tires lose traction with the road, instead skidding forward on a thin film of water. This can commonly cause accidents or collisions on wet surfaces, Raziq said.

Once you feel this happen, do not slam on the brakes as many new drivers do, she continued, explaining: “Your car will rotate and you will lose control of your vehicle.”

Similarly, avoid turning the vehicle too much, which could cause it to spin further out of control. Steer in the direction that you’re sliding, instead of against it.

Finally, ease off the accelerator and slow down gradually, eventually coming to a stop.

It might seem obvious, but you should avoid flooded areas and pools of standing water if at all possible, Raziq said. Similarly, if you hear a storm is on the way, it’s a good idea to move your car to an area of higher elevation if possible to avoid damages.

“We always tell our students, don’t risk going through deep flooded roads or areas,” she said. “When you plan ahead, you know that certain areas are going to be flooded, especially if you drive a lot.”

As climate change worsens storms, many people don’t realize they’re in a flood-risk area. Use our interactive map to see Toronto’s hidden flood zones.

On Tuesday, the city of Toronto is warning residents to avoid Lake Shore Boulevard near Ontario Place and the bike lanes of the westbound Bloor Viaduct due to flooding; you can check current road closures and restrictions in Toronto, including flooding, using the city’s interactive map here .

If your car breaks down on the side of the road and it’s currently raining, Raziq urges you not to pop the hood and investigate yourself. The rain could damage the car’s electronics and make matters worse, she said.

“If your car breaks down, walk out of the vehicle, find a safe spot by the vehicle and call a tow truck or whoever,” she continued. ”... We never invite you to open the hood yourself, unless you know what you’re doing and it’s a day where it’s not raining.”

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives unravel as seven MLAs walk away
stories.summary: The B.C. Conservatives are losing MLAs at a startling pace, just months after Kerry-Lynne Findlay took over as leader, leading one political scientist to describe the party as 'imploding before our eyes.'
stories.author: Andrew Johnson
stories.content:
Vancouver – The B.C. Conservatives are losing MLAs at a startling pace, just months after Kerry-Lynne Findlay took over as leader, leading one political scientist to describe the party as “imploding before our eyes.”

Seven Conservative MLAs have left the caucus since the beginning of August, including the latest defection announced Monday.

University of the Fraser Valley political scientist Hamish Telford says the departures reflect a fundamental shift in what the party is trying to become.

“I’ve never seen anything quite like this in Canadian politics before,” he said. “A party sort of imploding before our eyes.”

Findlay won the Conservative leadership in May after campaigning on a socially conservative platform focused on “faith, family and freedom.”

“I’m fighting for nothing less than the future of British Columbia. Our way of life,” Findlay said on May 30 after winning the leadership.

But Telford says the party had functioned as a coalition of conservative and more liberal-minded members united primarily by their opposition to the NDP. That coalition has now fractured.

“Kerry-Lynne Findlay campaigned for leadership and has, since she became leader, indicated that she doesn’t want to lead a coalition-style party.”

“She wants this to be a decidedly conservative and populist party. Those who are not on board with that program are leaving.” Telford said.

The departures have also opened the possibility of a new centre-right political option in B.C.

“There is a wide space now between the NDP and Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s Conservatives,” Telford said. “There are many voters in that space that are not happy with the NDP, particularly on fiscal matters. And they’re not happy with Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s Conservatives, particularly on social matters.”

One potential alternative is CentreBC, led by former B.C. Liberal cabinet minister Mike Bernier. Former Conservative MLA Peter Milobar has also discussed creating a centre-right alternative.

For now, the governing NDP is watching its main opposition party weaken. “I understand that the Conservatives are in significant chaos,” Premier David Eby said Tuesday. “Our focus remains on delivering for British Columbians.”

Telford says the Conservatives’ survival could hinge on their support in rural B.C. “What’s really important for Kerry-Lynne Findlay and the Conservatives is that they have a territorial base in the Interior and the North,” he said.

In the middle of all this, Findlay is also facing a make-or-break test of her leadership – winning a seat in the legislature. She says she is “focusing her full attention and full energy” on winning the seat in Abbotsford-Mission on Sept. 26.

Telford says a victory would likely solidify her position.

“If she wins that seat, I think she’s here to stay for a while,” he said. “If she doesn’t win it, there will be a lot of pressure on her to step down.”

stories.title: Alberta Motor Association student patrollers return to province’s crosswalks
stories.summary: Classes are back in Lethbridge, Alta., and that means the Alberta Motor Association's student patrollers are once again holding their stop signs.
stories.author: Justin Sibbet
stories.content:
For more than 85 years, the Alberta Motor Association (AMA) has trained Grade 5 students across the province to become safety patrollers.

It has a strong track record of keeping kids safe.

“During that time, there have been zero serious injuries or fatalities when a patroller has been on a crosswalk,” said Allison Purcell, AMA school safety patrol coordinator.

For first-time patrollers Charlotte Loewen and Briar Maret, it brings confidence to their school.

“I was not allowed to cross by myself for a long time and this will help adults feel more safe for their kids,” said Loewen, a Grade 5 student at West Coulee Ridge Elementary School in Lethbridge.

Maret also attends that school and she believes patrolling gives her experience in leadership as well.

“It shows the kids younger than us that this is how you’re supposed to cross behave and this is how you’re supposed to cross the crosswalk.”

But safety patrol requires cooperation from the entire community.

“It’s just a good reminder that we are watching for patrollers when we are coming up to a crosswalk, we’re paying attention to what their commands are. It’s pretty easy to see their stop signs when we need to stop,” said Purcell.

Police say drivers who fail to follow the rules of the road could face consequences.

“We’ll have an extra push to remind drivers, pedestrians and students that we’re back in class now. There will be automated enforcement as well as conventional enforcement,” said Sgt. Tony Ramotowski of the Lethbridge Police Service’s traffic response unit.

He says pedestrians also need to be responsible, though.

“Look both ways, use a crosswalk, if there’s lights, turn the lights on. If you’re walking up to the school zone, you see a driver, make eye contact with them, make sure they see you.”

In Lethbridge, all playground and school zones are harmonized. This means both zones have a 30 km/h speed limit from 7:30 a.m. until 9:00 p.m. every day.

stories.title: Hegseth’s post belittling Canadian cadet program draws condemnation from across political spectrum
stories.summary: Social-media episode is playing out amid an increasingly acrimonious relationship between the two countries, with trade talks stalled and tariffs escalating
stories.author: Andrea Woo, Mike Hager
stories.content:
A photo of a Canadian Forces cadet instructor and a young participant at a summer training camp made its way from the fringes of Canada’s online right to the account of U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose post featuring the image has drawn condemnation across the political spectrum.

The social-media episode is playing out amid an increasingly acrimonious relationship between the two countries, with trade talks stalled and tariffs escalating.

Mr. Hegseth has made military fitness a central theme of his leadership at the Pentagon, pushing tougher physical standards and testosterone testing while shaming “fat generals .” His post about the image included what seemed to be a derisive swipe at the physical appearances of the two women shown.

The image came from an Aug. 24 Instagram post by the Vernon Cadet Training Centre in B.C.’s North Okanagan, celebrating the conclusion of its 2026 summer program. It depicts a commanding officer of one of the Western Canada cadet squadrons in military camouflage handing a medal to a cadet wearing a scarlet beret.

The first woman, a Cadet Instructor Cadre officer, is paid by the reserve forces of Canada’s military to train young cadets.

On Monday, an account called Veterans for Freedom, which purports to be a Canadian veterans community group, posted the image in a reply on the social-media platform X, deriding the fitness of military members. Popular conservative Montreal-based streamer Nick Belanger, also known as the Pleb Reporter, posted the image a few hours later.

Mr. Hegseth shared the image with his two million followers later that night, along with a Canadian flag emoji and the words “This is real” in brackets. The post prompted a mix of ridicule and criticism in the replies, with some users piling on with further mockery and others scolding Mr. Hegseth for targeting a Canadian youth program.

The instructor’s family declined to comment on Tuesday.

Canada’s Department of National Defence said the cadet program provides youth aged 12 to 18 with opportunities to develop leadership skills, knowledge and self-confidence.

“We are proud of the professionalism and contributions of all our dedicated Canadian Armed Forces members,” it said in a statement.

The Pentagon, meanwhile, stood by Mr. Hegseth’s comment.

“The X post speaks for itself,” deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss said.

Mr. Hegseth’s post drew swift and bipartisan condemnation from political leaders across Canada. Asked about the post on Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters on Parliament Hill that “it’s beneath their office.”

B.C. Premier David Eby called the post an embarrassment.

“It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to right now,” he said in response to a reporter’s question at a news conference in Burnaby on Tuesday.

“That includes a pointless, stupid, self-defeating trade war against Canada, of all countries in the world. I look forward to a change in that leadership. I’m astonished at the depths they continue to explore with their public rhetoric.”

Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, who served as minister of national defence in 2015, also pushed back against Mr. Hegseth’s post.

“In the midst of a hot war against a mortal enemy of the United States, the Secretary of War of the world’s only super power finds time to troll folks at a cadet camp for teenagers in Vernon, British Columbia,” Mr. Kenney wrote. “To our many friends in the great United States of America: What’s going on?”

Dimitris Soudas, former director of communications to prime minister Stephen Harper, said the Canadian Cadet Organizations help young Canadians develop leadership, discipline, self-confidence and a commitment to their communities.

“Mocking these young people says far more about the person doing the mocking than it ever will about the young people wearing the uniform,” he wrote on X.

Conservative MP Garnett Genuis replied to Mr. Hegseth’s post saying that “cadets do great work, and are not members of the military.”

He continued: “158 members of the Canadian military gave their lives in Afghanistan after your country was attacked. Canada and the US have a great history of fighting together for freedom and justice. It’s history worth remembering.”

Mr. Belanger, the libertarian livestreamer who gained a substantial following while covering the last federal election campaign of Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, told The Globe in an interview that he at times feels guilty for helping craft national news cycles despite having only a surface-level understanding of politics. This episode with Mr. Hegseth is not one of those times, though, he said.

“I posted my opinion and the Secretary of War agrees with me,” he said.

With a report from The Canadian Press

U.S. Sen. Ruben Gallego, an Arizona Democrat and former marine, says he is concerned by American rhetoric denigrating Canada's military. On a visit to Ottawa, he said rhetoric from Trump officials has been disrespectful and risks compromising work by American allies to keep the U.S. safe.

The Canadian Press

It depicts a commanding officer of one of the Western Canada cadet squadrons in military camouflage handing a medal to a cadet wearing a scarlet beret.
The first woman, a Cadet Instructor Cadre officer, is paid by the reserve forces of Canada’s military to train young cadets.

On Monday, an account called Veterans for Freedom, which purports to be a Canadian veterans community group, posted the image in a reply on the social-media platform X, deriding the fitness of military members. Popular conservative Montreal-based streamer Nick Belanger, also known as the Pleb Reporter, posted the image a few hours later.

Mr. Hegseth shared the image with his two million followers later that night, along with a Canadian flag emoji and the words “This is real” in brackets. The post prompted a mix of ridicule and criticism in the replies, with some users piling on with further mockery and others scolding Mr. Hegseth for targeting a Canadian youth program.
The instructor’s family declined to comment on Tuesday.
Canada’s Department of National Defence said the cadet program provides youth aged 12 to 18 with opportunities to develop leadership skills, knowledge and self-confidence.
“We are proud of the professionalism and contributions of all our dedicated Canadian Armed Forces members,” it said in a statement.
The Pentagon, meanwhile, stood by Mr. Hegseth’s comment.
“The X post speaks for itself,” deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss said.

Mr. Hegseth’s post drew swift and bipartisan condemnation from political leaders across Canada. Asked about the post on Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters on Parliament Hill that “it’s beneath their office.”
B.C. Premier David Eby called the post an embarrassment.

“It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to right now,” he said in response to a reporter’s question at a news conference in Burnaby on Tuesday.

“That includes a pointless, stupid, self-defeating trade war against Canada, of all countries in the world. I look forward to a change in that leadership. I’m astonished at the depths they continue to explore with their public rhetoric.”
Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, who served as minister of national defence in 2015, also pushed back against Mr. Hegseth’s post.

“In the midst of a hot war against a mortal enemy of the United States, the Secretary of War of the world’s only super power finds time to troll folks at a cadet camp for teenagers in Vernon, British Columbia,” Mr. Kenney wrote. “To our many friends in the great United States of America: What’s going on?”

Dimitris Soudas, former director of communications to prime minister Stephen Harper, said the Canadian Cadet Organizations help young Canadians develop leadership, discipline, self-confidence and a commitment to their communities.
“Mocking these young people says far more about the person doing the mocking than it ever will about the young people wearing the uniform,” he wrote on X.
Conservative MP Garnett Genuis replied to Mr. Hegseth’s post saying that “cadets do great work, and are not members of the military.”

He continued: “158 members of the Canadian military gave their lives in Afghanistan after your country was attacked. Canada and the US have a great history of fighting together for freedom and justice. It’s history worth remembering.”

Mr. Belanger, the libertarian livestreamer who gained a substantial following while covering the last federal election campaign of Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, told The Globe in an interview that he at times feels guilty for helping craft national news cycles despite having only a surface-level understanding of politics. This episode with Mr. Hegseth is not one of those times, though, he said.
“I posted my opinion and the Secretary of War agrees with me,” he said.

stories.title: London Health Coalition joins national protest over Alberta healthcare legislation
stories.summary: Health coalitions across Canada are calling on the federal government to take action to protect the country’s public healthcare system as controversial legislation in Alberta takes effect today.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Health coalitions across Canada are calling on the federal government to take action to protect the country’s public healthcare system as controversial legislation in Alberta takes effect today.

The London Health Coalition is among groups participating in a National Day of Action Tuesday, with protesters gathering outside the London office of federal MP Arielle Kayabaga.

The protests come as Alberta’s Bill 11, the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 (No. 2), takes effect.

The legislation allows physicians to charge patients for medically necessary healthcare services while also billing the public healthcare system. It also opens the door to private, for-profit health insurance.

Health coalitions across the country say the changes could lead to a two-tier healthcare system and are calling on the federal government to enforce the Canada Health Act.

Peter Bergmanis with the London Health Coalition says the federal government has a responsibility to protect Canada’s public healthcare system.

“The federal government is the guardian of our national healthcare system,” Bergmanis said.

“We’re saying you have the right to enforce it. So, by that, start enforcing it.”

Bergmanis says allowing for-profit health insurance in one province could lead to similar changes elsewhere, including Ontario.

“If it opens up the for-profit health insurance industry in one province, it is inevitable that it will happen in other provinces, and in Ontario is poised to do just that,” he said.

The National Day of Action includes protests in communities across Canada, including several in Ontario.

stories.title: Humane Society London & Middlesex welcomes 12 rescued animals from Northern Ontario wildfires
stories.summary: The Humane Society London & Middlesex has welcomed 12 animals rescued from communities across Northern Ontario.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
The Humane Society London & Middlesex has welcomed 12 animals rescued from communities across Northern Ontario.

The shelter received five puppies, two adult bully-mix dogs and five cats Saturday as part of a collaboration with non-profit pet rescue Northern Reach Network.

The animals were transferred to London over a three-week period.

The five puppies are currently staying in a foster home while they become socialized and adjusted to their new surroundings.

Once they are ready, the puppies will be made available for adoption.

The two adult dogs and five cats are going through the shelter’s intake process, including health assessments, to ensure they are healthy and ready for adoption.

Melanie Paterack, director of community and animal supports at the Humane Society London & Middlesex, says the community will play an important role in helping the animals find new homes.

“This is so meaningful for us, an organization and also for a community, because it’s not just us who are going to help these animals,” Paterack said.

She says the shelter is also looking for people who can foster animals and is asking for donations.

The Humane Society London & Middlesex has a current wish list on its website outlining items the organization needs.

stories.title: ‘Every kid gets a chance to have books,’ Dolly’s Imagination Library in St. Marys looks to create endowment fund
stories.summary: Dolly Parton’s legacy of philanthropy is living on in the town of St. Marys one month, ON book at a time.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Dolly Parton’s legacy of philanthropy is living on in the town of St. Marys one month, one book at a time.

The local chapter of Dolly’s Imagination Library has stepped up its fundraising campaign to create a permanent endowment fund to make sure young children in the community will always have books to read.

“There’s an array of books. There’s lots of different cultural things to read up on. It’s really neat just to see what they come up with every month that we receive. So, it most often would be books that I wouldn’t even think to buy,” said Stephanie Schellenberger, whose son Harrison, almost four, is enrolled in the program.

With International Literacy Day on September 8, the St. Marys chapter of Dolly’s Imagination Library has stepped up its fundraising campaign. Local partner and founder Chantal Lynch says they’re trying to raise the final $54,000 in their goal of creating a $300,000 endowment fund.

“So, we have 300 children every month that are getting age appropriate, selected by professionals, books. And those are gifted to them. So, they go to the post office, they show up in their mailbox, and the book has their name on it the kid’s name. It’s amazing,” said Lynch.

Five-year-old Beau Doucette is also a member. He enjoys reading with his grandmother, Debbie Baker.

“And of course a lot of it is educational, and it gets them prepared for school,” said Baker.

The fundraising campaign had already been underway when Dolly passed, last week. Lynch says it makes their efforts that much more meaningful.

“And it started because her father is illiterate. She understands the struggle that her father had being illiterate. And so it was just fundamental,” said Lynch.

Supported entirely by the local community, the program does not discriminate. It’s available to any child who lives within the St. Marys postal code area.

And in addition to the educational aspect for young Harrison, Schellenberger says that’s part of why she was attracted to the program.

“I think it’s wonderful because not everyone can afford to buy books, and I think that’s kind of the whole point that Dolly Parton started. Every kid gets a chance to have books every month,” she said.

Anyone interested in supporting the campaign can donate through the St. Marys Imagination Library website .

stories.title: Wellington Gateway BRT project enters final phase amid commuter headaches
stories.summary: The ambitious Wellington Gateway Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) project is now entering its final construction phase, marking a significant step towards the completion of the city’s Rapid Transit corridor.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
The ambitious Wellington Gateway Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) project is now entering its final construction phase, marking a significant step towards the completion of the city’s Rapid Transit corridor.

While the promise of enhanced transit, upgraded utilities, and improved infrastructure looms, commuters are bracing for continued disruptions as major work ramps up.

Construction on Phase 2B, the remaining section of Wellington Road between Watson Street and south of Base Line Road East, officially commenced on Monday. This final push involves widening the road, installing two centre-running transit lanes, constructing new transit stations, and undertaking critical replacements of aging underground infrastructure.

Jennie Dann, Construction and Infrastructure Director, highlighted the extensive scope of the subterranean work. “That sewer is large enough for me to walk through and about three stories deep,” Dann explained, referring to the installation of a trunk line sewer. “We’re trying to fix all that while we’re doing the road.”

This comprehensive approach aims to address existing issues, including local flooding, and provide the city with reliable infrastructure for decades to come.

The Wellington Gateway project, a major component of London’s Rapid Transit network, has been a source of frustration for many drivers. The current phase is expected to create further “headaches for commuters,” as the final phase gets underway. However, city staff maintain that the long-term benefits will significantly outweigh the short-term pain.

To mitigate traffic impacts, city officials assure that at least one lane of traffic in each direction will be maintained throughout the construction process, ensuring continued access to businesses and properties. “We will always be maintaining one lane of traffic in each direction... and trying to keep traffic flowing,” Dann stated.

Work in the Wellington and Commissioners area is anticipated to be wrapped up by the summer of 2027. The broader project, however, is extensive. Construction north of Whetter Avenue is slated for 2026 and 2027, with work shifting south towards Base Line Road East by late 2027.

The entire Wellington Gateway project is now projected to continue through 2029, with some final restoration work carrying over into 2030.

Beyond transit and utilities, the project includes incorporating active transit lanes for cyclists and scooter users.

Furthermore, land acquisition has addressed the notorious Wellington Road ‘S’ curve, promising a “much more comfortable curve” for drivers upon completion.

City staff have acknowledged concerns regarding cut-through traffic in residential neighbourhoods and impacts on local businesses, emphasizing ongoing efforts to lessen these effects.

Adjustments to signal timing, such as at Base Line, have already been implemented to improve traffic flow, including for emergency vehicles traveling too and from the London Health Sciences Centre Victoria Campus. It also addresses hospital staff shift changes.

As Wellington Gateway moves into its final stages, other elements of London’s Rapid Transit network are also progressing. Notably, Clark’s Bridge has been widened and completed, now featuring two traffic lanes, dedicated transit lanes, and a new multi-use path for pedestrians and cyclists.

Drivers are advised to follow posted signs and detour routes, exercise caution, allow for extra travel time, and plan ahead as they navigate the ongoing construction zones.

stories.title: Saugeen First Nation elects new chief in Bruce County
stories.summary: Sonya Roote is the new chief of the Saugeen First Nation.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Sonya Roote is the new chief of the Saugeen First Nation.

Roote, a long time councillor, beat out incumbent Conrad Ritchie by a mere 13 votes for the top job.

Roote says she plans to increase transparency and communication between Saugeen First Nation council, and band members, as well as, try to bring Anishinabek Police to the community to provide policing.

Ritchie will remain on Saugeen First Nation council, as one of nine councillors. He’s now one of three former Saugeen chiefs, sitting on Saugeen council.

He congratulated Roote on her victory, following Friday’s vote.

stories.title: Federal government commits $29M to north Calgary water main project
stories.summary: The North Calgary Water Servicing project will deliver 100 million litres of drinking water to northside communities when it's complete in 2029, city officials said Tuesday.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Although it isn’t the water main at the centre of Calgarians’ attention, a major piece of infrastructure for the city’s northern neighbourhoods has received a multi-million dollar boost from the federal government.

Calgary-Confederation Liberal MP and parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Corey Hogan , joined city officials on Tuesday to announce a $29 million contribution to the North Calgary Water Servicing project .

“The ability to turn on a tap and receive drinkable water is a miracle of modern civilization that’s become absolutely mundane, most of the time,” Hogan said.

“But as Calgarians, we unfortunately know too well, it’s not always mundane. It’s mundane until availability and reliability is challenged.

“I’m just so glad that working with the city, we’re able to bring a little more mundane into the lives of Calgarians.”

The federal funding, from the Build Communities Strong Fund, is earmarked for the first stage of the North Calgary Water Servicing project, where shovels got in the ground last fall in northwest Calgary.

11:35 Calgary close-up: Experts say feeder main rupture findings critical to future decision making

The first stage includes the construction of nearly several kilometres of feeder main, as well as upgrades to connect existing facilities such as the Top Hill Reservoir, Big Hill East Reservoir and Mountain View Pump Station.

“That will go into operation next year, providing 30 million additional litres of water to Calgarians from the Bearspaw Water Treatment Plant,” said Michael Thompson, the city’s general manager of infrastructure services.

The project has a total budget of $533 million. The first phase is set to cost $123 million, with $94 million of that coming from city funds.

At full build out, expected in 2029, the north feeder main is slated to run 22 kilometres and include up to 10 support facilities between the treatment plant connecting to the Northridge Feeder Main at 144 Avenue and 14 Street N.W.

According to city officials, the project will deliver 100 million litres of drinking water to north Calgary communities when it’s complete, and that could increase to more than 400 million litres daily once a new water treatment plant is built.

“This is a great first step in delivering increases in infrastructure for Calgarians, to move more water to Calgarians and provide additional redundancy so that if we do have issues, there’s a backup in place that people can rely on,” Thompson said.

2:09 Bearspaw feeder main replacement enters home stretch on schedule, on budget

The reliability of Calgary’s water system has been top of mind for many due to two critical ruptures along the Bearspaw feeder main: a major line that carries 60 per cent of the city’s drinking water.

Fast-tracked construction continues on replacing that feeder main, which is set to be complete by the end of the year.

To help pay for the projects, city council approved a $609.5 million increase to the upcoming budget, as well an expansion of the city’s borrowing capacity by more than $500 million to help cover the water infrastructure projects.

City officials said at the time the move will result in a 14-per cent rate increase in 2027, or an additional $17 monthly.

1:49 Calgary city council approves $609M for feeder main, water system upgrades

Calgary mayor Jeromy Farkas said Tuesday’s announcement marks a key step in improving the city’s water infrastructure, but noted more collaboration would be required with other orders of government to pay for it.

“We’re going to continue making the case for not just Alberta’s fair share of funding from the federal government but also Calgary’s fair share of investment from the provincial government,” Farkas told reporters.

City officials noted temporary outdoor water restrictions may be required starting Sept. 15 related to the North Calgary Water Servicing Project, but that will be dependent on weather conditions and water demand.

A final decision is expected to be announced next week.
