stories.title: Calandra’s comments spark confusion over Ontario’s new high school attendance rules
stories.summary: Ontario Principals’ Council says it lacks clarity on which absences can be excused after the minister’s latest comments
stories.author: Dave McGinn, Laura Stone
stories.content:
As the school year begins in Ontario , a new policy linking high school students’ attendance to grades has been thrown into confusion for principals across the province following comments made by Education Minister Paul Calandra on Tuesday.

Starting this school year, attendance and participation will count for 15 per cent of the final mark for students in Grades 9 and 10, and 10 per cent for those in Grades 11 and 12.

The government announced the change in April , as part of an effort to tackle high absentee rates .

Many parents wondered what the new policy would mean for their children’s grades in cases in which they need to take them out of class for sports or for other reasons.

In an interview with The Globe and Mail in June, Mr. Calandra said those parents have nothing to worry about. Students who are absent from school because of hockey tournaments, other extracurricular activities or even family vacations will not see their grades docked so long as parents notify the school, he said.

At a press conference in Hamilton on Tuesday, when asked by The Globe about the new policy, Mr. Calandra said: “Look, parents still have the ability to excuse their children. They’ll have to inform the school, the principal, that it is their intention to excuse their child.”

But in a follow-up answer, the minister seemed to suggest that the decision as to which absences count as excused or not will rest on principals’ discretion.

This came as a surprise to the Ontario Principals’ Council, which was not consulted on any parts of the policy, said president Amy Johnson.

“It starts the school year with uncertainty and instability,” she said on Tuesday. Some school boards’ classes started today. High school started today. So on the course outlines going out today, if anyone who watched the news was like, ‘So how does the attendance thing work?’ people don’t know, or else they’re answering in a vacuum. Certainly, as an organization, we haven’t gotten enough clarity ourselves to put something out to all of our members at this point.”

Mr. Calandra’s office did not respond to a request from The Globe on Tuesday when asked to clarify his remarks.

Principals will almost always allow students to participate in sports or go on family vacations without penalty, Ms. Johnson said.

“We do that as a matter of course,” she said.

“The problem now is that we don’t have clarity on all of the answers to the complex other ways that attendance plays out in schools,” she added. “We’re asking those questions right now of the ministry because all of those haven’t been spelled out in the policy.”

Leaving these decisions to the discretion of principals without more clarity will not only add to principals’ workload but create more conflict between parents and administrators, said Kelly Gallagher-Mackay, an associate professor at Wilfrid Laurier University and the co-director of the Annual Canadian School Survey, a national initiative launched by People for Education and the Centre for Leading Research in Education.

This year’s inaugural survey of more than 450 principals across the country found only one-quarter said they had never had in-person interactions with parents or guardians that involved physical violence, threats or intimidation.

More than a third of principals reported being the subject of, or receiving, threatening or intimidating messages from parents or guardians by phone, e-mail or social media at least once or twice a month.

“The potential for that to flare up is for sure there,” Ms. Johnson said. “Principals, the vice-principals, we’re there to support students and their families, not be distracted by, frankly, arguing with them or delivering bad news that we hadn’t had clarity on in the first place.”

The policy is intended to target students who aren’t in class because they are “just deciding not to go to school,” Mr. Calandra said in June.

Attendance rates in the province are so poor that something had to be done to get students back at their desks on a more regular basis, he added. In previous years, attendance did not factor into grades.

The government expects students to be at school 90 per cent of the time, otherwise they are considered to be chronically absent.

However, only about a quarter of Grade 12 students and less than 34 per cent of those in Grade 11 are meeting the threshold of 90-per-cent attendance. Among students in Grades 9 and 10, 43 and 36 per cent, respectively, are meeting it.

At a press conference in Hamilton on Tuesday, when asked by The Globe about the new policy, Mr. Calandra said: “Look, parents still have the ability to excuse their children. They’ll have to inform the school, the principal, that it is their intention to excuse their child.”
But in a follow-up answer, the minister seemed to suggest that the decision as to which absences count as excused or not will rest on principals’ discretion.
This came as a surprise to the Ontario Principals’ Council, which was not consulted on any parts of the policy, said president Amy Johnson.

“It starts the school year with uncertainty and instability,” she said on Tuesday. Some school boards’ classes started today. High school started today. So on the course outlines going out today, if anyone who watched the news was like, ‘So how does the attendance thing work?’ people don’t know, or else they’re answering in a vacuum. Certainly, as an organization, we haven’t gotten enough clarity ourselves to put something out to all of our members at this point.”
Mr. Calandra’s office did not respond to a request from The Globe on Tuesday when asked to clarify his remarks.
Principals will almost always allow students to participate in sports or go on family vacations without penalty, Ms. Johnson said.
“We do that as a matter of course,” she said.

“The problem now is that we don’t have clarity on all of the answers to the complex other ways that attendance plays out in schools,” she added. “We’re asking those questions right now of the ministry because all of those haven’t been spelled out in the policy.”

Leaving these decisions to the discretion of principals without more clarity will not only add to principals’ workload but create more conflict between parents and administrators, said Kelly Gallagher-Mackay, an associate professor at Wilfrid Laurier University and the co-director of the Annual Canadian School Survey, a national initiative launched by People for Education and the Centre for Leading Research in Education.

This year’s inaugural survey of more than 450 principals across the country found only one-quarter said they had never had in-person interactions with parents or guardians that involved physical violence, threats or intimidation.

More than a third of principals reported being the subject of, or receiving, threatening or intimidating messages from parents or guardians by phone, e-mail or social media at least once or twice a month.

“The potential for that to flare up is for sure there,” Ms. Johnson said. “Principals, the vice-principals, we’re there to support students and their families, not be distracted by, frankly, arguing with them or delivering bad news that we hadn’t had clarity on in the first place.”
The policy is intended to target students who aren’t in class because they are “just deciding not to go to school,” Mr. Calandra said in June.

Attendance rates in the province are so poor that something had to be done to get students back at their desks on a more regular basis, he added. In previous years, attendance did not factor into grades.
The government expects students to be at school 90 per cent of the time, otherwise they are considered to be chronically absent.

However, only about a quarter of Grade 12 students and less than 34 per cent of those in Grade 11 are meeting the threshold of 90-per-cent attendance. Among students in Grades 9 and 10, 43 and 36 per cent, respectively, are meeting it.

stories.title: RCMP ask to meet ex-B.C. Conservative who says he was offered job to quit as MLA
stories.summary: B.C. legislator Ian Paton says he expects the RCMP to ask about allegedly being offered a job to give up his seat so Conservative Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay could run.
stories.author: Ashley Joannou The Canadian Press
stories.content:
British Columbia legislator Ian Paton said RCMP have asked to interview him on Wednesday, and expects them to ask about allegedly being offered a job to give up his seat so Conservative Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay could run.

Paton, who quit the Conservative caucus last week among an exodus of MLAs from the official Opposition, said Findlay’s chief of staff Chris Delaney asked him in July to step down in Delta South, saying he would be given a job as an adviser for two years with the same salary as an MLA.

stories.title: Bluewater Golf Course reopens days after devastating fire
stories.summary: Golfers were back on the course, just days after a devastating fire destroyed the Bluewater Golf Course’s clubhouse, near Bayfield.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Golfers were back on the course, just days after a devastating fire destroyed the Bluewater Golf Course’s clubhouse, near Bayfield.

The fire broke out last Wednesday, Aug. 26, around 8 p.m., near where the electric golf carts were being stored.

No one was injured in the blaze, but the clubhouse was destroyed.

Undeterred, Bluewater Golf Course owners, reopened the 9 hole course this morning.

They thanked first responders, and their staff, for allowing them to get the course re-opened, with no other damage reported to the course, or neighbouring trailers.

stories.title: Canada, U.S. remain close on military front despite rising political tensions, top soldier says
stories.summary: Military leadership was friendly at Indo-Pacific conference in Victoria, B.C., this week co-hosted by U.S. and Canada
stories.author: Pippa Norman
stories.content:
Canada’s military relationship with the United States remains unchanged despite the collapse of trade talks and escalating tension at a political level, the country’s top soldier says.

At a conference of the chiefs of defence for the Indo-Pacific held in Victoria, B.C., this week, General Jennie Carignan said Canada’s military collaboration with the U.S. remains strong, ensuring the two countries can continue to work together to defend key regions, including the Indo-Pacific. Her comments were echoed by her U.S. counterparts.

“The chiefs of defence, our job is to translate political objectives into military effects. We both do this with our government, and we constantly meet to align our work and collaborate,” Gen. Carignan, who has served as Canada’s Chief of the Defence Staff for two years, told The Globe and Mail in an interview on Monday.

She added that Canada’s fighter jet contract with American company Lockheed Martin and Canada’s role in the U.S.’s Golden Dome missile defence system are a “different conversation” than the one the country is having with the Trump administration about trade, despite media reports saying U.S. officials pressed Canada on these topics as part of negotiations.

The conference in Victoria is being held over three days, ending Wednesday, with 29 countries in attendance. It’s an annual event that rotates locations across the Indo-Pacific and was last held in Canada in 2017. Back then, the discussion centred around countering violent extremism and peacekeeping operations.

As a U.S. Pacific Command event, the country is always one of two co-hosts. This year, its organizing partner is Canada.

It’s a timely collaboration given that the relationship between Canada and the U.S. at a political level is on thin ice, with barbs being thrown back and forth by politicians on both sides since trade negotiations broke down last month. Most recently, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy claimed Canada has no military, U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent cracked a joke about the country’s ability to respond to threats and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posted a controversial remark about the Canadian cadet program to social media.

While speaking to reporters at a press conference on Tuesday, Defence Minister David McGuinty called Mr. Hegseth’s post, which mocked two cadets, “below the dignity of the office.”

Yet, in the military-to-military conversations happening in Victoria this week, it was impossible to count on ten fingers the number of times words such as “collaboration,” “partner,” or “interoperability” have been uttered by Canadian and American senior military officials in their public remarks.

Gen. Carignan’s friendly tone when speaking about her U.S. counterparts was matched by General Dan Caine, chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, and Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of the U.S. Pacific Command, while addressing the sea of uniforms in attendance at the conference.

Gen. Caine called for a “round of applause for Canada” before going on to emphasize the importance of interoperability between each country’s militaries and for the Indo-Pacific nations in the room to build up their own military might.

“We owe it to our citizens to invest in our own capabilities to protect our sovereignty and our interests as they intersect around the globe,” he said. “That type of strength is built on interoperability and integration, and yielded through great partnerships. Our forces must be interoperable.”

Adm. Paparo thanked his Canadian counterparts for their leadership and hospitality, before speaking about the importance of operating together to “compound” deterrence.

Gen. Carignan and Adm. Paparo are scheduled to hold a joint press conference with reporters Wednesday morning, on the last day of the conference. The U.S. delegation declined individual interview requests with reporters attending the conference.

The two co-host delegations were seated side by side in the conference’s main ballroom inside the Fairmont Empress hotel on Tuesday, presenting a united front before the other delegates. Mr. McGuinty sat among them before his own opening remarks, which he began by acknowledging his U.S. counterparts, adding to the abundance of pleasantries.

Gen. Carignan told the crowd on Tuesday that Canada and the U.S. have “a lot in common” in terms of their activities and posture in the Indo-Pacific.

“Canada, as a maritime nation, is surrounded on three sides by ocean and has the longest coastline in the world. And on the fourth side of our border, we share with our longtime ally, the United States,” she said.

For now, Canada’s operational and strategic relationship with the U.S. seems distant from that of its faltering political relationship.

Mr. McGuinty told reporters he thinks Canadians “understand the difference between the performative nature of an administration in the United States and the importance of the military-to-military co-operation, which continues.”

stories.title: B.C. government overstates gas revenue forecasts by $1.46-billion due to errors
stories.summary: Administrative errors should be corrected in province’s quarterly fiscal report, officials say
stories.author: Brenna Owen
stories.content:
Errors including botched currency conversions led the British Columbia government to overstate its forecasted natural gas revenues by about $1.46-billion over five fiscal years, officials confirmed on Tuesday.

Energy Minister Adrian Dix said the most significant error, a 44-cent overstatement in the forecasted per-gigajoule price of natural gas this fiscal year, was a “serious mistake.”

But he said the errors affect the province’s forecasting, not its actual revenues, which can vary in a given year. Price fluctuations, including the spike and subsequent decline linked to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, have led the province to both underestimate and overestimate its revenues over the years, Dix said.

“That part is a normal part. What isn’t a part of it is human error that we’re acknowledging today and correcting in the budget,” he told reporters in Vancouver.

Senior staff with the ministries of energy and finance told a technical briefing earlier Tuesday that the errors had been independently verified and corrections would be included in the province’s quarterly fiscal report expected later this month.

The briefing heard the impact on B.C.’s deficit – last pegged at $7.7-billion for fiscal year 2025-2026 – would be made clear with the release of that report.

The most substantial of the errors made by Energy Ministry staff related to U.S.-Canadian dollar conversions, when a formula was incorrectly applied across a spreadsheet.

The province’s forecasting is based on private-sector estimates of natural gas prices, which are provided in Canadian or U.S. dollars.

Dix said the error involved an incorrect assumption that figures were shown in U.S. dollars, when in fact they were Canadian dollars. The numbers were “again translated into Canadian dollars, leading to an overstatement of revenue,” he said.

The briefing heard correcting that error resulted in a price decrease of 44 cents per gigajoule of natural gas in B.C.’s forecasting for 2026-2027.

Budget 2026 shows incorrect forecasted prices per gigajoule ranging from $2.34 to $4.83 at plant inlet, referring to gas that hasn’t yet been processed.

“We’re making changes to the way the process happens to ensure that such errors do not occur in the future,” Dix said.

The Opposition B.C. Conservatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but last week, their finance critic Gavin Dew called for the auditor general to examine the flawed revenue forecasts, after they were originally reported by Business in Vancouver.

“This isn’t just an accounting error. It’s a credibility problem,” Dew said in a statement, while Opposition Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay said B.C. could not afford budgets “built on wishful thinking.”

The information in Tuesday’s technical briefing was provided on background, meaning it was not for attribution to an individual.

A second error involving the conversion of energy units amounted to a five-cent decrease in the forecasted price.

Two other errors stemming from the use of data from 2025 instead of this year’s figures resulted in a decrease in the plant inlet price of 1 cent per gigajoule, while adding three cents to the outlet price.

Combined, correcting the errors amounted to an average annual decrease in expected revenues of $292-million from this fiscal year to the one starting in 2030.

The impact for the current fiscal year is $306-million, reducing forecasted revenue by about 24 per cent, from $1.297-billion to $991-million.

The Energy Ministry is working with experts to improve its quality assurance process in forecasting moving forward, staff told the briefing.

The briefing heard Treaty 8 First Nations in northeastern B.C. had alerted government officials to what they believed to be an error in the province’s accounting of processing and transportation costs for natural gas in June.

Staff said the province reviewed its calculations and confirmed those costs were appropriately incorporated into its forecasting, but in July uncovered the series of errors related to the conversion of currency units of natural gas.

The errors come as the province works on an updated framework for collecting natural gas royalties that’s set to come into force on Jan. 1, with the goal of returning 50 per cent of profits after accounting for companies’ production costs.

Staff at the briefing acknowledged concerns among Treaty 8 First Nations that the framework won’t hit that target and said further information would be available this fall.

Dix said officials were confident they were “on the right track.”

He said the goal was to establish a new royalty framework that’s “fair for the taxpayers and the owners of the resources,” including First Nations.

It must also strike a balance with the industry, he said.

“We have to make sure (there’s) a good return for the people so that we can help pay for things that are really important to me, like health care and education, on the one hand, and you’ve got to ensure that we have an industry that’s in the province.”

stories.title: Encampment cleared at downtown gateway. But where do the people go now?
stories.summary: Advocates say a lack of daytime spaces and full shelters leaves people with few options when encampments are cleared.
stories.author: Norman De Bono
stories.content:
The city of London and social agencies are locked in an ongoing “chess match” that sees homeless people evicted from one encampment only to relocate elsewhere and eventually cycle through the same sites, the director of London Cares says.

There are few places for homeless people to go during the day, leaving them trapped in a cycle of moving tents and tarps, said Chris Moss, executive director of the agency that works to get people off the street and into housing.

“It comes and goes, police and city bylaw officers move people from block to block. There’s no getting ahead of it anymore,” she said. “It’s a chess match. There’s no space they can go where they’re not kicked out. There’s nowhere for them to go.”

Tuesday, the city moved to clear an encampment at the northwest corner of Horton and Wellington streets, a gateway to downtown. About 20 people were staying in several makeshift shelters, including tents and tarps. They were given notice Monday to leave the site, and London police officers were among those clearing the location Tuesday, city officials said.

“The co-ordinated informed response (CIR) team monitors the area daily to conduct outreach and cleanup. The team continues to address concerns in the area as they arise,” Paul Ladouceur, the city’s director of emergency management and security services, said in an email response to Free Press questions.

The street corner is near the Salvation Army Centre of Hope. The centre works closely with the response team, and when it requests enforcement, the team responds, Ladouceur added.

That intersection saw a similar encampment a few weeks ago that moved to a site near Beal secondary school, Moss said. Another area on Bathurst Street has also seen encampments established.

Drug-possession clause pulled from shelter guidelines after heated debate

London homeless agency faces 'precarious' spot amid stalled federal cash

Advertisement 1Story continues below

The city tracks homelessness in London, and there are now more than 2,200 homeless people and 34 encampments in the city, Moss said.

“At any one time there are several hundred on the street,” Moss said. “Homelessness and drug use is bad and it’s getting worse.”

Ward 13 Coun. David Ferreira, who represents downtown, agreed the movement of encampments and lack of resources for homeless people remain ongoing issues.

“We don’t have enough space and we have to open more spaces to get people off the street,” he said. “I’m not happy about the fact we move people around.”

Ferreira said he argued at a recent city council meeting for a citywide search for more spaces for homeless people to ease pressure on the core, but did not get support. “I want the entire city to realize it’s not a downtown or Old East issue. It’s a city of London issue.”

Sarah Campbell, executive director of Ark Aid Mission that provides shelter and other supports to homeless people, said the city works with London police to tell people at encampments they have to move but can’t tell them where to go.

“We move people along often and the problem is there’s no place for people to go. It’s getting worse,” she said. “There are fewer services and people don’t have access to resources. We don’t know where to send people. The shelters are full.”

stories.title: ‘Cruel’: Legal community questions N.S. move to exclude tents from higher income assistance
stories.summary: Members of Halifax's legal community are reacting after the provincial government prevented people living in tents from accessing higher income assistance.
stories.author: Mitchell Bailey, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Members of Halifax’s legal community are reacting after the provincial government prevented people living in tents from accessing higher income assistance benefits.

Human rights lawyer Vince Calderhead has been fighting for years to secure better income supports for people living in tents. On Aug. 5, he saw his position validated by the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal, which ruled tents count as a legal accommodation.

However, two weeks later, the province changed the criteria for income assistance , which effectively cancelled out the court ruling.

“By choosing the option of rewriting the law to overturn that decision, they’ve effectively forced people back onto that $400 a month rate,” said Calderhead.

2:08 Ruling in NS homelessness case sets precedent for people who live in tents

The courts overturned a decision that Bradley Lowe, who died in 2023, didn’t qualify for additional “accommodation” support because he lived in a tent.

Calderhead says that legal recognition of a tent as an “accommodation” would have seen those sleeping rough earn at least $300 more per month.

Nova Scotia revised its income assistance legislation to exclude tents on Aug. 25. The changes repealed the definition of a “home” and limited it to residential units with a kitchen and bathroom or spaces like municipally-approved rooming homes.

“For the province to have a broad income assistance program and then say, ‘By the way, we’re excluding a certain category of people.’ That doesn’t smell right,” said Calderhead.

He says his legal team is reviewing whether the province is discriminating against people based on their housing situations.

After the court ruling, Dalhousie Legal Aid began helping people in tent encampments apply for the enhanced rate, only for them to be disqualified two weeks later.

“The effect of the changes to the regulations are to lower the benefits to which unhoused people are entitled,” said Mark Culligan, a Dalhousie Legal Aid worker.

He says he disagrees with the argument that people living in a rental unit have higher expenses than those in a tent.

“They need to buy food. If they can’t store the food, that means they have to buy more fresh food or more packaged food. It means higher food costs. It means you can’t buy in bulk,” he said.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the province said that the “Court interpreted the regulations as they were written at the time and identified that some language could be clearer, including how accommodation was described.”

“While previous decisions had supported the department’s interpretation of the regulations, the Court of Appeal reached a different conclusion, highlighting the need for greater clarity,” the statement read.

“These amendments provide clearer direction on how different living situations are considered when determining eligibility for income assistance rates, so the program can be administered consistently and transparently across the province.”

The province says the amendments do not change who is eligible for income assistance and that people experiencing homelessness “will continue to be able to access income assistance and other supports for which they qualify.”

As for Calderhead, he’s calling the decision “cruel.”

“The province decided to go low on this rather than take the high road and ensuring that that group of people in need were treated with respect and dignity,” he said.

stories.title: Advocates say gender-based violence still overlooked in N.S. mass shooting response
stories.summary: The chair of the monitoring committee said 30 recommendations still need to be addressed. Advocates say more needs to be done to deal with the culture of gender-based violence.
stories.author: Angela Capobianco, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
The final progress monitoring report on the implementation of recommendations from the inquiry into the 2020 Nova Scotia mass shooting included gender-based and intimate partner violence for the first time.

The chair of the independent committee, Myra Freeman, said Monday that the province is in better shape than in 2020, but some say more needs to be done to address the culture of violence.

“Whether people like it or not, we have to note that the findings found that this all sparked off because of an incident of intimate partner violence, which was a massive red flag,” said Liz Leclair, an advocate who speaks out against gender-based violence.

“It rarely gets mentioned.”

The April 2020 attacks began in Portapique, N.S., when the shooter, Gabriel Wortman, assaulted his partner, Lisa Banfield.

In total, 22 people were killed during a 13-hour rampage that included multiple shootings and fires. Wortman was ultimately shot and killed by RCMP.

2:29 Final report from committee tracking Nova Scotia mass shooting recommendations released

The final report released Monday highlights that of the 130 recommendations released in 2023, 40 still require “significant work.”

Freeman noted that gender-based violence was one of those areas.

“We know that change takes time and government cannot address gender-based violence, intimate partner … violence by themselves,” she said.

Freeman added that the epidemic requires large-scale societal change, however, Leclair says she doesn’t see enough being done.

“The patterns I continue to see coming out of the premier’s office and the cabinet and caucus of the government do not in any way, shape or form indicate to me that they take this as seriously as they should,” said Leclair.

Kristina Fifield, a trauma therapist who sat on the most recent monitoring committee, agrees that not much has changed since 2020.

“Survivors are continuing to experience harm and system-induced trauma and systemic injustices and being failed or not believed when they’re trying to get support or when they’re seeking justice,” she said.

Premier Tim Houston issued a statement Monday, asserting the province’s commitment.

“We must break down barriers and improve safety and resilience in our communities,” he wrote in part.

“We must continue to work together to realize the significant and systemic change that is required to address complex and interconnected issues facing our society.”

But Leclair says in order to see significant change, front-line organizations need sustainable core funding.

“I think stabilized core funding would allow a lot of these organizations to work on really significant systems-level change pieces and do the advocacy work they need instead of having to constantly be writing grants or chasing down more funding,” she said.

stories.title: Alberta's Smith says Tennessee trip isn't sending wrong message during trade war
stories.summary: Smith said the Tennessee capital made changes 25 years ago to make itself a music industry haven and economic powerhouse and that she wants to find out how.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith denied suggestions Tuesday that her upcoming trip to Tennessee could be sending the wrong message amid a trade war between Canada and its southern neighbour.

“I hope no one’s surprised to hear that I believe it’s my job to continue reaching out at all levels to various influencers in the United States and get our message across that we have an incredible partnership,” Smith told reporters at an unrelated news conference in Calgary.

stories.title: U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra among dignitaries visiting Newfoundland for 25th anniversary of 9/11
stories.summary: Gander has held commemoration event every year since hosting thousands of stranded travellers after terrorist attacks in 2001
stories.author: Devin Stevens
stories.content:
U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra will be among the dignitaries heading to central Newfoundland this month to mark the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

The community of Gander has held a commemoration event every year since hosting thousands of stranded travellers after officials closed U.S. airspace and ground dozens of planes, said mayor Percy Farwell.

He said the event is about commemorating the nearly 3,000 people who were killed when hijackers slammed planes into the World Trade Center in New York and crashed into The Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

“We also acknowledge the connection that transpired with our little neck of the woods here and how meaningful that turned out to be,” Farwell said Tuesday.

“(We were) responding to people that were in distress and needed a lot of life’s necessities like food and shelter. Mostly they needed love and compassion because it was a very distressing time.”

The town of about 9,500 people became forever linked to the 9/11 attacks when its airport took in 38 passenger planes carrying more than 6,500 travellers. The people of Gander rallied around what they called the “plane people,” converting schools and church halls into shelters and taking many travellers into their own homes while providing food, hot showers and more. The outpouring of support was recounted in the hit stage musical “Come From Away.”

Cory Abbott, marketing manager for Steele Hotels, which operates four properties in Gander, says the town is pretty much booked solid for the commemoration.

“We’ve been blocked-in there for a fair bit,” Abbott said in an interview Tuesday. “We did have some (rooms) available … but it’s really filled in, in the last month or so.”

Dignitaries expected at the commemoration include Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour, former prime minister Jean Chrétien, Premier Tony Wakeham, Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson and Hoekstra.

Hoekstra has caused controversy by criticizing the “elbows up” campaign against U.S. tariffs and by expressing irritation with Canadians’ response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s rhetoric about making the country the 51st state. Tens of thousands of Canadians have signed a petition asking the federal government to kick Hoekstra out of the country and request his removal as ambassador.

In a statement, Hoekstra said the 9/11 attacks left a lasting mark on him and the United States, with the people of Newfoundland showing what community really means during a dark time.

“On this 25th anniversary, I am returning to say a heartfelt thank you not just on behalf of those who were stranded, but for an entire nation that remains moved by Gander’s generosity. I look forward to meeting many of those who opened their hearts and homes and honouring the enduring bond built that week,” the ambassador said.

Farwell said there’s no question that it’s a delicate time in the Canada-U.S. relationship, but the events in Gander 25 years ago are outside the realm of trade policy and politics.

“The humanity of what happened here, I think that rises above the political discussions and all the other sabre rattling,” he said. “Hopefully this is a bit bigger than all that.”

Farwell said the town holds an event every Sept. 10 to share stories that have not yet been featured in books, films or other media. This year’s list of speakers include David Collenette, who was Canada’s minister of transportation in 2001 and helped oversee Operation Yellow Ribbon, Canada’s emergency response to help safely land 200 diverted aircraft and care for the people on board.

Gander’s arena will host the formal ceremony on Sept. 11 with speeches by dignitaries and musical performances by Newfoundland artists including the Ennis Sisters and Great Big Sea’s Alan Doyle. The facility can usually accommodate 2,000 people, but Farwell said he wouldn’t be surprised if 2,500 crammed in.

An invite-only performance of “Come From Away” for dignitaries is also planned.

Farwell said the community was nervous at first about people writing a musical about “what we described as a bunch of people making sandwiches,” but is proud of the role Gander played.

He said he is sometimes contacted by U.S. students on Zoom who weren’t alive at the time, looking to learn about what happened.

“I think Canadians, and Atlantic Canadians and Newfoundlanders, the more isolated you get, the more dependent on each other, historically, we have been,” he said.

“So we tend to understand that (if) someone’s got a problem, it’s everybody’s job to help them fix it. And so that’s certainly true of our culture here.”

stories.title: U.S. senator says Democrats will have a tough time curtailing Trump’s tariff policy
stories.summary: Democrats are hopeful that they will have good results during the Nov. 3 midterm elections, amid Trump’s low approval ratings.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – U.S. Senator from Arizona Ruben Gallego tempered expectations around the prospect of Democrats gaining a majority in the House of Representatives and the Senate and using that power to curtail U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canada.

“I do think they’ll use their power,” said Gallego, during a press conference at the U.S. embassy in Ottawa on Tuesday. “The question is, do you have enough to overcome vetoes and things of that nature.”

Democrats are hopeful that they will have good results during the Nov. 3 midterm elections, amid Trump’s low approval ratings.

Gallego, who was in Ottawa visiting with embassy staff and Canadian politicians to discuss the ongoing trade dispute, said Congress and the Senate have historically given up too much of their power to the president when it comes to trade policy.

Trump has applied most of his tariffs through executive action. The tariffs he enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (Ieepa) were struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court in February, but the president has since found other pieces of legislation to apply more levies on goods from other countries.

The president also has the power to veto legislation.

“There’s going to be a strong incentive for Democrats to actually engage on oversight when it comes to tariffs,” said Gallego. “The…number one reason why is because by the Constitution, it’s the Senate and Congress in general that actually has tariff policy.”

Canada walked away from a potential interim trade deal with the U.S. on Aug. 21, after weeks of negotiations between Canadian and American officials.

The potential deal would have provided tariff relief on Section 232 levies on Canadian autos, steel and aluminum, as well as the avoidance of a 50 per-cent tariff under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which applies to $28 billion worth of Canadian goods. In exchange, Canada would have ended its moratoriums on U.S. alcohol in several provinces and dropped tariffs on American autos.

Prime Minister Mark Carney ultimately decided to hit pause on negotiations, citing several last-minute demands on the U.S. side that made the deal untenable.

Canada has now threatened dollar-for-dollars tariffs on U.S. goods, which are set to take effect Sept. 8, in response to the Section 338 tariffs.

The prospect of Canada gaining tariff-free access to the American market remains in question for the time being.

Last week, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is a Democrat hopeful for the presidency in 2028, told CTV News he could not guarantee the complete removal of tariffs.

Gallego said he could not clarify what Newsom meant in terms of his comments, but said it should be his party’s goal to remove tariffs.

“I think the anybody who is running for president should be very clear,” he said. “It should be the goal of a Democratic president to remove these tariffs, 100 per cent.”

Senate Democratic Leader Senator from New York Chuck Schumer also intends to introduce a bill to strike down the Section 338 on Canadian goods and the Section 301 tariffs introduced under the Trade Act of 1974 that targets forced labour in supply chains. Schumer cited the growing cost of living crisis among American consumers as the reason for the legislation.

The bill is not expected to pass the Republican-controlled Congress and does not address Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum.

stories.title: Canadian lotteries say new prediction market restrictions don’t go far enough
stories.summary: Group argues new rules for investment platforms still allow trades that are more akin to bets
stories.author: Meera Raman
stories.content:
Canadian lottery corporations say new restrictions on prediction markets don’t go far enough, arguing that some of the trades Canadians can still make through investment platforms function more like bets than investments.

Last week, the Canadian Securities Administrators, an umbrella organization of provincial and territorial securities regulators, and the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, or CIRO, said in a joint statement that prediction contracts tied to sports and entertainment should not be regulated as securities or derivatives, keeping them off platforms operated by regulated investment dealers. Contracts tied to certain economic, financial and environmental outcomes, however, can still be offered.

While the guidance brings some clarity to the debate over whether prediction contracts should be regulated by securities regulators or gaming commissions, the Canadian Lottery Coalition, which represents gaming and lottery organizations in seven provinces, says the bigger question of where investing ends and gambling begins remains unresolved.

The group has registered to lobby provincial officials over prediction markets, arguing that prediction contracts still available to Canadian investors can function like gambling and should face stronger consumer protections and regulatory safeguards, warning that the products could otherwise divert revenue from provincially regulated channels.

“We appreciate the further clarity, but I just feel like it’s too far to say that it’s a line in the sand,” said Molly Cormier, executive director of the Canadian Lottery Coalition. “The time to act is now before they expand further in Canada.”

The organization represents publicly owned lottery and gaming corporations in British Columbia, Manitoba, Quebec, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Nova Scotia.

Prediction markets allow people to wager on real-world events. Two companies have received CIRO approval to provide Canadians with access to certain event contracts: Wealthsimple Inc., which partnered with U.S. prediction-market operator Kalshi , and Interactive Brokers Group Inc.

Those approvals are restricted to prediction contracts based on economic, financial, or climate-related events, and does not allow contracts for sports results or elections.

“CSA members have consulted a wide range of stakeholders over the past several months, including local gaming regulators, and intend to continue to do so in the future as assessments in this area continue,” said Ilana Kelemen, a spokesperson for the CSA, in a statement.

Certain event contracts “are regulated as options contracts and are subject to the same regulatory oversight as all other listed options offered by CIRO dealer members,” said Ariel Visconti, a spokesperson for CIRO, in a statement. CIRO is a self-regulatory organization that oversees all investment dealers and mutual fund dealers, as well as all trading activity on Canada’s debt and equity marketplaces.

Canada’s provincial gambling systems generate revenue that flows back to governments to support public services. The Lottery Coalition is concerned that, as prediction markets grow, some spending that would otherwise take place through provincially regulated gambling could migrate to products offered outside those systems.

Ron Segev, a partner at law firm Segev LLP who specializes in betting, said prediction markets do raise gambling-related regulatory questions, but he is skeptical that they pose a major competitive threat to traditional lottery products.

The lottery “is a completely different beast,” Mr. Segev said. “I don’t know that it would necessarily cannibalize the lottery business.”

Prediction markets may compete more directly with forms of gambling such as sports betting, he said, where customers believe their knowledge or analysis can give them an advantage in predicting an outcome.

Ms. Cormier said provincial lottery corporations have historically adapted their offerings as gambling habits and technology have changed. While she is not aware of any member currently planning to launch its own prediction-market product, she said they could consider new products that fit within their existing regulatory frameworks.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that sports and entertainment contracts fall outside the 2017 binary-options ban. This version has been updated to remove that reference.

stories.title: Indigenous involvement, Canadian materials required in restoration of 24 Sussex Drive: Ottawa
stories.summary: Public Services and Procurement Canada issued a request for qualifications for companies interested in restoring 24 Sussex Drive.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
In its search for a “world class design vision” to restore the official prime minister’s residence at 24 Sussex Drive in Ottawa, the federal government is prioritizing the use of Canadian materials and mandating Indigenous involvement in the multi-million-dollar project.

Last month, Public Services and Procurement Canada published its request for qualification (RFQ), the first of two stages in its design-building competition for the historic home’s rehabilitation.

The largely technical, 97-page document “defines the requirements for the qualification of respondents,” sets a “basis for selection,” and breaks down the scoring system that’ll be used to create a list of up to seven firms that will be invited to partake in stage two and submit a formal request for proposal, which is expected to be issued this winter.

The RFQ deadline is Sept. 22 at 2 p.m.

A successful bidder will be awarded in fall 2027, which is later than the July 1 date Prime Minister Mark Carney set when announcing the non-partisan fundraising campaign led by the Rideau Hall Foundation to fund the project.

“The time period between the announcement of the winning proposal and the estimated contract award of Fall 2027 is reserved for any final negotiations that May be required between Canada and the winning team,” Pspc told National Post in an email.

“Given its national and historical significance, the rehabilitated residence must be completed by Canadians for Canadians,” reads the RFQ, issued on Aug. 21.

“In that spirit, the use of Canadian materials and innovations must be considered and incorporated throughout the project.”

Companies need not be Canadian to meet the mandatory requirement of being considered a “Canadian supplier,” but they must have a place of business and office in Canada, where they are registered and pay taxes, and employ Canadians or conduct “day-to-day business activities in Canada.”

It also means they “will not subcontract work to non-Canadian suppliers or individuals located outside Canada, in a manner that results in minimal value-added activities being performed within Canada.”

Respondents must also submit an “Indigenous Participation Plan (IPP)” that ensures at least five per cent of project work is carried out by Indigenous businesses and people. Public Services and Procurement Canada said any IPP commitments made in the RFP stage “will become deliverables in the resulting contract, subject to regular progress monitoring and reporting (and potentially other measures).”

Sussex Drive, along with the rest of Parliament Hill, is the ancestral territory of the Anishinabe Algonquin Nation, with which Pspc said “engagements have been undertaken” and will be reflected in the RFP and “inform the site’s design.”

As for the design, the RFQ offers little in the way of new details about the work that’s needed to repair and modernize the more than 160-year-old house that became the official prime minister’s residence in 1950 — the last time it had “a comprehensive rehabilitation.”

“The project shall provide a secure, dignified, functional, and adaptable environment that supports residential, official, ceremonial, and administrative functions while meeting current codes, standards, and operational requirements,” it notes.

The successful bidder’s “work will include the modernization of building systems, upgrades to meet applicable codes and standards, and the integration of security, sustainability and accessibility requirements.”

The 35-room, 12,000-square-foot home has been vacant since 2015 when prime minister Stephen Harper left office. His successor, Justin Trudeau, lived there as a child when his father was prime minister but opted to move his own family to Rideau Cottage, across the street on the grounds of the Governor General’s residence at Rideau Hall. Carney and his family followed suit when he was elected last year.

The National Capital Commission decommissioned the site in 2022.

The RFQ also doesn’t indicate any construction budget, with Pspc noting it will show up in the RFP. Earlier this year, architects interviewed by National Post estimated that, depending on specifications, the bill for this type of major project could be anywhere between $40 million and $100 million.

That figure tracks with a requirement for prospective designers to submit a completed “complex building project” worth at least $50 million pre-tax as part of their RFQ response.

stories.title: B.C. government confirms errors worth $1.46B in gas revenue forecasts
stories.summary: Errors including botched currency conversions led the British Columbia government to overstate its forecasted natural gas revenues by about $1.46 billion over five fiscal years, officials confirmed on Tuesday.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Errors including botched currency conversions led the British Columbia government to overstate its forecasted natural gas revenues by about $1.46 billion over five fiscal years, officials confirmed on Tuesday.

Energy Minister Adrian Dix said the most significant error, a 44-cent overstatement in the forecasted per-gigajoule price of natural gas this fiscal year, was a “serious mistake.”

But he said the errors affect the province’s forecasting, not its actual revenues, which can vary in a given year. Price fluctuations, including the spike and subsequent decline linked to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, have led the province to both underestimate and overestimate its revenues over the years, Dix said.

“That part is a normal part. What isn’t a part of it is human error that we’re acknowledging today and correcting in the budget,” he told reporters in Vancouver.

Senior staff with the ministries of energy and finance told a technical briefing earlier Tuesday that the errors had been independently verified and corrections would be included in the province’s quarterly fiscal report expected later this month.

The briefing heard the impact on B.C.‘s deficit — last pegged at $7.7 billion for fiscal year 2025-2026 — would be made clear with the release of that report.

The most substantial of the errors made by Energy Ministry staff related to U.S.-Canadian dollar conversions, when a formula was incorrectly applied across a spreadsheet.

The province’s forecasting is based on private-sector estimates of natural gas prices, which are provided in Canadian or U.S. dollars.

Dix said the error involved an incorrect assumption that figures were shown in U.S. dollars, when in fact they were Canadian dollars. The numbers were “again translated into Canadian dollars, leading to an overstatement of revenue,” he said.

The briefing heard correcting that error resulted in a price decrease of 44 cents per gigajoule of natural gas in B.C.‘s forecasting for 2026-2027.

Budget 2026 shows incorrect forecasted prices per gigajoule ranging from $2.34 to $4.83 at plant inlet, referring to gas that hasn’t yet been processed.

“We’re making changes to the way the process happens to ensure that such errors do not occur in the future,” Dix said.

The Opposition B.C. Conservatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but last week, their finance critic Gavin Dew called for the auditor general to examine the flawed revenue forecasts, after they were originally reported by Business in Vancouver.

“This isn’t just an accounting error. It’s a credibility problem,” Dew said in a statement, while Opposition Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay said B.C. could not afford budgets “built on wishful thinking.”

The information in Tuesday’s technical briefing was provided on background, meaning it was not for attribution to an individual.

A second error involving the conversion of energy units amounted to a five-cent decrease in the forecasted price.

Two other errors stemming from the use of data from 2025 instead of this year’s figures resulted in a decrease in the plant inlet price of 1 cent per gigajoule, while adding 3 cents to the outlet price.

Combined, correcting the errors amounted to an average annual decrease in expected revenues of $292 million from this fiscal year to the one starting in 2030.

The impact for the current fiscal year is $306 million, reducing forecasted revenue by about 24 per cent, from $1.297 billion to $991 million.

The Energy Ministry is working with experts to improve its quality assurance process in forecasting moving forward, staff told the briefing.

The briefing heard Treaty 8 First Nations in northeastern B.C. had alerted government officials to what they believed to be an error in the province’s accounting of processing and transportation costs for natural gas in June.

Staff said the province reviewed its calculations and confirmed those costs were appropriately incorporated into its forecasting, but in July uncovered the series of errors related to the conversion of currency units of natural gas.

The errors come as the province works on an updated framework for collecting natural gas royalties that’s set to come into force on Jan. 1, with the goal of returning 50 per cent of profits after accounting for companies’ production costs.

Staff at the briefing acknowledged concerns among Treaty 8 First Nations that the framework won’t hit that target and said further information would be available this fall.

Dix said officials were confident they were “on the right track.”

He said the goal was to establish a new royalty framework that’s “fair for the taxpayers and the owners of the resources,” including First Nations.

It must also strike a balance with the industry, he said.

“We have to make sure (there’s) a good return for the people so that we can help pay for things that are really important to me, like health care and education, on the one hand, and you’ve got to ensure that we have an industry that’s in the province.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Scientists make possible breakthrough in hunt for dark matter
stories.summary: Dark Matter is invisible to the human eye and to telescopes, but scientists are confident it exists due to its gravitational effects at galactic scales
stories.author: Will Dunham
stories.content:
Scientists have made a possible breakthrough in the hunt for dark matter – observing hints of it during an experiment about a 1.6 kilometres underground in South Dakota – though they stopped short of saying they have finally detected this elusive cosmic component.

The researchers described a particle interaction documented at the Sanford Underground Research Facility – built in a former gold mine in the state’s Black Hills region – that May have involved a hypothesized particle called a Wimp, short for “weakly interacting massive particle.” This is one of the proposed candidates for being a dark matter particle.

Ordinary matter makes up stars, planets, people and everything else we can see. But it represents only about 15 per cent of all the matter in the universe. The rest is thought to be dark matter, which does not emit or reflect light, making it invisible to the human eye and to telescopes. But scientists are confident dark matter exists because of its gravitational effects at galactic scales.

Particle physicist Sam Eriksen of the University of Bristol in England, lead author of a study describing the work, said it “could be the first hint of a dark matter observation.”

Dark matter is thought to interact only extremely rarely with ordinary matter. The ongoing LUX-Zeplin, or LZ, experiment in which the observation occurred is designed to catch such interactions and is optimized to look for WIMPs.

It employs ten tonnes of the chemical element xenon in liquid form inside a detector device – a large cylindrical vessel – that is managed by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

The researchers are searching for dark matter scattering off xenon atoms. When a particle scatters, they would observe flashes of light, with the properties of these flashes revealing what type of particle interacted with the xenon.

In an announcement made on Tuesday at a scientific conference in Japan and described in the study submitted to the journal Physical Review Letters, they described the detection of an interaction between a xenon atom and another particle that appeared to unfold in a way hypothesized for a Wimp.

They said what they May have observed was a Wimp colliding with a xenon atom’s nucleus, transferring a small amount of energy that produced a faint flash of UV light that was detected in the experiment. And the collision caused the xenon atom’s nucleus to jolt forward in what is called a nuclear recoil.

While the researchers said the interaction acted as they would expect a Wimp to act, they cautioned that the observation does not yet meet the statistical threshold needed to claim a discovery of dark matter.

“Importantly, as it’s just a single event, we are not claiming that it is dark matter,” Eriksen said.

The researchers are working to rule out other explanations.

“We May be looking at something extraordinary, but we have to be exceptionally rigorous before drawing that conclusion,” Ucla astrophysicist and study co-author Alvine Kamaha said.

Scientists are unsure of the nature of dark matter, just as they are uncertain about the nature of the mysterious cosmic force called dark energy.

“There could be millions of dark matter particles passing through our bodies every second, and yet almost none of them will ever interact with an atom in our bodies,” Kamaha said.

A leading hypothesis is that dark matter is made of a type of particle produced in the early universe and still present today.

“When we observe galaxies and clusters of galaxies, we see that they behave as though they contain much more mass than the matter we can see. So although we cannot see dark matter itself, we can observe what its gravity does,” Kamaha said.

“You can think of dark matter as the cosmic glue that helped enable the formation of galaxies like our Milky Way. Without dark matter, the universe would have evolved very differently, and the structures that eventually led to our solar system May not have formed in the same way,” Kamaha said.

Scientists are searching for dark matter in several ways.

“We study its gravitational effects on galaxies and the universe. We try to produce dark matter particles in particle accelerators. And we perform direct detection using experiments buried deep underground, like LZ, to shield them from cosmic rays and other sources of background while we look for the extremely rare occasion when a dark matter particle interacts with ordinary matter,” Kamaha said.

stories.title: Why buying Canadian makes us feel good
stories.summary: It’s not purely about patriotism – it’s also about agency
stories.author: Gary Mason
stories.content:
My wife was an early adopter of the Buy Canadian movement.

It began around the time U.S. President Donald Trump decided to start insulting us last year, referring to former prime minister Justin Trudeau as “ Governor ” and Canada as America’s “ 51st state .” Then there were the tariffs Mr. Trump was hitting Canada with that would hurt our economy.

It all boiled over – for her and many others - during the infamous ambush of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office on Feb. 28. It prompted us to cut short an American holiday by several weeks.

Things haven’t been the same since.

My wife became single-minded in her determination to not see a cent of our money spent on an American product. Some things have snuck past her detection techniques. But mostly she has been an unabashed patriot, determined to keep as much of our money in this country as she can, with travel dollars spent in destinations not marked with an American flag.

Then came last week when she went to our local grocery store to buy apples.

Our local Thrifty’s, it needs to be said, has done an admirable job sourcing fruits and vegetables, in particular, from countries other than the U.S. We have seen Asian pears from China, Valencia oranges from Egypt and tangerines from South Africa. It’s not uncommon to see food in the produce aisles from countries such as Vietnam, Ecuador and Brazil. And those are just some examples. But recently she went to buy apples and there were tons of them – almost entirely from Washington State.

She was shocked.

The Okanagan region of B.C. used to be known for its apple crop. But years ago, many orchard growers decided there was more money to be made in wine than fruit, so the great conversion took place. Apples are still grown, but not nearly to the same extent. And today, much larger orchards in Washington State are squeezing out the much smaller Okanagan growers. Even when local apples soon arrive in B.C. stores they won’t be able to compete with the price of the Washington State apples. Therein lies the dilemma for many.

For my wife, buying Canadian is as much about helping to protect Canadian jobs as it is punishing U.S. producers. She understands her choices may not be other people’s. She doesn’t believe in shaming those who don’t share her Buy Canadian enthusiasm. She also understands people have limits: many want to help workers in this country out, but not at any price.

And this would seem to describe a prevailing ethic in the country.

Abacus Data recently did a deep dive into people’s attitudes when it comes to Buy Canadian. Its research, conducted in late June and early July, found that buying Canadian has become a regular decision for many of us. And a majority said they go out of their way to choose a Canadian product over a non-Canadian one. But the findings revealed something else: this behaviour isn’t purely about patriotism.

It’s about agency.

“When asked how choosing Canadian makes them feel, the largest single response is that it makes them feel ‘more in control, like I have some say in what happens to the country.’” David Coletto, CEO of Abacus, wrote in a report last month.

Here are some numbers I found interesting:

Fifty-three per cent of those surveyed said they go out of their way to choose a Canadian product often or almost always. Somewhat surprisingly – make that a lot surprisingly – that number shoots to 59 per cent in Quebec – the highest percentage of any region in the country on that question. The closest is Saskatchewan/Manitoba at 57 per cent. The lowest? Alberta at 42 per cent. (The province also has the highest share of those who say they “rarely or never go out of their way” to buy Canadian – 20 per cent.)

I agree with Mr. Coletto’s assessment that Buy Canadian does give people a sense they are having some input in this trade war. And that’s important, given the utter lack of control we have over any number of other things affecting our lives: inflation, housing costs, tariffs, climate change, war and the overwhelming feeling that the world seems to be spinning out of control.

Sure, putting down an orange you discover is from California and picking up one that says Mexico isn’t going to change the trajectory of trade talks with the U.S. But it’s something.

And let’s face it, it feels good to take a stand. Especially when you know you’re on the right side of the issue.

stories.title: Quebec Cardinal Marc Ouellet says he’ll donate $100K from defamation suit win
stories.summary: Superior Court Justice Martin Castonguay ruled on Monday that Paméla Groleau's accusations against Ouellet were unfounded and ordered her to pay him $100,000.
stories.author: Pierre Saint-Arnaud
stories.content:
By Pierre Saint-Arnaud The Canadian Press

Posted September 1, 2026 4:32 pm

Updated September 1, 2026 4:34 pm

Quebec Cardinal Marc Ouellet expressed his gratitude today after winning a civil defamation suit against a woman who accused him of sexual misconduct as part of a class-action lawsuit.

Superior Court Justice Martin Castonguay ruled on Monday that Paméla Groleau’s accusations against Ouellet were unfounded and ordered her to pay him $100,000.

Ouellet issued a brief written statement today from his residence in Rome, Italy.

In it, he expresses his gratitude to the civil justice system and thanks his lawyers and the witnesses who testified.

Groleau had accused Ouellet of touching her without consent on three occasions between 2008 and 2010, while she was training or working for the church.

Ouelette reiterated his plan to donate the $100,000 in damages to organizations fighting sexual abuse against Indigenous Peoples in Canada.

“I pledge to continue the fight within the Church and in society against every form of abuse, particularly sexual abuse, and I unreservedly support substantiated victims in their pursuit of restorative justice,” he writes.

Castonguay’s 52-page ruling, handed down Monday at the Montreal courthouse, is harsh on Groleau.

The judge concluded that her testimony “was neither credible nor reliable.” He noted that she changed her account of the facts several times and that the alleged incidents took place during public events attended by other people.

stories.title: London under heat warning, temperatures forecast to reach 32 C
stories.summary: Humidex values could approach 40 as the Middlesex-London Health Unit urges residents to take precautions.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
Environment Canada has issued a yellow-level heat warning for London and the surrounding region for Tuesday and Wednesday, with the hot weather possibly lasting into Thursday.

At 2:30 p.m. Tuesday, the national weather agency issued the alert, warning of hazardous conditions that may pose health risks, with maximum temperatures expected to reach 30 to 32 C on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Minimum temperatures are expected to range from 20 to 23 C, with humidex values near 40.

For Tuesday, Environment Canada is calling for a high of 30 C, with a 30 per cent chance of showers this afternoon and a risk of a thunderstorm. Temperatures are expected to fall only to a low of 21 C overnight.

“The heat event may continue into Thursday, particularly for Windsor and Essex County, however, confidence is low,” officials wrote in the alert.

The Middlesex-London Health Unit also urged residents Tuesday afternoon to take precautions during the heat.

“Be safe and check in on family, friends and neighbours – especially those who may be more vulnerable to extreme heat,” health unit officials wrote.

The health unit recommends drinking plenty of water, even if you don’t feel thirsty; avoiding caffeinated and alcoholic beverages; and limiting time outdoors. Those who must be outside should seek shade and, where possible, plan activities for the early morning or evening.

Residents are also advised to keep drapes or blinds closed on the sunny side of their homes, take cool showers and use fans to draw in cooler air at night, but not rely on fans as a primary cooling device during prolonged heat.

The health unit also urged residents never to leave a child or pet in a parked car or sleeping outside in direct sunlight.

stories.title: Former Montreal priest convicted in 2019 of abusing boys facing new charges
stories.summary: Montreal - A former Montreal priest who was found guilty in 2019 of sexually abusing two boys is facing charges of possessing and accessing child sexual abuse material.
stories.author: Morgan Lowrie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A former Montreal priest who was found guilty in 2019 of sexually abusing two boys is facing charges of possessing and accessing child sexual abuse material.

Brian Boucher’s lawyer appeared in a Montreal courtroom today on his behalf, and the case was postponed to Sept. 8.

Court documents say the alleged offences occurred between April 7 and April 9.

The 64-year-old was sentenced in 2019 to eight years in prison for sexually assaulting two boys, after being found guilty in one case and pleading guilty in the other.

Boucher worked in 10 Montreal-area churches between 1985 and 2015. The abuse took place at two churches, between 1995 and 1999 in the case of one victim and between 2008 and 2011 in the other.

Boucher was granted statutory release in 2024 and was serving the remainder of his sentence in the community at an approved residential facility before his recent arrest.

In a 2024 report before his release, the Parole Board told Boucher that his case management team “mentions that there is a strong possibility that you have committed other sexual acts in the past.”

“In fact, a public inquiry report in September 2020 revealed that several complaints were made against you since the early 1980s concerning your unacceptable behaviour and interest in young boys,” it read. “In 2002, your name was included on an official list of potential pedophiliac priests, produced by a member of the clergy.”

Under the law, statutory release is granted after an inmate has served two-thirds of their sentence, but the board imposed a number of conditions, including requiring Boucher to live at an approved facility and not be in contact with children or the victims.

In late 2025, the Parole Board modified Boucher’s release conditions to order him to stay away from sections of the Côte-des-Neiges-Notre-Dame-de-Grace and Town of Mount-Royal boroughs, unless for medical reasons, after one of the victims reported seeing him.

He has also been seen in locations where the victim and their family are likely to be present, the report noted.

“The (Correction Service of Canada) assesses that you are not trustworthy, have a history of not respecting the emotional boundaries of others which puts the victims and the victims’ families at risk of further trauma,” read the report.

Boucher was formally stripped of his priesthood in 2020. His conviction and the subsequent independent inquiry sparked criticism of Montreal’s Catholic diocese for failing to take complaints against Boucher seriously.

Montreal’s archbishop promised in 2020 to implement a series of recommendations stemming from the inquiry, including strict protocols for dealing with abuse and sanctions for those who violate rules.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Alberta’s revised statement celebrating province’s birthday removes reference to Indigenous peoples
stories.summary: Updated version was ‘issued in error’ and the original ‘stands,’ government spokesperson says
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
The Alberta government released a statement celebrating the province’s birthday on Tuesday, but an hour later, a revised version was sent out that removed any reference to Indigenous peoples.

The misstep unfolded at a time when relations between the government and the First Nations in Alberta have been strained over the coming referendum on Oct. 19.

Several First Nations have said that any vote on whether Alberta should separate from Canada is a violation of treaty rights.

Shortly after 10 a.m. local time on Tuesday, the government published a statement on behalf of Premier Danielle Smith commemorating the day Alberta joined Confederation in 1905 and became a province of Canada.

The third paragraph of the first statement read: “We recognize the Indigenous Peoples whose enduring connection to and stewardship of this land continues to shape Alberta. Over generations, people from many backgrounds have strengthened our communities through hard work, innovation, entrepreneurship, and a shared belief in opportunity.”

But an hour after it came out, the province sent an edited, expanded statement that removed any reference to Indigenous peoples from the English-language statement.

“Generations of Albertans from many backgrounds have helped build our province through hard work, innovation and a shared belief in freedom. Their legacy can be seen in the strong communities, thriving industries and quality of life we enjoy today,” Ms. Smith’s new statement read.

The original French-language statement mentioning Indigenous peoples was not revised in the second release.

Yonathan Sumamo, a government spokesperson, said the revised version was “issued in error” and the original, which mentioned First Nations, “stands.”

“We apologize for this error and any confusion that it May have caused,” Mr. Sumamo said in an e-mailed statement.

Ms. Smith, at an unrelated news conference, blamed Alberta’s public service for the revision.

“The public service posted one statement and then took it down and put up another one. I said, ‘Why didn’t you put up the original one?’ And so I’m not exactly sure what happened with that glitch,” Ms. Smith said, adding that Indigenous communities are one of many groups that have “helped build the province.”

Trevor Mercredi, the Grand Chief of Treaty 8 First Nations, called the change made to the Premier’s statement “deeply troubling.”

“Treaty 8 Sovereign First Nations and all First Nations across Alberta have always been part of the history, present and future of this province. Our Nations are not a footnote to Alberta’s story,” Mr. Mercredi said in a statement. “Treaty Nations were here long before Alberta existed, and our place in this land cannot be erased when it becomes politically inconvenient.”

He went on to say that the omission was concerning given the Oct. 19 referendum, which he says challenges “the constitutional status of Treaty rights and the duty to consult.”

“Respect for First Nations must be reflected in the government’s words, actions and relationships,” Mr. Mercredi said.

The revised statement remains on Ms. Smith’s social-media accounts on X and Instagram.

stories.title: Temperatures feeling close to 40 as heat warning continues
stories.summary: Temperatures in London and surrounding areas will feel close to 40 C as the heat warning persists.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Temperatures in London and surrounding areas will feel close to 40 C as the heat warning persists. “Intense heat and humidity. It will be brief, it’s not going to last through the weekend,” said CTV Meteorologist Julie Atchison.

“The risk of scattered showers and thunderstorms develop overnight and through the early morning hours. You will likely hear some rumbles of thunder, especially towards the Bruce Peninsula.” Storms could push through first thing in the morning.

Upwards of 20 millimetres is expected Wednesday, bringing a mix of sun and cloud by the afternoon. “Then, the risk of thunderstorms once again developing in parts of southern Ontario,” Atchison added. “Lots of instability over the next seven days at temperatures close to where we should be for this time of year.” Here’s a full look at your forecast: Tuesday night: A few clouds.

Increasing cloudiness this evening, then a 40 per cent chance of showers late this evening and overnight. Showers beginning before morning, risk of thunderstorms late in the evening and overnight. Low 21 C. Wednesday: Showers ending in the morning, then mainly cloudy with a 40 per cent chance of showers in the afternoon.

Showers or thunderstorms beginning late in the afternoon. High 31 C, humidex 41 C. Thursday: Cloudy with 40 per cent chance of showers. High 26 C. Friday: Cloudy with a 30 per cent chance of showers. High 26 C.
