stories.title: U.S. strikes targets in Iran as hostilities flare again after a month without military action
stories.summary: The U.S. military hit targets in Iran on Tuesday after it said Tehran tried to attack commercial ships and American forces in the Middle East, as hostilities flare once again in an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content: Washington -- The U.S. military hit targets in Iran on Tuesday after it said Tehran tried to attack commercial ships and American forces in the Middle East, as hostilities flare once again in an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months. The U.S. strikes, and others on Sunday, abruptly ended a month without military action and threaten to fully reprise a conflict that has spiked global oil prices and posed political problems for Republicans in November’s midterm congressional elections. The renewed fighting comes after U.S. President Donald Trump had appeared to pivot toward trying to bend Iran to his will through economic sanctions. “If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings,” Trump warned on social media after U.S. Central Command announced the latest strikes. Iran’s Armed Forces General Staff and its joint military command, however, said the armed forces would deliver what they described as “crushing and devastating blows” against the United States. Iranian state television said the U.S. struck a fishmeal factory on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz as well as several civilian targets in Hormozgan province. It said a fishing pier and a Ports and Maritime Organization tower in Sirik were among the sites hit by U.S. forces. The U.S. and Iran are both seeking control over the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway off Iran’s coast through which 20 per cent of the world’s oil normally flows. Tehran effectively closed it after the war began. Oil prices have moved sharply higher this week with renewed clashes between Iran and the United States. Crude, already up about seven per cent this week, continued to rise following the strikes on Tuesday. The price of crude has jumped more than 50 per cent this year and it’s dragged the cost of gasoline upward with it. The cost for a gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S. ticked higher again overnight to US$4.10, according to AAA. Last year at this time, a gallon cost $3.19. Before military action began again this week, the Trump administration had argued that hitting the right economic target would get Tehran to its breaking point. Now, military strikes are renewing even as U.S. stockpiles of advanced interceptors have been diminishing and the war has been unpopular among many Americans. A return to open conflict would be dangerous for the region, where Iran has targeted U.S. military bases and infrastructure in Gulf countries since the war began. In the previous strikes on Sunday, U.S. Central Command said its forces struck Iranian rocket launchers that would sea mines into the strait. Iran responded to Sunday’s attacks by launching missiles at U.S. sites in Jordan, which were intercepted, while United Arab Emirates said it stopped an Iranian drone over its waters. The American military in recent days has cast the renewed fighting as limited, though Trump had acknowledged Monday that more strikes might be necessary. U.S. Central Command said Monday on X that its attacks on Iranian targets on Sunday were narrowly focused on preventing Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard forces from placing new mines in the Strait of Hormuz. “U.S. forces took limited, precise action against Irgc minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz,” U.S. Central Command said. “In essence, Iran created the threat and the U.S. military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce.” Central Command reiterated Tuesday that its attacks followed Iranian aggression against commercial vessels and American troops in the region. --- Ben Finley, The Associated Press

stories.title: Nunavik police officer charged with assault after Quebec watchdog investigation
stories.summary: Montreal - An officer with the Nunavik Police Service appeared in court Monday to face charges of assault and assault with a weapon, announced Quebec’s police watchdog in a release.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - An officer with the Nunavik Police Service appeared in court Monday to face charges of assault and assault with a weapon, announced Quebec’s police watchdog in a release.

The officer, 29, appeared in court in Kuujjuarapik, a town on the shore of Hudson’s Bay in northern Quebec, said the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes, or BEI, who investigated the allegations.

stories.title: ‘Do you know how much new signs cost?’: U.S. businesses vow to keep ‘Ontario’ in names
stories.summary: Business owners in upstate New York say they have no plans to drop ‘Ontario’ from their names following Trump’s ‘Lake America’ executive order.
stories.author: Daniel Otis
stories.content: Business owners in upstate New York say they have no plans to drop “Ontario” from their names following Trump’s “Lake America” executive order. “Our business was named after Lake Ontario, and most of our equipment, attractions, and décor were designed with the lake, water, and nautical themes in mind,” Ontario Play & Café owner Pouya Seifzadeh told CTVNews.CA in an email Monday. “When the renaming was announced, we had a great laugh about unexpectedly finding ourselves in the middle of the story.” Amid trade tensions with Canada, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to rename the lake, which has been known as Lake Ontario for more than four centuries. The switch to “Lake America” has been met with firm condemnation from Canadians as well as Trump’s opponents in the U.S. The change also prompted a cheeky Instagram post from Seifzadeh’s indoor playground and café, which is located in Rochester, N.Y., the largest American city on the lake. “POV: You named your entire business after Lake Ontario… and then woke up today,” Ontario Play & Café posted on Friday. “Do you know how much new signs cost?” After more than a decade in business, thousands of children have celebrated their birthdays or frolicked at Ontario Play & Café. With a pirate ship play structure, water station and sand table, the 1,300-square-metre indoor playground leans heavily into its nautical theme. The “Ontario” name is also featured on everything from staff T-shirts to plastic cups. “The name has become part of our identity and our relationship with local families,” Seifzadeh, a dual Canada-U.S. citizen, explained. “Therefore, our official position regarding our own business is simple: Ontario Play & Café is not changing its name.” ‘We’re always going to carry Lake Ontario merchandise’ Amanda Miller is the owner of both the Lake Ontario Gift Shop and Lake Ontario Realty in New York’s Jefferson County, which sits at the eastern end of the lake. Citing brand recognition and associated costs, Miller says she has no intention to change the names of her businesses – but she isn’t against the idea of stocking “Lake America” souvenirs at her gift shop in the future “We’re going to prepare for what consumers are requesting,” Miller told CTVNews.CA by phone on Tuesday. “But at the end of the day, we’re always going to carry Lake Ontario merchandise.”Located near the water in Rochester, the Lake Ontario Press screen printing shop also has no plans to change its name. “The name change is just a silly waste of time,” owner Matt Saxon told CTVNews.CA by email on Monday. “My business will remain Lake Ontario Press.” The business prominently sells “Lake Ontario” t-shirts and posters on its website. “I will not be calling it anything other than Lake Ontario,” Saxon added. “We cannot move on from this quick enough.” ‘A clear distraction’ Rochester’s city council has also flatly rejected the “Lake America” name. In a proclamation released on Friday, the nine-member council unanimously slammed the name change as being as “childish as it is futile” and vowed to continue referring to “Lake Ontario” in all official capacities. “This desperate and flaccid stunt by the President is a clear distraction from the issues that matter most to U.S. voters: the failing economy, housing, affordability and, lest we forget, President Trump’s unwanted and unwarranted war with Iran,” the proclamation read. “No serious person from the Native Tribes or U.S. and Canadian cities which share the Lake will ever call Lake Ontario ‘Lake America.’” The proclamation also criticized the “futile trade conflict with Canada – among our nation’s most important and dependable allies.” Following the “Lake America” name change, Seifzadeh said he remains focused on the “fun and humour” of the situation, joking that “nobody had consulted us.” “We will leave the politics, the reasons behind the decision, and predictions about whether the new name will stick to others,” Seifzadeh added. “We will continue concentrating on what we do best, which is creating a fun and enjoyable place for children and families.”

stories.title: Calgary home with pro-Trump flags vandalized amid cross-border trade war
stories.summary: Asked why they remain in Canada even with their support for the Trump administration, the U.S. homeowner who came here for work said it's because they have built a life in Calgary.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
paragraphs: If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .
Some Calgarians frustrated by the renewed U.S. tariff trade war appear to be taking out their anger on one pro-Trump home by using eggs, dog feces and online suggestions of arson.
The homeowner says while his life is in Canada, he’s a strong supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump. He calls the anger fundamentally offside.

“The position of some would be to say, ‘Hey, this guy, he doesn’t agree with what we agree in, politically (even though) he goes to work, he pays his taxes … (so) let’s run them out of town,'” the homeowner said in an interview.
“That’s not a good look in my opinion, in any democratic society.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That's not a good look in my opinion, in any democratic society."
He spoke on the condition of anonymity, noting that the police have become involved, and he and his wife fear for their safety.
Since the recent attention, he said, many people have approached him positively, while others have egged the house and thrown bagged dog excrement onto the property.
Some have made comments on social media suggesting torching their home.

A spokesperson for Calgary police confirmed they had received a report of vandalism on Aug. 23, and that the homeowners were concerned about online attacks, but they say there were not sufficient grounds to support criminal charges.
The homeowners say they were born and grew up in the United States, moving to Canada for work reasons more than a decade ago.
Their home near Calgary’s downtown displays two large pro-Trump flags. A massive American flag often hangs from their balcony.
“We’re proud Americans, we support the president, and that was the idea behind the flags,” the homeowner said, stating the intention was originally to showcase their patriotism.
He said it has developed into a sign of acceptance of conservatives who, he believes, have had their views suppressed and marginalized.
One of the pro-Trump flags says “Trump: Make America Great Again” while the other says “Trump 2028: Third Term and Beyond.”

The homeowner says while he supports the Trump administration’s policies — such as taxes, immigration and spending — the reference to 2028 is a joke given that presidents cannot, under the U.S. Constitution, serve a third term.
It’s not the first time his home has been in the firing line, he said.
A retaining wall was defaced with graffiti during the 2024 U.S. presidential election that saw Trump defeat Democrat challenger Kamala Harris.
He said the pro-Trump flags were up long before the tariff war, which began just over a week ago, when the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about $28 billion in Canadian exports.
Canada has responded with its own tariffs, which take effect Sept. 8.

The Calgary house is not the only collateral damage. Last week, Trump signed an order changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America to hit back against sharp criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford.
Asked why they remain in Canada even with their support for the administration, the homeowner said it’s because they have built a life in the country.

stories.title: B.C. boaters warned to avoid mysterious floating island
stories.summary: Boaters in northern British Columbia are being warned to stay away from a mysterious floating island that has reappeared on a lake after drifting about 30 kilometres in two weeks.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content: Boaters in northern British Columbia are being warned to stay away from a mysterious floating island that has reappeared on a lake after drifting about 30 kilometres in two weeks. BC Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer says he initially thought reports of the island covered in trees and foliage on Williston Lake, the reservoir for the W.A.C. Bennett Dam in the northern Interior, were a hoax, but satellite images confirmed its existence in mid-August. The island measuring about one hectare then disappeared, but Gammer says it was spotted again on Monday, having travelled about 30 kilometres. He says boaters should resist the urge to visit the island, theorizing that it’s based on an unstable mass of logs and decaying debris that May have broken free from the shore when the lake recently filled for the first time since 2012. Rocky Avery shared images of the island that drew worldwide attention after it was spotted by a friend at the lake north of Avery’s hometown of Mackenzie. He says the water under the island at the time was about 60 metres deep. “When I saw the video, it was just kind of in awe because you can see from his boat — he was making the ripples, and you could see along the island it was all just going up and down, and it was actually real,” said Avery. “It was crazy.” Avery said he had lived in the area for more than 48 years and never heard of anything like the island before. He said he wanted the island to be named Rocky Island “even though it’s not that rocky.” Avery shared the discovery with BC Hydro and members of the Tsay Keh Dene First Nation. Gammer said when he first heard about the island on Aug. 13, he questioned the report. “I checked internally and nobody that I have with contacts in the company had heard of this either. So, at the time, we basically thought it was maybe a hoax, and we didn’t give it much more attention,” said Gammer, manager of northern community relations with BC Hydro. But a few days later, engineers with the Crown utility spotted it on satellite imagery in Finley Bay, near the centre of the lake. “This is a rare occurrence, and certainly the first that we’ve heard of for Williston Reservoir,” said Gammer. He said they tried to track the island but it seemed to vanish, before it was spotted again against the shoreline where the Ospika River flows into the lake. “It’s moved about 30 kilometres northwest on the reservoir into a more remote location,” said Gammer. “It looks like the island appears to be intact.” Gammer said he also received a photo from a boater, providing double confirmation. Based on satellite imagery, the island is about 140 meters long and about 70 meters wide, he added. Avery cheered news the island hadn’t sunk, after being told by members of the Tsay Keh Dene First Nation that they too had spotted it again. “We’re just waiting for the water to calm down so we can take a jet boat and take a better look at it,” said Avery, adding a former chief from the nation would join the trip to inspect the island. Gammer said the island’s origin was not certain but it’s normal for trees that fall into the reservoir to clump together in a sheltered bay. “You can imagine, like a tree falling down in the forest, and the trunk is laying flat, and over a long period of time, it starts to break down, and other plants, moss, and even trees start growing on top,” said Gammer. The rising waters of the reservoir then could have lifted the mass free, calling it the “best theory” of how the island came to be. Gammer said waves in the reservoir can become violent during a windstorm and he feared they could tear apart the mass of logs and woody debris. “It’s just naturally unstable, and so it’s unsafe to climb onto the island or land a boat on it. It would be dangerous to do that,” he said. BC Hydro will continue to monitor the island to see if it starts moving again. “I mean, there will be people who will probably want to study it and get close to it. So, there May be more information to come about the island as the weeks go by,” said Gammer. This report by Nono Shen, The Canadian Press, was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, takes over from Tim Cook after 15 years
stories.summary: the helm of the tech giant, ending Tim Cook’ tenure during which the company’s value skyrocket to US$4.6 trillion.
stories.author: The Associated Press
paragraphs: the helm of the iconic tech giant on Tuesday, ending Tim Cook’s 15-year tenure during which the company’s value skyrocket to US$4.6 trillion thanks to the iPhone’s enormous popularity.

The transition to a new CEO comes at a pivotal time for Apple. Artificial intelligence has unleashed the greatest upheaval within the industry since Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPhone in 2007. Apple has gotten off to a rough start in AI after stumbling in its efforts to deliver new features built on the technology, as promised nearly two years ago.

Earlier this year, it unveiled new artificial intelligence advances, including upgrades to its Siri assistant, emphasizing a focus on privacy and day-to-day use as the iPhone maker tries to catch up with rivals.
Latest updates on company news here

Ternus faces challenges that will force him to step outside his comfort zone in hardware engineering. Beyond finding ways to keep Apple competitive in the artificial intelligence race, he will need to navigate supply chain questions and relationships with figures such as President Donald Trump, who offered public praise for his predecessor on Tuesday.

Serving as Apple CEO will also require soft skills, including developing relationships with important figures. Cook cultivated ties with Trump as he navigated the company through business challenges, including Trump’s trade and tariff war targeting countries in Asia, where Apple has extensive manufacturing supply chains. Although he is handing over the CEO reins at Apple, Cook is widely expected to help the company maintain a good relationship with Trump after he shifts to his new role as executive chairman.

Ternus worked on some of Apple’s signature products under Cook, including the Apple Watch, AirPods and Apple Vision Pro. He will headline next week’s launch of the latest iPhone at Apple’s Cupertino, California, headquarters.

stories.title: London explosives probe: Accused faces new voyeurism, child porn charges
stories.summary: Zekun Wang, 27, surrendered to police and was released with the Crown’s consent while under strict house-arrest bail conditions.
stories.author: Jane Sims
paragraphs: One of the four people charged in the north London guns and explosives probe that began earlier this year is facing additional voyeurism and child pornography charges.

Zekun (Alex) Wang, 27, who is currently under strict house-arrest bail conditions and living in the Toronto area, was charged with two counts of voyeurism and one count of possession of child pornography on Aug. 20. He surrendered to police and was released with the Crown’s consent.

His new charges were discussed briefly during a case-management court appearance in London on Tuesday, when Ontario Court justice of the peace Kristine Diaz ordered a publication ban on anything that could identify any complainants in the separate court filing.
Wang wasn’t in court and wasn’t required to be there. His brief court appearance was handled by an agent for defence lawyer Nick Cake.
Cake confirmed the new charges and had no comment except that “we will litigate this matter in court.”

Wang, Jerry Tong, 27, Fei (Frank) Han, 26, and Feiyang (Astrid) Ji, 21, were all arrested and charged with multiple counts after a series of bizarre events that London police have said began with an attempted break-in on Jan. 24 at a Western University engineering building and led to the discovery of a cache of hazardous chemicals and firearms at 212 Chesham Place, west of the university.
All four have ties to the university, and Wang, Tong and Han have specific links to the engineering school. All three were involved with MORS LAB, an engineering startup.

In the months before their arrests, they had been working on and promoting an anti-drone defence system to pitch to both the Canadian Armed Forces and NATO. Videos of their project were available online before they were charged.
More charges were laid last month against all four accused, bringing the total number of counts before the court to 31.

All four face joint charges involving guns and specific materials, including manufacturing guns and possession of stolen property over $5,000 belonging to Western University . Other charges specifically name Wang and Tong.

Wang faces additional charges that include break-and-enter, occupying a motor vehicle with a firearm and accessing computer data pertaining to firearm design that could be used on a 3D printer, metal milling machine or other computer systems to make and traffic guns.

Tong is charged with carrying a concealed weapon, careless use of a firearm, resisting arrest, break-and-enter, occupying a motor vehicle with a firearm and a spate of firearms-related charges, both in London and the Ottawa area.

The investigation began when police were called to the university to investigate reports of a possible break-in at the Claudette MacKay-Lassonde Pavilion, an engineering building on campus. One man was arrested and police recovered a loaded handgun.
The focus shifted to the Chesham Place home where, over several days, London police, with the assistance of five other police services, uncovered a trove of hazardous chemicals and firearms.
There was further investigation in the Ottawa area, where two homes were searched and more firearms were seized.
There are no links to any national security threat, police have said.

Only Wang and Ji have been granted bail and are out of custody. Wang’s bail hearing in March resulted in his release to his parents’ home under strict house-arrest terms and a $410,000 no-deposit bail with his parents as his two sureties, after spending five weeks in custody. One of his bail conditions is wearing a GPS tracking device.
He has already asked that his case be tried by a Superior Court judge.

Ji, the only woman charged in the matter, was released on $500 no-deposit bail in late March after two months in custody. She required no bail hearing or sureties and was released with the Crown’s consent.
Both Wang and Ji’s cases are slated to be back in court on Sept. 29, when it’s hoped an Ontario Court of Justice preliminary hearing date will have been selected for all four accused.
Han remains in custody after an unsuccessful bail hearing held just days after his arrest. His next court appearance is Friday.
Tong hasn’t requested a bail hearing. His next court appearance is Sept. 8.

One of the four people charged in the north London guns and explosives probe that began earlier this year is facing additional voyeurism and child pornography charges.

Zekun (Alex) Wang, 27, who is currently under strict house-arrest bail conditions and living in the Toronto area, was charged with two counts of voyeurism and one count of possession of child pornography on Aug. 20. He surrendered to police and was released with the Crown’s consent.

stories.title: Canadian actor Tedde Moore was part of a family of outstanding creative artists
stories.summary: She started her career on stage at the Stratford Festival, but was best known for her performance in the classic holiday film A Christmas Story
stories.author: Fred Langan
stories.content:
Tedde Moore, who died at age 79 on Aug. 5 in Huntsville, Ont., was a classically trained actor who performed for years at the Stratford Festival and later appeared in movies such as A Christmas Story .

The 1983 film was a modest success on its release but later became a holiday rerun classic. She played Miss Shields, a schoolteacher who gives a student named Ralphie, played by Peter Billingsley, a failing grade for a paper saying he wanted a BB gun for Christmas. She attends to another student, Flick, who got his tongue stuck on a cold flagpole. Ms. Moore was nominated for a Genie for her performance.

She reprised the role of Miss Shields in 1994 in My Summer Story .

Dorothea Mavor Moore was born in Toronto on April 11, 1947. She later dropped “Dorothea” for the more manageable “Tedde” (pronounced “Teddy”) at the start of her acting career. Her father was Mavor Moore, an artistic polymath who was everything from drama critic to television producer. Her mother, Darwina (Faessler) Moore, stayed at home to take care of the family. Darwina and Mavor divorced when the children were quite young.

Ms. Moore went to North Toronto Collegiate Institute, but was expelled. “I believe she got into a huge tiff with her teachers because she took a position that there was a homosexual encounter in Othello ,” said her son, Noah Shebib. She then went to a boarding school on Prince Edward Island.

Young Tedde started acting around the age of 13. After high school, she landed at London’s Royal Academy of Dramatic Art – known as Rada – one of the best classical theatre schools in the English-speaking world. On graduating in 1967, she won the Principal’s Medal of Honour. Other winners over the years have included such luminaries as Glenda Jackson and Alan Rickman.

Other Rada graduates played coveted roles in films and on the British stage, but Ms. Moore headed home to Canada, where she was an instant star at the Stratford Festival. Early on, she appeared in A Midsummer Night’s Dream with Christopher Walken.

She continued to be a mainstay at Stratford.

“My mother was Juliet in Romeo and Juliet . She was everything you could be at Stratford for the next four or five seasons,” her son said.

When her first daughter, Zoe, was born she shifted from theatrical work to film and television. In retrospect, her younger daughter Suzanna said, “She should have stayed in the theatre.”

Ms. Moore was part of a multigenerational clan of creative artists stretching back to her grandmother, Dora Mavor Moore, who came to Canada from Scotland as a six-year-old in 1894; she was the first Canadian accepted to the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art, graduating in 1912. Back in Canada she was one of the founders of the Stratford Shakespearean Festival, as it was then known, and an early appointee to the Order of Canada. She was made an officer in 1970 for her contributions to Canada’s theatrical world. She died at 91 in 1979.

Tedde’s father, James Mavor Moore (known as Mavor), started acting on radio when he was 13. He was an intelligence officer during the Second World War and then head of CBC’s International Service in the late 1940s, which was run by External Affairs and was a subtle propaganda service. He moved to CBC Television a couple of years before it went on the air in September of 1952, and started CBC National News. He continued to act, was a drama critic at Maclean’s magazine, taught drama at York University, chaired the Canada Council and was named to the highest level of the Order of Canada. In the middle of all that he played the detective Nero Wolfe on CBC Radio in 1982.

The men in Ms. Moore’s romantic life were also famous artists. Fellow actor Patrick Christopher was her partner and the father of her first child, Zoe, born in 1973.

Later, Ms. Moore began a relationship with the filmmaker Don Shebib, who made the groundbreaking 1970 film, Goin’ Down the Road. She had a role in a 2011 sequel, Down the Road Again.

“Tedde was an elegant, sophisticated, friendly person,” said Piers Handling, former director and CEO of the Toronto International Film Festival and a close friend of Mr. Shebib’s. He wrote a book called The Films of Don Shebib . “Don could be pricklier and Tedde was the perfect foil. Don’s early films had a working-class flavour. But when they became more middle class, Tedde fitted the part perfectly.”

Along with Down the Road Again , Ms. Moore was in two of Mr. Shebib’s earlier films, Rip Off , in which she played a small role, and Second Wind, in which she was more prominent.

She and Mr. Shebib had two children together, Suzanna and Noah.

“My mother never married anyone, and not my father, though they lived together for decades,” Noah Shebib said. “I was in my mother’s belly when she was shooting A Christmas Story in 1983.”

Noah has continued the family’s creative legacy. A successful music producer known as 40, he helped launch the recording career of the Canadian rapper and singer Drake. “Drake came to my studio to rent recording space for $200 a day. By the fifth day I realized I had taken all his money so we made a decision to work together.” He has won two Grammy Awards (Best Rap Album and Best Rap Song) for his work with Drake. Mr. Shebib was executive producer of almost all of Drake’s albums, more than 100 songs.

His sister Suzanna was a child actor but is now a schoolteacher. His sister Zoe Carter is a writer.

Tedde Moore also had experience in the literary world; she co-edited the book Standing Naked in the Wings : Anecdotes from Canadian Actors. It was published in 1997 by Oxford University Press.

In her long acting career, Ms. Moore appeared in about 50 films and television programs. Among other honours, she won a Canadian Film Award in 1976 as best supporting actress for her role in Second Wind .

Ms. Moore had been suffering from multiple sclerosis since 2009. She continued to work and in 2011 she played Mrs. Claus in Mistletoe Over Manhattan, a made-for-TV movie . Her final role in 2017 was also Christmas-themed, in the romance/drama Magical Christmas Ornaments.

Ms. Moore leaves her children, Zoe Carter, Suzanna Shebib, Noah Shebib and Chaunce Drury, along with three sisters and five grandchildren. Don Shebib predeceased her in 2023.

stories.title: How the cap on international study permits is changing campuses this fall
stories.summary: As post-secondary students get ready to return to campuses for the fall semester, Canada’s international student arrivals are tracking well below the target it has set for this year.
stories.author: Kamil Karamali
stories.content:
Toronto — As post-secondary students get ready to return to campuses for the fall semester, Canada’s international student arrivals are tracking well below the target it has set for this year — resulting in Ontario colleges suspending programs and universities and student groups pushing Ottawa to hand out more study permits.

Ottawa’s target for this year is 155,000 new international student arrivals, but data from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (Ircc) shows just 22,405 arrived during the first six months of 2026, tracking well below the full-year target.

However, international student arrivals are highly seasonal and typically surge ahead of the fall semester.

In January 2024, then-Immigration Minister Marc Miller announced a temporary cap on international study student permits. There were 292,885 new international student arrivals in 2024 — followed by a more than 60-per-cent drop in 2025, to 115,005. That’s much lower than the target that was actually announced for 2025, at 305,900 new arrivals.

The international student population has dropped one-third since 2024, according to an email statement from Ircc, with the goal of reducing pressures on housing, infrastructure, and services.

“We are seeing those positive signs that recent measures are working,” Briannah Dale, spokesperson for Ircc, said in an email to CTV News.

“A recent TD Economics report found that cuts to immigration levels have already eased the pressure on social and economic infrastructure, lowering condo demand for both home ownership and the secondary rental market,” added Dale. “Lower immigration rates have also caused a reduction in asking rents across major cities in Canada.”

Colleges hit harder than universities

Since the temporary cap was issued, Ontario colleges have been hit the hardest, with hundreds of programs suspended and thousands of job losses

Centennial College has had a total of 61 programs suspended between the two years — 54 in 2025 and an additional seven this year.

“Current students who are progressing through affected programs as scheduled can continue their studies toward completion and will have the opportunity to graduate,” said a Centennial College spokesperson to CTV News via email.

Meanwhile, Fanshawe initially announced 40 program suspensions last year, followed by another 10 later that year and nine additional suspensions announced this March.

“Over the last two years Fanshawe has experienced an approximately 40 per cent decline in total student term enrolments due to changes in federal policies related to international students,” a spokesperson from Fanshawe College told CTV News, which highlights it’s welcoming more than 2,000 international students this year.

Algonquin College, meanwhile, approved the suspension or cancellation of another 30 programs effective this fall. Neither college responded to CTV News’ request for comment.

“We’re seeing a decrease in the amount of students on our campuses, meaning there’s a decrease in services as well from that result in terms of students,” Georgina Cabrol, president of the College Student Alliance, said in a Zoom interview with CTV News Sunday.

“From my perspective, we’ve seen a loss in our academic support, such as career services, loss of job employment for students on campus — and it’s just been quite a situation where individuals have been impacted in various ways.”

Ontario initially cushioned universities from much of the impact of the federal cap. The province maintained 2023 application levels at 22 of its 23 universities, compared with just 11 of 24 colleges, saying its allocations would prioritize public programs supporting in-demand jobs.

‘Attracting higher-quality students’

In Ircc’s email to CTV News, Dale says that the current policy is focusing on attracting “higher quality students” and keeping the “world’s best talent” — highlighting that new arrivals of study permit holders at the university level increased by ten percentage points, from 30 per cent in 2024 to 40 per cent in 2025.

“As overall international student admissions decrease, the proportion of university students relative to college students is increasing,” said Dale. “Ircc is expecting this trend to continue with new measures directed at graduate students in 2026 and a continued focus on attracting talent at the master’s and PhD level.”

Data from the University of Toronto shows that although international student intake fell six per cent in the fall of 2024, the institution is now anticipating a nine per cent increase in its international student body this fall.

“When it comes to Trinity, our number (of international students) generally is about 30 per cent,” said Kristen Moore, director of student experience at Trinity College to CTV News Sunday. “That’s been pretty consistent for us over the last few years.”

“It’s fair to say that Toronto fared better than many other universities in the province and in the country, because of here of the international appeal of our programs is very strong,” said Vice-Chancellor of Trinity College at University of Toronto, Nicholas Terpstra, to CTV News Sunday. “We have not had the kind of fall-off, drop-off in international numbers of some other smaller universities have had.”

More stringent requirements

While universities have generally been less affected than colleges, international students who were accepted to Canadian schools say the process of obtaining a study permit has become more difficult.

“I got my (student) visa in under 10 days, so it was very much a miracle for me to get it,” said Aurin Kabir, who is an international student at Toronto Metropolitan University, told CTV News Sunday. “But I know some students who are waiting for almost a year to two years for that visa — and to be honest, a very uncertain thing now.”

The Bangladeshi student studying economics said the process of applying for a student visa from Canada has gotten even more “difficult” since the Canadian government limited the number of study permits it administers.

“When I applied, you had to show proof of almost $25,000 Canadian — but before that it was only $15,000, so it’s almost double now,” she added. “We have to show in our bank that we had that much to cover our first year here in Canada, we have to show proof of assets and other stuff — and we have to show proof that we have intent to go back to Bangladesh after I’m done with my studies. You have to show that intent.”

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada requires a single applicant outside Quebec to demonstrate at least $22,895 for living expenses, in addition to tuition and transportation costs. That requirement rises to $23,448 for applications submitted beginning Sept. 1.

stories.title: Art Gallery of Ontario's CEO Stephan Jost to depart at the end of this year
stories.summary: Toronto - The Art Gallery of Ontario says its top executive is stepping down after a decade in the role.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - The Art Gallery of Ontario says its top executive is stepping down after a decade in the role.

In a news release, the AGO says director and CEO Stephan Jost is leaving at the end of this year.

A person leaves the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto, Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Cole Burston

The AGO credits Jost with securing significant art collections during his tenure, including a recent donation of 450 works from the late patrons Carol and Morton Rapp.

It says Jost also led a project to expand the gallery space by 40,000 sq. feet, set to open next year.

The AGO has also weathered controversy in recent months. The Globe and Mail earlier this year reported on the fallout after the gallery backed away from acquiring work by Jewish-American photographer Nan Goldin, who had been critical of Israel’s miliary campaign in Gaza.

The AGO says it will launch a global search for Jost’s replacement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

stories.title: U.S. Senator to introduce bill to repeal Trump’s latest tariffs on Canada
stories.summary: Legislation is unlikely to pass, but comes as Democrats focus on affordability issues heading into the midterm elections
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is set to introduce legislation to stop U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest tariffs as Democrats ramp up their affordability messaging ahead of midterm elections.

The new bill backed by the Democrat from New York attempts to rein in the latest tariffs on Canadian goods and the separate duties the Trump administration says are linked to forced labour in supply chains.

“While inflation rages, families struggle to pay their bills and small businesses close, Trump – detached from reality – continues his bluster on the global stage, doubling down on a chaotic trade war that has meant only pain for American families, farmers and manufacturers,” Schumer said in a news release Tuesday.

“Republicans won’t stand up to Trump’s nonsense and Americans are crying out for relief.”

The legislation is largely symbolic, since it’s unlikely to pass a Republican-controlled Congress or overcome Trump’s presidential veto.

But it gives Democrats ammunition against Republicans – who are heading into November elections as an unpopular war on Iran drives up inflation and gas prices, and as affordability remains the top issue cited by voters.

Trump last month hit Canada with 50-per-cent tariffs on multiple goods, ranging from hockey sticks and cement to honey, after trade talks between the two nations broke down.

Canada is set to respond with its own set of retaliatory duties next week.

The Trump administration in July also used Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to hit Canada and dozens of other countries with double-digit tariffs, after claiming those countries weren’t doing enough to fight forced labour in supply chains.

The Canadian government has told the Trump administration that new legislation combatting forced labour in supply chains should have shielded Canada from those 10 per cent tariffs.

Those duties do not apply to goods compliant under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as Cusma.

A coalition of U.S. states is already challenging the use of Section 301 for the forced-labour duties.

Schumer’s new legislation – which would repeal both sets of tariffs and require refunds – comes as polling shows that Trump’s tariffs on Canada and the president’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” are widely unpopular.

A new Reuters/Ipsos poll released Tuesday found a majority of Americans oppose both moves.

The nationwide Aug. 28 to Aug. 30 poll of 1,023 registered voters – which was conducted online, so it can’t be assigned a margin of error – found only 20 per cent of respondents support the higher tariffs on Canada and 14 per cent support changing the name of Lake Ontario.

stories.title: 49 Quebecers become millionaires after $55M Lotto Max win
stories.summary: Forty-nine Quebecers are now millionaires after winning a share of a $55 million Lotto Max jackpot. Some of them only learned the news when Loto-Québec contacted them, with reactions ranging from laughter and disbelief to tears.
stories.author: Marisela Amador
stories.content: Forty-nine Quebecers are now millionaires after winning a share of a $55 million Lotto Max jackpot. Some of them only learned the news when Loto-Québec contacted them, with reactions ranging from laughter and disbelief to tears. Most of the new millionaires didn’t know each other, but they had all purchased at least one share of the winning Formule groupe ticket on the Loto-Québec website. On Tuesday, the winners gathered at Loto-Québec’s head office in Montreal to receive their share of the prize money. The 49 jackpot winners come from 12 different regions across the province, from the Outaouais to the Côte-Nord. Laurentians resident François B. said he purchased his ticket just minutes before the draw and checked the results the following morning. “My heart skipped a beat!” he said. He added that he plans to buy a more luxurious vehicle and spoil his children. ‘It’s hard to believe’ Another winner, Côte-Nord resident Jacques V., said he became emotional upon discovering his win. “I had two sleepless nights. It’s hard to believe, but it feels good.” Loto-Québec said it was the first time in its history that it had handed out so many cheques worth more than $1 million in a single day. “It’s incredible to think that 49 families here in Quebec will enjoy part of this jackpot. Loto-Québec generates significant spinoffs for the community, in addition to the money paid out to lottery winners,” said Isabelle Jean, executive vice-president and COO of Lottery Games at Loto-Québec. “This summer alone, dozens of Quebecers shared jackpots of $25 million, $40 million and $55 million, becoming millionaires in the process. We’re so proud of this contribution.” According to Loto-Québec, the online Formule groupe allows players to purchase one or more shares in a lottery group and pool them with those of other group members.

stories.title: Stephan Jost to depart role as Art Gallery of Ontario CEO
stories.summary: AGO accessioned more than 18,000 works of art since Jost joined in 2016
stories.author: Lana Hall
stories.content:
The Art Gallery of Ontario has announced that director and chief executive Stephan Jost will be stepping down, effective Dec. 31, 2026.

Jost joined the AGO in 2016 after holding roles at the Honolulu Museum of Art in Hawaii, the Shelburne Museum in Vermont and the Mills College Art Museum in California.

Under his leadership, the AGO accessioned more than 18,000 works of art and secured more than $500-million in commitments in gifts of art and funds for the museum. Jost also led a successful campaign to expand the AGO, namely through the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary gallery, which will expand the Ago’s gallery space by 40,000 square feet when it opens in 2027.

“Over the summer, I reflected on arriving at the AGO 10 years ago and establishing the Strategic Plan we call AGO 2028,” Jost said in a press release. “I realized that we have met our goals ahead of schedule. Now is the time to set the AGO up for the future with new leadership.”

In an interview, Jost said he does not have another role lined up, and plans to take “a bit of a break” for three to nine months before seeking a leadership role elsewhere.

“Let me be blunt. There’s no shortage of opportunities for major museum directors,” he said.

The AGO has said they will appoint someone on an interim basis before commencing a global search for a new director and CEO.

Jost’s tenure has not been without controversy. During his time at the AGO, three curatorial staff members stepped down, including chief curator and deputy director Julian Cox, modern and contemporary curator John Zeppetelli, and inaugural curator of Indigenous art Wanda Nanibush.

Earlier this year, the AGO dissolved a committee that declined to acquire a Nan Goldin artwork after a debate over whether the Jewish-American artist’s views are “antisemitic,” prompting four resignations and a governance review at the gallery.

In an e-mail statement at the time, Jost acknowledged that the committee’s purpose had been undermined by discourse that has spilled into the public. “I can assure you we are focused on our mission and working to take the necessary actions to ensure our processes are about art and respectful dialogue,” he said.

Now, Jost said he’s proud of the programming the AGO has done to attract younger and more diverse audiences over the past decade. Fifty two per cent of the gallery’s visitors, not including school groups, are now under the age of 39, and 60 per cent come from “non-European heritage,” he said.

“That’s a shift that we’ve done very intentionally to reflect Toronto,” he said. “... The last 10 years haven’t been without challenges for any cultural leader. But we had a plan and stuck to it, and I feel good about that.”

In a press release, AGO board of trustees co-president Beth Horowitz praised Jost’s programming shifts and initiation of the gallery’s expansion.

“Stephan has transformed the AGO over the past decade. The collection is broader, deeper and more inclusive,” she said. “His leadership of the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery project – fully funded and on track – is his legacy and will have a lasting impact.”

Reflecting on conversations about art and nationalism that have dominated cultural headlines in the wake of the trade war with the United States, Jost said it’s more important than ever for cultural institutions to frame global conversations through Canadian art.

“If we don’t use Canadian content and artists to tell the world what’s important, other places we will.”

stories.title: Mysterious floating island reappears on B.C. lake
stories.summary: Boaters should resist urge to visit island, which could be based on an unstable mass of logs and decaying debris, BC Hydro spokesperson says
stories.author: Nono Shen
stories.content:
Geologist John Joseph Clague said when he first heard that a floating island, bigger than a football field, had been spotted on a lake in British Columbia’s northern Interior, he dismissed it as an “AI stunt.”

But Clague – a professor of earth sciences at Simon Fraser University and an emeritus scientist of the Geological Survey of Canada – is now convinced that the island is very real, but is mystified by its origins.

Boaters have been being warned to stay off the island that reappeared on Monday on Williston Lake, the reservoir for the W.A.C. Bennett Dam.

BC Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer said it had travelled about 30 kilometres, adding to the mystery surrounding the island that he theorized had been formed when it was lifted free by rising water levels in the reservoir.

Clague, who has previously worked around the Williston Lake area, was not convinced by that explanation. He said he had seen evidence of erosion along the lake, but “nowhere near that in scale.”

“There is erosion occurring, and trees do collapse into the lake, but they don’t kind of form this very large mat of forested material,” said Clague. “This is unusual. I’ve never heard of such a thing before.”

He said it also remained a mystery why the island had not broken apart after travelling so far.

“I think a lot of people view it as something that’s very thick, but it can’t be thick if it’s moving around the lake at speeds,” said Clague, “So, you know, it’s a curiosity.”

BC Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer says he initially thought reports of a floating island covered in trees on Williston Lake in northern British Columbia were a hoax, before satellite images confirmed its existence. It then vanished, but has now reappeared, 30 kilometres from where it was previously seen.

The Canadian Press

Rocky Avery shared images of the island that drew worldwide attention after it was spotted by a friend at the lake north of Avery’s hometown of Mackenzie last month.

He said the water under the island at the time was about 60 metres deep.

“When I saw the video, it was just kind of in awe because you can see from his boat – he was making the ripples, and you could see along the island it was all just going up and down, and it was actually real,” said Avery. “It was crazy.”

Avery notified BC Hydro and members of the Tsay Keh Dene First Nation of the discovery.

Gammer said he too initially thought the reports of a floating island covered in trees and foliage were a hoax when BC Hydro received them on Aug. 13.

“I checked internally and nobody that I have with contacts in the company had heard of this either. So, at the time, we basically thought it was maybe a hoax, and we didn’t give it much more attention,” said Gammer, manager of northern community relations with BC Hydro.

But a few days later, engineers with the Crown utility spotted it on satellite imagery in Finley Bay, near the centre of the lake.

“This is a rare occurrence, and certainly the first that we’ve heard of for Williston reservoir,” said Gammer.

He said they tried to track the island but it seemed to vanish, before it was spotted again on Monday against the shoreline where the Ospika River flows into the lake.

“It’s moved about 30 kilometres northwest on the reservoir into a more remote location,” said Gammer. “It looks like the island appears to be intact.”

Gammer said he also received a photo from a boater, providing double confirmation of the island’s reappearance. Based on satellite imagery, the island is about 140 metres long and about 70 metres wide, he added.

He said boaters should resist the urge to visit the island, theorizing that it was based on an unstable mass of logs and decaying debris that May have broken free from the shore when the lake recently filled for the first time since 2012.

Gammer said the island’s origin was not certain but it was normal for trees that fall into the reservoir to clump together in sheltered bays.

“You can imagine, like a tree falling down in the forest, and the trunk is laying flat, and over a long period of time, it starts to break down, and other plants, moss, and even trees start growing on top,” said Gammer.

The rising waters of the reservoir then could have lifted the mass free, calling it the “best theory” of how the island came to be.

Gammer said waves in the reservoir can become violent during a windstorm and he feared they could tear apart the mass of logs and woody debris.

“It’s just naturally unstable, and so it’s unsafe to climb onto the island or land a boat on it. It would be dangerous to do that,” he said.

BC Hydro would continue to monitor the island to see if it started moving again, Gammer said.

“I mean, there will be people who will probably want to study it and get close to it. So, there May be more information to come about the island as the weeks go by,” said Gammer.

Avery cheered news the island hadn’t sunk, after being told by members of the Tsay Keh Dene First Nation that they too had spotted it again.

“We’re just waiting for the water to calm down so we can take a jet boat and take a better look at it,” said Avery, adding a former chief from the nation would join the trip to inspect the island.

Avery said he had lived in the area for more than 48 years and never heard of anything like the island before.

He said he wanted the island to be named Rocky Island – “even though it’s not that rocky.”

stories.title: Carney urges Trump administration to ‘stop doing memes’ and get serious about trade talks
stories.summary: Carney didn't hesitate to defend walking away from the table when it became clear Canada's sovereignty was at stake.
stories.author: Michael Talbot
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney still believes the United States and Canada can reach a “mutually beneficial” trade deal, but first President Donald Trump and his administration need to show Canadians some respect and get serious about negotiations, he told reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday.

Since trade talks fell apart , President Trump has not only unleashed additional tariffs, but his usual barrage of social media tirades directed at Canada — a nation he feels has long taken advantage of the U.S. on the subject of trade.

With a sharpie scrawl, Trump even declared he was renaming Lake Ontario ‘Lake America’ and has claimed Canada has nothing the U.S. wants or needs.

U.S. Department of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth added to the animosity with a distasteful social media post mocking female members of a Cadet Training Centre in Vernon, B.C.

Pentagon deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss seemed to defend Hegseth’s post, saying it “speaks for itself.”

On Tuesday, Carney said the post was “beneath their office” and indicative of a nation that isn’t taking Canada, or the increasingly precarious trade situation, seriously.

“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those (trade) discussions, we can have those discussions,” the PM said. “It’s not constructive,” he said of the online trolling, “but that’s their democracy.”

In all fairness, not all Canadian politicians have chosen the high road during the cross-border sparring.

Notably, Ontario Premier Doug Ford has called Trump “a loser” and mocked him for his previous bankruptcies in the private sector, before toning things down and admitting he got a bit carried away.

Carney, meanwhile, refuted speculation that Ford had anything to do with trade talks falling apart.

“The premiers play a very important role in this process, labour plays an important role in this process, all stakeholders play a role in this process,” Carney said. “We consult with the premiers, take into account their views … (but) the decisions on trade are the decisions of the government of Canada, I’m the Prime Minister, ultimately I’m responsible, with the cabinet, for those decisions.”

While Carney is hopeful a deal can be reached, he didn’t hesitate to defend walking away from the table when it became clear Canada’s sovereignty was at stake.

“The attitude of the United States in these discussions, and subsequently, has been one that core Canadian industries would either be subsidiaries effectively of the United States’ industries, or would put in place terms where those industries would be gradually wound down in Canada and wiped out, of course we are not going to accept those terms.”

Canada has since fired back at the United States with counter tariffs , but Carney still remains hopeful that cooler heads may prevail.

“There is a mutually beneficial deal, there were elements of that mutually beneficial deal that we were moving towards … but we never viewed that we had that deal and it diverged towards the end, and at some point maybe it will converge again.”

stories.title: Calgary home with pro-Trump flags becomes vandalism target in cross-border trade war
stories.summary: The homeowner says while his life is in Canada, he's a strong supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Some Calgarians frustrated by the renewed U.S. tariff trade war appear to be taking out their anger on one pro-Trump home by using eggs, dog feces and online suggestions of arson.

The homeowner says while his life is in Canada, he’s a strong supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump. He calls the anger fundamentally offside.

“The position of some would be to say, ‘Hey, this guy, he doesn’t agree with what we agree in, politically (even though) he goes to work, he pays his taxes … (so) let’s run them out of town,’” the homeowner said in an interview.

“That’s not a good look in my opinion, in any democratic society.”

He spoke on the condition of anonymity, noting that the police have become involved, and he and his wife fear for their safety.

Since the recent attention, he said, many people have approached him positively, while others have egged the house and thrown bagged dog excrement onto the property. Some have made comments on social media suggesting torching their home.

A spokesperson for Calgary police confirmed they had received a report of vandalism on Aug. 23, and that the homeowners were concerned about online attacks, but they say there were not sufficient grounds to support criminal charges.

The homeowners say they were born and grew up in the United States, moving to Canada for work reasons more than a decade ago.

Their home near Calgary’s downtown displays two large pro-Trump flags. A massive American flag often hangs from their balcony.

“We’re proud Americans, we support the president, and that was the idea behind the flags,” the homeowner said, stating the intention was originally to showcase their patriotism. He said it has developed into a sign of acceptance of conservatives who, he believes, have had their views suppressed and marginalized.

One of the pro-Trump flags says Trump: Make America Great Again, while the other says Trump 2028: Third Term and Beyond. The homeowner says while he supports the Trump administration’s policies — such as taxes, immigration and spending — the reference to 2028 is a joke given that presidents cannot, under the U.S. Constitution, serve a third term.

It’s not the first time his home has been in the firing line, he said. A retaining wall was defaced with graffiti during the 2024 U.S. presidential election that saw Trump defeat Democrat challenger Kamala Harris.

He said the pro-Trump flags were up long before the tariff war, which began just over a week ago, when the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about $28 billion in Canadian exports. Canada has responded with its own tariffs, which take effect Sept. 8.

The Calgary house is not the only collateral damage. Last week, Trump signed an order changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America to hit back against sharp criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

Asked why they remain in Canada even with their support for the administration, the homeowner said it’s because they have built a life in the country.

Also, he said the trade fight, as with past trade fights, is fleeting. Canada and the U.S. will eventually “kiss and make up,” he said.

“It’s just a matter of when.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec government websites changing ‘Lake America’ back to Lake Ontario on maps
stories.summary: The Quebec government is taking steps to keep the name of Lake Ontario after President Trump signed an order to change lake's name to 'Lake America.'
stories.author: Joe Lofaro
paragraphs: It’s Lake Ontario, as far as the Quebec government is concerned.
For a brief period on Monday, users visiting the provincial transportation ministry’s interactive traffic map saw “Lake America” appear on their screen.
The change on Quebec511.info came after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order in the Oval Office last week to change the name of the smallest of the Great Lakes to “Lake America.”

A spokesperson for the Ministère des Transports et de la Mobilité durable said the name of the lake was changed because the map uses data from Google Maps. The online tech giant confirmed that Google Maps also changed the name of the lake because it relies on information from government sources, notably the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (Gnis).

“Depending on the regional settings applied by this provider, certain geographic names May vary, and a recent adjustment made by Google explains the unusual display observed,” wrote Émilie Lord, a transportation ministry spokesperson, in an email.
“The issue has been corrected. The official name, ‘Lake Ontario,’ is now displayed.”
Google has said, however, that users in Canada using Google Maps should still see Lake Ontario, and that only U.S. users would see “Lake America” after the company updated its maps on Saturday.
The Ministry of Transport isn’t the only government website to show the wrong name.

Quebec’s liquor control board, known as the Société des alcools du Québec (SAQ), told CTV News that it has asked its third-party provider “to make the correction on our website first thing this morning to revert the name to Lake Ontario.”
Former U.S. ambassador to Canada Gordon Giffin on the ‘Lake America’ fiasco and why he believes the name change will be reversed.
The maps change also affected the website of the Sqdc, the government-owned corporation that handles the sale of recreational cannabis.

“The naming issue on the maps used by the Sqdc was corrected on Monday morning. It was caused by a supplier, who was able to resolve the issue as soon as it was brought to their attention,” a spokesperson said in an email.
Name changed on other government maps
Several government agencies in Ontario, such as Metrolinx, HydroOne, and the Lcbo , also displayed “Lake America,” blaming third-party mapping services for the change. They later reversed the change.
Meanwhile, MapQuest has said it will refuse to change the name of Lake Ontario on its maps.

U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in an interview that Trump contacted Apple directly to force the company to change the name Lake Ontario to “Lake America” and that the change would happen very soon.
With files from CTV News’ Kayla Thompson and The Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. boaters warned to avoid floating island that has mystified experts
stories.summary: Geologist John Joseph Clague said when he first heard that a floating island, bigger than a football field, had been spotted on a lake in British Columbia's northern Interior, he dismissed it as an "AI stunt."
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Geologist John Joseph Clague said when he first heard that a floating island, bigger than a football field, had been spotted on a lake in British Columbia’s northern Interior, he dismissed it as an “AI stunt.”

But Clague — a professor of earth sciences at Simon Fraser University and an emeritus scientist of the Geological Survey of Canada — is now convinced that the island is very real, but is mystified by its origins.

Boaters have been being warned to stay off the island that reappeared on Monday on Williston Lake, the reservoir for the W.A.C. Bennett Dam, after BC Hydro confirmed its existence in mid-August but then lost track of it..

BC Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer says he initially thought reports of a floating island covered in trees on Williston Lake in northern British Columbia were a hoax, before satellite images confirmed its existence. It then vanished, but has now reappeared, 30 kilometres from where it was previously seen. (Sept. 1, 2026)

BC Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer said it had travelled about 30 kilometres, adding to the mystery surrounding the island that he theorized had been formed when it was lifted free by rising water levels in the reservoir.

Clague, who has previously worked around the Williston Lake area, was not convinced by that explanation. He said he had seen evidence of erosion along the lake, but “nowhere near that in scale.”

“There is erosion occurring, and trees do collapse into the lake, but they don’t kind of form this very large mat of forested material,” said Clague. “This is unusual. I’ve never heard of such a thing before.”

He said it also remained a mystery why the island had not broken apart after travelling so far.

“I think a lot of people view it as something that’s very thick, but it can’t be thick if it’s moving around the lake at speeds,” said Clague, “So, you know, it’s a curiosity.”

Rocky Avery shared images of the island that drew worldwide attention after it was spotted by a friend at the lake north of Avery’s hometown of Mackenzie last month.

He said the water under the island at the time was about 60 metres deep.

“When I saw the video, it was just kind of in awe because you can see from his boat — he was making the ripples, and you could see along the island it was all just going up and down, and it was actually real,” said Avery. “It was crazy.”

Avery notified BC Hydro and members of the Tsay Keh Dene First Nation of the discovery.

Gammer said he too initially thought the reports of a floating island covered in trees and foliage were a hoax when BC Hydro received them on Aug. 13.

“I checked internally and nobody that I have with contacts in the company had heard of this either. So, at the time, we basically thought it was maybe a hoax, and we didn’t give it much more attention,” said Gammer, manager of northern community relations with BC Hydro.

But a few days later, engineers with the Crown utility spotted it on satellite imagery in Finley Bay, near the centre of the lake.

“This is a rare occurrence, and certainly the first that we’ve heard of for Williston reservoir,” said Gammer.

He said they tried to track the island but it seemed to vanish, before it was spotted again on Monday against the shoreline where the Ospika River flows into the lake.

“It’s moved about 30 kilometres northwest on the reservoir into a more remote location,” said Gammer. “It looks like the island appears to be intact.”

Gammer said he also received a photo from a boater, providing double confirmation of the island’s reappearance. Based on satellite imagery, the island is about 140 metres long and about 70 metres wide, he added.

He said boaters should resist the urge to visit the island, theorizing that it was based on an unstable mass of logs and decaying debris that may have broken free from the shore when the lake recently filled for the first time since 2012.

Gammer said the island’s origin was not certain but it was normal for trees that fall into the reservoir to clump together in sheltered bays.

“You can imagine, like a tree falling down in the forest, and the trunk is laying flat, and over a long period of time, it starts to break down, and other plants, moss, and even trees start growing on top,” said Gammer.

The rising waters of the reservoir then could have lifted the mass free, calling it the “best theory” of how the island came to be.

Gammer said waves in the reservoir can become violent during a windstorm and he feared they could tear apart the mass of logs and woody debris.

“It’s just naturally unstable, and so it’s unsafe to climb onto the island or land a boat on it. It would be dangerous to do that,” he said.

BC Hydro would continue to monitor the island to see if it started moving again, Gammer said.

“I mean, there will be people who will probably want to study it and get close to it. So, there may be more information to come about the island as the weeks go by,” said Gammer.

Avery cheered news the island hadn’t sunk, after being told by members of the Tsay Keh Dene First Nation that they too had spotted it again.

“We’re just waiting for the water to calm down so we can take a jet boat and take a better look at it,” said Avery, adding a former chief from the nation would join the trip to inspect the island.

Avery said he had lived in the area for more than 48 years and never heard of anything like the island before.

He said he wanted the island to be named Rocky Island — “even though it’s not that rocky.”

Gammer said he also received a photo from a boater, providing double confirmation of the island’s reappearance. Based on satellite imagery, the island is about 140 metres long and about 70 metres wide, he added.

He said boaters should resist the urge to visit the island, theorizing that it was based on an unstable mass of logs and decaying debris that may have broken free from the shore when the lake recently filled for the first time since 2012.
Gammer said the island’s origin was not certain but it was normal for trees that fall into the reservoir to clump together in sheltered bays.

“You can imagine, like a tree falling down in the forest, and the trunk is laying flat, and over a long period of time, it starts to break down, and other plants, moss, and even trees start growing on top,” said Gammer.
The rising waters of the reservoir then could have lifted the mass free, calling it the “best theory” of how the island came to be.
Gammer said waves in the reservoir can become violent during a windstorm and he feared they could tear apart the mass of logs and woody debris.
“It’s just naturally unstable, and so it’s unsafe to climb onto the island or land a boat on it. It would be dangerous to do that,” he said.
BC Hydro would continue to monitor the island to see if it started moving again, Gammer said.
“I mean, there will be people who will probably want to study it and get close to it. So, there may be more information to come about the island as the weeks go by,” said Gammer.
Avery cheered news the island hadn’t sunk, after being told by members of the Tsay Keh Dene First Nation that they too had spotted it again.
“We’re just waiting for the water to calm down so we can take a jet boat and take a better look at it,” said Avery, adding a former chief from the nation would join the trip to inspect the island.
Avery said he had lived in the area for more than 48 years and never heard of anything like the island before.
He said he wanted the island to be named Rocky Island — “even though it’s not that rocky.”

stories.title: Élections Québec says it will send out voting information in French only to comply with language laws
stories.summary: This year’s documents will include a QR code for voters to access information online in English, spokesperson says
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
A group representing anglophones in Quebec is calling on the provincial elections authority to reverse its decision to only send out voter information in French.

Élections Québec said Tuesday that printed voter cards will only be available in French for the first time in its history, in order to comply with language laws.

In previous elections, voter information cards were printed in both English and French.

Spokesperson Julie St-Arnaud-Drolet said in an e-mail that Élections Québec must follow legislation adopted in 2022 making French the sole language of communication for public institutions. However, this year’s documents will include a QR code for voters to access information online in English, she added.

Indigenous voters and those eligible to receive English instructions must contact Élections Québec to request English information.

But Eva Ludvig, the director of a lobby group that represents the anglophone community in Quebec, says the new measures are creating unnecessary barriers for voters. She says Élections Québec, as a neutral and independent institution, should encourage maximum participation in democracy.

“I think this goes contrary to all that,” said Ludvig, the director of Talking Advocating Living in Quebec. “This limits participation. It marginalizes English speakers. It limits participation to those who aren’t adept at using technology.”

According to Statistics Canada, around five per cent – or roughly 400,000 voters in Quebec – only speak English. Ludvig says anglophone seniors, many of whom are unilingual, will be especially affected, especially if they don’t know how to scan a QR code.

St-Arnaud-Drolet said the elections authority will multiply its efforts to reach anglophone and allophone voters throughout the campaign period.

She said the agency repeatedly asked both the commissioner of the French language and the minister of the French language to be allowed to provide basic information in both languages during the election period, but “these efforts were unsuccessful.”

“We will run advertisements in English-language media … as well as on several websites and online streaming platforms, such as Spotify,” she said.

But Ludvig says those measures are not enough. She worries the new directives could prevent anglophones from showing up at the ballot, especially as Quebec has flip-flopped over who can access services in English since it expanded its language laws.

“All voters need to be treated equally and have equal access to clear information as to the process,” she said. “This is fundamentally an issue of democratic participation, not language politics.”

Duff Conacher, co-founder of Democracy Watch, agrees with Ludvig.

He says that not having printed materials hinders access to information, even if it can be found online. He says that the provincial election guide, which gives thorough information on voting options, is not as easy to read as a notice with the address of a polling station.

“It’s a bad idea to put up barriers to any voters voting, and this is a barrier,” he said. “People are not being mailed printed information directly in the language that they speak and read.”

Donal Gill, a political-science professor at Dawson College, says that while he understands the concerns of the anglophone community, he does not expect to see a drop in voter turnout as a result of the new rules. He says most anglophones in Quebec are functionally bilingual.

“Political parties have very well-oiled machines to make sure that older voters get to the ballot box,” he said. “So I think that will fill any gaps there.”

He said those pressuring Élections Québec are “barking up the wrong tree,” as the agency’s changes are in line with the law and not meant to favour any one political party.

However, he warns against favouring the protection of the French language over making democracy as accessible as possible.

“The law is written oftentimes in a kind of a clumsy way, and this is one of the ways in which it’s going to take effect,” he said. “It’s a furtherance of a process that’s been ongoing that can be debated, but it can also be reversed if a different government came in with different priorities.”

Voters should receive information cards by Sept. 18, ahead of the election on Oct. 5, according to Élections Québec.

stories.title: Ontario to remove stretch of Toronto bike lane after recent court win
stories.summary: Work will begin ‘almost immediately’ to remove a stretch of the Bloor Street bike lane east of Islington station, minister Prabmeet Sarkaria says
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
A stretch of bike lane on a major Toronto road is set to be removed, Ontario’s transportation minster said Tuesday as the province pressed ahead with its plan to overhaul the cycling network over the city’s objections after a recent court win.

The province said it had put out a bid request to study and design options to restore vehicle traffic on bike lane sections of Bloor Street, Yonge Street, Avenue Road and around Queen’s Park.

The successful bidder will also be expected to look for ways to retain or reconfigure the bike lanes, “where they make sense and do not make gridlock worse,” the province said in a news release.

In the meantime, work will begin “almost immediately” to remove a stretch of the Bloor Street bike lane east of Islington station, minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said. He did not say how much would be removed and his office did not immediately respond to a request for details.
