stories.title: ‘Immediately stop using’: Thousands of walking pads sold at Canadian Tire recalled
stories.summary: Health Canada has announced a recall for an electric walking pad sold at Canadian Tire due to an 'electrical hazard.'
stories.author: Aarjavee Raaj
paragraphs: Health Canada has announced a recall for an electric walking pad sold at Canadian Tire due to an “electrical hazard.”
The recall involves the PowerG Walking Pad, Model Number 499-4052 (UPC 8 46325 03115 8), the federal agency said in a recall notice posted last week.
“The affected product does not meet the requirements of the relevant standard for this product category, which poses an electrical hazard,” the notice said.
The federal agency has asked customers to “immediately stop using” the recalled product and return it to a Canadian Tire store for a refund or in-store credit.
The company reported that 7,000 units of the affected products were sold in Canada between January 2025 to July 2026.
There have been no reports of incidents or injuries in Canada, as of Aug. 10, the notice added.
Customers are advised to contact Canadian Tire by telephone or visit the company’s website for more information.

stories.title: ‘Dream job: Retirement’: Canadian little leaguer goes viral after World Series
stories.summary: A 12-year-old from Vancouver is going viral after his appearance at the Little League World Series. And it's not for his playing.
stories.author: Shannon Paterson
paragraphs: “It’s like a dream come true. It’s a baseball paradise, basically. You play on the best fields in the world, and you get interact with other countries,” said Huang, who plays for Vancouver’s Little Mountain Baseball.
The games are televised, and the broadcast crew at Espn wanted to learn a little bit about every player.
“There’s a survey, they ask you about your favourite foods, your favourite actors and stuff like that. One of the questions was, what’s your dream job?” said Huang.
During an at bat against South Korea, his answer appeared on screen. Daniel’s dream job? Retirement.
“I did not know that is what he said on his answer, retirement,” said Daniel’s coach Brad Dorwart. “Someone sent that in our group chat, and I just rolled my eyes. Of course he did.”
“He’s always the guy who makes jokes,” said Daniel’s mom Nicky. “He always comes up with the response that is very not typical. So, I wasn’t super shocked, but I also had a good laugh.”
After Barstool Sports posted about Daniel saying “This Kid Gets It” to its nearly seven million X followers, Huang was internet famous.
“And still today, people are sending me links and news where Daniel’s name is mentioned. It’s actually pretty cool,” said his mom.

“It was pretty sad to have such an amazing season come to an end, but I think it was a really good game. They had pretty good sportsmanship and it showed that they worked hard to get here, so they deserved it,” Daniel said.

“One of your jobs as a coach is to teach them the skills, but also let them understand that it’s OK, the sun will come up tomorrow. It’s a game. We all want to win the game, but it’s a game,” said Dorwart.
For Daniel, it was the end of an era. This was his last season of little league.
“He’s definitely retired from Little League, but not from work,” joked his coach. “You have to start before you retire.”
And Daniel’s not planning on starting work anytime soon.
“It’s just best if I don’t have to work these next couple of years,” he said. “Just enjoy and relax.”

stories.title: The election campaign to replace Macron in France is heating up as the summer vacation season ends
stories.summary: Here’s what to know at these early stages of what promises to be among the most consequential leadership votes anywhere in the world next year, and which comes as France is grappling with multiple challenges, including the disruptions of Donald Trump’s U.S. presidency.
stories.author: The Associated Press
paragraphs: Paris — With the end of France’s summer vacation season, the election campaign to replace Emmanuel Macron as president next May is bursting to life.

An unusually large and broad field of candidates is forming to lead the European Union’s largest country, its second-largest economy and only nuclear-armed power, their appetites whetted by the fact that Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive presidential term himself.
Some won’t get the support they will need from sponsors and their political camps to be on the starting line when the first round of voting is held on April 18.

Still, a crowded field could boost far-right candidate Marine Le Pen — just as it did for Jean-Marie Le Pen, her father, in 2002. The record 16 candidates splintered the first-round vote, creating an electoral earthquake when the elder Le Pen qualified for the decisive second round.

Socialist Party leader Olivier Faure became the latest to declare his candidacy this weekend. He joined more than two dozen others who say that they intend to stand or are contemplating a run in 2027.

Here’s what to know at these early stages of what promises to be among the most consequential leadership votes anywhere in the world next year, and which comes as France is grappling with multiple challenges, including the disruptions of Donald Trump’s U.S. presidency.
Polls suggest Le Pen is the candidate to beat

After decades of trying, first by her father and then her, Marine Le Pen’s fourth campaign for the French presidency is already shaping up as the strongest opportunity for her nationalist, anti-immigration National Rally party to take power.

Such an outcome would rock the European Union, putting a politician, who has long been hostile to the bloc of 27 nations and many of their collective rules and policies, in charge of one of the EU’s most important countries.

“It’s clearly a crucial election, just because the far right might win this one and it never was the case before,” said Gilles Ivaldi, a researcher at the Paris-based Sciences Po university who specializes in populism and radical right-wing politics.
“With Le Pen as president, we know that the EU will be weakened. To what extent we don’t know, but we know she’s against the EU,” he said. “This would create a lot of instability.”

Polls have for months suggested that Le Pen is the front-runner and could possibly sail into the winner-takes-all runoff on May 2 as the first-round vote leader, which would be a first for her. She trailed Macron in the 2017 and 2022 first-round voting and then lost decisively to him in round two.

It was a giant upset when her father qualified in 2002 for round two. His associations with people who collaborated with France’s Nazi occupiers in the Second World War and his multiple hate-speech convictions, including Holocaust denial, made him anathema to many voters.

This time, it would a giant upset if his 58-year-old daughter doesn’t advance. Marine Le Pen has worked for years to distance herself from his extremism. She’s already begun reaping the fruits at the ballot box: Since 2024, her National Rally has become the largest party in parliament’s powerful lower house.

She got another boost in July when a Paris appeals court cleared her path for another presidential campaign, by shortening a ban on seeking elected office that a lower court had handed down to Le Pen for embezzlement.
Behind Le Pen, the picture is uncertain
With Le Pen widely expected to secure one of the spots in the decisive second-round duel, the battle for the other is becoming hard fought, its outcome highly uncertain.

For now, Le Pen’s strongest opponents include veteran far-left and anti-capitalist firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who hopes to make his first runoff after placing third in 2022 and fourth in 2017 and 2012, and two former prime ministers under Macron — Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, both centrists.

Other prominent possibilities include conservative former Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau and multiple figures from the mainstream left, including European Parliament lawmaker Raphaël Glucksmann and Ecologists leader Marine Tondelier, campaigning before the expected birth within weeks of her second child.

Those seven took part in a debate last week at the storied Roland Garros tennis arena in Paris. In what served as an unofficial starting gun for the campaign, they batted around proposals for fixing some of France’s economic problems. Some took shots at Le Pen, which she hit back.

The potential scenario of a Le Pen-Mélenchon second-round duel that polls suggest could end with a Le Pen victory could ultimately prompt some candidates to drop out, to concentrate votes behind mainstream alternatives.
“What we don’t know is who’s going to be against her” in a possible second-round matchup, Ivaldi said. “The more the fragmentation, the more the chances that Mélenchon will be that person.”
Wars, Trump and Macron’s mixed legacy hang over the election
No French presidential election campaign this century has taken place in such choppy waters.

The Iran war has hit France’s stagnating economy with higher energy costs. The war in Ukraine has Paris worrying that Russia might next target one of France’s Nato allies, a potential path to wider conflict.

Trump’s presidency is rattling French faith in the trans-Atlantic alliance. The manufacturing and exporting might of China and the artificial intelligence revolution are heightening concerns of France being left behind economically and technologically.
But France’s mounting and increasingly expensive public debt is narrowing the financial room for maneuver that Macron’s successor will inherit.
Many voters also blame Macron for France’s woes and took their anger to the streets during his two-term presidency.

Ultimately, the election May hinge on whether voters want to upset the established order by propelling Le Pen and Mélenchon into a duel of the right and left extremes, or will back a more mainstream candidate, as a possibly safer option.
“It will be quite interesting to see which of these two forces will win in the end,” Ivaldi said. “These are two different forces, two antagonistic forces that are playing against one another.”
John Leicester, The Associated Press

Trump’s presidency is rattling French faith in the trans-Atlantic alliance. The manufacturing and exporting might of China and the artificial intelligence revolution are heightening concerns of France being left behind economically and technologically.

But France’s mounting and increasingly expensive public debt is narrowing the financial room for maneuver that Macron’s successor will inherit.

Many voters also blame Macron for France’s woes and took their anger to the streets during his two-term presidency.

Ultimately, the election May hinge on whether voters want to upset the established order by propelling Le Pen and Mélenchon into a duel of the right and left extremes, or will back a more mainstream candidate, as a possibly safer option.

“It will be quite interesting to see which of these two forces will win in the end,” Ivaldi said. “These are two different forces, two antagonistic forces that are playing against one another.”

John Leicester, The Associated Press

stories.title: Members of Toronto cancer community shocked by abrupt closing of local Gilda’s Club chapter
stories.summary: Club offered services for cancer patients and their families, including group therapy
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
paragraphs: Three years ago, kindergarten teacher Laura Hughes learned she had breast cancer. Three days after her diagnosis, she contacted Gilda’s Club Greater Toronto, hoping to access support.
The weekly online group that she found through Gilda’s quickly became a lifeline during her medical journey.

She began attending virtual sessions on Friday afternoons, which followed her chemotherapy appointments earlier in the day. Through the group, she connected with other patients grappling with cancer at a time when she felt particularly alone.
“I could just safely connect with my friends in this group, and they knew all the right questions to ask because they had all been there that same week,” she said.
Like the other Gilda’s Club chapters across the United States and Canada, the Greater Toronto club offered services for cancer patients and their families, including group therapy.
It abruptly announced on Aug. 21 that it had ceased operations after nearly 25 years, with no explanation given.
Days later, on Aug. 24, records show the organization filed for bankruptcy. It is scheduled to meet with creditors on Sept. 10.
Patients who recently received therapy through Gilda’s Club Greater Toronto have been directed to other resources, including the organization’s Simcoe Muskoka chapter.
Last week, the sister club said it would support individuals and families affected by the Toronto closing.
“Our focus is on helping people feel welcomed, supported and connected to the resources that are right for them,” executive director Lana Hann said.
Ms. Hughes was among the patients saddened to learn of the shutdown.
She described how the members of her online group later forged in-person connections and even showed up for each other at the hospital.
“They would sit with me in the waiting room, as I would for them,” she said. “It was pretty amazing.”
Three years after meeting online, they continue to see each other regularly and have a group chat they call “Friday Friends,” a nod to those weekly Zoom sessions that first drew them together.
Gilda’s Club Greater Toronto closed weeks after the group lost its charitable status with the Canada Revenue Agency.
CRA requires charities to comply with the Income Tax Act, including filing annual returns.
The agency’s website shows the organization’s status was revoked on July 11 after it missed a deadline to file a return. The group cited the loss of its charitable status in its bankruptcy filing.
A representative for the organization could not be reached for comment through an e-mail address listed on its website. An automatic reply said the account is no longer monitored.
“We are deeply grateful to everyone who has been part of this community and for the compassion, generosity, and sense of connection fostered over the years,” it said.

Gilda’s Club works to address the emotional and social changes that result from patients’ cancer diagnoses. Cancer specialists say patients and loved ones may experience emotional challenges, such as depression and anxiety, and barriers in interpersonal relationships.

The organization was named after the late actress Gilda Radner, who began her career in Canada in the early 1970s at the comedy theatre Second City Toronto. Ms. Radner died in 1989, three years after her own diagnosis with ovarian cancer.

Garrett Harrison, who works in arts management for the City of Oakville, accessed group therapy online through Gilda’s Club Greater Toronto after his mother was diagnosed with ovarian cancer in August, 2025.

He first learned about the organization’s work through his time at Second City. In January, Mr. Harrison began attending weekly therapy sessions online on Wednesday nights, alongside other caregivers.

Over eight weeks, around eight to 10 people joined the sessions and shared their experiences. The discussion was guided by a psychotherapist. The caregivers found it helpful to access online therapy while meeting loved ones’ medical needs.

Mr. Harrison said he lost his 72-year-old mother, Liz Zavitz , on Friday, March 6, before the last scheduled Wednesday night group session. Ms. Zavitz, a devoted educator and theatre enthusiast, died just 200 days after her diagnosis.
Her son, an only child, decided he would attend that concluding therapy session, even though he found it very difficult.
“I was very quiet,” he said. ”I just wanted to show my support."
Mr. Harrison also hoped to access grief support services through Gilda’s Club. He said learning about the club’s closing through an e-mail was “very disheartening.”
“I’ve kept in touch with a few people from my group, and we were all very confused and shocked,” he said, adding they too maintain a group chat on WhatsApp.
Other organizations that support cancer patients and their families were also saddened to learn of the club ceasing operations.
On Instagram, Childhood Cancer Canada called Gilda’s a valued partner and a place where families could find “connection and community during some of the most unimaginable moments of their lives.”

Brenda Delodder, chief executive officer of the Wellspring Cancer Support Foundation, also offered support to volunteers and staff. Beyond treatment, she said, individuals need to be able to access understanding, guidance and community.
Mr. Harrison echoed this sentiment and said he hopes the situation with Gilda’s Club Greater Toronto can be resolved.
If not, he added, ”I hope others are able to step up and fill the hole that will be left with all the families.”
With reports from Stephanie Chambers in Toronto
Editor’s note: A photo caption accompanying this article incorrectly named Garrett Harrison’s mother. Her name was Liz Zavitz.

stories.title: For Hamiltonians battling addiction, peer support is a dose of empathy
stories.summary: Pilot program at St. Joseph’s Healthcare gives recovered drug users a chance to help others
stories.author: Molly Hayes, Photography by Laura Proctor
stories.content:
Perched on a hospital bed on the third floor of St. Joseph’s Healthcare in Hamilton , Madison Tatlock remembers watching her boyfriend nod off in a recliner there, after the birth of their baby 3½ years ago.

He was high, she remembers – and she remembers getting him to sneak in drugs for her, too, before he fell asleep against the freezer in the obstetrics unit’s communal kitchen and got kicked out.

For the most part, Ms. Tatlock acknowledges, her memories of that postpartum period are foggy, and tainted by shame. She and her boyfriend, Matthew Cheeseman, were both well over a decade into active addiction at the time, both heavily using fentanyl and crystal meth.

The then-29-year-old couldn’t be trusted alone with her baby. Mr. Cheeseman, then 37, wasn’t allowed into the hospital, period, after the freezer incident, unless he was escorted by his mother. Ms. Tatlock recalls how family members would visit with baby gifts, and then just sit there, silently.

“Everyone was just really sad,” she says.

But just a few years later, the pair are back roaming the same hospital’s halls – this time with employee badges. They are members of a novel, hospital-wide peer support program that helps patients struggling with substance use, from admission through discharge and beyond.

For two days this summer, The Globe and Mail was granted rare access to the team, shadowing Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman throughout the hospital to get a glimpse of their work firsthand.

The four-year pilot project, which launched in March, 2025, is being funded through a $4.3-million grant from Health Canada’s Substance Use and Addictions Program .

A year and a half in, colleagues say the project has not only filled a critical gap in care for some of the hospital’s most vulnerable patients, but has also empowered those providing the support with a sense of purpose. Since its inception, the peer support team has logged more than 14,000 patient interactions, across virtually every unit of the hospital.

“It’s quite incredible when you see the impact that this small team is having,” says Brooke Cowell, the hospital’s chief nursing executive and executive vice-president of clinical operations.

The patients they see are not necessarily admitted because of substance use, Tim O’Shea, an infectious disease specialist and co-head of the hospital’s addictions medicine program, explains.

“They could be in hospital because they have had a heart attack, a stroke, or need gallbladder surgery,” he says. “But the substance use piece is going to play into the quality of care that they get, because if it’s ignored, obviously that’s going to get in the way of them getting the care that they need.”

Discrimination and stigma are still deeply ingrained within the health care system , and sanctimony from providers has historically left many people – especially those who are homeless or use drugs – reluctant to seek care at all.

As big Canadian cities and small towns alike continue to struggle with converging crises of housing affordability, mental health and addictions, peer workers have become critical in helping to build back support and trust.

“We’re trying to provide good care to people, and this is a way to help provide good care – by making people more comfortable, more trusting,” Dr. O’Shea says.

“It provides better outcomes for the patients.”

Karen Haan, Darrin Marchand and Joseph Snelgrove are among hundreds of patients that the peer-support team has helped at St. Joseph’s so far. The pilot project is about a year-and-a-half old.

At the start of their shift one Monday morning in July, Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman join their team – which also includes social workers, physicians and a part-time nurse – around a boardroom table. It’s time to go over their patient list, which on this day includes roughly 10 people.

There’s a woman who had been admitted the day before, in psychosis. She was too agitated to speak with support workers when she first arrived, but they are hoping she might be up for a visit today.

There’s another patient they’ve been working with for months, since his admission for surgery on both knees, due to septic arthritis. He is just about ready to go home – but needs help getting wheelchair accommodations for his apartment before he can be discharged.

There’s a man who was transported from the local jail, and is in withdrawal in the ICU.

Another man on the list was admitted a few days ago, after an overdose, and is being treated for a serious blood infection. Despite his condition, he is itching to leave; he is worried about losing his bed – and the belongings he left behind – at a local homeless shelter.

Leaving against medical advice is one of the main things the team is trying to prevent, because they know these patients will likely wind up back in the emergency room, usually sicker than when they left.

The peers have conducted hundreds of surveys with patients so far. Virtually all of the nearly 200 patients they spoke with upon intake reported having previous hospitalizations. The average number of hospitalizations in the past year was 4.52 – and the average number of times they left against medical advice was 1.36. The top reasons patients gave for having left early included drug cravings and withdrawal symptoms, but also not feeling welcome or supported within the hospital – which is what the team is hoping to prevent.

During The Globe’s visit, that support takes on different forms. Sometimes a peer worker simply pops by a patient’s room to say hello, and to let them know they’ve been where they are. Other times they take the patient out for a cigarette break, or help co-ordinate a visit from a relative or friend. One former patient they are still working with recalls how touched he was that when he grew bored and restless in the hospital during his months-long stay, they were able to bring him his guitar.

As they build relationships throughout their patients’ stays, Ms. Tatlock says they have been able to connect some people with community resources, assist them with replacing their government IDs, and even help them secure or hang onto housing.

The team follows a harm-reduction model, meaning no one is pressed into addiction treatment. If a patient does want to use drugs, the peers will try to ensure they are doing so safely and offsite. But the majority of patients they’ve worked with – 86 per cent of 187 patients specifically surveyed about their substance use – said they were ready to make a change.

The team works with substance-use physicians such as Dr. O’Shea, who can prescribe medications, such as suboxone, to ease pain or withdrawal symptoms.

In at least a dozen cases she can think of – the ones that make her eyes well up, just thinking about them – Ms. Tatlock says they have been able to get patients into treatment programs. In at least five cases, the programs were the very same ones that she and Mr. Cheeseman credit with saving their own lives.

Mr. Cheeseman, playing hockey on his street, gets invited by a neighbour to a backyard concert while Ms. Tatlock tidies up at home. The couple have lived in this house since May. They were homeless four years ago when they learned they were expecting a child.

Back in August, 2022, when Ms. Tatlock saw the two red lines pop up on her pregnancy test, she panicked.

She and Mr. Cheeseman were both homeless at the time, and had not known each other long. They were both deeply unwell and in survival mode.

The couple turned to Dr. O’Shea and peer support worker Marcie McIlveen, whom they’d gotten to know through their outreach work in the community .

With their help, Ms. Tatlock was admitted into St. Joseph’s Inpatient Program for Substance Use in Pregnancy (iPROSPR), where she attempted four different times, unsuccessfully, to titrate off the drugs. They got her a prenatal bed at the YWCA.

Social worker Sarah Simpson, who worked with Ms. Tatlock at the time on the women’s health, newborn and pediatric care unit, remembers her as one of the sickest patients ever admitted to the program. Her addiction was just so severe.

At one point, while Ms. Tatlock was in the hospital during her pregnancy, Mr. Cheeseman was admitted to another floor after suffering from a stroke – his second in only a few years. He’d also previously had open-heart surgery and a pacemaker installed, and had been hospitalized multiple times after overdoses.

“I’ve been all over this hospital,” he remembers today, shaking his head.

It was Mr. Cheeseman who got sober first. When he checked into a detox centre in Sarnia, Ont., in the fall of 2023, Ms. Tatlock – still high and totally paranoid – remembers thinking he was lying and cheating on her.

But then he graduated to a transitional program. And then a sober living house, St. Stephen’s House in London.

As the months passed, and he talked more and more about his hopes for their little family, she realized he was really doing it this time – and began wondering if she could do it, too. By January, 2024, just before her baby’s first birthday, she did.

Though their baby had gone into foster care after leaving the hospital, they kept up visits, and eventually Mr. Cheeseman was even able to take the baby on his own to visit Ms. Tatlock, in treatment. They’d go on stroller walks. Take the baby to the library. Slowly, a new life came into view. By the time the baby was 2, they had regained full custody.

They got an apartment across the street from a big park. Mr. Cheeseman’s mom helped cover their rent while they were on social assistance.

But even with the mountainous task of achieving sobriety behind them, the two new parents had trouble picturing their next steps. Neither had worked in years. They both had criminal records. Who would hire them?

paragraphs: Perched on a hospital bed on the third floor of St. Joseph’s Healthcare in Hamilton , Madison Tatlock remembers watching her boyfriend nod off in a recliner there, after the birth of their baby 3½ years ago.
He was high, she remembers – and she remembers getting him to sneak in drugs for her, too, before he fell asleep against the freezer in the obstetrics unit’s communal kitchen and got kicked out.

For the most part, Ms. Tatlock acknowledges, her memories of that postpartum period are foggy, and tainted by shame. She and her boyfriend, Matthew Cheeseman, were both well over a decade into active addiction at the time, both heavily using fentanyl and crystal meth.

The then-29-year-old couldn’t be trusted alone with her baby. Mr. Cheeseman, then 37, wasn’t allowed into the hospital, period, after the freezer incident, unless he was escorted by his mother. Ms. Tatlock recalls how family members would visit with baby gifts, and then just sit there, silently.
“Everyone was just really sad,” she says.

But just a few years later, the pair are back roaming the same hospital’s halls – this time with employee badges. They are members of a novel, hospital-wide peer support program that helps patients struggling with substance use, from admission through discharge and beyond.
For two days this summer, The Globe and Mail was granted rare access to the team, shadowing Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman throughout the hospital to get a glimpse of their work firsthand.
The four-year pilot project, which launched in March, 2025, is being funded through a $4.3-million grant from Health Canada’s Substance Use and Addictions Program .

A year and a half in, colleagues say the project has not only filled a critical gap in care for some of the hospital’s most vulnerable patients, but has also empowered those providing the support with a sense of purpose. Since its inception, the peer support team has logged more than 14,000 patient interactions, across virtually every unit of the hospital.
“It’s quite incredible when you see the impact that this small team is having,” says Brooke Cowell, the hospital’s chief nursing executive and executive vice-president of clinical operations.
The patients they see are not necessarily admitted because of substance use, Tim O’Shea, an infectious disease specialist and co-head of the hospital’s addictions medicine program, explains.

“They could be in hospital because they have had a heart attack, a stroke, or need gallbladder surgery,” he says. “But the substance use piece is going to play into the quality of care that they get, because if it’s ignored, obviously that’s going to get in the way of them getting the care that they need.”

Discrimination and stigma are still deeply ingrained within the health care system , and sanctimony from providers has historically left many people – especially those who are homeless or use drugs – reluctant to seek care at all.

As big Canadian cities and small towns alike continue to struggle with converging crises of housing affordability, mental health and addictions, peer workers have become critical in helping to build back support and trust.
“We’re trying to provide good care to people, and this is a way to help provide good care – by making people more comfortable, more trusting,” Dr. O’Shea says.
“It provides better outcomes for the patients.”
Karen Haan, Darrin Marchand and Joseph Snelgrove are among hundreds of patients that the peer-support team has helped at St. Joseph’s so far. The pilot project is about a year-and-a-half old.

At the start of their shift one Monday morning in July, Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman join their team – which also includes social workers, physicians and a part-time nurse – around a boardroom table. It’s time to go over their patient list, which on this day includes roughly 10 people.
There’s a woman who had been admitted the day before, in psychosis. She was too agitated to speak with support workers when she first arrived, but they are hoping she might be up for a visit today.

There’s another patient they’ve been working with for months, since his admission for surgery on both knees, due to septic arthritis. He is just about ready to go home – but needs help getting wheelchair accommodations for his apartment before he can be discharged.
There’s a man who was transported from the local jail, and is in withdrawal in the ICU.

Another man on the list was admitted a few days ago, after an overdose, and is being treated for a serious blood infection. Despite his condition, he is itching to leave; he is worried about losing his bed – and the belongings he left behind – at a local homeless shelter.

Leaving against medical advice is one of the main things the team is trying to prevent, because they know these patients will likely wind up back in the emergency room, usually sicker than when they left.

The peers have conducted hundreds of surveys with patients so far. Virtually all of the nearly 200 patients they spoke with upon intake reported having previous hospitalizations. The average number of hospitalizations in the past year was 4.52 – and the average number of times they left against medical advice was 1.36. The top reasons patients gave for having left early included drug cravings and withdrawal symptoms, but also not feeling welcome or supported within the hospital – which is what the team is hoping to prevent.

During The Globe’s visit, that support takes on different forms. Sometimes a peer worker simply pops by a patient’s room to say hello, and to let them know they’ve been where they are. Other times they take the patient out for a cigarette break, or help co-ordinate a visit from a relative or friend. One former patient they are still working with recalls how touched he was that when he grew bored and restless in the hospital during his months-long stay, they were able to bring him his guitar.

As they build relationships throughout their patients’ stays, Ms. Tatlock says they have been able to connect some people with community resources, assist them with replacing their government IDs, and even help them secure or hang onto housing.

The team follows a harm-reduction model, meaning no one is pressed into addiction treatment. If a patient does want to use drugs, the peers will try to ensure they are doing so safely and offsite. But the majority of patients they’ve worked with – 86 per cent of 187 patients specifically surveyed about their substance use – said they were ready to make a change.
The team works with substance-use physicians such as Dr. O’Shea, who can prescribe medications, such as suboxone, to ease pain or withdrawal symptoms.

In at least a dozen cases she can think of – the ones that make her eyes well up, just thinking about them – Ms. Tatlock says they have been able to get patients into treatment programs. In at least five cases, the programs were the very same ones that she and Mr. Cheeseman credit with saving their own lives.

Mr. Cheeseman, playing hockey on his street, gets invited by a neighbour to a backyard concert while Ms. Tatlock tidies up at home. The couple have lived in this house since May. They were homeless four years ago when they learned they were expecting a child.
Back in August, 2022, when Ms. Tatlock saw the two red lines pop up on her pregnancy test, she panicked.
She and Mr. Cheeseman were both homeless at the time, and had not known each other long. They were both deeply unwell and in survival mode.
The couple turned to Dr. O’Shea and peer support worker Marcie McIlveen, whom they’d gotten to know through their outreach work in the community .

With their help, Ms. Tatlock was admitted into St. Joseph’s Inpatient Program for Substance Use in Pregnancy (iPROSPR), where she attempted four different times, unsuccessfully, to titrate off the drugs. They got her a prenatal bed at the YWCA.

Social worker Sarah Simpson, who worked with Ms. Tatlock at the time on the women’s health, newborn and pediatric care unit, remembers her as one of the sickest patients ever admitted to the program. Her addiction was just so severe.

At one point, while Ms. Tatlock was in the hospital during her pregnancy, Mr. Cheeseman was admitted to another floor after suffering from a stroke – his second in only a few years. He’d also previously had open-heart surgery and a pacemaker installed, and had been hospitalized multiple times after overdoses.
“I’ve been all over this hospital,” he remembers today, shaking his head.

Though their baby had gone into foster care after leaving the hospital, they kept up visits, and eventually Mr. Cheeseman was even able to take the baby on his own to visit Ms. Tatlock, in treatment. They’d go on stroller walks. Take the baby to the library. Slowly, a new life came into view. By the time the baby was 2, they had regained full custody.

stories.title: Volunteer program aims to comfort patients without loved ones in their final moments
stories.summary: No One Dies Alone pairs those who are nearing death and have no family or close friends available to sit with them with trained volunteers
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Sitting at the bedside of a dying man, Nanette Godbout flipped slowly through an illustrated book about life after death. Although the gentleman was unresponsive, Ms. Godbout said he managed to open his eyes, which drifted across the pages of The Next Place .

“The next place that I go will be as peaceful and familiar as a sleepy summer Sunday and a sweet, untroubled mind,” the book opens before detailing a gentle transition into the next realm. “There will be no room for darkness in that place of living light.”

Ms. Godbout, who volunteers her time sitting with strangers in Winnipeg who are nearing the end of their lives, has come to understand that death doesn’t follow a schedule. Nurses told her that it would likely be days before the man died, but he closed his eyes for the final time after the book was read aloud.

“It just seemed to speak to him,” Ms. Godbout said. “One would never know, but it’s just my intuition, my interpretation of what he was feeling. There was something in that book that I felt he maybe needed to hear.”

For roughly six years, Ms. Godbout, 59, has volunteered with No One Dies Alone, a program where trained volunteers provide comfort to individuals who are nearing death and have no family or close friends available to sit with them.

The program, which began in 2019, is run through the provincial charity Palliative Manitoba, and takes place at two Winnipeg locations that provide end-of-life care, Riverview Health Centre and Deer Lodge Centre.

The concept of No One Dies Alone, or NODA, was born in Eugene, Ore., in the 1980s. Sandra Clarke, a registered nurse working the night shift at Sacred Heart Medical Center, said a dying patient who could barely speak asked her to sit with him. She promised him that she would come back after making her rounds, but he died by the time she returned, Ms. Clarke explained in a 2013 interview with Mayo Clinic.

“The sense of frustration and anger was overwhelming. He had a simple wish that was easily granted, and I couldn’t do it,” she said, tears gathering in her eyes.

“I always say it’s a man whose name I have no idea, but it’s a man I’ll never forget.”

In 2001, Ms. Clarke’s No One Dies Alone program was founded, serving as the model for hundreds of chapters that have since launched across the United States, Canada and around the world, including in the United Kingdom and Singapore.

While each group operates independently, all have the same underlying mission, a hope made clear in its very name. That no one dies alone.

In places where it is available, these volunteers make it so health care workers can focus solely on medical care. But service availability does vary, especially in rural and remote regions, making it difficult at times to fulfill every patient’s last wish.

Asked how she became a volunteer with NODA Manitoba, Ms. Godbout said it traces back to her first encounter with death.

She was just a teenager when her aunt died suddenly, and the adults in her life were so consumed with their own grief that she was left to navigate hers alone. The death, for many years, haunted a young Ms. Godbout, who was left with uncomfortable, difficult questions about her own finite existence.

Rather than drown in those feelings, the lifelong educator decided to confront them, beginning an enduring journey demystifying death and dying. She is trained as an end-of-life doula and has a master’s degree in education, with a specialization in grief and bereavement, and another one in counselling.

Through schooling, Ms. Godbout took a 10-week compassionate care course offered through Palliative Manitoba, a prerequisite for any volunteer with the organization who supports individuals with life-limiting illnesses and the bereaved.

It covers topics such as spiritual care and how to differentiate between spirituality and specific religious beliefs, end-of-life ethical issues and how to comfort the dying.

Her volunteer work started soon after, first as a co-facilitator with children’s grief groups, then with the telephone bereavement program and as an end-of-life companion, supporting people with an incurable illness and their families. In 2019, she raised her hand to join NODA and has since been called to the bedsides of 16 individuals.

“Being with someone at the end of life is like standing in a doorway between two worlds. It feels like being present for a birth in that we both stand at opposite ends of the same sacred mystery,” Ms. Godbout said.

“At a birth, we watch someone take their first breath, and at death, we may witness their last. And in each case, we’re powerless to control the moment itself. All we can do is provide care and comfort and support.”

Despite the emotional weight of being a NODA volunteer, Kathleen Williamson, Palliative Manitoba’s end-of-life volunteer co-ordinator, said they have not had difficulties finding people willing to step up.

She said they have about 40 volunteers, all of whom have varying availabilities to take on bedside vigils. Typically, volunteers are called to sit with people who are expected to die in the next 24 to 72 hours, typically taking on three-hour shifts between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.

In addition to the completion of the compassionate care course, volunteers are required to have enhanced criminal-record checks, provide personal references and complete additional training.

Still, some applicants are denied for various reasons – for example, if they have recently experienced a personal loss and are still grieving, Ms. Williamson explained.

Most often, people nearing the end of life refer themselves for NODA, but family or a power of attorney can also make a referral. Referral forms, Ms. Williamson said, detail the individual’s cognitive and mental state, comfort with touch, their cultural or religious background and any other relevant details.

For example, someone may write about their love for classical music, wanting the Bible read to them or having their hand held.

Ms. Godbout has what she calls a “vigil bag” that she can pack quickly to leave with a moment’s notice. Inside are books on life and death, some religious, with sticky notes peeking out of their pages, which are filled with highlights and scribbles. There are also essential oils and a portable speaker to play gentle music.

She prefers to drive in silence to vigils and purposefully parks her vehicle a distance away, giving herself time to mentally transition before sitting at an individual’s bedside. She always introduces herself, whether the person is responsive or not, as a “new friend who has come to spend some time with them.”

What happens next varies. Sometimes they pray or read a book. Sometimes they listen to music or sit in silence, Ms. Godbout’s hand gently resting on theirs.

“It’s the act of consciously bearing witness to their transition, and so I try to offer a calm, loving and safe environment so the individual can pass away on their own terms and timeline,” she said.

When she leaves, Ms. Godbout says a special prayer for the individual and their life, thanking them for allowing her into that sacred space.

She said that through “befriending” death, she has healed her teenage self and unearthed a passion to provide comfort to others who must confront death themselves.

“I have been so inspired to live more deeply.”

Care Between the Lines was a summer series that introduced you to volunteers in health care who fill gaps and provide compassion in a system that can be isolating and scary. This was the final instalment.

stories.title: London Transit seeks $2M in budget funding amid rising fuel costs, tariffs
stories.summary: London Transit is asking the city for an additional $2 million in funding for the 2027 budget to increase its service hours and keep up with the rising cost pressures from the rise in diesel fuel costs and U.S. tariffs.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London Transit is asking the city for an additional $2 million in funding for the 2027 budget to increase its service hours and keep up with the rising cost pressures from the rise in diesel fuel costs and U.S. tariffs.
· Posted: Sep 01, 2026 5:22 AM EDT | Last Updated: September 1

The London Transit Commission (LTC) is asking the city for a $2 million funding boost for its 2027 budget to increase its service hours and keep up with rising cost pressures stemming from the price of fuel and U.S. tariffs.
The city politician-led commission says it's going to advocate to the provincial and federal governments for financial support as transit agencies deal with these impacts.

"Given the rising fuel costs and the fact that they're driven by global events more so than domestic, it might be advantageous to us to communicate to our provincial and federal partners the pressures that rising diesel costs are putting on transit commissions and request that they consider increasing their levels of support as well," said Mayor Josh Morgan.

"Certainly, we can pass this motion today but I think it has to be paralleled with an advocacy piece to other levels of government to recognize that these forces are beyond the control of any individual transit commission or even municipality and it's something many are facing together."

At its meeting on Monday, the LTC unanimously voted to work with public transit advocacy organizations such as the Ontario Public Transit Association (OPTA) and the Canadian Urban Transit Association (CUTA) to raise the issue to upper levels of government.

A staff report said 2026 has been a "volatile year" for diesel fuel prices due to the ongoing uncertainty in the Middle East and that predicting a budget for it is challenging. The agency said it's relied on reserve funding to cover these costs but that won't be viable next year.
"In 2026, there was a requirement of around $3.6 million in reserve funding to balance that budget," said Mike Gregor, LTC's director of finance.
"The reserves aren't sustainable. This will result in a significant drawdown on our reserves that could be managed for 2026 but is not recommended going forward."

The costs resulted in fuel prices, increased costs for bus maintenance, an additional 2,000 service hours and a $50,000 allocation for service improvements that were also funded through reserves, Gregor added.

The original 2026 fuel budget was based on an estimated price of $1.21 per litre, noting it was reduced later in the year amid price trends at the time and council's request to find savings. This year's projected actual is expected to be $2.6 million over budget and will require the use of the Energy Management Reserve to manage this overage, the report said.
For 2027's budget, the diesel price is based on the recent average of $1.65 per litre, marking an 8.8 per cent increase in fuel expenses.
London Transit also seeks to add a permanent 2,400 service growth hours.

The LTC also approved an application for $3.5 million assessment growth funding for its new proposed Route 40 and an Alternative Service Delivery (ASD) model. The money comes through property taxes from developments each year.
The ASD model is recommended for areas that may not initially warrant a full conventional route based on estimated ridership demands but can grow in those areas to eventually get a full route.

LTC found two possible ASD zones which include th F ox Hollow area bounded by Hyde Park, Wonderland, Fanshawe Park Road and Sunningdale. Stops would be located within the main areas of the Hyde Park Power Centre at Fanshawe and Hyde Park and Masonville Mall.

A second zone includes t hree, non-adjacent areas within north Lambeth and south Byron. Stops would connect to Hyde Park and Oxford and Westmount Mall allowing for connections to the fixed route network.
Route 40 would run between the Hyde Park Power Centre and Western University via Dalmagarry, Coronation, South Carriage, Hyde Park, Sarnia and Western Road.

The new route would expand service into the growing residential neighbourhood which currently lacks a transit service within the standard 400 meter travel distance. It aims to operate on a 40 minute frequency and is expected to be operational in fall 2028.

stories.title: ‘Evolving global context’: School boards across Canada cancel, tweak field trips
stories.summary: Edmonton — Zoe Cogger says two trips to the United States were going to be the highlight of her senior year in high school.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

Posted September 1, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 1, 2026 5:20 am.

Edmonton — Zoe Cogger says two trips to the United States were going to be the highlight of her senior year in high school.

The 16-year-old was set to go with fellow Edmonton students to the National High School Dance Festival in Pittsburgh and to Spokane, Wash., for the annual Bloomsday Run.

But the trips are no more.

Edmonton Public Schools has cancelled all international excursions for the school year, including to Thailand, France, the United Kingdom, Costa Rica and Portugal.

“I was pretty sad when I found out,” Cogger said.

Cogger is among thousands of students across Canada whose school trip plans have been cancelled or tweaked for this school year for various reasons, including global conflicts and uncertainty.

Supt. Rob Thompson with the Edmonton public board said in a letter to parents in June that a recent field trip had students come face to face with civil unrest. The board didn’t specify what country the students were in.

“Couple this with reported global fuel shortages, recently reported public health concerns and ongoing military conflict, which introduces further unpredictability and risk to international travel,” Thompson said.

He added that he doesn’t take the cancellations lightly and that the board would reassess its decision before the 2027-28 school year.

The Vancouver School Board and the Calgary Catholic School District both said they’re approving field trips on a case-by-case basis.

“We are operating within an evolving global context and are carefully considering a range of factors in our review processes,” the Vancouver board said in an email.

Last year, the public Calgary Board of Education cancelled all international trips while it reviewed policies on how trips are planned and students prepare for the rigours of international travel. It said recently that trips have resumed for this year.

In Winnipeg, the Louis Riel School Board has cancelled trips to the United States since last October, after Ottawa posted a travel advisory warning Canadians that the U.S. government is no longer accepting gender markers.

The Winnipeg School Division said it’s allowing school trips — but not to the United States.

“Travel to other international destinations May still be considered if it supports student learning or business operations,” spokesperson Jillian Recksiedler said in an email.

Public boards in Toronto and Saskatoon say none of their trips have been cancelled.

Some experts say school trip changes are understandable.

“We live in really complex times and international trips are a complex thing to pull off,” said Maren Aukerman, an education professor at the University of Calgary.

“The other side is it is a real loss . There’s lots of research that compares virtual field trips with real field trips and, not surprisingly, you cannot replace being in a different place, exploring a different culture.”

Aukerman said some schools are choosing instead to plan trips within Canada.

Wayne Smith, a hospitality and tourism professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, said the cost of living has made it more difficult for parents to sign up their children for trips.

Planning trips has also become complicated, he said. With Canada’s population growth, teachers are seeing students with more diverse citizenship statuses.

“I know in Toronto, for example, the amount of paperwork (teachers) have to file to do a class trip is pretty phenomenal,” he said.

“It’s just got really complicated over the last few years, and especially since the vast majority of the trips are south of the border.”

Aukerman said that the trade war has complicated travel to the United States.

Edmonton high school student Nyla Ahmadzai said she isn’t going on any international school trips this year. But she spent all last year helping friends raise money for their planned excursions.

“They did bottle drives, sold chocolates, candies, even posting on social media, asking family members for donations and stuff,” she said. “I had a friend clean cars.

“Now it’s taken away from them, and it’s really, really frustrating.”

Cogger said she had hoped Edmonton Public Schools would consider trips on a case-by-case basis instead of cancelling them altogether.

“It’s better to find a way to make it work because these experiences are a high school experience.”

But there’s an upside.

Cogger said her school is planning a run in Jasper National Park instead of the one in Washington, and she’s not upset.

“I’m glad that they were able to find a replacement. “

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

stories.author: News Staff
paragraphs: TORONTO — When writer-director David Bezmozgis set out to adapt his 2014 novel “The Betrayers” for the big screen, he wasn’t just changing its format. He also had to adjust to a new geopolitical landscape.
The film, which is set in Ukraine and Israel, is one of 61 Canadian features and shorts programmed at this year’s edition of the Toronto International Film Festival.
The Canadian Press spoke to Bezmozgis and four other homegrown directors about their films.
“THE BETRAYERS”

Bezmozgis’s second novel was an unmitigated hit when it was published. It made numerous best-of-the-year lists — from the Wall Street Journal to the New Yorker — and was shortlisted for the Giller Prize.
Twelve years later, Bezmozgis has revisited the story of a disgraced Israeli politician who flees to Crimea and comes face-to-face with the former friend who betrayed him.
Those 12 years were consequential, Bezmozgis said. The book deals with Russia’s relationship with Ukraine and Israel’s relationship with the occupied West Bank.
“That subject has continued to be current and pressing, and also of interest to Canadians, which is why it was worth doing (the story) again,” Bezmozgis said.
In 2014, Russia had annexed Crimea and Israel was at war with Gaza. In 2026, Russia is four years into a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Israel is three years into its war on Hamas.

Bezmozgis said that in writing the script, he found himself “choosing different storylines that relate to what’s happening in the world right now. It made sense at the time, dealing with Ukraine and Crimea, and Israel, and we’ve updated it.”
Showtimes: Saturday, Sept. 12 and Monday, Sept. 14
-Nicole Thompson

Ashley Da-Le Duong only ever knew the barest outline of her father’s young life: that he had grown up in Vietnam during the war, and eventually moved to Canada to work as an engineer. She asked him for more, but he never gave it. Until, that is, he emailed her his memoir — a project she didn’t know he was working on — written in the form of letters to her.
As a way to process what she learned about her father’s childhood, Duong decided to adapt it into a documentary.
The resulting film is as much an adaptation of the memoir as it is a chronicle of making that adaptation.

Duong flew to Vietnam to connect with her father’s family and recreate scenes from his memoir. Also caught on film are interactions between the family and the young actors cast to play them as children, and conversations about what will be included in the documentary and why.
“He’s not in contact with his family in Vietnam, so It was a way of bringing the family together to talk about these difficult things,” she said.
In the end, the family members’ questions about how their story will be shown on screen are just as revelatory as the re-enactments themselves.
Showtimes: Tuesday, Sept. 15; Thursday Sept. 17; Saturday, Sept. 19
“NEIL PEART: NO ONE’S DISCIPLE”

For legions of music nerds who measure greatness in polyrhythms, Neil Peart was a prog-rock deity. The lyricist and stickman for Canadian power trio Rush was considered one of the greatest to ever sit behind a kit before his death from brain cancer in 2020.
But while he played the tom-toms virtuosically, he played his cards close to his vest.

So when making this heartfelt documentary about Peart, filmmakers Scot McFadyen and Sam Dunn spoke to those closest to him: Rush bandmates Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson, as well as drumming titans Stewart Copeland, Danny Carey, Chad Smith and Gavin Harrison.
“I didn’t really have a sense of how much of an inspiration he was to people that knew him, and how loyal of a friend he was,” said Dunn.

“He was a notoriously private person… but when we sat down with his close friends, we learned he was a real inspiration, a real motivator. He set the bar really high for everyone. It gave us a deeper sense of what Neil was like as a person — the person behind the genius.”
Showtimes: Wednesday, Sept. 16; Saturday, Sept. 19
-Alex Nino Gheciu
Director Serville Poblete’s latest feature is a sweaty contribution to the pantheon of coming-of-age hangout films.
Inspired by Greta Gerwig’s “Lady Bird” and its ability to put him in the shoes of a white girl from the Sacramento suburbs, Poblete set out to paint a portrait of the kids in his community.
“There aren’t a lot of stories that just allow kids that are darker-skinned, POC backgrounds to have fun and be themselves,” he said.
“And so ‘Sunburn’ is really a ‘Lady Bird’ for the hood.”

Set in Toronto during a blackout on the hottest, stickiest day of the year — much like a massive 2003 power outage — the film follows a group of teens cut off from their phones, wandering around their neighbourhood and finding themselves.
It revels (sometimes simultaneously) in the grossness of city heat and the sweetness of adolescent summer.
Showtimes: Monday, Sept. 14; Wednesday, Sept. 16; Saturday, Sept. 19
“TURTLE ISLAND RAP”
This documentary about three Indigenous rappers has been in the works for nearly five years.
“We were interested in exploring what the Indigenous hip hop scene looked like five years ago and we found some really exciting things happening,” said director Alexandra Lazarowich.

She ended up connecting with Wiidaaseh, a Toronto-based Anishinaabe rapper from Wiikwemkoong Unceded First Nation; A$h Da Hunter, who lives in Phoenix and is from Yavapai-Apache Nation; and Travis Thompson, a Navajo artist from the suburbs of Seattle.
Before she brought out the cameras, Lazarowich spent time connecting with the musicians and their communities, leading to an intimate portrait of their lives and artistic processes.
“It’s more of a snapshot of the culture that’s happening right now than it is sort of a prescriptive documentary about indigenous hip hop,” Lazarowich said.
Showtimes: Sunday, Sept. 13 and Tuesday, Sept. 15
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.
Nicole Thompson and Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press

As a way to process what she learned about her father’s childhood, Duong decided to adapt it into a documentary.

The resulting film is as much an adaptation of the memoir as it is a chronicle of making that adaptation.

Duong flew to Vietnam to connect with her father’s family and recreate scenes from his memoir. Also caught on film are interactions between the family and the young actors cast to play them as children, and conversations about what will be included in the documentary and why.

“He’s not in contact with his family in Vietnam, so It was a way of bringing the family together to talk about these difficult things,” she said.

In the end, the family members’ questions about how their story will be shown on screen are just as revelatory as the re-enactments themselves.

Showtimes: Tuesday, Sept. 15; Thursday Sept. 17; Saturday, Sept. 19

“NEIL PEART: NO ONE’S DISCIPLE”

For legions of music nerds who measure greatness in polyrhythms, Neil Peart was a prog-rock deity. The lyricist and stickman for Canadian power trio Rush was considered one of the greatest to ever sit behind a kit before his death from brain cancer in 2020.

But while he played the tom-toms virtuosically, he played his cards close to his vest.

So when making this heartfelt documentary about Peart, filmmakers Scot McFadyen and Sam Dunn spoke to those closest to him: Rush bandmates Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson, as well as drumming titans Stewart Copeland, Danny Carey, Chad Smith and Gavin Harrison.

“I didn’t really have a sense of how much of an inspiration he was to people that knew him, and how loyal of a friend he was,” said Dunn.

“He was a notoriously private person… but when we sat down with his close friends, we learned he was a real inspiration, a real motivator. He set the bar really high for everyone. It gave us a deeper sense of what Neil was like as a person — the person behind the genius.”

Showtimes: Wednesday, Sept. 16; Saturday, Sept. 19

-Alex Nino Gheciu

Director Serville Poblete’s latest feature is a sweaty contribution to the pantheon of coming-of-age hangout films.

Inspired by Greta Gerwig’s “Lady Bird” and its ability to put him in the shoes of a white girl from the Sacramento suburbs, Poblete set out to paint a portrait of the kids in his community.

“There aren’t a lot of stories that just allow kids that are darker-skinned, POC backgrounds to have fun and be themselves,” he said.

“And so ‘Sunburn’ is really a ‘Lady Bird’ for the hood.”

Set in Toronto during a blackout on the hottest, stickiest day of the year — much like a massive 2003 power outage — the film follows a group of teens cut off from their phones, wandering around their neighbourhood and finding themselves.

It revels (sometimes simultaneously) in the grossness of city heat and the sweetness of adolescent summer.

Showtimes: Monday, Sept. 14; Wednesday, Sept. 16; Saturday, Sept. 19

“TURTLE ISLAND RAP”

This documentary about three Indigenous rappers has been in the works for nearly five years.

“We were interested in exploring what the Indigenous hip hop scene looked like five years ago and we found some really exciting things happening,” said director Alexandra Lazarowich.

She ended up connecting with Wiidaaseh, a Toronto-based Anishinaabe rapper from Wiikwemkoong Unceded First Nation; A$h Da Hunter, who lives in Phoenix and is from Yavapai-Apache Nation; and Travis Thompson, a Navajo artist from the suburbs of Seattle.

Before she brought out the cameras, Lazarowich spent time connecting with the musicians and their communities, leading to an intimate portrait of their lives and artistic processes.

“It’s more of a snapshot of the culture that’s happening right now than it is sort of a prescriptive documentary about indigenous hip hop,” Lazarowich said.

Showtimes: Sunday, Sept. 13 and Tuesday, Sept. 15

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

Nicole Thompson and Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘You just move forward’: Greenland Energy oil exploration delayed by a year
stories.summary: Calgary — A drilling rig was being retooled in Alberta. Trucks and cranes were set to ship from Denmark. More equipment was due from Houston.
stories.author: News Staff
paragraphs: By Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press
Posted September 1, 2026 4:00 am.
Last Updated September 1, 2026 5:21 am.
Calgary — A drilling rig was being retooled in Alberta. Trucks and cranes were set to ship from Denmark. More equipment was due from Houston.

And a Quebec shipping firm was preparing to receive cargoes from those far flung locales at a port west of Montreal, load them Tetris-style onto vessels and sail this fall to Greenland’s rugged and inhospitable east coast. All this, in preparation for what would be the first oil wells to be drilled in the barren tundra of Jameson Land Basin.
But then, in mid-August, authorities in the mostly autonomous Danish territory said they needed more time to review Greenland Energy Co.’s plans to tap what it believes could be an oil bonanza.

“We literally shut everything down in its tracks,” Robert Price, Greenland Energy’s chief executive, said in a recent interview. Equipment has been put into storage and plans set aside for “a good year” until November or December of 2027.
“You just take a deep breath and you just move forward,” he said.
“We’re going to be in Greenland for a long time. We’re there for the long term. It’s a delay, but it’s not an insurmountable delay.”

Also on-hold is a six-part documentary series chronicling the Greenland exploration program hosted by Phil McGraw, better known as the TV personality Dr. Phil, and produced by McGraw’s firm Envoy Media Co.
The area Greenland Energy aims to explore is covered by pre-existing licences held by its joint-venture partner, U.K.-based 80 Mile PLC.

80 Mile obtained the licences long before the Greenland government banned new oil and gas exploration in 2021. Those permits — two granted in 2015 and one in 2018 — are still valid, Greenland’s Ministry of Trade and Natural Resources says in an online information page.
“A revocation of the existing permits would require special steps and can be considered expropriation,” it said. The permits are valid until the end of 2028, and could be extended.
Getting the go-ahead to actually get to work has been another matter.

“We had what we thought were assurances to get the permits to drill the wells before the end of this year and as it turned out, the government said that they wanted more time to review it,” Price said.
Initially, the regulator asked Greenland Energy to drill one exploratory well instead of two, and the company agreed, Price said.
The Greenland government said in an Aug. 12 news release that government and company officials met in July and that the firm presented plans to begin exploration this winter.

“The department expressed concern at the meeting about the very tight schedule and reviewed the regulatory process that must be completed before drilling activities can be approved,” it said. Among other things, social sustainability and environmental impact assessments must be completed, as well as public consultations.
“It’s just a process,” Price said. “We’re drilling the Arctic Circle, and we expect delays in the Arctic Circle.”
Other than storage and maintenance costs, Greenland Energy isn’t taking much of a financial hit from the delay, he added.

This summer, Greenland Energy and its partner ran afoul of local authorities when equipment was transported to near the planned drilling site from elsewhere on the island without the approval of the mineral resources ministry. The government decided it would not be “proportional” to order the drilling bed be moved back to its previous location, but instead issued “a strong warning” that the company must inform the government of any logistical matters in the future.

Price said the company obtained a permit last year to land the equipment, but it had expired. It believed moving the equipment to its airport in Jameson Land would be allowed, but the mineral resources regulator disagreed such a carve-out existed. Price said “we apologized” and “our equipment there right now is lawfully stored there.”

Two Canadian companies enlisted in the effort — Calgary-based Stampede Drilling and Desgagnés, which specializes in shipping in harsh environments — have sought to make clear that they had nothing to do with that issue.
Stampede Drilling said a rig that’s being upgraded for “potential deployment” to Greenland remains in Canada.

“Stampede further confirms that it will not be landing a drilling rig in Greenland unless Greenland Energy’s drilling program receives all required regulatory consents and approvals of Greenlandic authorities.”
Desgagnés said none of its vessels have unloaded cargo in Greenland, nor have they been scheduled to travel there.
“Desgagnés conducts its operations in strict compliance with all applicable laws, regulations, and requirements in Canada and internationally,” it said.
“The management, authorization, and implementation of the project fall exclusively under the jurisdiction of the competent Greenlandic authorities, whose decisions will be respected by Desgagnés.”

The drilling plans were coming together at the same time U.S. President Donald Trump set his sights on Greenland for U.S. annexation. The government on the island, whose population of about 56,000 is mostly Inuit, has fiercely rejected such an idea. Price has said he does not believe a U.S. takeover of Greenland is on the table, and that his company is committed to respecting Greenland’s independence.

Oil drilling May be on pause in Greenland, but Price said he’s still busy with work elsewhere in the territory. Another company he runs, Usfm Corp., has been involved in a nickel exploration project on the west side of the island.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.
Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Pilot Jack Tucker was famous for his nerves of steel and curling rink skills
stories.summary: Jack’s family takes comfort in knowing that he is flying with the angels now, reunited with his beloved Maureen
stories.author: Jennifer Power
stories.content:
Jack Edward Tucker: Pilot. Curler. Adventurer. Family man. Born Oct. 12, 1940, in Kelowna, B.C.; died April 29, 2026, of chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder, in Surrey, B.C.; aged 85

Trained as a Royal Canadian Navy pilot, Jack Tucker flew off Canada’s last aircraft carrier HMCS Bonaventure in the 1960s. The nerves of steel required for landing on a moving target in North Atlantic seas came in handy during his long career as a commercial airline pilot, especially when quick thinking was required, as on one memorable occasion.

Jack was the middle of three sons born to Alfred and Millicent Tucker. Summer days were spent swimming in the lake with brothers Brian and Trevor. Winters were spent on the ice and curling rinks. Jack always made the hockey and curling teams both in high school and while serving in the navy.

Jack met Maureen Power at the Kelowna Regatta, when she was visiting from Victoria with her high-school band. So began a lifelong love story that almost didn’t happen. After high school, Jack moved to Esquimalt to join HMCS Venture, a program designed to boost officer numbers during the Cold War. Maureen lived nearby and they set up their first date with other navy recruits and some of Maureen’s friends. Everyone was on time except for Jack who was in the finals of a Venture ping pong tournament. He won the tournament and then raced to the meeting spot. Maureen wasn’t impressed, but she did get a sense of Jack’s competitive nature very early.

Jack and Maureen married in 1960 and moved to Halifax where Jack flew CS2F Tracker aircraft on submarine patrols. While stationed on the Bonaventure he would do leather work in his spare time, making wallets and belts.

In 1965 Jack left the navy and joined Canadian Pacific Airlines. He commuted to Vancouver from the Okanagan for his flights. He took up curling again and competed for British Columbia’s team as third in the 1968 Brier. He went on to skip the B.C. team in the 1973 Brier. (Later in life, Jack served as a curling judge during the 2010 Olympics.)

Jack and Maureen welcomed two children, Laurie and James. Jack was an adventurous and mischievous father. He took the family on holidays to remote lakes and exotic locales. One morning, in Fiji, Jack solemnly told everyone not to move because a snake was curled up on the pillow between Jamie and Laurie. Maureen bolted while Jack pounced with a pillowcase as if to capture the snake, yelling “April Fools!”

In 1973 Jack co-piloted a Royal Flight during the Queen and Duke of Edinburgh’s Canadian tour. It became a matter of family amusement that when the Queen unexpectedly came forward to thank the pilots, Jack was bent over the controls and showed her a little more of his backside than he would have liked.

In 1995, Jack was mostly flying long-haul routes. One day, departure was delayed on a flight to Taiwan because of an engine problem. Eventually, the DC10 with 257 people on board was cleared for takeoff. During takeoff, an explosive bang was heard and the plane shuddered violently. Jack made the decision to reject takeoff and braked heavily bringing the plane to a safe stop off the runway, nose wheel collapsed but all spirits intact. Throughout the Transport Canada investigation, Jack maintained that he would make the same call again. When he retired at the mandatory age of 60, Jack was hired by Mandarin Airlines as its chief trainer.

Jack returned to the sea and cruised to many destinations with Maureen and other family members. As a passenger on flights, he would explain the details of what was happening and remain wide awake when everyone else slept. Ironically, though Jack could operate huge aircraft he was baffled by cellphones and personal computers.

Jack was a Renaissance man. His artistic pursuits transitioned from leather to antique refinishing and eventually to wood carving. He carved birds and other wildlife and entered competitions, winning numerous best of show awards.

After Maureen died in 2020, Jack’s life was quieter, but he continued to cruise with his family and to enjoy weekly meetings with friends over pancakes at the Surrey IHOP.

Jack’s family takes comfort in knowing that he is flying with the angels now, reunited with his beloved Maureen.

Jennifer Power is Jack’s niece.

To submit a Lives Lived: lives@globeandmail.com

Lives Lived celebrates the everyday, extraordinary, unheralded lives of Canadians who have recently passed. To learn how to share the story of a family member or friend, go to tgam.ca/livesguide .

In 1965 Jack left the navy and joined Canadian Pacific Airlines. He commuted to Vancouver from the Okanagan for his flights. He took up curling again and competed for British Columbia’s team as third in the 1968 Brier. He went on to skip the B.C. team in the 1973 Brier. (Later in life, Jack served as a curling judge during the 2010 Olympics.)

Jack and Maureen welcomed two children, Laurie and James. Jack was an adventurous and mischievous father. He took the family on holidays to remote lakes and exotic locales. One morning, in Fiji, Jack solemnly told everyone not to move because a snake was curled up on the pillow between Jamie and Laurie. Maureen bolted while Jack pounced with a pillowcase as if to capture the snake, yelling “April Fools!”

In 1973 Jack co-piloted a Royal Flight during the Queen and Duke of Edinburgh’s Canadian tour. It became a matter of family amusement that when the Queen unexpectedly came forward to thank the pilots, Jack was bent over the controls and showed her a little more of his backside than he would have liked.

In 1995, Jack was mostly flying long-haul routes. One day, departure was delayed on a flight to Taiwan because of an engine problem. Eventually, the DC10 with 257 people on board was cleared for takeoff. During takeoff, an explosive bang was heard and the plane shuddered violently. Jack made the decision to reject takeoff and braked heavily bringing the plane to a safe stop off the runway, nose wheel collapsed but all spirits intact. Throughout the Transport Canada investigation, Jack maintained that he would make the same call again. When he retired at the mandatory age of 60, Jack was hired by Mandarin Airlines as its chief trainer.

Jack returned to the sea and cruised to many destinations with Maureen and other family members. As a passenger on flights, he would explain the details of what was happening and remain wide awake when everyone else slept. Ironically, though Jack could operate huge aircraft he was baffled by cellphones and personal computers.

Jack was a Renaissance man. His artistic pursuits transitioned from leather to antique refinishing and eventually to wood carving. He carved birds and other wildlife and entered competitions, winning numerous best of show awards.
After Maureen died in 2020, Jack’s life was quieter, but he continued to cruise with his family and to enjoy weekly meetings with friends over pancakes at the Surrey IHOP.
Jack’s family takes comfort in knowing that he is flying with the angels now, reunited with his beloved Maureen.
Jennifer Power is Jack’s niece.
