stories.title: Wildfires. Flooding. Drought. Majority of Canadians personally affected by climate change events this year: Study
stories.summary: This year, more than 60 per cent of Canadians have been personally affected by climate disasters, the Elbows Up For Climate campaign has found.
stories.author: Marco Chown Oved
paragraphs: Climate change is causing natural disasters across Canada that are burning down homes, evacuating communities, washing away livelihoods, drying out crops, poisoning the air and killing people, according to a newly published study.
This year, more than 60 per cent of Canadians have been personally affected by climate disasters, the Elbows Up For Climate campaign found when producing its 2026 Climate Impacts Map .

Multicoloured dots representing wildfires, flooding, drought, hazardous air quality and extreme heat warnings splatter across every province and territory in the country, having affected 934 communities, representing more than 26 million Canadians so far this year — triple the number from 2025.

“We’ve almost normalized in many towns and cities across Canada people having to pack a go bag so they can evacuate at a moment’s notice, which is shocking. If you think about that from 10 years ago, it was inconceivable,” said David Miller, former mayor of Toronto and co-chair of the nearly 300 mayors and municipal councillors behind the Elbows Up For Climate campaign.

“This is climate change. And unless we really get serious about addressing climate change and dramatically lowering our greenhouse gas emissions in Canada, because we’re becoming a laggard, it’s going to get much, much, much worse.”

Between Jan. 1 and Aug. 12 of this year, 68 communities declared a local state of emergency, and many more faced multiple climate-fuelled hazards over the course of the summer. Extreme heat affected the largest number of communities at 669, followed by unsafe air quality in 320, flooding in 138, wildfire in 49, severe storms in 40 and drought in 12, the study found. Among Indigenous people, wildfires have affected 81 different First Nations, forcing 9,131 people from their communities since April 1.

This doesn’t include millions more Canadians struggling with the economic fallout of climate change: increased heating and cooling bills or reduced municipal services as communities struggle to pay for climate-related damages and infrastructure costs, the campaign said in a statement.
The wildfires will get bigger, stronger and more frequent — but that’s not to say there’s nothing we can do.

The local leaders behind Elbows Up For Climate are calling for nation-building projects that protect Canada from the dual crises of climate breakdown and economic instability. As federal political priorities turn away from climate and toward defending Canada’s economy from American tariffs, the group says both problems share a common solution.

“You can answer both challenges with the same strategy if you ask the right question ... The question is, how do we build an economy that works for Canadians and our environment? And when you ask that, the answer becomes obvious,” Miller said.

The local leaders are advocating for three nation-building projects: a clean electricity grid, federal housing that’s energy-efficient and affordable, and a national resilience, response and recovery strategy.

Canadians should “recognize the very positive potential economic strategy of trying to build an economy that’s a lot less reliant on oil and gas and the necessity to build resilience and the ability to recover from these disasters,” Miller said. “You put that together, and you have a very strong economy that’s creating the jobs of the future and is also doing our part to dramatically lower our greenhouse gas emissions.”
To help pay for these programs, the local leaders are also calling for an excess-profits tax on oil and gas companies, which have been reaping benefits from increased fossil fuel prices.

The Canadian oil industry stands to collect an estimated $90 billion in first-quarter windfall profits from the price shock linked to the 2026 conflict in Iran, according to the study, which calculated that Canada’s four largest publicly traded oil producers made almost $150 million a day in after-tax profit in the second quarter of 2026. The U.K. and Portugal have already introduced a similar levy on the fossil fuel industry.

Two in three Canadians support such a tax, according to a 2026 Liaison Stratégies poll commissioned by Climate Caucus. Another poll, released last week by EKOS, found a strong majority of Canadians care “very deeply” about nature conservation , even at the expense of economic development.

Prioritizing the environment is a view held by the overwhelming majority of people in the world , according to polling of more than 130,000 people in 125 countries done last year, which found 89 per cent thought their national government “should do more to fight global warming.”
This silent majority is consistently underrepresented in politics, Miller said.

“People vastly overestimate the opposition to climate action. Why? Because it’s really loud. It’s very well-funded and it’s aggressive,” he said. “Even in the face of the prime minister walking away from the trade deal, (Canadians) still prize nature and the environment and they expect governments to build an economy that works in harmony with the climate.”
The 2026 Climate Impacts Map from Elbows Up for the Climate.

stories.title: In Ontario, a proposed gold mine could release pollutants and require water treatment ‘in perpetuity,’ federal reports reveal
stories.summary: Federal reports warn Kinross Gold’s proposed Great Bear mine in Ontario could release arsenic and require water treatment ‘in perpetuity.’
stories.author: Savannah Ridley; Emma McIntosh
paragraphs: At first, the findings by government scientists felt like validation for Grassy Narrows First Nation , which had long raised concerns about plans for a gold mine upriver.
The First Nation has feared the planned mine would worsen the effects of mercury in the water , industrial pollution that has poisoned its people for generations.
The company behind the mine downplayed those concerns, saying its own studies show only minimal impact.
But a flurry of reports by federal agencies released earlier this year as part of a review by the federal Impact Assessment Agency have cast that into doubt.
Internal documents raise questions on whether Kevin Rombout’s move violated ethics law, an allegation that the province and the mining company deny.

Kinross Gold’s conclusion that the mine wouldn’t worsen water quality is “not scientifically sound,” Environment and Climate Change Canada determined, finding the company relied on flawed data and models. The department said it flagged issues with the company’s work as early as February 2025, but Kinross did not fix them.

In a separate report, Natural Resources Canada warned the area “could require water treatment in perpetuity,” noting that more than 80 per cent of the rock set to be mined has the potential to release arsenic or sulphate , a chemical that can worsen mercury contamination.
Health Canada sounded its own alarm, finding Kinross did not have a plan in place to monitor mercury trends or communicate results to First Nations.
Despite the warnings from federal scientists, the Impact Assessment Agency recently told the First Nation it is moving to expedite permits for the mine.
Government accused of putting profits before Indigenous health

The mine has not yet been approved and the fast-tracking does not guarantee the project will ultimately move forward. But it does signal the agency wants to be ready to hit the gas pedal if the mine receives a green light.

“Over and over, we have told the government that we need to heal our people and our land. It feels like Canada is doing the opposite by fast-tracking this dangerous, polluting mine upstream from us,” said Joseph Fobister, the director of the Grassy Narrows Land Protection Team.
“This shows that the government cares more about Kinross’ profits than it does about our health.”
A Kinross spokesperson told the Star that the company stands by its assessment of the mine’s environmental impact, calling it “comprehensive and supported by extensive scientific expertise.”

The company rejected the suggestion that federal scientists found its assessment flawed and misleading, saying that conclusion misrepresents the nature of the federal process, in which submissions are refined and improved upon based on issues raised by regulators.

“Kinross continues to work with regulators throughout the review process and will consider additional analysis, data collection, or revisions where appropriate in response to regulatory feedback,” spokesperson Samantha Sheffield said in an email.
She said the company believes it can develop the mine without harming nearby communities.
“We recognize the concerns expressed by Grassy Narrows and will continue to consider the community’s perspectives as part of our engagement and the regulatory review process.”
Kinross did not ask the agency to fast-track the mine’s permitting, Sheffield said, adding that it was a decision by the federal government.

The Impact Assessment Agency did not directly answer when asked about the legal mechanism it’s using to do so, but said it is “maximizing Indigenous participation” by co-ordinating consultations about the permits with Indigenous communities.
A new study has found current sulphate emissions from a paper mill are exacerbating the impact of the old mercury still in the river system.

“This makes the process more efficient and predictable for consultations that would be required before certain construction activities can begin, should the project proceed to permitting,” the agency said in a statement.

Richard Lindgren, a lawyer with the Canadian Environmental Law Association (CELA) who is representing Grassy Narrows, said it’s not clear what legal authority the federal government has to speed up the mine’s approval process. Though the Carney government has designated some “major projects” it wants to expedite, the Kinross mine isn’t one of them. And although the Carney government has signalled plans to fast-track more projects through different mechanisms, it has not yet introduced a bill to make them law.
Lindgren said Grassy Narrows has asked the federal government but has not received an answer.
A legacy of industrial pollution

From 1962 to 1970, a pulp and paper mill dumped tonnes of mercury into the Wabigoon River upstream from Grassy Narrows, also known as Asubpeeschoseewagong Netum Anishinabek. The potent neurotoxin contaminated the river’s fish, poisoning the people who rely on one of the remote community’s primary food sources.

The proposed site of the Kinross Great Bear mine would be about the same distance upstream, along a different waterway. As federal and provincial regulators have considered the project, one of the key questions has been how it could affect the area’s still-tainted waterways.

Grassy Narrows has raised concern about one chemical in particular: sulphate. In wet, low-oxygen environments like lake bottoms, sulphate can help bacteria turn mercury into an even more toxic form called methylmercury. As it migrates up the food chain from fish to humans, the poison becomes even more concentrated.
Treated wastewater from the mine could double concentrations of sulphate in the nearby Chukuni River, and methylmercury “remains a concern,” Environment and Climate Change Canada found.
The findings validate what Grassy Narrows has been saying all along, Fobister said.

“I feel that Kinross is not telling the truth about how their proposed gold mine will make our mercury poisoning worse,” he said. “Kinross seems to ignore our concerns, and it looks like they haven’t even taken Environment Canada’s concerns seriously.”
Kinross’s Sheffield said the company’s studies and analysis “do not support” Fobister’s view, adding that Kinross will continue to consider Grassy Narrows’ perspective.

The company has done a number of things in response to concerns raised by Environment Canada, Sheffield said, including expanding downstream study boundaries, completing additional water, sediment and fish sampling, and adding seasonal monitoring.

Federal scientists responding to Kinross’ plans also raised concerns about the rock to be mined. Once exposed, the majority of that material has a high risk of emitting sulphate and arsenic into the environment, Natural Resources Canada said, noting that some contaminated water from the mine would be allowed to seep into the environment by design.
Kinross Gold says it adheres to the highest environmental standards. But there is growing concern about its history of alleged pollution.

Kevin Morin, an expert in water contamination from mines who was hired by Grassy Narrows to review Kinross Gold’s plans, found the mine would cause a “long-term toxic scenario.” Based on the company’s estimates, Morin said in a report submitted to the federal government, there’s a 25-per-cent chance of “at least one” damaging toxic release or spill in about 26 years of mine operation — and a 100-per-cent chance of one damaging spill at the site every century, even after the mine itself is long closed.
The company’s plans would allow contaminated water to flow “passively and unabated” into the environment once it has shut down the site, Morin wrote.
Kinross did not directly respond to Morin’s comments, but noted that regulators are still reviewing the mine.
Ontario ministry also raises concerns
Kinross Gold’s plans have also raised concerns for First Nations who have so far been more open to considering the project.

Lac Seul and Wabauskang First Nations, whose land the Great Bear mine is proposed to sit on, told the federal government that their review found the environmental risks have been “underestimated significantly,” and that Kinross’ water quality predictions are “optimistic and likely unrealistic.”
But the nations also said they were “optimistic” Kinross could remedy the issues they flagged, and that through an Anishinaabe-led assessment, they’re still weighing their stances on the project.
Lac Seul Chief Clifford Bull and Wabauskang Chief William Petiquan did not answer questions from the Star. Sheffield said the company has a strong working relationship with both nations.
“We take the views of Lac Seul First Nation and Wabauskang First Nation seriously,” she said.

The Ontario government — which has been vocally supportive of the Great Bear mine and fast-tracked its provincial vetting earlier this year — also filed concerns to the Impact Assessment Agency. The Ministry of Energy and Mines found Kinross’s plan for decommissioning the site after mining is done “does not conform” to Ontario’s rules. It also found Kinross had focused on too small of an area to properly assess how the mine could impact the land around it.
Kinross said its current plans for the decommissioning of the site are a “conceptual draft,” and that is still finalizing details and consulting Indigenous communities.

Ontario’s Ministry of Energy and Mines would not say whether it is factoring the federal scientific assessments into its ongoing review of the mine proposal. Ministry spokesman Robert Quartarone said the province is “moving with speed to unlock this opportunity” while still maintaining regulatory standards, and that Kinross will still need Ontario’s sign-off on key requirements, like its plans to eventually close the mine site.
Amid questions about whether Kevin Rombout’s move violated an ethics law, both Ontario and the

Earlier this year, a Star investigation found that a Ford government staffer who had worked to advance the Kinross project had then moved on to work for the mining company. The investigation also showed Kinross enjoyed close and constant access to the provincial government, while Grassy Narrows was often sidelined in discussions about the mine.
Final decision to be made by environment minister

Lindgren, the lawyer with CELA, said the issues raised by federal scientists and experts hired by Grassy Narrows are “fundamental concerns” that could take months or years to resolve, if it’s even possible to fix them.

“It’s far from clear that this thing is a done deal,” Lindgren said. “The approach is pretty questionable or inappropriate because of the large amount of time and effort and resources that my client, Grassy Narrows, has to expend in responding to these permit applications … You may be wasting everybody’s time.”

Kerrie Blaise, the founder of Legal Advocates for Nature’s Defence, an environmental law non-profit, said it’s unclear what the federal government’s new streamlined process could look like, or how it might affect the Impact Assessment Agency’s review of the mine.

“If you enter a process and then, when those rules start changing while you’re going through the process, that is not helpful. That’s not helpful to anyone, government workers, staffers, industry, the proponent themselves or communities,” Blaise said.

The agency did not directly answer when asked what the streamlined process will look like, but said it will mean “clarity on permitting requirements, timelines and processes through the development of detailed federal permitting plans.” The agency also said it will give Indigenous communities a single point of contact, and that details of the permitting process will be posted publicly.

The Impact Assessment Agency is still assessing Kinross’s plans, along with feedback it has received from federal experts and First Nations. It will eventually submit a report to federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, who can decide whether to approve or reject the mine. The timeline for that process is uncertain, as the agency is still deciding whether it needs more information to move ahead.
Fobister said the findings from federal scientists should be a “wake-up call” for regulators.
“Each time more industry is forced on our land, we pay the price with our health.”

stories.content:
At first, the findings by government scientists felt like validation for Grassy Narrows First Nation , which had long raised concerns about plans for a gold mine upriver.

The First Nation has feared the planned mine would worsen the effects of mercury in the water , industrial pollution that has poisoned its people for generations.

The company behind the mine downplayed those concerns, saying its own studies show only minimal impact.

But a flurry of reports by federal agencies released earlier this year as part of a review by the federal Impact Assessment Agency have cast that into doubt.

Internal documents raise questions on whether Kevin Rombout’s move violated ethics law, an allegation that the province and the mining company deny.

Kinross Gold’s conclusion that the mine wouldn’t worsen water quality is “not scientifically sound,” Environment and Climate Change Canada determined, finding the company relied on flawed data and models. The department said it flagged issues with the company’s work as early as February 2025, but Kinross did not fix them.

In a separate report, Natural Resources Canada warned the area “could require water treatment in perpetuity,” noting that more than 80 per cent of the rock set to be mined has the potential to release arsenic or sulphate , a chemical that can worsen mercury contamination.

Health Canada sounded its own alarm, finding Kinross did not have a plan in place to monitor mercury trends or communicate results to First Nations.

Despite the warnings from federal scientists, the Impact Assessment Agency recently told the First Nation it is moving to expedite permits for the mine.

Government accused of putting profits before Indigenous health

The mine has not yet been approved and the fast-tracking does not guarantee the project will ultimately move forward. But it does signal the agency wants to be ready to hit the gas pedal if the mine receives a green light.

“Over and over, we have told the government that we need to heal our people and our land. It feels like Canada is doing the opposite by fast-tracking this dangerous, polluting mine upstream from us,” said Joseph Fobister, the director of the Grassy Narrows Land Protection Team.

“This shows that the government cares more about Kinross’ profits than it does about our health.”

A Kinross spokesperson told the Star that the company stands by its assessment of the mine’s environmental impact, calling it “comprehensive and supported by extensive scientific expertise.”

The company rejected the suggestion that federal scientists found its assessment flawed and misleading, saying that conclusion misrepresents the nature of the federal process, in which submissions are refined and improved upon based on issues raised by regulators.

“Kinross continues to work with regulators throughout the review process and will consider additional analysis, data collection, or revisions where appropriate in response to regulatory feedback,” spokesperson Samantha Sheffield said in an email.

She said the company believes it can develop the mine without harming nearby communities.

“We recognize the concerns expressed by Grassy Narrows and will continue to consider the community’s perspectives as part of our engagement and the regulatory review process.”

Kinross did not ask the agency to fast-track the mine’s permitting, Sheffield said, adding that it was a decision by the federal government.

The Impact Assessment Agency did not directly answer when asked about the legal mechanism it’s using to do so, but said it is “maximizing Indigenous participation” by co-ordinating consultations about the permits with Indigenous communities.

A new study has found current sulphate emissions from a paper mill are exacerbating the impact of the old mercury still in the river system.

“This makes the process more efficient and predictable for consultations that would be required before certain construction activities can begin, should the project proceed to permitting,” the agency said in a statement.

Richard Lindgren, a lawyer with the Canadian Environmental Law Association (CELA) who is representing Grassy Narrows, said it’s not clear what legal authority the federal government has to speed up the mine’s approval process. Though the Carney government has designated some “major projects” it wants to expedite, the Kinross mine isn’t one of them. And although the Carney government has signalled plans to fast-track more projects through different mechanisms, it has not yet introduced a bill to make them law.

Lindgren said Grassy Narrows has asked the federal government but has not received an answer.

A legacy of industrial pollution

From 1962 to 1970, a pulp and paper mill dumped tonnes of mercury into the Wabigoon River upstream from Grassy Narrows, also known as Asubpeeschoseewagong Netum Anishinabek. The potent neurotoxin contaminated the river’s fish, poisoning the people who rely on one of the remote community’s primary food sources.

The proposed site of the Kinross Great Bear mine would be about the same distance upstream, along a different waterway. As federal and provincial regulators have considered the project, one of the key questions has been how it could affect the area’s still-tainted waterways.

Grassy Narrows has raised concern about one chemical in particular: sulphate. In wet, low-oxygen environments like lake bottoms, sulphate can help bacteria turn mercury into an even more toxic form called methylmercury. As it migrates up the food chain from fish to humans, the poison becomes even more concentrated.

Treated wastewater from the mine could double concentrations of sulphate in the nearby Chukuni River, and methylmercury “remains a concern,” Environment and Climate Change Canada found.

The findings validate what Grassy Narrows has been saying all along, Fobister said.

“I feel that Kinross is not telling the truth about how their proposed gold mine will make our mercury poisoning worse,” he said. “Kinross seems to ignore our concerns, and it looks like they haven’t even taken Environment Canada’s concerns seriously.”

Kinross’s Sheffield said the company’s studies and analysis “do not support” Fobister’s view, adding that Kinross will continue to consider Grassy Narrows’ perspective.

The company has done a number of things in response to concerns raised by Environment Canada, Sheffield said, including expanding downstream study boundaries, completing additional water, sediment and fish sampling, and adding seasonal monitoring.

Federal scientists responding to Kinross’ plans also raised concerns about the rock to be mined. Once exposed, the majority of that material has a high risk of emitting sulphate and arsenic into the environment, Natural Resources Canada said, noting that some contaminated water from the mine would be allowed to seep into the environment by design.

Kinross Gold says it adheres to the highest environmental standards. But there is growing concern about its history of alleged pollution.

Kevin Morin, an expert in water contamination from mines who was hired by Grassy Narrows to review Kinross Gold’s plans, found the mine would cause a “long-term toxic scenario.” Based on the company’s estimates, Morin said in a report submitted to the federal government, there’s a 25-per-cent chance of “at least one” damaging toxic release or spill in about 26 years of mine operation — and a 100-per-cent chance of one damaging spill at the site every century, even after the mine itself is long closed.

The company’s plans would allow contaminated water to flow “passively and unabated” into the environment once it has shut down the site, Morin wrote.

Kinross did not directly respond to Morin’s comments, but noted that regulators are still reviewing the mine.

Ontario ministry also raises concerns

Kinross Gold’s plans have also raised concerns for First Nations who have so far been more open to considering the project.

Lac Seul and Wabauskang First Nations, whose land the Great Bear mine is proposed to sit on, told the federal government that their review found the environmental risks have been “underestimated significantly,” and that Kinross’ water quality predictions are “optimistic and likely unrealistic.”

But the nations also said they were “optimistic” Kinross could remedy the issues they flagged, and that through an Anishinaabe-led assessment, they’re still weighing their stances on the project.

Lac Seul Chief Clifford Bull and Wabauskang Chief William Petiquan did not answer questions from the Star. Sheffield said the company has a strong working relationship with both nations.

“We take the views of Lac Seul First Nation and Wabauskang First Nation seriously,” she said.

The Ontario government — which has been vocally supportive of the Great Bear mine and fast-tracked its provincial vetting earlier this year — also filed concerns to the Impact Assessment Agency. The Ministry of Energy and Mines found Kinross’s plan for decommissioning the site after mining is done “does not conform” to Ontario’s rules. It also found Kinross had focused on too small of an area to properly assess how the mine could impact the land around it.

Kinross said its current plans for the decommissioning of the site are a “conceptual draft,” and that is still finalizing details and consulting Indigenous communities.

Ontario’s Ministry of Energy and Mines would not say whether it is factoring the federal scientific assessments into its ongoing review of the mine proposal. Ministry spokesman Robert Quartarone said the province is “moving with speed to unlock this opportunity” while still maintaining regulatory standards, and that Kinross will still need Ontario’s sign-off on key requirements, like its plans to eventually close the mine site.

Amid questions about whether Kevin Rombout’s move violated an ethics law, both Ontario and the

Earlier this year, a Star investigation found that a Ford government staffer who had worked to advance the Kinross project had then moved on to work for the mining company. The investigation also showed Kinross enjoyed close and constant access to the provincial government, while Grassy Narrows was often sidelined in discussions about the mine.

Final decision to be made by environment minister

Lindgren, the lawyer with CELA, said the issues raised by federal scientists and experts hired by Grassy Narrows are “fundamental concerns” that could take months or years to resolve, if it’s even possible to fix them.

“It’s far from clear that this thing is a done deal,” Lindgren said. “The approach is pretty questionable or inappropriate because of the large amount of time and effort and resources that my client, Grassy Narrows, has to expend in responding to these permit applications … You may be wasting everybody’s time.”

Kerrie Blaise, the founder of Legal Advocates for Nature’s Defence, an environmental law non-profit, said it’s unclear what the federal government’s new streamlined process could look like, or how it might affect the Impact Assessment Agency’s review of the mine.

“If you enter a process and then, when those rules start changing while you’re going through the process, that is not helpful. That’s not helpful to anyone, government workers, staffers, industry, the proponent themselves or communities,” Blaise said.

The agency did not directly answer when asked what the streamlined process will look like, but said it will mean “clarity on permitting requirements, timelines and processes through the development of detailed federal permitting plans.” The agency also said it will give Indigenous communities a single point of contact, and that details of the permitting process will be posted publicly.

It will eventually submit a report to federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, who can decide whether to approve or reject the mine. ByJoe McGinty Reporter

One of Canada’s biggest artists has teamed up with the University of Waterloo to drop a new clothing collaboration celebrating Canadian universities.

Drake and his clothing company OVO (October’s Very Own) picked six universities from across Canada to release a back-to-school, campus-inspired collaboration.

The University of Waterloo joins other institutions including the University of Toronto, McMaster University,Dalhousie University,Western University and York University, which have their school’s logos and colours on various clothing items.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Toronto Island waitlist life: why one man will never give up his dream of living lakeside

The collection dropped online Aug. 28 and, in only a few hours, nearly the entire UW line was sold out.

Dubbed Part 1 of the 2026 campus collection, the brand said on its social media it is “celebrating the legacy, prestige and pride of some of Canada’s top universities.”

The UW collaboration sports a black and gold design across five items, with some including the founding year, 1957, and the school’s iconic Greek-inspired warrior logo helmet.

“Bringing OVO to campus was a direct response to feedback we received from students,” said Shawn Gilbertson, interim director of print and retail solutions at the University of Waterloo.

“They showed a strong interest in W Store partnering with OVO. This exciting collection is unlike anything else we have offered and allows us to showcase our brand in new spaces.”

This isn’t the first time a university in Waterloo has gotten a nod from one of the world’s most streamed artist. Last year, OVO partnered with Wilfrid Laurier University for its 2025 campus collection.

For those who missed out on buying items for this year’s collection online, the school will be hosting an in-person pop-up shop on campus Sept. 8 and 9 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. across from the UW Store at the South Campus Hall.

All items will be available on a first come basis. Items not sold in-store will be available on the school’s website on Sept. 10.

Joe McGinty is a reporter with the Waterloo Region Record.

[](http://london.ca/newsroom/new-online-options-make-it-easier-report-bylaw-concerns-city-london)

Tuesday, September 1, 2026

Beginning on September 3, residents can report a wider range of bylaw-related concerns online through the Service London Portal. The expanded service creates a simpler, more direct way to submit non-emergency concerns and connect with the appropriate City team.

The expanded options include occupant noise, such as people, parties and loud music; general noise, such as construction, equipment and barking dogs; property standards violations; vermin, rats or pest infestations; and other bylaw complaints not captured in the drop-down menu.

As part of the change, non-emergency noise complaints should be submitted through the Service London Portal at service.london.ca, rather than reporting them to the London Police Service.

“We want reporting a noise concern to be simple and the response to be timely,” said Amanda Pfeffer, Director, Municipal Compliance. “By moving occupant noise reporting to Service London, complaints will come directly to the staff responsible for responding, while residents will receive immediate confirmation that their concern has been received.”

Residents can visit service.london.ca to view the available reporting options and submit a complaint.

Municipal Compliance works with residents and property owners to help keep London’s neighbourhoods safe, healthy and well maintained. Staff provide education, conduct inspections and enforce City bylaws when needed.

As always, call 911 in an emergency.

Tuesday, September 1, 2026

Beginning on September 3, residents can report a wider range of bylaw-related concerns online through the Service London Portal. The expanded service creates a simpler, more direct way to submit non-emergency concerns and connect with the appropriate City team.

The expanded options include occupant noise, such as people, parties and loud music; general noise, such as construction, equipment and barking dogs; property standards violations; vermin, rats or pest infestations; and other bylaw complaints not captured in the drop-down menu.
As part of the change, non-emergency noise complaints should be submitted through the Service London Portal at service.london.ca, rather than reporting them to the London Police Service.

“We want reporting a noise concern to be simple and the response to be timely,” said Amanda Pfeffer, Director, Municipal Compliance. “By moving occupant noise reporting to Service London, complaints will come directly to the staff responsible for responding, while residents will receive immediate confirmation that their concern has been received.”
Residents can visit service.london.ca to view the available reporting options and submit a complaint.

Municipal Compliance works with residents and property owners to help keep London’s neighbourhoods safe, healthy and well maintained. Staff provide education, conduct inspections and enforce City bylaws when needed.
As always, call 911 in an emergency.

stories.title: Mark Carney fires back after Pete Hegseth mocks Canadian cadets in online post: ‘Stop doing memes’
stories.summary: Hegseth posted a screenshot to X of a cadet from Vernon, B.C. to social media Monday.
stories.author: Kristjan Lautens
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney called for Americans to respect Canadian culture after U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth mocked cadets from British Columbia on social media Monday night.

Hegseth posted a screenshot to X of a cadet from Vernon, B.C. receiving an award at summer training session, with the Canadian flag and the caption “this is real.” The post has garnered nearly 7 million views by Tuesday morning.

“Stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough,” Carney said when asked about the post Tuesday, adding it was “beneath their office.”

The Army Cadet League of Canada said they stand “firmly” with their volunteers, staff and officers in a statement Tuesday that did not directly address or mention Hegseth.

“We strongly condemn any online harassment, or mockery of cadets’ achievements,” the group said in a statement on Facebook. “Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable.”

The prime minister responded to the incident while speaking about the ongoing trade war with the U.S. and reiterating that his government’s plan is “standing up for Canada first and foremost.”

Carney said the possibility has always been there for a “mutually beneficial trade deal” with the United States, with the caveat that they have to “respect Canadian sovereignty, the French language and culture and Canadian culture.”

When asked about the post on Tuesday, Pentagon deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss said “the X post speaks for itself.”

Cadets are between 12 and 19 years old in Canada, and there are more than 60,000 who are led by about 9,000 military members and volunteers.

Many defended the cadet program, and the two in the photo, online after the post, with some accusing Hegseth of body-shaming women and unfairly targeting youth in an attempt to disparage the Canadian Armed Forces.

“Cadets do great work, and are not members of the military,” Conservative MP in Saskatchewan Garnett Genuis said. “Canada and the U.S. have a great history of fighting together for freedom and justice. It’s history worth remembering.”

Hegseth previously sparked controversy when he said during a podcast appearance in 2024 before U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term that he doesn’t believe women should be in military combat roles.

“It hasn’t made us more effective, hasn’t made us more lethal, has made fighting more complicated,” Hegseth, who served in the U.S. army National Guard, said on the “Shawn Ryan Show.”

Since taking office in 2025, Hegseth has also repeatedly commented on the weight of his own troops, using the phrase “fit not fat” to describe his vision for the military.

Former Republican congressman and veteran of the U.S. Air Force Adam Kinzinger jumped to criticize Hegseth Tuesday, saying the comments were “making fun of children.”

Jason Kenney, former premier of Alberta , referenced the ongoing conflict between the U.S. and Iran in his response to the post and questioned why this was a priority for the defence secretary.

“In the midst of a hot war against a mortal enemy of the United States, the Secretary of War of the world’s only super power finds time to troll folks at a cadet camp for teenagers in Vernon, British Columbia,” he wrote.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: This B.C. party’s deepening ties to Alberta’s separatist movement raise eyebrows in the west
stories.summary: Jake Bregolisse is the second B.C. Conservative hire with links to the separatist Republican Party of Alberta, deepening controversial Western ties.
stories.author: Alex Boyd; Emma McIntosh

Further ties have emerged between the separatist Republican Party of Alberta and the top levels of the B.C. Conservative Party, deepening a political relationship that has raised eyebrows in the west.

Jake Bregolisse, who previously worked for a political strategy firm co-directed by Republican Party of Alberta (RPA) leader Cameron Davies, appears to have been recently hired to work in B.C. Conservative Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s office. The RPA is a provincial party that has campaigned for Alberta to separate from Canada .

Bregolisse is Findlay’s second known hire with ties to the separatist movement in Alberta.

The other is Apollo Chung , who had recently worked as executive director of the RPA. He was director of operations for Findlay’s B.C. Conservative Party until Wednesday, when Findlay announced he had been fired.

Findlay did not give a reason for the move, which followed the surfacing of alleged audio recordings of a Findlay staffer talking about monetizing their work in politics. The Star cannot independently verify the authenticity of the audio, which a Canadian Press report said was allegedly of Chung.

Party backers are supposed to live in the province when they contribute. Donations in 2025 were apparently made by B.C. residents.

A Star investigation published earlier this month found that Chung was among a group of four donors who in 2025 each gave the maximum allowable $5,000 donation to the Republican Party of Alberta while apparently living in B.C., seemingly in violation of Elections Alberta’s campaign finance rules. Chung did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

A person with the name Jake Bregolisse also donated the maximum amount to the Republican party last year, according to public donation records, but Bregolisse has public ties to Alberta. He registered a political consulting business in Calgary in early 2025, corporate records show, and his LinkedIn profile lists work experience in both Alberta and B.C.

He has also worked for Republican leader Davies’ political consulting company, Sovereign North Strategies, two sources told the Star.

He is now Findlay’s director of legislative affairs and strategic planning, according to a B.C. government directory that was recently taken offline.

Apollo Chung

When reached by phone, Bregolisse asked the Star to send an email, to which he did not respond. Chung and Findlay also did not respond to requests to comment for this story.

When Findlay won the race to lead the Conservative Party in May, she pledged it to “faith, family and freedom,” a common political slogan also used by the RPA. She has said she would maintain an economic relationship with Alberta, should it decide to separate, though her office previously told the Star she believes in federalism and is a “Canadian, born and bred.”

Philippe J. Fournier, who runs the polling website 338Canada, told the Star he interacted with Bregolisse, then director of research for the strategy firm Sovereign North, about a poll by the Alberta company in 2024.

The second source for this story, who works in politics and asked not to be named for fear of professional repercussions, provided the Star with a photo of a Sovereign North business card showing the same name and job title, with a phone number associated with Bregolisse’s LinkedIn profile. This source also said that the Jake Bregolisse who worked for Sovereign North is the same person now working for Findlay.

The Star searched public records in and social media sites and could find no evidence of a different Jacob Bregolisse in Alberta and B.C.

When Findlay campaigned for leader, she tracked more populist and right wing than some of her competitors, and she also made clear that she saw her province as part of a distinct, western part of Canada with a more adversarial relationship to Ottawa, said Stewart Prest, a political scientist at the University of British Columbia.

In some ways, Prest added, Findlay’s version of the B.C. Conservative Party and the Republican Party of Alberta are “ideological fellow travellers.”

“There’s a strong affinity for that kind of populist world view (in Findlay’s camp) … and it lends itself to sympathy for the kinds of causes that Alberta separatists believe in, even if not coming out right and endorsing the idea of a separate Alberta.”

Findlay’s office — which has been embroiled in internal scuffles this month, with seven MLAs leaving the party — did not respond to questions from the Star about Bregolisse’s hiring, and the relationship between the B.C. Conservatives and the Alberta Republicans. Alberta Republican Party leader Davies also did not reply to requests for comment.

(Updated September 2 at 6:20 a.m.)

Power has been restored to the London Campus and buildings will reopen as usual on Wednesday, September 2. All regularly scheduled work, classes and events will resume as scheduled.

Due to an electrical safety concern, employees and students in buildings F, G, H, L and K are advised to evacuate immediately.

Students and employees in other buildings should avoid the area but may remain on campus.

London Hydro will be on scene shortly to investigate a hydro issue. Updates will be provided by email and on social media channels.

London Hydro will be on scene shortly to investigate a hydro issue. Updates will be provided by email and on social media channels.

stories.title: Confusion deepens on Ontario’s new student absence policy after education minister says principals will get final say
stories.summary: The province's principals say they wish they had been consulted beforehand, especially with mid-term marks required a couple of months into the school year.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
The province is targeting students who skip under its new policy that will dock marks for missed classes — but principals get to make the final call whether extended vacations or non-school sports tournaments will count as authorized absences.

These “can still be an excused absence, but the parent has to inform the principal, who can still make the determinant,” Education Minister Paul Calandra said in answering questions about the new rules for Ontario teens while at an unrelated announcement Tuesday in Hamilton.

But with the start of the fall classes already underway in some boards, and starting in most next week, confusion remains about how the policy will work — and be enforced — on the ground, and what will be allowed on a school-by-school basis.

Toronto’s Leaside High School has already sent out a memo to parents, saying allowable absences include “illness or other unavoidable circumstances, such as inclement weather or approved absences such as cultural days and holy days” meaning marks will not be deducted.

However, it adds, “please note that family vacations are not considered excused absences from schools.”

The province’s new rules — which Calandra has said are based on pleas from teachers who saw first-hand the growing numbers of teens missing class on a regular basis — now mandate that attendance and participation comprise 15 per cent of final marks in all classes in Grades 9 and 10, and 10 per cent for those in Grades 11 and 12. J ust 40 per cent of high school students meet acceptable standards for attendance, a recent report said.

Excused, or allowable, absences should not impact final grades, but if teens miss 2.5 to 4.5 classes per credit without authorization — or the stamp of approval from a principal — their mark in that area drops to a level 3, or a B, and to a level 2 when they hit five to seven classes.

“Parents still have the ability to excuse their children,” Calandra also said Tuesday. “They’ll have to inform the school, the principal, that it is their intention to excuse their child” for things like outside sports, music, dance or other activities.

“This isn’t targeting those kids who are busy and are doing the right thing,” Calandra added. “What this is about is those kids who don’t have an excused absence from their parents — who sometimes their parents don’t even know that they’re skipping a class ... Ultimately, you have to participate, and you have to be there.”

Concerns around the lack of clear details around the new policy are especially high for students in Grades 11 and 12, given post-secondary schools look at those marks and even a slight drop can make the difference when applying to competitive programs.

The province’s principals are still waiting for more details and say they wish they had been consulted beforehand, especially with mid-term marks required a couple of months into the school year.

“Principals have already been doing things like that — giving permission” for extended vacations or tournaments, said Ontario Principals’ Council president Amy Johnson, adding parents typically email administrators or teachers in advance of such absences.

Rates were much better before COVID. Here are some reasons for teenagers’ absenteeism — and what some other jurisdictions are doing.

“That’s the easy part — it’s not the part we’re struggling with,” she added. “It’s the many other situations that weren’t accounted for in (the minister’s) comments and aren’t outlined in the policy.”

Vulnerable families may not notify a school of an absence in a timely manner, and principals are also unsure how to deal with 16- and 17-year-olds who live independently.

In general, she added, “principals work to accommodate families who wish to take their children on holiday” but will intervene to discuss concerns when student achievement is at issue.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said the minister has given conflicting messages on the policy when it comes to sports and vacations.

“I think this is the third different answer he’s given on this ... this doesn’t help our kids in school and it doesn’t help the people who help them in schools, our teachers and principals,” he said.

Education unions have been urging the province to instead invest in more mental health services and school supports to address the underlying causes of absenteeism.

NDP education critic Chandra Pasma considers the policy a “stunt.”

“One student at one school will have one set of rules, and the student at the school next door will have a totally different set of rules, and it affects their marks. It doesn’t matter when they’re applying for university what the rules were — what matters is their grade.”

The plan “made for a good announcement for (Calandra) to say that grades were going to be tied to attendance,” she said. “Then you look at the details and that’s not quite what’s happening.”

stories.title: Mark Carney says trade talks will resume when Americans ‘start being serious’
stories.summary: Carney says the Trump administration must respect Canadian sovereignty and adopt a more serious tone before Canada returns to the negotiating table.
stories.author: Alex Ballingall
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney says there is still a “positive opportunity” for a trade deal with the United States, but that the Trump administration must respect Canadian sovereignty and adopt a more serious tone before Canada returns to the negotiating table.

Speaking to reporters Tuesday morning outside his office on Parliament Hill, Carney said there were multiple issues that alone would have been enough for Canada to reject the deal that fell apart in August, including concerns about French-language protections and Canada’s freedom to pursue its own trade deals with other countries.

He also said U.S. officials need to stop taunting Canada online — a day after U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth posted an image on social media mocking Canadian military cadets — which Carney panned as “beneath their office.”

“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” Carney said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has taken the position in trade talks that Canadian industries must become U.S. subsidiaries or be "wiped out." (Sept. 1, 2026)

He added that before he told Canadian negotiators to abandon the talks, “there were elements of that mutually beneficial deal that we were moving towards, which is why we were still at the table, but we never viewed that we had that deal and it diverged towards the end.”

When the talks collapsed last month, the Trump administration slapped new 50 per cent tariffs on almost $28 billion worth of Canadian goods, adding to the suite of import duties that have hammered sectors like automaking, steel and aluminum manufacturing, and the forestry industry. The federal government intends to strike back on Sept. 8 with counter-tariffs.

Since then, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has suggested the Trump administration will take further action if Canada follows through with those retaliatory tariffs. Trump had already threatened to hike import taxes on Canadian autos from 25 to 50 per cent, and Greer told the CBC last week that, “if there’s further retaliation from the Canadian side … we’re not going to just sit down and take that.”

Escalating trade war dashes hopes of ending the 18-month provincial liquor boycott.

Tensions have also escalated in recent days, with Premier Doug Ford lampooning U.S. President Donald Trump as a “dictator” and a “loser” who can “kiss my ass,” and Trump declaring that Lake Ontario will now be called “Lake America.”

At a G20 meeting in Asheville, N.C. on Tuesday, federal Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne was scheduled to meet with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent later in the day. Speaking before the meeting, Champagne told reporters he would be “firm” yet “constructive,” while looking to “reduce the friction” of recent days while Canada stays true to its position that it had to walk away from a bad trade deal.

Earlier this week, Bessent dismissed the idea of a “tit-for-tat” trade war between the U.S. and Canada, noting that the American economy is several times larger than Canada’s. He claimed Carney had turned the situation into a “political shouting match” that is only in the interest of his governing Liberal party.

“We’re not at war with Canada. How are we going to be at war with Canada? … Are they going to take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sic them on us?” Bessent told CNBC this week, referring to the now-defunct submarine attraction at the West Edmonton Mall.

Meanwhile, Carney welcomed the result of three byelections on Monday, where voters in North Vancouver—Capilano, Toronto’s Beaches—East York and Quebec’s Chicoutimi—Le Fjord elected Liberal MPs. Calling the result a “vote of confidence” in his government, Carney noted that more than 50 per cent of ballots were cast for victorious Liberal candidates.

He credited the win in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord, a seat held by the Conservatives since 2018, to the local candidate and the government’s plan to grow the economy and guard French language and dairy protections.

“The attitude of the United States in these discussions and subsequently has been one that the core Canadian industries either would be subsidiaries effectively of the United States industries, or would put in place terms where those industries would be gradually wound down in Canada,” Carney said, repeating his view that Trump’s aim is to destroy certain sectors of the Canadian economy for the benefit of the U.S.

Carney said he remains focused on boosting the Canadian economy and doubling trade with countries other than the U.S. over the next decade, as he argues the “rupture” on trade and relations with Canada’s closest commercial partner south of the border is a sign of a fundamentally changing world.

stories.title: Say it ain’t snow! Sunshine Village in Banff posts photos of first snow of season
stories.summary: Didn’t they just wrap up a summer snow season at Sunshine Ski Resort?
stories.author: Stephen Hunt
stories.content:
Didn’t they just wrap up a summer snow season at Sunshine Village Ski Resort?

The Banff National Park-based ski resort, which extended ski season for a couple of weeks on June 21, posted photos of its first snow day of the fall on Sunday, a full three weeks before fall officially arrives.

“We’ve got a snow day on our hands,” Sunshine posted. “Hello winter! Who’s ready for ski and snowboard season to begin?”

View this post on Instagram

While it might be presumptuous to answer, ‘absolutely nobody’, the first snow day of 2026 in the Rocky Mountains actually arrived almost a full week later than the first snow day of 2025, which CTV News reported last Aug. 24, 2025.

On that day, four resorts, including Sunshine Village, Nakiska, Lake Louise and Kicking Horse Ski Resort all reported snow.

At Sunshine Village, the snowfall brought on the first snow creature of the season when employee Liv Bergstrom built a snow bear — complete with snowy paws.

Liv Bergstrom made the most of the first snowfall at Banff Sunshine Village over the weekend to build a snow bear.

And on Sunday, Kicking Horse Resort posted some snow day photos of its own on its social media feed.

“First snow has entered the chat,” Kicking Horse posted. “A little snow? No problem. A few more bike laps? Absolutely. Winter mode? Loading...

“One foot in summer, one foot in winter. We’ll take it.”

No word yet on when either resort anticipates opening for winter ski season.

stories.title: Felix Auger-Aliassime advances with opening-round win at U.S. Open
stories.summary: Auger-Aliassime, the third-ranked man at the U.S. Open, won his first-round singles match on Monday night by defeating Australia's Rinky Hijiata 7-5, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
paragraphs: Felix Auger-Aliassime is well aware that New York claims to be the city that never sleeps.

After starting late and then playing for three hours and 19 minutes — and enduring a 55-minute rain delay between the second and third set — the Montreal tennis star can relate to the lack of rest in The Big Apple.
Auger-Aliassime, the third-ranked man at the U.S. Open, won his first-round singles match on Monday night by defeating Australia’s Rinky Hijiata 7-5, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5.

“We’ve known each other since we were like 10 years old, but this is the first time we’ve played one another. He caused me a lot of problems out there … but most importantly I’m through to the next round,” said Auger-Aliassime after the match.

The Canadian finished with 17 aces, 48 winners and 11 double faults. He had 50 unforced errors. Auger-Aliassime won 18 of 22 service games, and six of 21 return games. He advances to play Russian Karen Khachanov, who beat Roman Burruchaga of Argentina in three straight sets.

Meanwhile, Denis Shapovalov of Richmond Hill, Ont., will play his second-round men’s singles match Wednesday against Luca Van Assche of France. Shapovalov defeated Miomir Kecmanovic of Serbia in four sets on Sunday, while Van Assche beat Britain’s Cameron Norrie, also in four sets.

Leylah Fernandez of Laval, Que., is scheduled to play her second-round women’s singles match Wednesday against Mananchaya Sawangkaew of Thailand. Fernandez bounced Shuai Zhang of China in straight sets on Sunday, while Sawangkaew defeated Panna Udvardy of Hungary in straight sets.

stories.title: Former Calgary teacher and sexual abuse convict Fred Archer back in court
stories.summary: Eighty-two-year-old Fred Archer appeared in a Calgary courtroom Monday to face charges stemming from allegations of sexual incidents going back decades.
stories.author: Tyler Barrow
stories.content:
Eighty-two-year-old Fred Archer appeared in a Calgary courtroom Monday to face charges stemming from allegations of sexual incidents going back decades.

Archer faces charges of sexual assault, sexual interference and sexual exploitation in connection with alleged incidents between June 1994 and September 1995 involving a boy who was then aged 13.

The boy, who cannot be identified due to a publication ban, is referred to as JR in court.

During opening arguments, Crown Prosecutor Gianna Argento told Justice Brandy Shaw that Archer first befriended JR’s father and later developed a “very close relationship” where Archer ended up in a caretaker role over JR.

She told court Archer would look after JR while his father worked out of town for weeks.

Archer is accused of sexually abusing JR during a 15-month period.

JR went to John Ware School, where Archer was a teacher.

Archer’s lawyer, Tim Dunlap, rejected the allegations, telling the court JR’s allegations are “for profit.”

Archer was convicted for abusing boys in the 1990s at Springbank Middle School.

He was also named along with another former teacher in a massive class-action lawsuit against the Calgary Board of Education involving a $15.7-million payment to 55 former students of John Ware School.

The trial is set to last five days.

stories.title: BC Conservatives lose another MLA, seventh to leave party caucus since mid-August
stories.summary: Chilliwack-Cultus Lake MLA Á’a:liya Warbus cited a ‘critical breakdown in communications’ in decision to leave party
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
The BC Conservative caucus lost another MLA on Monday, the seventh to leave the ranks of the province’s Official Opposition party since mid-August.

The exodus presents a growing challenge to party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay as the former Conservative MP runs in a by-election to win a seat in the provincial legislature.

Monday’s departure of Á’a:liya Warbus, the only Indigenous MLA on the party benches, is the latest domino to fall for the BC Conservatives. A succession of defections, senior staff departures and internal controversies has rocked the party since Ms. Findlay was elected leader in late May, throwing both her leadership and the Conservatives’ future into question.

The upheaval is also a boon to Premier David Eby ’s NDP, which won 47 seats to the Conservatives’ 44 in the 2024 election and could now benefit from a fractured opposition and divided centre-right.

Ms. Warbus, who represented the Chilliwack-Cultus Lake riding and served as the party’s house leader, joins Peter Milobar, Ian Paton, Rosalyn Bird, Teresa Wat, Brennan Day and Bruce Banman. All have left the caucus since Aug. 14 and now sit as independent MLAs.

Mr. Milobar and Mr. Paton last week announced their intention to form a new political party with Mr. Milobar as interim leader. They will be up against former BC Liberal cabinet minister Mike Bernier, who was named leader of the CentreBC party in July, in vying for the votes of those seeking a more centrist political home than Ms. Findlay’s Conservative Party.

The BC Conservatives did not respond to an interview request on Monday.

In announcing her decision, Ms. Warbus cited the party’s departure from core issues and a “critical breakdown in communication” under Ms. Findlay’s leadership, both with the public and internally, across MLAs and staff.

“Caucus members have learned of hirings, firings, critic appointments and leadership positions through any and all channels including social media before being informed by leadership,” Ms. Warbus said in a statement.

She also highlighted the inability of the caucus to discuss serious allegations that surfaced last week, which prompted the firing of operations director Apollo Chung after audio recordings circulated purportedly capturing a staffer discussing a fundraiser “so we can steal everything.”

Another recording allegedly captured Ms. Findlay telling caucus members that if an MLA gave up their seat to trigger a by-election, she “could give them a role as a senior adviser in the same portfolio.” Reann Gasper resigned as Abbotsford-Mission MLA on Aug. 22, giving Ms. Findlay a chance to run; she has since become the leader’s deputy chief of staff. It is a violation of the Criminal Code to offer a legislator an inducement to resign from office.

Neither Ms. Findlay nor the party have confirmed the authenticity of the recordings. Ms. Findlay announced Mr. Chung’s firing on Aug. 26 in a one-sentence statement, with no reason given. In a post to social media the following day, she referenced a “surreptitious recording” and called allegations that comments about the party’s future plans May constitute a criminal offence “a political smear job and nothing more.”

A caucus meeting that was planned for Monday was cancelled without explanation on Sunday. Ms. Warbus said it reflected “the lack of value being placed on caucus members and their opinions.”

In an interview, Ms. Warbus said “a number of staff hirings and firings” happened without so much as a courtesy e-mail to MLAs, causing confusion and leaving them not properly informed to speak on behalf of the party and do their jobs effectively. She also underscored the seriousness of the allegations raised by the leaked audio recordings.

“There were some very critical, pivotal points in the past two weeks that deserve time, answers, accountability and transparency,” she said.

Ms. Warbus said unity is needed among like-minded people, and that divisions, personal attacks and culture wars are unhelpful.

“I’m open, and my door’s open, my phone’s open, to anybody that wants to have those conversations,” she said. “I think we have to come together before we can ask British Columbians to govern at all.”

Ms. Warbus is not alone in citing a breakdown of communications as a factor in leaving the party. Randy Hawes resigned as the B.C. Conservatives’ riding association president for Abbotsford-Mission on Aug. 24 after learning through media reports that Ms. Gasper had stepped down.

In an interview, the former BC Liberal MLA and former mayor of Mission said he was shocked by the outcome of May’s leadership contest, when Ms. Findlay was elected on the fourth ballot with 51 per cent of the vote, to Caroline Elliott’s 49 per cent.

“She’s what I would call hardcore right-wing, and I don’t think that’s what the BC Conservative Party was supposed to be,” Mr. Hawes said.

He cited as examples Ms. Findlay’s attack on Mr. Milobar during the leadership contest, suggesting he is in a conflict of interest because his wife is Indigenous, and a July report that Ms. Findlay and her senior staff directed MLAs to no longer use the term “First Nations” in describing people but instead use terms such as “Indian.”

Mr. Hawes also said that Ms. Findlay did not repudiate comments made by her husband, Brent Chapman, the party’s South Surrey MLA, who in old social-media posts described Palestinian children as “inbred walking, talking, breathing time bombs” and suggested mass shootings such as Sandy Hook were fake.

“My conscience will not allow me to sit in a party that has that woman at the head,” Mr. Hawes said.

He, too, is hopeful that Mr. Milobar’s and Mr. Bernier’s groups will work together.

“What’s going on now is insane,” he said. “As far as people who are in the centre, you can’t split that vote. You need a uniting formula.”

stories.title: New $54.3M Regina Mundi school opens, but old building to remain in use amid enrolment growth
stories.summary: Students and staff at Regina Mundi Catholic College are preparing to return to a brand new school this fall, but the school’s former building will remain in use as enrolment continues to outpace capacity.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Students and staff at Regina Mundi Catholic College are preparing to return to a brand new school this fall, but the school’s former building will remain in use as enrolment continues to outpace capacity.

The $54.3-million replacement school, built on the grounds of the existing Regina Mundi campus off Wellington Street South, has capacity for approximately 700 students.

However, the school currently has about 1,100 students enrolled.

As a result, the London District Catholic School Board has decided to keep the former school open for at least another year rather than add up to 24 portable classrooms to accommodate the growing student population.

“We’ve decided to keep the existing school for one year and continually review the plan as we move forward with the students and enrollment that we’re seeing currently today,” said LDCSB’s executive manager of capital projects Daryl Diegel.

The existing building was originally constructed in 1963 as a junior seminary. The new school, which began construction in spring 2024, has been nearly a decade in the making.

While the new facility includes updated technology and classroom spaces designed to connect and work together, elements of the former school have also been incorporated into the design.

Among them is the distinctive arched ceiling in the school’s cafetorium, which was replicated from the original building.

“It’s airy, open and well designed,” said Diegel as he walked down the high ceiling hallways.

The decision to operate both buildings reflects a broader challenge facing the London District Catholic School Board as enrolment continues to grow.

The board says it has grown by more than 30 per cent over the past five years and now serves more than 28,000 students.

It currently has 10 major construction projects underway, including nine new schools and one major addition. The cost of recent and upcoming construction projects is approaching $600 million, before additional land costs.

For now, Regina Mundi students will be split between the new and old buildings.

School officials say that despite operating in two separate spaces, the goal is to maintain the same sense of community.

“Even though we’re working in two buildings, we’re still one school and one family,” said RMC principal, Kevin Barnes.

Students are expected to begin the new school year next week.

Among them is the distinctive arched ceiling in the school’s cafetorium, which was replicated from the original building.

The decision to operate both buildings reflects a broader challenge facing the London District Catholic School Board as enrolment continues to grow.
The board says it has grown by more than 30 per cent over the past five years and now serves more than 28,000 students.

It currently has 10 major construction projects underway, including nine new schools and one major addition. The cost of recent and upcoming construction projects is approaching $600 million, before additional land costs.
For now, Regina Mundi students will be split between the new and old buildings.
School officials say that despite operating in two separate spaces, the goal is to maintain the same sense of community.
“Even though we’re working in two buildings, we’re still one school and one family,” said RMC principal, Kevin Barnes.
Students are expected to begin the new school year next week.

stories.title: Nearly 80 rescued from Grand Canyon flooding. 2 others died and 1 is unaccounted for, officials say
stories.summary: Nearly 80 people were rescued during Grand Canyon flooding, while two others died and one is unaccounted for, officials said Monday.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Grand Canyon National Park, Ariz. — -- The bodies of a Texas chiropractor and at least one other person have been found after a major weekend flash flood swept through the Grand Canyon, and forecasters warned more flooding was possible as heavy rain shrouded the canyon walls.

Saturday’s flash flood severely damaged the only water pipeline into the canyon. Officials barred tourists from staying at lodges and hotels inside Grand Canyon National Park and issued emergency water restrictions for year-round residents. Waves of rain hit the Bright Angel Creek area of the tourist destination that hosts 4.4 million visitors a year.

Nearly 80 people were rescued during the flooding. Officials are seeking information on one person who remains unaccounted for.

Incident Cmdr. Dave Black said officials used night vision and other equipment to find people who needed to be evacuated over the weekend.

The flood threatened people who hike far into the Grand Canyon

The flood happened deep in the canyon near where the Colorado River flows, around popular lodges and camping areas where people hiking from one rim of the Grand Canyon to the other stop for the night.

Scores of visitors had to be evacuated from the area by helicopter. They talked of a massive deluge and rangers warning of rockslides, and saw huge pools of logs and debris rolling down the river as they stood nearby awaiting rescue.

Hiker Daniel Evans said it rained several times before the worst 30-minute downpour Saturday afternoon. He had been planning to rest through the hot day and spend the night near the hard-hit Bright Angel campground area.

Earlier, rangers told him it looked to be safe. Then, as the rain poured, they told him it was time to go. He thought of Nepal and the massive floods and landslides that poured down mountain valleys last week.

“The entire time it was raining -- the entire time I’m going through all this and packing -- I’m just keeping my eyes upstream, just praying that a wall of water isn’t coming toward us,” Evans said.

One hiker killed is identified as rescuers search for his friends

The family of John Giusti, 53, said the Texas chiropractor set out Thursday on a trip he dreamed of with two buddies -- Texas martial arts studio owner Brent Rosenkranz, 42, and Wyoming pilot Timothy Smith, 53. They planned to spend two nights at the bottom of the canyon fishing and hiking.

They spoke to their families Thursday and found their campsite Friday. They have not been heard from since, the three families said in a joint statement released Monday.

All three men had ties to Granbury, Texas. Their families said they planned “several days of hiking, camping, fishing and exploring together.”

Park officials said they recovered the body of a 46-year-old man Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River and were trying to recover a second body. Their email provided no other details.

Shannon Cahill said her brother and his daughter are missing somewhere in the Grand Canyon region.

Michael Wilhoit, 53, Mystic Wilhoit, 30, and her boyfriend left Saturday for a three-night camping trip. She hasn’t heard from any of them since. Phone calls go straight to their voicemail, and they have not posted on social media.

“That’s not like Mystic. If she’s doing something, she’s posting. She posts constantly,” Cahill said. Cahill wasn’t sure where they were going to camp.

Late Monday morning, more rain fell as the state Department of Emergency and Military Affairs was coordinating with the park service and county emergency management officials in search and recovery efforts.

It’s `monsoon season’ in the Grand Canyon

Visiting the Grand Canyon can be particularly dangerous in the summer because of the risk of flash flooding that accompanies the monsoon, or rainy season. Clear days can quickly give way to thunderstorms and downpours. Forecasters warned more flooding could happen Monday or just about any time storms pop up.

Rain also fell on part of the Dragon Bravo fire scar, a burn area left by a lightning-caused wildfire in July 2025. It burned for days before exploding into a fast-moving conflagration that forced evacuations and consumed the historic Grand Canyon Lodge, some cabins and other structures.

Without vegetation, a barren burn scar allows runoff to flow more quickly.

The steep, rocky nature of the canyon itself funnels water rapidly. What might be a normal summer downpour somewhere else can become a charging wall of water in the canyon.

El Nino has this year’s monsoons in the desert especially intense

This year’s heavy monsoon rains are especially intense because there is a higher amount of water vapour in the atmosphere, mostly because of a strong El Nino, said A. Park Williams, a hydroclimatologist at the University of California, Los Angeles.

The natural warming of parts of the Pacific Ocean can warp weather globally. That extra water vapor in the southwest U.S. gets wrung out in the storm in the form of rainfall, he said.

The link to human-caused climate change and the heavy Arizona rain is pretty strong, said climate scientist Daniel Swain of the California Institute for Water Resources.

A few months ago, Swain and colleagues published a study in the journal Weather and Climate Extremes finding that during the summer, short-term intense downpours in the West -- akin to the one that hit the Grand Canyon -- have become 10 per cent stronger since 2000.

The flood hits water supply in the canyon

The flood was a major blow to an enduring effort to modernize the water pipeline that serves visitors and the roughly 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village.

A US$208 million rehabilitation of the pipeline and upgrades to the associated water delivery system started in 2023, with the park service calling it a crucial investment to ensure the park can meet the needs of residents and visitors. The project was expected to be completed next year.

While the Grand Canyon has large storage tanks for potable water on the South Rim, they won’t be refilled while the pipeline is out of service.

Stengle reported from Dallas. Seth Borenstein in Kensington, Md.; Julie Walker in New York City, Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, S.C.; Kathy McCormack in Concord, N.H.; and Christopher Weber in Los Angeles contributed.

Jamie Stengle and Ty Oneil, The Associated Press
