stories.title: Toronto sex offender faces new charges of drugging, sexually assaulting woman
stories.summary: A disgraced Toronto pharmacist who drugged and sexually assaulted 18 women more than 15 years ago has been charged with similar offences.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Warning: This story deals with sexual assault.

A 73-year-old former Toronto pharmacist on statutory release was arrested last week and charged with sexually assaulting a woman.

Before being released in 2025, Allen SIU Ming Chow was serving time for drugging and recording himself sexually assaulting 18 young prostitutes more than 15 years ago.

What’s more, Peel Regional Police say investigators in their special victims unit believe there are additional alleged victims of Chow.

Chow was released from federal prison in March 2025, after serving approximately nine years and four months of a 14-year sentence for 36 counts of administering a stupefying drug and sexually assaulting 18 women between 2009 and 2012.

“Between December 2025 and April 2026, it is alleged that the accused met an adult female victim online and subsequently met with her in person on multiple occasions. During these encounters, the accused allegedly rendered the victim unconscious and unresponsive before sexually assaulting her,” police wrote in a Saturday press release , adding that he used his phone to record the sex acts “without the victim’s knowledge or consent.”

The Oakville man is charged with overcoming resistance by administering or attempting to administer a drug, sexual assault causing bodily harm and voyeurism.

Previously, Chow was the owner, manager and licensed dispensing pharmacist at Bridletowne Pharmacy in Toronto, according to a sanctioning decision by the Ontario College of Pharmacists. Police were on the way to arrest Chow in relation to a sexual assault allegation on Dec. 4, 2012, when they saw him stagger out of his pharmacy and get in his vehicle while severely impaired.

While he was in custody, a search of his residence uncovered several camera memory cards that contained 70 hours of footage in 95 separate videos of himself engaged “in all manner of sexual activity” with female sex workers who’d been rendered unconscious with drinks or food laced with Lorazepam, according to a sentencing decision by Ontario Superior Court Justice Gregory Mulligan.

“Chow subjected his victims to degrading and dehumanizing activity,” which included spitting on them and having unprotected sex, according to the agreed statement of facts quoted by the judge.

“He treated the women as objects, manipulating their bodies as he pleased.”

The judge explained that when Chow completed his “disgusting sexual conduct, he showed no concern for his victims’ recovery or ability to get home safely,” often exiting the hotel room where the assaults occurred, leaving his victims “to regain consciousness on their own and make their way home in spite of the condition he had subjected them to.”

Some of the women were victimized more than a dozen times each.

During a forensic psychiatric evaluation requested by the defence, Chow explained that he “felt justified in making them unconscious for sexual gratification” because they were prostitutes providing a paid service.

Chow was released on conditions a week after his arrest, but was arrested again in March 2013 after police went through a “painstaking and thorough investigation” to identify and interview 18 of the victims — none of whom were aware “that they were subject to this degrading and humiliating activity while being videotaped.”

Upon learning what happened to her, one woman “became physically ill in the waste basket of the interview room,” the decision reads.

Many of the victims provided victim impact statements to the court, some of whom chose to read them aloud in front of a then 62-year-old Chow at his November 2015 sentencing.

“I have had numerous hospitalizations for suicide attempts and post-traumatic disorder from what happened to me,” one victim stated. “He, of all people, a medical professional, purposely and knowingly preyed on me numerous times.”

“When I think of you, my chest gets tight, I feel sick to my stomach,” another offered. “I have had some major anxiety attacks when thinking about what you have done to not only me, but many other women and young ladies.”

Another said she felt sick watching her own video statement in court.

“When I got home that was all I could think about, I cried constantly and didn’t even want to hold my daughter because I didn’t think I was good enough,” she said.

Chow also addressed the court during the sentencing hearings, apologizing to his victims and calling his actions “callous, heinous, selfish and degrading.”

According to the decision, Chow immigrated from Hong Kong on a student visa to attend York University, where he met his wife of over 30 years, with whom he shares an adult daughter. He’d been running his pharmacy for 17 years when he was first arrested, at which time he was about 59 years old.

Chow’s psychiatric evaluation determined that he started drinking significantly more three years earlier following a prostate cancer diagnosis, including while at work. He “presented with a major depression without psychotic features,” alcoholism and paraphilia, specifically “sexual sadism,” one the psychiatrist said will now be a “lifelong disorder.”

“He stated that if a person in these circumstances were to re-offend, it would more likely be the same type of offence, and that once these offences start, they can escalate over time,” Mulligan wrote.

Another psychopathy checklist found Chow externalized blame, lacked empathy for victims and that “he May resort to these maladaptive strategies when faced with future stressors or recurrence of his major depressive disorder.”

The judge said his assessments show signs of someone who lacked “insight into their conduct” and cited a section of Chow’s letter as an example.

“I indulged my sexual fantasy to the fullest degree. I wanted to feel young again by associating with young escorts to reassert my virility,” he wrote.

“I am not misogynistic. My actions were never meant to harm, nor were they carried out with violent, malicious or criminal intent. They were pure sexual fantasy merely, nothing more. I was naïve and ignorant not to have realized the criminality of my actions.”

While Chow pleaded guilty to all charges, avoiding having his many victims testify at trial, Mulligan ruled “a substantial period of incarceration” was required and handed down a sentence of 14 years after credit for nearly three years spent in custody.

“Mr. Chow is at a low risk to re-offend provided he consents to treatment such as that described … and maintains sobriety upon release,” Mulligan wrote. “It is in society’s interest that Mr. Chow receives treatment as soon as possible, so that its effectiveness can be monitored and measured.”

It’s not clear what, if any, treatments Chow engaged in while in custody. National Post has contacted the Parole Board of Canada to obtain a copy of his release decision. It’s also unclear if a warning to the public was issued at the time of his release.

Meanwhile, Peel police ask anyone who May have had similar interactions with the accused or people with information to share to contact their special victims unit at 905-453-2121, ext. 3460.

Editor’s note: This story was updated to reflect new information that Chow was not paroled, as originally indicated by Peel Regional Police. Rather, Chow is out on statutory release, which requires, under federal law, that Correctional Service of Canada automatically release an inmate after they’ve served two-thirds of their sentence.

He “presented with a major depression without psychotic features,” alcoholism and paraphilia, specifically “sexual sadism,” one the psychiatrist said will now be a “lifelong disorder.”

Another psychopathy checklist found Chow externalized blame, lacked empathy for victims and that “he May resort to these maladaptive strategies when faced with future stressors or recurrence of his major depressive disorder.”
The judge said his assessments show signs of someone who lacked “insight into their conduct” and cited a section of Chow’s letter as an example.
“I indulged my sexual fantasy to the fullest degree. I wanted to feel young again by associating with young escorts to reassert my virility,” he wrote.

“I am not misogynistic. My actions were never meant to harm, nor were they carried out with violent, malicious or criminal intent. They were pure sexual fantasy merely, nothing more. I was naïve and ignorant not to have realized the criminality of my actions.”

It’s not clear what, if any, treatments Chow engaged in while in custody. National Post has contacted the Parole Board of Canada to obtain a copy of his release decision. It’s also unclear if a warning to the public was issued at the time of his release.
Meanwhile, Peel police ask anyone who May have had similar interactions with the accused or people with information to share to contact their special victims unit at 905-453-2121, ext. 3460.

Editor’s note: This story was updated to reflect new information that Chow was not paroled, as originally indicated by Peel Regional Police. Rather, Chow is out on statutory release, which requires, under federal law, that Correctional Service of Canada automatically release an inmate after they’ve served two-thirds of their sentence.

stories.title: Thinking of leaving your desk job and entering the trades? Here’s what you should know first
stories.summary: For many Canadians, skilled trades have started to become more attractive as a career option, partly as various levels of government invest heavily in these professions while a boom in artificial intelligence creates fear over the future of many desk jobs.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
More than 25 years into his job as a business administrator, Simon Hardcastle felt there was nothing left for him to learn.

He didn’t hate his job, but it wasn’t thrilling either, Hardcastle recalled.

Then, one day at work, he signed up to drive a skid steer to plow snow, and he knew it was time for a shakeup.

“I moved snow, and about two hours later I thought, ‘Wow, this is really good fun! What else can I do?” the 49-year-old Ancaster, Ont., resident said. “So, I spoke to my wife and I was like, ‘I’m thinking of changing careers.’”

He knew going from a desk job to a skilled trade wasn’t going to be easy. It meant giving up a stable paycheque for a while, and temporarily transitioning to a single-income household while also raising two kids.

But he was sure that’s what he wanted to do.

For many Canadians, skilled trades have started to become more attractive as a career option, partly as various levels of government invest heavily in these professions while a boom in artificial intelligence creates fear over the future of many desk jobs.

Some career counsellors say they’re seeing more interest among mid-career workers to make a switch. However, not knowing where to begin often delays the process.

Start by understanding the different trade opportunities, said Rachel Buesink, general manager at Express Employment Professionals in Hamilton, Ont.

Online assessment tools can help you figure out where your strengths lie — whether that’s building things, mathematics and problem-solving, or even general handyman work, she said.

But just having an interest isn’t enough.

Buesink said a lot of times, people come to her with misconceptions.

“So many people come in and say: ‘I’ve hung pictures, I can build anything from Ikea, I want to be a carpenter,’” she said.

But many don’t realize how lengthy and demanding the journey is, she said. It can take four years of school and several exams. You also need an employer who can document your progress and is willing to hire you as an apprentice.

Shelley Gray, chief executive officer of SkilledTradesBC, says exposure to your desired job or industry can help cement that decision.

Gray said several institutions offer sampler or pre-apprenticeship programs to try out various trades. That could also be a help in getting into a full-time program or finding an employer, she said.

Buesink said switching careers is about “looking at understanding what each skilled trade opportunity is, trying to best match it with your strengths and interest, and then trying to keep up with the ever-changing economic demands for that trade.

“It is a bit of a balancing act.”

Keeping up with bills and supporting a family during the transition can also be a challenge.

“The biggest thing is the wage cut until you’re trained and able to add value to the company,” Buesink said.

She said workers in transition can get employment insurance or make some money from apprenticeships. But overall, it takes time to get to a well-paid job.

For Hardcastle, switching to operating heavy equipment was a calculated financial risk.

He and his wife saved up for a couple of months before he could finally quit his day job, and he took out a loan for his certification.

Getting certified is crucial to landing a well-paying job. But that could take time, depending on the program you choose.

For example, it can take about four months to become a truck driver, a year to become a welder and five years to become a qualified electrician.

Gray said many skilled trades offer a level of flexibility to apprentices to learn at their own pace.

But she said it’s crucial to find an employer who can sponsor you. “Eighty per cent of apprenticeship happens in the workplace.”

College programs with co-ops can help with placements in most cases, Buesink said. But if there aren’t enough spots, she said this is where your previous desk job could help boost your resumé and show your eagerness to work.

“If you have a strong resume, if you have a good background and a willingness (that shows): ‘Hey, I’m in school, this is what I want to do,’ — that makes you more attractive to the potential employer,” she said.

While it can take a while to get trained, Gray said she often hears from people about high levels of job satisfaction alongside good pay.

That’s true in Hardcastle’s case. He didn’t have to take a pay cut and now gets to do something that excites him.

“Right now, it’s like a kid in a sandbox,” he said. “I’m playing with these big machines and I’m moving material.

“Every day is different. It’s so much fun, like, I can’t even explain.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

stories.title: 2 tornadoes confirmed in Manitoba and Saskatchewan this weekend
stories.summary: Multiple tornadoes were confirmed in Manitoba and Saskatchewan after a stormy Sunday, they are the newest twisters amid a record-breaking storm season in the Prairies, Eccc said.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
paragraphs: If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .
Editor’s Note: a previous version of this story indicated three tornadoes were confirmed. However, only two tornadoes had been confirmed as of Monday afternoon.
Multiple tornadoes have been confirmed in Manitoba and Saskatchewan after a stormy Sunday on the Prairies, according to Environment Canada.
Environment Canada confirmed a tornado touched down in Maryfield, Sask., on Sunday, it said. Maryfield is located slightly more than 250 km east of Regina.

“There was a line of storms that formed in the late morning and afternoon hours in Saskatchewan, they pushed towards the Manitoba border. And then a few other storms were formed just in front of that line,” Dylan Painchaud-Niemi, a research meteorologist with the Northern Tornadoes Project (NTP), told Global News, noting that it triggered tornado warnings for potentially affected areas.
“(The weather) was conducive for tornado development, and one did produce.”
The twister landed five km south of the community around 4 p.m. Sunday, according to Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC).
Terri Lang, a meteorologist with ECCC, told Global News that the heaviest rainfall fell in southeastern parts of the province, near the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border.

“It originated in Alberta and deepened as it came over Saskatchewan. It brought in some moisture from the south and that’s really what spawned these thunderstorms,” noting such storms typically occur in early summer, not at the end of August.
Lang said the combination of those storms, moisture and other atmospheric conditions led to the Maryfield tornado.
A NTP team is also investigating reports of a tornado approximately 45 km away, in Kelso, Sask., along with other areas that were hit by the storm.
In Manitoba, at least one tornado occurred on Sunday, Dave Phillips, a senior climatologist with ECCC told 680 CJOB Monday morning.

The agency said twisters touched down more than 300 km west of Winnipeg in Elkhorn, Man. The province has seen more tornado activity than average this summer, with at least 11 confirmed tornadoes thus far — compared to the usual annual total of seven or eight, Phillips said.
Painchaud-Niemi said a team started tracking the Manitoba system after being notified there was a chance of tornadoes.
“We knew there was some severe weather potential, as well as some of our local meteorologists warned us that there was something that was going to occur,” he recalled.
“Then there were some storms that popped up near the border with Manitoba, and then those ended up producing some tornadoes.”
NTP received reports of damage from the Manitoban side of the border, but none have been reported from Saskatchewan, said Painchaud-Niemi.
Environment Canada’s senior climatologist said this summer’s heat and humidity added to the stormy weather.

“If you look at the Prairies, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, we’ve had a record number of tornadoes,” Phillips said, noting ECCC’s records on that topic are limited to about the last 10 years when technology allowed round-the-clock monitoring. Before that, he said, tracking twisters was hit or miss.
“We’ve had, I think, in total, 77 tornadoes this year on the Prairies,” Phillips said. “That’s certainly the most number of tornadoes you’ve had in that last, say eight, or nine, (or) 10 years.”

The agency said twisters touched down more than 300 km west of Winnipeg in Elkhorn, Man. The province has seen more tornado activity than average this summer, with at least 11 confirmed tornadoes thus far — compared to the usual annual total of seven or eight, Phillips said.

Painchaud-Niemi said a team started tracking the Manitoba system after being notified there was a chance of tornadoes.

“We knew there was some severe weather potential, as well as some of our local meteorologists warned us that there was something that was going to occur,” he recalled.

“Then there were some storms that popped up near the border with Manitoba, and then those ended up producing some tornadoes.”

NTP received reports of damage from the Manitoban side of the border, but none have been reported from Saskatchewan, said Painchaud-Niemi.

Environment Canada’s senior climatologist said this summer’s heat and humidity added to the stormy weather.

“If you look at the Prairies, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, we’ve had a record number of tornadoes,” Phillips said, noting ECCC’s records on that topic are limited to about the last 10 years when technology allowed round-the-clock monitoring. Before that, he said, tracking twisters was hit or miss.

“We’ve had, I think, in total, 77 tornadoes this year on the Prairies,” Phillips said. “That’s certainly the most number of tornadoes you’ve had in that last, say eight, or nine, (or) 10 years.”

stories.title: Ottawa asks court to quash lawsuit over projected missed emission targets
stories.summary: Federal Court doesn’t have power to order government to meet emissions targets, government lawyers argue
stories.author: Nick Murray
paragraphs: The federal government is asking a Federal Court judge to toss out a lawsuit accusing Ottawa of having no intention of meeting its 2030 greenhouse gas emissions target.
In recent court filings, government lawyers argued the Federal Court doesn’t have the power to order the government to take steps to meet its emissions targets.
The government also argued it wasn’t up to the court to “opine on the political and policy issues” at the heart of the lawsuit.
“Climate change is a real and important issue. Accountability, however, with respect to concerns expressed by the Applicants, lies with Parliament, not with the Court,” the government wrote.

“There is no basis on which a court could order any of the relief sought in the Application. The Act creates no duties which could be owed to the Applicants and instead establishes a framework that includes a series of targets, plans, assessments, and reporting to track progress on emission reductions over time.”

A group of climate advocates filed a lawsuit against the federal government in June arguing recent policy changes have knocked Ottawa off its track to meet Canada’s legislated greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets.
Environmental Defence, the Canadian Association of Physicians for the Environment and climate activists Marie Maltais, Sophia Mathur and Shirley Barnea brought the lawsuit forward.

They asked the Federal Court to order the government to bring its 2030 emissions reductions plan into compliance with the Net-Zero Accountability Act – or to declare Ottawa’s emission reductions plan unlawful under the act.

The Net-Zero Accountability Act, which passed in 2021, legally commits Canada to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 and requires the government to set national emission reduction targets along the way – though there are no consequences for missing them.
A progress report published in December shows the government is nowhere near on track to meet its current target of cutting emissions to 40 to 45 per cent below 2005 levels.
In a statement, the director of communications for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said that because the matter is before the courts, they could not comment on the federal legal submission.
“The Government of Canada is committed to fighting climate change and reaching net-zero emissions by 2050,” Chris Zhou wrote.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has been accused of backsliding on climate policy for the better part of the last year.

He eliminated the consumer carbon price in March 2025 – on his first day in office. While he promised a strengthened industrial carbon pricing system, he was accused of weakening that system through an agreement with Alberta in May that has ramifications for every other province and territory.

His government is also moving to repeal the electric vehicle sales mandate – Ottawa has promised stronger tailpipe standards but those are still years away – and to cancel the oil and gas emissions cap. Carney’s government also has delayed methane regulations in Alberta.
In a video released two weeks after the suit was filed, Carney said federal climate policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau was too expensive and divisive.

“I want to be clear on this point. The changes we have made will mean that our emissions will be higher in the next few years than they were projected to be under the previous government’s plan,” Carney said in the video.
“But in my judgment, that plan was not sustainable over the long term.”

stories.title: Greece cuts grocery prices nearly 10 per cent to support households
stories.summary: Prices of more than 1,700 grocery and school supplies items fell by an average of 9.5 per cent in Greece on Monday as a government-backed measure kicked in to confront concerns over purchasing power.
stories.author: AFP Staff
stories.content:
Prices of more than 1,700 grocery and school supplies items fell by an average of 9.5 per cent in Greece on Monday as a government-backed measure kicked in to confront concerns over purchasing power.

The measure “provides relief to households and citizens confronted with the high cost of living,” said Development Minister Takis Theodorikakos.

The price reductions will be in place in the EU nation until the end of the year, the government of Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis noted in a statement.

The conservative Mitsotakis is seeking a third mandate in legislative elections due in the spring next year, and on Sunday he spoke of the measure as providing temporary relief for Greeks faced with high grocery prices and housing costs while salaries remain low.

“This is not a solution for all of the problems weighing on household budgets today. But it provides concrete relief,” Mitsotakis said on Facebook.

The measure adds to a reduction of 10 cents per litre on petrol and five cents per litre on diesel which has been in place for two months.

The Greek economy took a major hit from the decade-long debt crisis that began in 2008, with earnings failing to keep pace with the rest of the EU.

Annual inflation ran at 3.3 percent in July in Greece, according to Eurostat data, as the war in the Middle East continues to push energy prices higher.

According to the Greek statistics agency Elstat annual food price inflation ran at 2.7 percent in June.

stories.title: Norway's Queen Mette-Marit joins procession to bring late King Harald V's coffin to royal chapel
stories.summary: The coffin of late King Harald V of Norway traveled through the royal palace to its chapel on Monday, with Queen Mette-Marit joining the procession in her first official appearance since assuming the title.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Oslo, Norway — The coffin of late King Harald V of Norway traveled through the royal palace to its chapel on Monday, with Queen Mette-Marit joining the procession in her first official appearance since assuming the title.

Harald passed away Friday at age 89, and his son, the crown prince, immediately became King Haakon Viii. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne.

Haakon, 53, will take the oath to Norway’s constitution on Tuesday. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction.

Mette-Marit has been largely absent from the public eye in the wake of her lung transplant in June. She was diagnosed in 2018 with pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive disease that damages and scars lung tissue. It can cause serious breathing problems, and there is no known cure.

Mette-Marit and Queen Sonja, Harald’s widow, held hands and walked behind the coffin during Monday’s procession.

Since Harald’s death, the royal family and the country have been in an official state of mourning. Norwegians and visitors expressed their grief over the weekend by laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital.

The coffin stayed in the palace’s Red Salon over the weekend before traveling to the royal chapel on Monday, where it will remain until the funeral. The public can go to the chapel to pay their respects to the late king beginning Tuesday, Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported.

The funeral is set for Sept. 9.

The Associated Press

stories.author: Isaac Callan

Firefighters were met with heavy and flames early on Monday morning when they rushed to the scene of a three-alarm blaze in Scarborough.
Toronto fire said it was called to the area of McLevin Avenue and Tapscott Road just before 2 a.m. to try and suppress the flames at a commercial building.
Facing a fierce fire, crews were quickly forced to transition to defensive firefighting, worrying about the deteriorating structural conditions of the building.
Toronto fire said its crews were worried about the condition of the building’s walls and roof.
As the city woke up on Monday, roads were still closed and crews were at the scene.
Officials said there were no longer visible flames, but there were still worries about the smoke emanating from the structure.
“Fire crews still remain on scene applying water to building,” Toronto fire wrote in a statement.

stories.title: TAP Air Portugal flies into red before privatization
stories.summary: TAP Air Portugal suffered a second-quarter loss due to high fuel prices, the airline said Monday, with the airline’s privatization to Air France-KLM or Lufthansa expected to be wrapped up soon.
stories.author: AFP Staff
stories.content:
TAP Air Portugal suffered a second-quarter loss due to high fuel prices, the airline said Monday, with the airline’s privatization to Air France-KLM or Lufthansa expected to be wrapped up soon.

The company recorded a net loss of 59.3 million euros (US$68.8 million) in the three months to the end of June, compared to a profit of 38.3 million euros in the same period last year.

While TAP carried a record 8.2 million passengers and took in record revenue of just over two billion euros over the first half of the year, higher fuel costs due to the war in the Middle East had a negative impact of 99.2 million euros, the company said.

Thanks to the “solidity of demand across our entire network”, the airline was “able to mitigate the significant impact of the sharp increase in fuel prices”, chief executive Luis Rodrigues said in a statement.

TAP, which was renationalized in 2020 to stem losses from the COVID-19 pandemic, is in the final stages of being reprivatized.

Both Air France-KLM and Lufthansa said in July they had submitted bids to acquire a controlling stake in the airline, with the government expected to announce the result in the coming days

The 40-year-old accused appeared by video Monday as the new charge was read in a London courtroom.

A window is covered with plywood, broken glass is visible on the sill and the front door is damaged at the deadbolt at 10 Raywood Ave. on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. A woman stabbed at the home later died in hospital. (Jack Moulton/The London Free Press)
A second-degree murder charge has officially been laid in the death of an elderly London woman attacked in her own home.

Monday morning, Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of no fixed address, appeared in a London courtroom by video link for five minutes from the Elgin-Middlesex Detention Centre as the new charge was read to him.

Cornejo is charged in the death of Lillian Leonard, 73, who died in hospital last week from stab wounds she received during a break-in at her Raywood Avenue home, north of the intersection of Wellington and Base Line roads.
A publication ban regarding evidence and reasons at a potential bail hearing was put in place by justice of the peace Kristine Diaz during Monday’s court appearance.

Cornejo appeared on the video link in a jail-issued orange T-shirt. His hair is long and he has a beard.
He told Diaz that he has contacted London defence lawyer Nicola Circelli. His case was put over to Sept. 10 to allow time for a legal aid application and to confirm retaining counsel.
Any potential bail hearing would be heard in the Superior Court of Justice, Diaz noted, because the charge is murder.

Police said last week that Leonard and Cornejo were not known to each other. She was stabbed after she heard a noise inside her home shortly after 6 a.m. on Aug. 22, which was a Saturday. She was able to call 911 after she was assaulted, police said.
Officers raced to the address, where London police said a man was found throwing glass at them at the home. An officer received minor injuries, police said.
Cornejo is also charged with aggravated assault, break and and enter with intent, assaulting a police officer with a weapon and obstructing a police officer.
A member of Leonard’s family declined comment when contacted by The Free Press on Monday.
With files from Ryan Goodison, The London Free Press

stories.title: Trump shares Christian group's proposal allowing Canadian Jews facing antisemitism to flee to the U.S.
stories.summary: Donald Trump has shared a report on a potential plan to create a legal pathway into the U.S. for Jewish Canadians facing antisemitism.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
paragraphs: As he finds new ways to poke Canada amid an ugly trade war, U.S. President Donald Trump has amplified a Christian group’s proposal to create a legal pathway into the United States for Canadian Jews facing antisemitism.

He shared on social media a news report about a letter written by the National Association of Christian Lawmakers (Nacl), which urges Trump to establish an expedited method of entry into the U.S. for Jewish Canadians “who are experiencing persecution or who credibly fear for their safety because they are Jewish.”

It points to “an alarming climate of harassment, intimidation, vandalism, threats, and violence” that Jewish Canadian families have faced since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, adding that “advocates working directly with these families report that more than 2,000 Jewish Canadians have expressed interest in relocating because of growing concerns for their safety.”

The letter continues: “Accordingly, we respectfully ask that you direct the Department of State and the Department of Homeland Security to identify and implement lawful, secure, and appropriately expedited pathways for eligible Jewish Canadian nationals and their immediate family members who face persecution.”

Nacl founder and president Jason Rapert signed the letter, alongside state representatives and religious leaders, and it was sent to the U.S. president, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and several U.S. senators and representatives on Thursday.

The letter said that any potential program should maintain national security safeguards such as identity, criminal history, medical and security screening and protect family unity. It also called for the Trump administration to work with states, local governments, Jewish organizations, churches, nonprofits and employers who are willing to assist arriving families.

The letter comes a month after Statistics Canada data showed that Jews were targeted in 71 per cent of religious hate crimes in Canada last year. While this represented a 16 per cent decline from the previous year, it remained 50 per cent higher than in 2022.

{'text': 'Marty York: Canadian Jews are fleeing antisemitism at record rates — and the numbers prove it', 'html': ' Marty York: Canadian Jews are fleeing antisemitism at record rates — and the numbers prove it'}
Jewish schools, synagogues and other institutions have been shot at, firebombed and targeted by hateful graffiti in Canada since Hamas’ October 7 attacks on Israel.

Simon Wolle, B’nai Brith Canada’s Chief Executive Officer, told National Post in an email: “While we have members of the Jewish community questioning their futures in Canada, make no mistake that this is our home and we are here to stay. Our community is strong and resilient and will not be made to live in fear.”

On the report shared by Trump, Wolle added: “At the same time, this should serve as a serious wake-up call for the Canadian government that immediate and concrete actions are needed to stem the tide of violence against our community.”

Meanwhile, in the U.S., the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) reported earlier in August that anti-Jewish hate crimes accounted for 63 per cent of all reported religion-based hate crimes last year, according to FBI data. It marked the third-highest year on record of anti-Jewish hate crimes in the U.S.

The letter states that an expedited pathway for Jewish Canadians would be consistent with “America’s historic commitment to stand against religious persecution,” adding, “We believe this moment presents another opportunity for America to demonstrate those principles.”

Elsewhere, the Nacl letter references Jewish and Christian leaders in Tulsa who have already offered to help receive Canadian Jewish families, and points out that Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt previously told Trump his state would welcome Jewish families who legally enter the United States .
In a July 22 letter, Gov. Stitt wrote that “Oklahoma would proudly welcome those who choose to make our state their home,” should Jewish families lawfully move to the U.S. in search of safety.

The Nacl letter concludes: “For generations, America has served as a refuge for people fleeing religious persecution. We urge you to ensure that, consistent with federal law and the security interests of the United States, that door remains open to our Jewish brothers and sisters in Canada who need it today.”

In a July 22 letter, Gov. Stitt wrote that “Oklahoma would proudly welcome those who choose to make our state their home,” should Jewish families lawfully move to the U.S. in search of safety.

The Nacl letter concludes: “For generations, America has served as a refuge for people fleeing religious persecution. We urge you to ensure that, consistent with federal law and the security interests of the United States, that door remains open to our Jewish brothers and sisters in Canada who need it today.”

stories.title: Ontario breaks ground on longest stretch of proposed Ring of Fire road network
stories.summary: Construction on the longest stretch of a road network to Ontario's mineral-rich Ring of Fire region has begun.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
paragraphs: The provincial government announced today that ground has been broken on a road to eventually connect the remote Marten Falls First Nation to the provincial highway network.
Chief Bruce Achneepineskum says the route will strengthen connections to health care and other essential services, while helping to accelerate the community’s growth.
Article continues below
Toronto Island waitlist life: why one man will never give up his dream of living lakeside
The provincial government says it’s part of a plan to unlock the economic potential of the Ring of Fire region and meet global demand for minerals.
That plan has been met with pushback by some First Nations, notably in response to legislation giving the government powers to fast-track projects.
The road to Marten Falls will span about 184 kilometres, or just over a third of the total network, and is expected to open by November 2031.
In June, the province and Webequie First Nation announced the start of construction on a 107-kilometre segment of the road network to that community.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

stories.title: London resident dies after head-on crash in Thames Centre
stories.summary: Dundas Street was closed for hours between Fairview and Shaw roads for the investigation.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
paragraphs: A London resident died in hospital after a head-on crash between an SUV and a transport truck in Thames Centre last week.
Middlesex County OPP and emergency crews responded shortly before 1 p.m. Aug. 26 to the collision on Dundas Street near Fairview Road.
The driver of the transport truck was taken to hospital with injuries not considered life-threatening, police said in a Monday release.
The SUV driver, a 40-year-old from London, was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries and later died.
Members of the OPP Traffic Incident Management Enforcement team attended the scene to assist with the investigation.
Dundas Street was closed for hours between Fairview and Shaw roads for the investigation.
Anyone with information is asked to contact OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Anonymous tips can be made to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 (TIPS).
Provincial police are investigating after people posing as Dorchester Fall Fair representatives collected money and information from prospective vendors for phony permits.
Middlesex County OPP responded to a fraud complaint on Hamilton Road in Thames Centre about 1:40 p.m. on Aug. 27.

The North Dorchester Agricultural Society, which manages the fair, learned potential vendors had provided information and paid an undisclosed amount of money to people posing as fair representatives to secure vendor permits, police said.
The fraudulent messages appeared on social media and in unsolicited emails, police said.
The suspects are unknown, and police believe there may be additional victims.
Anyone who believes they were victimized is asked to contact Middlesex County OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Anonymous tips can be made to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 (TIPS).
For more information about fraud, contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501.

stories.title: Seventh B.C. Conservative quits caucus, says she’s lost confidence in Findlay
stories.summary: The Indigenous MLA and former House leader cited the cancellation of a caucus meeting she said had been called for Monday in light of a "reasonable cause for concern."
stories.author: Chuck Chiang
paragraphs: If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .

B.C. Conservative MLA A’a:liya Warbus, one of the Opposition’s most prominent legislators, has joined the exodus from the party’s caucus, saying she has lost confidence in it under new leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.
Warbus said in a statement on Monday morning she would sit as an Independent, becoming the seventh Conservative MLA to quit the caucus this month, including five last week.
The Indigenous MLA and former House leader cited the cancellation of a caucus meeting she said had been called for Monday in light of a “reasonable cause for concern” about last week’s “implosion.”
“The decision to postpone today’s caucus meeting for a month reflects the lack of value being placed on caucus members and their opinions,” she said in her statement.
“It is one thing to ask for people’s trust, and quite another to blindfold someone and expect faith alone to substitute for transparency and accountability.”
The Chilliwack-Cultus Lake MLA also said she was concerned about the circumstances surrounding the resignation from the legislature of Reann Gasper to make way for Findlay to stand in a byelection.

Findlay, who was narrowly elected party leader on May 30 but does not have a seat in the legislature, had said last week that suggestions a leaked audio recording showed she illegally offered jobs to MLAs, in exchange for resigning so she could stand in a byelection, were “preposterous.”

Gasper has taken a paid position as Findlay’s deputy chief of staff. RCMP said they were aware of the purported recording of Findlay addressing Conservative legislators, but “does not confirm or deny any investigation, or the identity of any person who may be subject to an investigation, until such time as charges have been laid.”

The party has been in a state of upheaval over the ideological direction and strategies of the party under Findlay since Peter Milobar quit on Aug. 14, saying they had a lack of “ideological alignment.”
Findlay, who has said she will focus on “faith, family and freedom,” has since suffered the losses of Ian Paton, Rosalyn Bird, Teresa Wat, Brennan Day and Bruce Banman.
Neither Warbus nor Findlay immediately responded to requests for comment.
Warbus said in her statement that there had been a “critical breakdown” of communication under Findlay.
“Caucus members have learned of hirings, firings, critic appointments, and leadership positions through any and all channels including social media before being informed by leadership,” she said.
She said it was not just MLAs leaving, but “critical and talented members of our riding associations and staff that we rely on.”
Paton and Milobar have said they will form an alternative party.

Banman rallied other Conservatives to join him as an Independent on Thursday “regardless of political affiliation.” He said many have told him Findlay is “unelectable,” and that under her another election win by the NDP was increasingly likely.

stories.title: This Dickie Dee-inspired ice cream cooler is turning heads on Saskatchewan streets
stories.summary: As students prepare to head back to class next week, a Saskatchewan boy is focusing his last days of summer on sales.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
paragraphs: Martensville, Sask. - As students prepare to head back to class next week, a Saskatchewan boy is focusing his last days of summer on sales.
Gus Fandrich has been serving up sweet treats and nostalgia all summer long from his Dickie Dee-inspired ice cream cooler.
“I’m a big fan of ice cream,” Fandrich told CTV News.
At 10 years old, the savvy businessman is too young to remember the Dickie Dee’s ice cream sellers of the 1980s.
But he was fascinated by the freezer-on-wheels concept when he first saw it at a hockey game.
“He was wondering what it was, so I explained to him they used to drive around neighbourhoods selling ice cream when I was a kid,” his dad Jason Fandrich said.
With help from his dad, Fandrich created his own ice cream cart called Gus’ Sweet Treats, which officially took to the streets in May.
“It is like a modern Dickie Dee bike,” Fandrich explained.
The pair connected an e-bike to a freezer and a couple of cupboards that store ice cream treats, snacks and pop.
It can hold about 200 ice cream treats and weighs about 300 lbs when it is fully stocked.
“It would take me a while to just get down one street because I do not have the leg muscle to do it, so it is easier with an e-bike motor,” Fandrich said.
Fandrich rolls through the streets of Martensville, Sask., a small city just north of Saskatoon, a few times every week.
He attracts customers of all ages with a jingle he plays through a speaker.
“Most of the adults that we come across are very excited when they hear the music,” Jason said.
“It brings them right back to childhood.”
Fandrich suspects he has visited every neighbourhood in the city at least once this summer. He hopes to continue sales until the snow falls.
“(Customers) are super supportive and people will give lots of tips if you are a young kid,” he said.
The soon-to-be Grade 6 student is saving up to buy new hockey cards, Lego sets and a dirt bike.
He initially hoped to make about $300, but his dad says sales are already “well over that.”
“It can definitely get him some hockey cards and can definitely get him that dirt bike if he wants it,” Jason said.
This is just Fandrich’s first summer doing business and he already has plans to expand.
Over the winter, he would like to build more ice cream carts to sell to other small communities in Saskatchewan and Alberta.
“I couldn’t be more proud of him,” Jason said.
“He is a great kid and he has always been motivated.”

stories.title: Canadian Nato intern facing espionage charges to remain in custody, Belgian prosecutor says
stories.summary: Prosecutor’s office announced on July 25 that ‘a Canadian national of Chinese origin’ had been arrested on accusations of espionage
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Belgian federal prosecutor’s office says a Canadian facing espionage charges will remain in custody.

After a hearing today of the woman’s appeal of a July decision to keep her in detention, Belgium’s Chamber of Indictments decided to extend her pretrial custody by one month.

The prosecutor’s office announced on July 25 that “a Canadian national of Chinese origin” had been arrested on accusations of espionage and participation in a criminal organization.

The suspect, who has not been named by the prosecutor’s office, worked as an intern at NATO’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe in Mons, Belgium.

The office said she came to the attention of the organization’s security services, who reported the matter to Belgium’s military intelligence agency.

A federal source not authorized to speak publicly about the issue said officials in Canada were proceeding on the basis the suspect is Biwei Zhang – also known as Claire Zhang – who was previously employed by Canadian government agencies.

stories.title: Canadian suspect in Belgian espionage case to remain in pretrial detention
stories.summary: The Belgian federal prosecutor’s office says a Canadian facing espionage charges will remain in custody.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Belgian federal prosecutor’s office says a Canadian facing espionage charges will remain in custody.

After a hearing today of the woman’s appeal of a July decision to keep her in detention, Belgium’s Chamber of Indictments decided to extend her pretrial custody by one month.

The prosecutor’s office announced on July 25 that “a Canadian national of Chinese origin” had been arrested on accusations of espionage and participation in a criminal organization.

The suspect, who has not been named by the prosecutor’s office, worked as an intern at Nato’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe in Mons, Belgium.

The office said she came to the attention of the organization’s security services, who reported the matter to Belgium’s military intelligence agency.

A federal source not authorized to speak publicly about the issue said officials in Canada were proceeding on the basis the suspect is Biwei Zhang — also known as Claire Zhang — who was previously employed by Canadian government agencies.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Second-degree murder charge added after woman dies from injuries in London stabbing attack
stories.summary: As previously reported, the 73-year-old woman suffered serious injuries after she was assaulted and stabbed during a break-in at her home in the area of Wellington Road and Base Line Road east on the morning of Aug. 22.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
paragraphs: A woman who was the victim of a stabbing attack in her south London home last week has died.

As previously reported, the 73-year-old woman suffered serious injuries after she was assaulted and stabbed during a break-in at her home in the area of Wellington Road and Base Line Road east on the morning of Aug. 22.
Police said the woman was sleeping at her residence when she was awakened by a loud noise at about 6:10 a.m.
Investigators said she saw a man she didn’t know, entering the home and was assaulted and stabbed before she was able to call 911.
The woman was initially taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, but has since died in hospital.
The death has been deemed a homicide, according to police.

In addition to the initial charges of aggravated assault, break and enter, assault a peace officer, and obstruct peace officer, Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, has also been charged with second degree murder.
The allegations have not been proven in court.

stories.title: Ontario woman questions $500 fee to transfer family's medical records to new doctor
stories.summary: An Ontario woman says her former family doctor's office quoted her $100 per person to transfer the medical records of her family of five to their new family physician.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: An Ontario woman says her former family doctor's office quoted her $100 per person to transfer the medical records of her family of five to their new family physician.
· Posted: Aug 31, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: August 31
Doctors say the new system will reduce administrative paperwork which takes time away from patients.(Shutterstock)
When Melissa Snider found a new family doctor closer to her home in Denfield, Ont., she was happy at the thought of no longer travelling to London for medical visits.
The relief turned to shock however when her former family doctor quoted Snider $100 per person to transfer her records, along with those of her husband and their three children, to a new physician.
"It was quite surprising to me that transferring medical records for a family of five would cost me $500," said Snider, whose kids are all under the age of nine.

"My kids are all healthy so it would just be vaccine records for them, and my husband and I are pretty healthy too, so our records themselves would not be very extensive. Half a grand in this economy is just not doable for something so silly."

Snider said she had previously paid around $35 for the service. She asked a Facebook group for moms if others have been in this situation. She said she received a variety of responses, with some saying their doctor did it for free, and others saying they had to pay varying fees.

Access to personal health information and related fees is governed by the Personal Health Information Protection Act and not c overed by the Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP), according to the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (CPSO).

The work involved in fulfilling a request for medical records may include locating and retrieving records, reviewing them, preparing the materials for disclosure, and securely transferring them to the patient or the receiving health-care provider, says the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario.(Copyright (c) 2017 Stokkete/Shutterstock.)

The work involved in fulfilling a request for medical records may include locating and retrieving records, reviewing them, preparing the materials for disclosure, and securely transferring them to the patient or the receiving health-care provider, said CPSO spokesperson Laura Zilke.

The Information Privacy Commissioner recommends a $30 fee for electronic transfers, according to the Ontario Medical Association, which sets out recommended fees in its Physicians’ Guide to Uninsured Services.

In some cases, doctors may charge $30 for the first 20 pages and then $0.25 per extra pages, but all other methods of reproducing records should be charged for at cost, the guidance states. This can include clerical labour costs, toner and paper costs, equipment, and storage space.

"Among other requirements, physicians must provide a fee estimate in advance and charge only reasonable fees that reflect cost recovery," said Zilke, adding that physicians must consider these recommendations and the patient's ability to pay.

"CPSO'spolicyrequires that fees be reasonable, reflect cost recovery, and be commensurate with the nature of the service provided, including factors such as the materials used, the time required to prepare the records, and the direct cost of sending them."
Snider wonders why there isn't a centralized system where every clinic charges the same fee, or bases fees on a patient's medical history.

The current system is "disconnected" because clinics have their own system of storing health information, with some using paper charts and others electronic records, said Dr. Jobin Varughese, president of the Ontario College of Family Physicians.
Canadian doctors say they’re losing 20 million hours a year to unnecessary paperwork

When patients move between clinics, doctors and their teams must spend hours preparing and sending those records manually, he said, adding that it contributes to paperwork and other administrative tasks that take away time doctors can spend with patients.

"It's pretty clear that we need to get to a point that patients shouldn't have to pay for their records and family doctors should be able to spend their time caring for patients rather than moving records through a disconnected system," he said.
"Patients should be focused on their health, not on how their medical records move from one doctor to another."

Dr. Jobin Varughese is president of the Ontario College of Family Physicians. He agrees that patients shouldn't have to pay to have their medical records transferred to a different clinic.(Submitted by the Ontario College of Family Physicians)
Varughese believes this issue should be eliminated once Ontario rolls out the provincewide Primary Care Electronic Medical Record, where patient records are integrated onto one accessible system.
Ontario plans to create connected primary care medical record system, minister says

The electronic record aims to provide clinicians with a more complete view of a patient’s health history, improving coordination across the health system and reducing delays caused by missing records. It also seeks to save patients money in transfer fees, unnecessary medical tests and lab work.

"Right now it's on the patients to have to remember dates and times and so being able to reduce that burden will be helpful. It will also reduce the need for patients to repeat the same information to different providers just because their records aren't available," said Varughese.
The province is currently in a procurement phase but Varughese said officials have consulted with family physicians and he's hopeful this will simplify the process for doctors and patients.
As for Snider, she plans to provide her new doctor with a verbal medical history and not pay the hefty transfer cost.

stories.title: Leaders of China, Russia and India are among heads of state meeting to counter U.S. influence
stories.summary: The leaders of China, Russia and India are among the heads of state gathering in Kyrgyzstan this week for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
The leaders of China, Russia and India gathered with other heads of state in Kyrgyzstan on Monday for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are attending the events in Bishkek, the capital of the Central Asian nation.

Putin met separately with Xi and Modi in two of the many bilateral sessions on the sidelines of the summit. Putin affirmed to Xi Moscow’s readiness to make the visa-free regime with China permanent, and he said Russia’s relationship with India is strengthening.

Talks between Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are expected Tuesday, the day of the official SCO sessions.

Russia, now 4.5 years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Iran, six months into a war with the United States and Israel, see the summit as an important platform to strengthen their relations with non-Western partners.

Modi told Putin through a translator that India supports efforts to end the war in Ukraine, and that “we need to move from endless war to the end of war, to the end of hostilities,” adding that “this is very important for all of humanity.”

The SCO was founded in 2001 by China, Russia and four Central Asian states as a security forum. Over the past quarter-century, it has grown in size and influence, although its goals and programs remain vague and its brand recognition low.

It now includes 10 nations: Russia, China, India, Iran, Pakistan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Many other countries have the status of “dialogue partners.”

Along with Russia, China has presented the SCO as an alternative to Western-aligned organizations like the G7, and in recent years has wanted to expand the scope and influence of the organization, pledging development and financial assistance.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said last week that the organization has successfully “explored a new path for regional cooperation.” Beijing has consistently promoted the idea of an alternative world order with Russia’s support.

Summit attendees have significant disagreements

For many SCO members, the summit will be an opportunity to show that they maintain strong ties on the global stage despite souring relations with the West.

The organization is not a unified political or military bloc, however, and analysts note that its members have significant disagreements and their own distinct interests.

For countries such as India, however, experts say the summit is likely to be more about optics and strategic signalling than substantive outcomes.

The forum is heavily influenced by China and includes Pakistan as a member -- both of which are rivals of India.

Dinakar Peri, a fellow in security studies at Carnegie India, said the SCO gives India a seat at the table in a region increasingly shaped by competition among the larger powers, allowing it to protect its interests, track shifting geopolitical currents and project itself as a reliable stakeholder.

“While it May not entirely shape the agenda, it gives New Delhi a first-hand view of the region and allows it to hedge its position with others,” Peri said.

Turkiye, which holds partner status within the SCO, also seeks to use the platform to strengthen its position in the region.

It views SCO membership as part of a balanced foreign policy that seeks to maintain its traditional ties with the West as a part of Nato, while strengthening its influence in Eurasia.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who brought his country into the SCO as a “dialogue partner” in 2012, has repeatedly stated that he wants Turkiye to become a permanent member. While Turkiye has close trade ties with the European Union under a 1995 trade deal, its EU membership bid has stalled for more than 25 years.

Security restrictions imposed in Bishkek

Major shopping malls, markets and other sites in the capital were closed for the duration of the summit as part of security measures, and commercial flights to and from Manas Airport were restricted.

“Traffic in central Bishkek will be regularly restricted,” said Askat Alagozov, a spokesman for Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov, urging residents to leave the city.

The start of the school year was postponed until Sept. 15, and authorities declared Tuesday a non-working day for public sector and civil servants in Bishkek.

stories.title: Tiff fans grapple with ticket price hikes
stories.summary: The hike they noticed this year marks the first time in recent memory that films, other than the opening and closing night galas, cracked the $100 mark
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
paragraphs: When Arjun Singh first started attending the Toronto International Film Festival in 2022, he remembers buying tickets to the world premiere of warrior drama The Woman King for about $50 each.
This year, he saw balcony seats at similar premium screenings, which often include a Q-and-A with the cast or director, selling for as much as $106.
“That makes you go, is this really worth it?” said the Toronto non-profit worker, who has cut back on TIFF galas and now mostly opts for regular festival screenings because of the prices.

While TIFF fans have grown accustomed to tickets edging up by a few percentage points every festival, the hike they noticed this year marked the first time in recent memory that films, other than the opening and closing night galas, cracked the $100 mark.

Fans reported tickets to the premieres of anticipated films like Palme d’Or winner Fjord , justice system thriller Prima Facie and the Ryan Gosling-produced Love of Your Life going for as much as $106. Others posted screenshots on Reddit of tickets in the first few rows of premieres selling for $128. Last year, screenings in the same tier went up to $98.
TIFF did not respond to multiple requests for comment on ticket pricing.

The increase has some diehards, who can see upwards of 30 films during TIFF’s 10 days, rethinking how many premieres they’ll attend. Others are wondering how long it will be until they’re priced out of the event once nicknamed “the people’s festival” because of its affordability and public access.

“It definitely adds up and when you’re getting tickets for friends too. You don’t really want to look at your credit card,” said Joel Chico, an actor who estimates he spends about $2,000 on up to 30 tickets to premium screenings each year.

Like many TIFF fans, he takes the grin-and-bear it approach to ticket prices because of the thrill of being in the room with the cast when a film is seen for the first time. Still, they wish it cost less.
“I love TIFF. It’s like my Christmas every year but the costs are just kind of crazy nowadays,” Chico said.
While TIFF typically releases price ranges for every kind of ticket it sells in the lead up to the festival, this year it didn’t tell attendees what seats in each category would top out at.

Regular screenings, which come after premieres and do not typically have cast members in attendance, were listed as starting at $30 for non-members. Premium screenings began at $46. When The Canadian Press browsed tickets, it found many premium seats at screenings going for up to $106.

In the lead-up to the festival, TIFF advertised a $2 discount on regular screenings for members. It also promised $15 tickets to select screenings but had yet to release more details about those seats with just over a week to go before festivities began.
Charlie Keil, a professor at the Cinema Studies Institute at the University of Toronto, said TIFF is likely increasing prices both because it can, and because it needs to.

Over its 51-year history, he figures festival organizers have more than realized film fans will pay big bucks to see a movie before anyone else and to see it with Hollywood’s biggest stars in attendance.
“If the demand is there, that, in a way, stimulates institutions to push the pricing envelope because they think people will keep coming,” Keil said.
But there’s more than demand at play.
Arts organizations are constantly turning to patrons to help them cope with strained budgets and higher costs. TIFF is likely no exception.
“Space costs more, transportation more, food more, hospitality more, accommodation more. Everything is more expensive,” Keil said.
On top of inflation, TIFF is still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in online and pared back versions of the festival.
In 2023, the Hollywood strikes kept many stars from promoting their films at the event. That same year, TIFF lost longtime sponsor Bell, which had supported the organization since 1995.
The federal government offered $23-million to help TIFF launch a film market this year and Rogers stepped in to fill Bell’s void with a three-year agreement that runs through 2027.

The latest financial information TIFF published in annual reports showed it had revenue of about $45.1-million and more than $41.9-million in expenses in 2024. The bulk of its revenue came from ticket sales, followed by corporate partnerships, while salaries made up about half of its expenses.
Its revenue was $39.6-million in 2023, when it had roughly $46.2-million in expenses, its annual reports show.
TIFF’s program, administrative and fundraising costs have all risen in recent years, according to Charity Intelligence Canada, an organization that analyzes and publicizes charity finances.

“There’s just so many factors that are making it tough,” Keil said. “I would not want to be in TIFF’s position right now, just trying to make it all work financially, sustain the reputation of the festival.”
Cathy Crowe understands it’s not cheap to put on a festival of TIFF’s stature – this year’s iteration will debut almost 300 films and TV shows – but she’s still disappointed in the prices.

After filmmaker friends turned the street nurse onto the festival in the late 1990s, she started treating it like an annual staycation. She recalls seeing between 20 and 30 films a year, often paying only $17 a ticket.
Crowe avoids the ritziest galas, which typically turn Roy Thomson Hall and the Princess of Wales Theatre into a buzzy spectacle, so that kept her festival affordable.
But last year, when she logged on to buy tickets during a members’ window, she found most screenings she wanted to attend sold out.

“I only got one of my 20 choices, which was so disappointing and then, when I got it, it was a $37 film,” she said. “For a really big deal film it was OK, but how could I do 20 or 30 films at that price?”
Simply put, she didn’t. She attended the one film – German historical drama “Silent Friend” – and then started contemplating how many more years she could realistically afford to be a TIFF diehard.
“I see it as the tail end,” she said.
This year, she hopes to see at least one movie – a Midnight Madness film – with her grandson, but she’s under no illusion that the festival will feel like it once did.

“It is not a people’s festival any longer,” said Crowe. “I know it will be packed. I know people will be going. I know people will be coming from all over the country, but they’re losing a lot of regular folks.”
That’s a problem, said Keil, because TIFF has long prided itself on how many members of the public attend every year.

In fact, that broad access is a selling point, helping TIFF lure in movies from filmmakers who want to test the public’s reaction or build buzz with an audience broader than the industry buffs at competing festivals.
“The whole point is to give people access to films they wouldn’t normally see from places they would not normally see films coming from,” Keil said.
“If you price those films out of the normal, let’s say, cinephile’s reach, then the festival won’t be as successful in meeting that mandate.”

When Arjun Singh first started attending the Toronto International Film Festival in 2022, he remembers buying tickets to the world premiere of warrior drama The Woman King for about $50 each.

This year, he saw balcony seats at similar premium screenings, which often include a Q-and-A with the cast or director, selling for as much as $106.

“That makes you go, is this really worth it?” said the Toronto non-profit worker, who has cut back on TIFF galas and now mostly opts for regular festival screenings because of the prices.

While TIFF fans have grown accustomed to tickets edging up by a few percentage points every festival, the hike they noticed this year marked the first time in recent memory that films, other than the opening and closing night galas, cracked the $100 mark.

Fans reported tickets to the premieres of anticipated films like Palme d’Or winner Fjord , justice system thriller Prima Facie and the Ryan Gosling-produced Love of Your Life going for as much as $106. Others posted screenshots on Reddit of tickets in the first few rows of premieres selling for $128. Last year, screenings in the same tier went up to $98.

TIFF did not respond to multiple requests for comment on ticket pricing.

The increase has some diehards, who can see upwards of 30 films during TIFF’s 10 days, rethinking how many premieres they’ll attend. Others are wondering how long it will be until they’re priced out of the event once nicknamed “the people’s festival” because of its affordability and public access.

“It definitely adds up and when you’re getting tickets for friends too. You don’t really want to look at your credit card,” said Joel Chico, an actor who estimates he spends about $2,000 on up to 30 tickets to premium screenings each year.

Like many TIFF fans, he takes the grin-and-bear it approach to ticket prices because of the thrill of being in the room with the cast when a film is seen for the first time. Still, they wish it cost less.

“I love TIFF. It’s like my Christmas every year but the costs are just kind of crazy nowadays,” Chico said.

While TIFF typically releases price ranges for every kind of ticket it sells in the lead up to the festival, this year it didn’t tell attendees what seats in each category would top out at.

Regular screenings, which come after premieres and do not typically have cast members in attendance, were listed as starting at $30 for non-members. Premium screenings began at $46. When The Canadian Press browsed tickets, it found many premium seats at screenings going for up to $106.

In the lead-up to the festival, TIFF advertised a $2 discount on regular screenings for members. It also promised $15 tickets to select screenings but had yet to release more details about those seats with just over a week to go before festivities began.

Charlie Keil, a professor at the Cinema Studies Institute at the University of Toronto, said TIFF is likely increasing prices both because it can, and because it needs to.

Over its 51-year history, he figures festival organizers have more than realized film fans will pay big bucks to see a movie before anyone else and to see it with Hollywood’s biggest stars in attendance.

“If the demand is there, that, in a way, stimulates institutions to push the pricing envelope because they think people will keep coming,” Keil said.

But there’s more than demand at play.

Arts organizations are constantly turning to patrons to help them cope with strained budgets and higher costs. TIFF is likely no exception.

“Space costs more, transportation more, food more, hospitality more, accommodation more. Everything is more expensive,” Keil said.

On top of inflation, TIFF is still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in online and pared back versions of the festival.

In 2023, the Hollywood strikes kept many stars from promoting their films at the event. That same year, TIFF lost longtime sponsor Bell, which had supported the organization since 1995.

The federal government offered $23-million to help TIFF launch a film market this year and Rogers stepped in to fill Bell’s void with a three-year agreement that runs through 2027.

The latest financial information TIFF published in annual reports showed it had revenue of about $45.1-million and more than $41.9-million in expenses in 2024. The bulk of its revenue came from ticket sales, followed by corporate partnerships, while salaries made up about half of its expenses.

Its revenue was $39.6-million in 2023, when it had roughly $46.2-million in expenses, its annual reports show.

TIFF’s program, administrative and fundraising costs have all risen in recent years, according to Charity Intelligence Canada, an organization that analyzes and publicizes charity finances.

“There’s just so many factors that are making it tough,” Keil said. “I would not want to be in TIFF’s position right now, just trying to make it all work financially, sustain the reputation of the festival.”

Cathy Crowe understands it’s not cheap to put on a festival of TIFF’s stature – this year’s iteration will debut almost 300 films and TV shows – but she’s still disappointed in the prices.

After filmmaker friends turned the street nurse onto the festival in the late 1990s, she started treating it like an annual staycation. She recalls seeing between 20 and 30 films a year, often paying only $17 a ticket.

Crowe avoids the ritziest galas, which typically turn Roy Thomson Hall and the Princess of Wales Theatre into a buzzy spectacle, so that kept her festival affordable.

But last year, when she logged on to buy tickets during a members’ window, she found most screenings she wanted to attend sold out.

“I only got one of my 20 choices, which was so disappointing and then, when I got it, it was a $37 film,” she said. “For a really big deal film it was OK, but how could I do 20 or 30 films at that price?”

Simply put, she didn’t. She attended the one film – German historical drama “Silent Friend” – and then started contemplating how many more years she could realistically afford to be a TIFF diehard.

“I see it as the tail end,” she said.

This year, she hopes to see at least one movie – a Midnight Madness film – with her grandson, but she’s under no illusion that the festival will feel like it once did.

“It is not a people’s festival any longer,” said Crowe. “I know it will be packed. I know people will be going. I know people will be coming from all over the country, but they’re losing a lot of regular folks.”

That’s a problem, said Keil, because TIFF has long prided itself on how many members of the public attend every year.

In fact, that broad access is a selling point, helping TIFF lure in movies from filmmakers who want to test the public’s reaction or build buzz with an audience broader than the industry buffs at competing festivals.

“The whole point is to give people access to films they wouldn’t normally see from places they would not normally see films coming from,” Keil said.

“If you price those films out of the normal, let’s say, cinephile’s reach, then the festival won’t be as successful in meeting that mandate.”
